subject: languages

descriptors.title: Interact in classroom routines and personal introductions
descriptors.description: interact in classroom-related routines and personal introductions
descriptors.knowledge: Students have used formulaic expressions and communicated personal meaning in supported interactions (AC9LCHF01). They can respond to familiar classroom instructions and share simple personal information with support. They have not yet participated in sustained two-way classroom exchanges, managed requests and responses, or used the target language independently for the full range of classroom social routines.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interact in classroom-related routines and personal introductions using appropriate greetings, terms of address, requests and formulaic expressions, with growing independence.
elaborations: greeting each other and using appropriate terms of address, gestures, and body language for different times of day and relationships
responding to classroom instructions and routines
sharing personal information about topics such as age, zodiac animal sign, class and school
making simple requests using appropriate manners
using puppets to perform role-play exchanges about family
expressing thanks, apologies, likes and dislikes
using formulaic exclamations spontaneously when interacting with peers
identifying which languages they know and are learning

nodes.label: Greetings, address and classroom routine language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use appropriate greetings and terms of address for different people and times of day, and respond to classroom routine instructions.
criteria: Uses an appropriate greeting and address form when initiating or responding to a classroom exchange
Responds correctly to at least three different classroom routine instructions through action or language
nodes.hinge_reason: Greetings, address forms and routine classroom language are the entry conditions for all classroom participation. Students who cannot manage these conventions cannot engage in the exchanges, introductions or collaborative activities that follow in this and subsequent descriptors.

width.minimum: Use at least two contextually appropriate greetings or address forms, and respond correctly to at least three classroom routine instructions.
width.typical: Use greetings appropriate to time of day and relationship (teacher, peers); respond to routine classroom instructions with appropriate action or language; use formulaic exclamations spontaneously in peer interaction; distinguish between formal address to teachers and informal address to peers.
wider: Compare greeting conventions in the target language with English and another language known in the class — identify what changes across contexts (time of day, relationship, formality)
Identify which languages they know and are learning, discussing how greetings differ across the languages they speak at home and at school

modes.reason: Routine language must become automatic for classroom participation to flow. Repeated daily use of greeting and address conventions — not occasional practice — builds the fluency that allows students to focus attention on content rather than form in later interaction tasks.

nodes.label: Personal information and introductions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share and request personal information in a structured introduction exchange, using modelled sentence structures.
criteria: Shares at least three pieces of personal information using target language sentence structures
Asks at least one question to request personal information from a partner

width.minimum: Share at least three pieces of personal information (e.g. name, age, school, family) and ask a peer for at least one piece of information using a modelled question form.
width.typical: Participate in personal introduction exchanges — sharing and requesting information about name, age, class, school, family and interests; use puppets, role-play or paired exchange structures to support the interaction; identify which languages they know and are learning.
wider: Conduct an extended role-play introduction exchange incorporating both personal information sharing and questions, sustaining the exchange for at least four turns
Create a bilingual personal profile combining target language and English, presenting it to the class or a small group

modes.reason: Personal introduction exchanges are context-dependent — students need to practise the same information-sharing moves across different partners, formats and purposes (face-to-face, puppet play, digital) to build flexible use rather than memorised performance.

nodes.label: Requests, thanks and everyday social expressions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use polite requests, thanks, apologies and expressions of likes and dislikes in familiar classroom and social contexts.
criteria: Uses at least two different social expressions (request, thanks, apology, or preference) appropriately in a real or role-play context
Demonstrates appropriate manner or gesture alongside the verbal expression

width.minimum: Use at least two formulaic social expressions appropriately in context — for example, making a polite request, thanking someone, or expressing a like or dislike.
width.typical: Use a range of social expressions across everyday classroom interactions — polite requests, thanks, apologies, expressions of preference — with appropriate manner and register; begin to use exclamations and formulaic responses spontaneously in peer interaction.
wider: Compare the politeness conventions of the target language with English — identify where the same communicative act (e.g. requesting, thanking) requires different forms or gestures
Role-play a series of short social interactions (e.g. asking to borrow something, thanking a peer, apologising) demonstrating appropriate language and gesture for each

modes.reason: Social expression use integrates greeting conventions (node 1) and personal exchange skills (node 2) into the broader repertoire of classroom social language. The teaching investment is in creating authentic occasions for these expressions — not drills, but real moments of requesting, thanking and responding.

descriptors.title: Collaborate in play-based activities
descriptors.description: collaborate with others in a range of play-based activities using modelled expressions and visual and spoken cues
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interact in classroom routines and personal introductions using familiar formulaic expressions (AC9LCH2C01). They can share personal information and respond to routine classroom language. They have not yet sustained collaborative activity using the target language — taking turns, giving instructions, leading games, or working with peers toward a shared goal in the target language.
descriptors.endpoint: Students collaborate with others across a range of play-based activities, using modelled expressions, visual and spoken cues to participate, take turns, give instructions and work toward shared outcomes.
elaborations: participating in singing songs, and reciting rhymes and chants that use repetitive language and actions
participating in play-based experiences using props or dress-up costumes
using pictures or prompts to participate in speaking and listening activities with peers
collaborating in games that involve taking turns, making choices or swapping items
playing matching games with target language and English words from big books
taking turns leading games or activities
giving instructions such as taking the role of a physical education teacher
working collaboratively to identify and label objects or places on a word wall or map

nodes.label: Participating in songs, rhymes and structured language play
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in songs, rhymes, chants and structured language games that use repetitive language and physical actions.
criteria: Participates actively in at least two songs, rhymes or structured games, demonstrating meaning through action or response
Can follow along with at least one familiar text without visual prompt
nodes.hinge_reason: Participation in structured language play is the entry condition for collaborative activity. Students who cannot engage with repetitive, scaffolded language routines cannot take on the more open collaborative roles — turn-taking, instruction-giving, role-play leadership — that the subsequent nodes require.

width.minimum: Participate actively in at least two songs, rhymes or structured games, demonstrating understanding of meaning through appropriate actions or responses.
width.typical: Participate in singing songs, reciting rhymes and chants with repetitive language and physical actions; play memory and matching games using target language words; respond with appropriate actions or words to game instructions and prompts.
wider: Lead a song, rhyme or chant for the class or small group, demonstrating understanding of both the language and the associated actions
Create a new verse or variation on a familiar song or chant using known vocabulary

modes.reason: Language play requires a growing repertoire of songs, rhymes, chants and games. Repeated encounters with varied texts build the language memory and confidence that students need before they can participate flexibly rather than only following along.

nodes.label: Taking turns, giving instructions and leading activities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can take turns in games and collaborative activities, give simple instructions in the target language, and take on a leading role in familiar activities.
criteria: Takes a turn leading or directing an activity, giving at least one instruction in the target language
Responds correctly to at least one instruction given by a peer in the target language

width.minimum: Take a turn leading or directing at least one game or activity, giving at least one instruction or prompt in the target language.
width.typical: Participate in games and activities that require taking turns, making choices, swapping items or following instructions; take turns leading games or activities; give instructions in the target language using modelled forms; respond appropriately to peers' instructions.
wider: Take the role of teacher or instructor in a physical activity — giving a sequence of instructions to the group and responding to peers' attempts
Design and explain the rules of a simple new game using target language instruction forms, then lead a small group through it

modes.reason: Turn-taking and instruction-giving skills transfer across game types — physical games, board games, word games, role-play. Varied activity contexts ensure students build flexible collaborative language use rather than performance in one rehearsed scenario.

nodes.label: Collaborating in role-play and shared creative activities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collaborate in play-based role-play and creative activities, using modelled expressions and props to communicate within a shared scenario.
criteria: Uses at least two modelled expressions appropriately within a role-play scenario
Maintains a collaborative role for the duration of the activity without defaulting to English

width.minimum: Participate in at least one role-play or shared creative activity, using at least two modelled expressions appropriate to the scenario.
width.typical: Participate in role-play scenarios — using props, dress-up and costumes — in contexts such as restaurants, shops, or familiar community settings; use pictures, prompts and visual cues to support participation; collaborate to identify and label objects or places in shared tasks.
wider: Extend a familiar role-play scenario with additional turns or a new episode, introducing a complication and resolution
Work collaboratively to create a labelled word wall or map — deciding on content, dividing tasks, and combining contributions into a shared product

modes.reason: Collaborative role-play integrates structured language play (node 1) and turn-taking skills (node 2) into open-ended creative activity. The teaching investment is in setting up meaningful scenarios with real communicative purpose — not only rehearsed scripts, but genuine negotiation within the play context.

descriptors.title: Locate key information in texts and respond
descriptors.description: locate, with support, key information in spoken and written texts, and respond using gestures, images, words and modelled sentences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can participate in classroom interactions and collaborative activities using modelled expressions (AC9LCH2C01, AC9LCH2C02). They can follow spoken instructions and respond through action. They have not yet systematically located and extracted key information from texts, made connections between text content and their own knowledge, or responded to texts with structured opinions or retelling.
descriptors.endpoint: Students locate key information in familiar spoken and written texts with support, and respond using gestures, images, words and modelled sentences — including identifying main points, making personal connections, and expressing opinions about characters and storylines.
elaborations: making connections between a simple text and self
making connections between world knowledge and target language to infer meaning of words
identifying details about people and events heard, seen or read in media

recognising that gestures and body language are integral to communicating in language for First Nations Australians, and showing examples of how they are also integral to communicating in the target language
showing understanding of main points in spoken and written texts
listening to imaginative texts and responding through play-acting or movement
identifying key words in familiar texts such as stories and rhymes
drawing and labelling a character or scene from rhymes or stories
participating in shared reading and responding to questions
identifying and justifying a favourite character using modelled language
expressing opinions about characters or retelling storylines after viewing or listening

nodes.label: Identifying key words and main points in texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify key words and main points in familiar spoken and written texts, demonstrating understanding through gesture, image, ordering or brief response.
criteria: Identifies at least three key words from a familiar text when prompted
Demonstrates understanding of a main point through gesture, image, sequencing or spoken response
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying key words and main points is the prerequisite for all text response work. Students who cannot locate information in a text cannot make personal connections, express opinions, or retell storylines — the higher-order demands of this descriptor and the creating strand.

width.minimum: Identify at least three key words or one main point from a familiar spoken or written text, demonstrating understanding through gesture, image selection or spoken response.
width.typical: Listen to, read or view familiar texts and identify key words; demonstrate understanding of main points through sequencing pictures, creating captions, drawing scenes or responding to guided questions; use world knowledge to infer meaning of unfamiliar words from context.
wider: Identify key words and main points across different text types — spoken story, rhyme, cartoon, and written text — comparing how information is conveyed in each
Use knowledge of the world to infer the meaning of unfamiliar target language words in context, explaining the reasoning used

modes.reason: Key word identification requires students to encounter a growing range of text types — stories, rhymes, songs, cartoons, informative texts — to build the reading and listening strategies that transfer across formats. Repeated exposure with varied texts builds this generalised comprehension capacity.

nodes.label: Making connections between texts and personal experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make connections between text content and their own experience or world knowledge, and identify details about characters and events.
criteria: Makes at least one explicit personal connection to a text, expressed in target language or English with target language key words
Identifies at least one detail about a character or event from a text

width.minimum: Make at least one personal connection to a text and identify at least one detail about a character or event from the text.
width.typical: Connect text content to personal experience and world knowledge; identify details about characters, settings and events in informative and imaginative texts; recognise that gestures and body language contribute to meaning in texts and in their own experience of communication.
wider: Compare the world of a familiar text (characters, settings, events) with personal experience — discuss what is similar, different or surprising
Identify examples from First Nations Australian communication contexts where gesture and body language carry meaning, connecting to how this also occurs in the target language

modes.reason: Making connections between text and experience requires scaffolded prompts — students at Y1-2 need explicit questioning frames (What does this remind you of? Who is like you in this story?) to move from comprehension to connection. Guided discussion and question supports develop this capacity before independent response.

nodes.label: Expressing opinions and retelling
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express a simple opinion about a character or text, and retell or summarise a storyline using modelled language.
criteria: Expresses at least one opinion about a character or text using a modelled sentence structure
Retells at least two key events from a text in correct sequence

width.minimum: Express at least one opinion about a character or story using a modelled sentence structure, and retell at least two key events in sequence.
width.typical: Express opinions about characters using modelled language with reasons; retell or summarise storylines after listening to, reading or viewing a text; identify a favourite character and justify the choice; use modelled exclamatory or evaluative expressions to respond to texts.
wider: Compare two characters or texts — what is the same, what is different, which do you prefer and why — using modelled comparison and opinion structures
Perform a scene from a familiar story, combining retelling with personal response and expression

modes.reason: Opinion expression and retelling integrate key word identification (node 1) and personal connection making (node 2) into productive response tasks. The teaching investment is in providing opinion and retelling frames that scaffold structure without eliminating personal choice — students decide what they think, the frame helps them say it.

descriptors.title: Language carries cultural meaning
descriptors.description: recognise that language carries cultural meaning in everyday social interactions
descriptors.knowledge: Students have used formulaic social expressions in classroom and play contexts (AC9LCH2C01, AC9LCH2C02). They have noticed that gestures and body language contribute to meaning. They have not yet examined why specific language forms are used — the cultural conventions behind politeness, address, etiquette — or identified expressions that carry cultural meaning with no direct English equivalent.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise that language choices in everyday social interactions carry cultural meaning — including conventions of politeness, address, etiquette, and culturally-specific expressions — and can identify examples and explain their significance.
elaborations: discussing the different implications of direct versus polite request forms
showing politeness in different contexts, making requests with appropriate register
learning about etiquette in everyday social contexts such as how to address adults
understanding cultural gestures, for example, standing up to greet a teacher, receiving an object with both hands
creating bilingual resources such as illustrated word charts or digital flashcards
discussing words or expressions that appear to have no equivalent in English
discussing meanings of colloquial phrases used on specific occasions
interpreting language, facial expressions and other visual cues in animations or songs

nodes.label: Politeness, address and social etiquette conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and use language conventions for politeness, appropriate address and social etiquette in familiar everyday contexts.
criteria: Identifies at least two politeness or address conventions in the target language and can explain why each is used
Demonstrates the correct form in at least one context — for example, a polite request or appropriate address for an adult
nodes.hinge_reason: Politeness and address conventions are the foundation for all culturally appropriate social interaction. Students who do not understand why specific language forms are used cannot interpret or produce culturally appropriate communication — a prerequisite for the cultural translation and mediation work that develops across Y3-4 and beyond.

width.minimum: Identify at least two conventions of politeness or address in the target language and use them correctly in context — for example, distinguishing a polite request from a demand, or using appropriate address for an adult.
width.typical: Demonstrate levels of politeness in different contexts — requests, thanks, address of adults and peers; identify cultural gestures and etiquette conventions; distinguish between polite and impolite forms of the same communicative act; use appropriate language when addressing people of different ages or authority.
wider: Compare politeness conventions in the target language with English — identify where the conventions differ and what this reveals about cultural values around respect and relationship
Explore a range of everyday social contexts (greeting an elder, receiving a gift, entering someone's home) and identify the specific language and gesture conventions for each

modes.reason: Politeness conventions require students to move from observing language use to understanding the cultural logic behind it. Explicit discussion of why a particular form is used — not just what is said — builds the cultural reasoning capacity that distinguishes background learners' insight from surface imitation.

nodes.label: Culturally-specific expressions and untranslatable language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify expressions in the target language that carry cultural meaning — including phrases with no direct English equivalent or phrases used on specific cultural occasions.
criteria: Identifies at least one culturally-specific expression and explains its meaning in context
Can explain why the expression does not translate directly into English

width.minimum: Identify at least one expression in the target language that carries specific cultural meaning and cannot be directly translated, and explain what it means in context.
width.typical: Explore colloquial phrases, occasion-specific expressions and culturally-embedded language; discuss the cultural meaning and context of these expressions; compare with how equivalent sentiments are expressed in English; create bilingual resources that explain the cultural context of key expressions.
wider: Research a culturally-specific occasion or celebration and identify the language specifically associated with it — explain why particular expressions are used on that occasion and not others
Compare culturally-specific expressions across two or more languages known in the class — identify where untranslatability reflects different cultural values

modes.reason: Culturally-specific expressions are encountered rather than deduced. Students need exposure to a range of occasions, contexts and expression types before the general insight — that language encodes cultural meaning — becomes visible. Varied cultural encounters build the repertoire from which this understanding emerges.

nodes.label: Non-verbal and visual cues as cultural meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how non-verbal cues — gesture, facial expression, body language — carry culturally-specific meaning in the target language, and interpret these in interaction and media texts.
criteria: Identifies at least two non-verbal cues in the target language and explains their cultural meaning
Demonstrates or describes the correct use of at least one culturally-specific gesture or non-verbal convention

width.minimum: Identify at least two non-verbal cues in the target language (gesture, facial expression, body language) and explain what they mean in their cultural context.
width.typical: Interpret cultural gestures and non-verbal communication conventions; identify how facial expressions and visual cues in animations, songs and stories contribute to meaning; compare non-verbal conventions between the target language community and English-speaking contexts.
wider: Analyse a short animated or video text and identify all the non-verbal cues that carry meaning — compare with a peer's reading to discuss what is shared and what is culturally interpreted

Discuss how non-verbal communication in the target language compares with gesture and body language in First Nations Australian communication — identify similarities and differences in how gesture carries meaning

modes.reason: Non-verbal meaning interpretation integrates politeness conventions (node 1) and cultural expression awareness (node 2) into a holistic reading of communicative acts. The teaching investment is in creating analysis tasks that require students to notice the full communicative package — verbal, non-verbal and contextual — not only words.

descriptors.title: Create spoken, written and multimodal texts
descriptors.description: with support, create spoken, written and multimodal texts, using familiar words, modelled phrases and sentences, copying known characters and writing system conventions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interact in classroom routines, collaborate in play-based activities, and locate information in familiar texts (AC9LCH2C01–C03). They can use formulaic expressions and communicate personal meaning. They have not yet created their own texts — combining target language words, phrases and writing with images and multimodal elements — for a defined purpose and audience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create spoken, written and multimodal texts using familiar words, modelled phrases and sentences, combining target language with images and other modes to communicate meaning for a purpose.
elaborations: writing captions with support for a photographic display about a class event
drawing a picture around a component or character depicting the meaning
creating posters on a cultural topic selecting images and texts
matching bilingual captions to images of First Nations Country/Place locations in their local area or elsewhere in Australia
presenting knowledge of places in the target language country and Australia using photographs
role-playing a modelled conversation related to daily life
creating short plays based on extracts from familiar stories using puppets and props
practising language using toys, puppets and dolls
making a birthday card or drawing and labelling a self-portrait

nodes.label: Copying and producing written target language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can copy and produce written target language words and phrases with attention to writing conventions, using known characters or script features.
criteria: Copies at least five target language words with correct script conventions
Can produce at least two words from memory with recognisable accuracy
nodes.hinge_reason: Producing written target language is the prerequisite for all text creation. Students who cannot form written words with attention to script conventions cannot create written or multimodal texts — the core demand of this descriptor.

width.minimum: Copy at least five target language words or a short phrase with attention to script conventions (stroke order, character formation, or script-specific features as applicable), demonstrating understanding of what the words mean.
width.typical: Copy and trace words and phrases with attention to writing conventions; make and form characters or script features using varied materials; connect written forms to their spoken equivalents and meanings; begin to write short known phrases from memory.
wider: Explore the relationship between the written form and meaning in the target language writing system — for example, how components or character elements contribute to meaning
Compare writing conventions in the target language with English — identify what is similar and what requires different knowledge or attention

modes.reason: Writing script conventions require repeated practice for accuracy and fluency. Varied production activities — chalk, sand, whiteboards, digital tools — build the muscle memory and visual attention needed before students can write with confidence in text creation tasks.

nodes.label: Creating short texts for a purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create short spoken, written or multimodal texts using familiar words and modelled sentence structures, for a specific purpose and audience.
criteria: Creates a short text using at least three target language words or a modelled phrase
The text has a clear communicative purpose and is directed at an identifiable audience

width.minimum: Create at least one short text (caption, card, poster, label) using at least three target language words or a modelled phrase, with a clear communicative purpose.
width.typical: Create a range of short texts — captions for photo displays, greeting cards, posters, illustrated sentences, self-portraits with labels — using familiar words and modelled sentence structures; combine target language with images and other modes; present personal knowledge about places, people or experiences.
wider: Create a bilingual text that communicates the same information in both the target language and English — compare the choices made and what is easier or harder to express in each language
Create a text for a specific audience (younger students, family, community) and adapt the language choices accordingly

modes.reason: Text creation for a purpose requires students to understand that different purposes and audiences call for different language choices. Varied creation tasks — personal, informative, celebratory — build this contextual awareness before students can make independent text choices.

nodes.label: Performing and presenting created texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform or present a created spoken or multimodal text — a role-play, short play, or oral presentation — using the target language with support.
criteria: Performs or presents a created text using at least four target language phrases appropriate to the context
Demonstrates awareness of audience through manner of delivery — for example, appropriate volume, pace or expression

width.minimum: Perform or present at least one created text (role-play script, short play, oral presentation) using at least four target language phrases appropriate to the context.
width.typical: Role-play modelled conversations incorporating personal information; perform short plays based on familiar stories using puppets and props; practise and present oral texts using toys, costumes or visual supports; create and present a birthday card, self-portrait or greeting in the target language.
wider: Create and perform an original short play or role-play — not based on a modelled script — using known language for a new scenario
Present a created text to a real audience (another class, family members, school community) and adapt the presentation for that audience

modes.reason: Performance and presentation integrates written production (node 1) and purposeful text creation (node 2) into a full communicative act. The teaching investment is in creating real or realistic audience conditions — students performing for peers, younger students or family — that give the communication genuine stakes.

descriptors.title: Sound patterns and tones
descriptors.description: recognise and use sound patterns and tones of the target language
descriptors.knowledge: Students have noticed distinctive sounds and sound patterns in the target language and compared them with English (AC9LCHF02). They can imitate familiar sounds and identify some similarities and differences. They have not yet systematically recognised and used tones or tone-marking conventions, identified syllable structure, or applied sound pattern knowledge to their own spoken production with accuracy.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise and use the sound patterns and tones of the target language — identifying tones, matching tones to meaning, representing sounds in written form, and developing spoken fluency through attention to rhythm, tone and stress.
elaborations: listening to and performing nursery rhymes and stories with rhythms, tones and sound patterns
participating in tone-guessing activities identifying the 4 tones and the neutral tone
writing syllables in the phonetic system with correct tone marks
recording own pronunciation of different tones and playing games with peers
singing a Pinyin alphabet song understanding that Pinyin is the romanisation of spoken sounds
playing pair-matching card games matching tones, initial to final
identifying syllables that make up target language words
developing fluency of sentences using gesture to demonstrate tone and stress

nodes.label: Recognising and distinguishing tones
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and distinguish the tonal system of the target language, identifying how different tones on the same syllable produce different meanings.
criteria: Correctly identifies at least two different tones when heard in isolation or in a word
Can give an example showing that a tone change produces a different meaning
nodes.hinge_reason: Tonal distinction is the foundational sound knowledge for the target language. Students who cannot distinguish tones cannot accurately produce or comprehend spoken target language — all subsequent sound pattern work and spoken fluency development depends on this perceptual foundation.

width.minimum: Correctly identify at least two different tones when heard, and demonstrate understanding that tone changes meaning by giving an example.
width.typical: Identify and distinguish the tonal system of the target language (including neutral tone where applicable); participate in tone-guessing activities and matching games; demonstrate awareness that the same syllable with different tones carries different meanings; respond with appropriate actions when identifying tone types.
wider: Record own pronunciation of different tones and compare with a peer — identify where tones sound the same or different and discuss
Investigate tone patterns in a familiar rhyme or song — identify which tones recur and whether they contribute to the rhythm or musical effect

modes.reason: Tone discrimination requires repeated listening and production practice before it becomes reliable. Tone-guessing games, matched pairs, and self-recording activities build perceptual accuracy through repetition in varied contexts — a single lesson encounter is insufficient.

nodes.label: Representing sounds in written form
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent target language sounds in written form using the romanisation or phonetic system of the target language, including tone marks where applicable.
criteria: Writes at least three syllables in the target language phonetic system with correct tone marks
Can match at least five written phonetic forms to their spoken equivalents

width.minimum: Write at least three syllables in the target language romanisation or phonetic system with correct tone marks, demonstrating understanding that the written form represents spoken sound.
width.typical: Write syllables and words in the target language phonetic or romanisation system with correct tone marks; match written phonetic forms to spoken sounds; understand that the romanisation system is a learning tool representing spoken language; play pair-matching games matching sound to written form.
wider: Investigate how the romanisation or phonetic system of the target language handles sounds that are different from English — identify sounds that require attention because they look like English letters but sound different
Analyse how tone marks or diacritic marks on the same vowel produce different words — create examples showing the same syllable in all tones with meanings

modes.reason: Students need explicit instruction on how the phonetic or romanisation system works — it is not intuitive for English speakers or for students who know the language only orally. Explicit mapping between spoken sound and written symbol, with attention to deceptive similarities with English, prevents systematic errors.

nodes.label: Syllable structure and spoken fluency
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify syllables in target language words and apply sound pattern knowledge to develop spoken fluency through rhymes, poems and familiar texts.
criteria: Correctly identifies syllables in at least five target language words
Recites a familiar rhyme, poem or sentence demonstrating attention to tone and rhythm

width.minimum: Identify syllables in at least five target language words and recite at least one familiar rhyme, poem or sentence with attention to tone, rhythm and stress.
width.typical: Identify syllables that make up words and understand that each syllable carries meaning in the target language; develop fluency through reciting rhymes, poems and familiar sentences with attention to tone and stress; use gesture to support tone and stress demonstration.
wider: Recite a classic short poem or rhyme from the target language culture, demonstrating tone accuracy and attention to rhythm — compare the effect of saying it with and without tonal accuracy
Analyse the syllable and tonal structure of a familiar tongue twister — explain why it is difficult and identify the specific tonal or sound contrasts it practises

modes.reason: Syllable structure and spoken fluency integrate tonal discrimination (node 1) and phonetic writing knowledge (node 2) into extended spoken production. The teaching investment is in creating performance conditions — recitation, reading aloud, recording — that require students to apply all sound pattern knowledge simultaneously.

descriptors.title: Language features construct meaning
descriptors.description: recognise that target language components and/or characters and features of language are used to construct meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students have noticed features of the target language writing system and compared them with English (AC9LCHF02). They can copy familiar words with attention to script conventions (AC9LCH2C05). They have not yet examined how components, characters or grammatical features of the target language systematically construct meaning — how word-building elements combine, how word order operates, or how grammatical categories function.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise that components, characters and grammatical features of the target language are used to construct meaning — including how characters or words are built, how word order works, and how grammatical features such as adjectives, prepositions, question words and measure words operate in context.
elaborations: making and copying components, characters and/or words using playdough, strings, found objects, blocks and chalk
copying and tracing words and phrases with attention to stroke order
making connections among characters sharing the same radicals and discussing the importance of the associated meaning
learning that target language words are made up of multiple characters, each contributing meaning
noticing similarities and differences between punctuation conventions in the target language and English
understanding that there are basic rules of word order: subject+verb+object
using common adjectives to describe people, animals and objects in modelled sentences
recognising common prepositions relating to location
using some question words in familiar contexts
using basic measure words in modelled sentences

nodes.label: How characters or words are built
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how the target language builds characters or words from components, recognising that elements combine to construct meaning.
criteria: Identifies at least two examples of component combination in the target language with an explanation of how the components contribute to meaning
Can make at least one connection between a shared component and related meaning across two or more words
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how characters or words are built is the prerequisite for all subsequent work with vocabulary, reading and writing in the target language. Students who treat each word as an arbitrary string cannot use component knowledge to infer meaning, extend vocabulary, or understand the logic of the writing system.

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples of how components or elements combine in the target language to build a word or character, and explain the connection to meaning.
width.typical: Explore how characters or words are constructed from components or morphemes; make connections between shared components and related meanings; understand that words may be made up of multiple meaningful units; create or copy characters and words with attention to how components contribute to the whole.
wider: Investigate a group of words or characters sharing a common component and identify the semantic or phonetic connection — explain the pattern to a peer
Compare how words are built in the target language with how compound words or word parts work in English — identify similarities and differences in word construction logic

modes.reason: Word and character construction is not transparent — students need explicit instruction on how components combine and why. Guided analysis of component patterns, with discussion of the semantic or phonetic logic, builds the systematic knowledge that allows students to approach unfamiliar words strategically.

nodes.label: Word order and basic grammatical structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify basic word order patterns in the target language and recognise how grammatical structures — adjectives, prepositions, question words, measure words — function in context.
criteria: Identifies subject-verb-object word order in at least two target language sentences
Correctly uses at least one grammatical feature (adjective, preposition, question word, or measure word) in a modelled sentence

width.minimum: Identify the basic subject-verb-object word order in at least two target language sentences and correctly use at least one grammatical feature (adjective, preposition, or question word) in a modelled sentence.
width.typical: Recognise and apply basic word order rules; use common adjectives to describe people and objects; use prepositions for location; use question words in familiar contexts; use measure words with numbers in modelled sentences; notice similarities and differences between word order in the target language and English.
wider: Compare the placement of adjectives, adverbs or question words in the target language with English — identify where they appear in the same position and where they differ
Create a set of target language sentences demonstrating different grammatical features — annotate each sentence to show how each part contributes to meaning

modes.reason: Grammatical structures at Y1-2 are best encountered in varied contexts — reading, listening, play and production — rather than through isolated exercises. Students need to recognise and use structures across different sentence types and topics before the patterns become reliable.

nodes.label: Punctuation conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify similarities and differences between punctuation conventions in the target language and English, and use target language punctuation correctly in short texts.
criteria: Identifies at least two target language punctuation marks and describes how they compare with English
Uses correct punctuation in at least one short created text

width.minimum: Identify at least two punctuation marks in the target language, describe whether they are the same as or different from English equivalents, and use them correctly in a short text.
width.typical: Notice and discuss similarities and differences between target language and English punctuation conventions; use correct punctuation in created texts; understand the function of key punctuation marks in the target language.
wider: Compare a target language and English text of the same type — identify every punctuation difference and discuss what each reveals about the two writing systems
Create a bilingual mini-guide to punctuation conventions, explaining to a peer what is the same and what is different

modes.reason: Punctuation conventions integrate character/word knowledge (node 1) and grammatical structure awareness (node 2) into the full writing system. The teaching investment is in contextualised writing tasks that require correct punctuation for meaning — not isolated punctuation exercises.

descriptors.title: Target language features similar to and different from English
descriptors.description: recognise that the target language has features that may be similar to or different from English
descriptors.knowledge: Students have noticed sound patterns and tonal features of the target language (AC9LCH2U01) and recognised how language features construct meaning (AC9LCH2U02). They have compared some sound and writing features with English. They have not yet systematically compared structural features, word order, vocabulary borrowing, or grammatical categories across the two languages using beginning metalanguage.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise that the target language has features that are similar to and different from English — including word order, sound patterns, borrowed vocabulary, text features and basic grammatical categories — and can describe comparisons using simple language.
elaborations: noticing that simple statements in Chinese tend to follow the same word order as in English: subject+verb+object
discussing the placement of words in Chinese, for example, 'happy' in Happy Birthday versus the target language equivalent
comparing the vowel sounds of English with the main vowel sounds of the target language
identifying the similarities and differences between cardinal and ordinal numbers in the target language and English
comparing bilingual texts noticing similarities and differences in punctuation and text organisation
recognising that languages use words borrowed from other languages
learning metalanguage for word types, for example, what are considered verbs in English and adjectival verbs in the target language

nodes.label: Word order and structural similarities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify where word order and sentence structure in the target language is similar to or different from English, with examples.
criteria: Identifies at least two examples of word order similarity between the target language and English
Identifies at least one example of word order difference with a correct explanation
nodes.hinge_reason: Recognising structural similarities and differences is the foundation for language comparison. Students who assume the target language works exactly like English will make systematic errors and cannot develop the comparative metalinguistic awareness that this descriptor and the Y3-4 strand require.

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples where word order in the target language is the same as English and at least one where it differs, using a simple sentence example for each.
width.typical: Compare word order in statements, questions and phrases across the target language and English; notice where modifiers, numbers, and descriptive words appear relative to nouns; discuss where the two languages follow similar logic and where they diverge.
wider: Investigate a specific structural difference — for example, how dates, names or expressions of time are ordered differently — and explain the rule in simple terms
Compare equivalent phrases in bilingual texts and map the structural differences — annotate a short text to show where target language and English word order matches and where it diverges

modes.reason: Structural comparison requires students to hold two language systems in mind simultaneously. Explicit comparison frames — 'in English this goes here, in the target language it goes there, because...' — scaffold the reasoning before students can conduct comparisons independently.

nodes.label: Vocabulary borrowing across languages
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise that languages borrow words from each other, and identify examples of borrowed words in the target language or English.
criteria: Identifies at least two borrowed words and explains their meaning in context
Can explain in simple terms why languages borrow words from each other

width.minimum: Identify at least two borrowed words in the target language (from English or another language) or in English (from the target language), and explain what they mean.
width.typical: Explore borrowed vocabulary in the target language — words adopted from other languages; recognise that English also borrows from the target language and other languages; discuss why languages borrow words and what this reveals about cultural contact and influence.
wider: Research a set of borrowed words in the target language and trace their origin — identify what cultural or historical contact led to the borrowing
Compare borrowed words in the target language with borrowed words in Australian English — identify patterns in what gets borrowed (food, technology, fashion) and why

modes.reason: Vocabulary borrowing is best understood through varied examples across categories — food, technology, transport, popular culture. Exposure to multiple examples across domains builds the general insight about language contact before students can reason about why borrowing occurs.

nodes.label: Text features and metalanguage for language types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify similarities and differences in text features across the target language and English, and use simple metalanguage to describe word types.
criteria: Identifies at least two text feature similarities or differences between a target language and English text
Correctly uses at least two metalanguage terms to describe language features

width.minimum: Identify at least two similarities or differences in text features between a target language and English text, and correctly use at least two metalanguage terms (e.g. verb, noun, adjective) to describe language features.
width.typical: Compare bilingual texts (picture books, songs, multimedia) and notice similarities and differences in punctuation, layout, and organisation; use simple metalanguage to describe word types in the target language and English; discuss grammatical categories that appear different across the two languages.
wider: Compare two bilingual versions of the same text (e.g. a folk tale in target language and English) — identify all the structural and textual differences and compile a class comparison list

Explore a grammatical category that works differently in the target language from English — for example, where English uses one word type and the target language uses a different structure — and explain the difference in simple terms

modes.reason: Text feature comparison and metalanguage use integrate structural comparison (node 1) and vocabulary knowledge (node 2) into a broader reading of how the two languages work as systems. The teaching investment is in making comparison explicit — naming what students notice — rather than leaving metalinguistic awareness implicit.

descriptors.title: Language reflects cultural practices
descriptors.description: notice that people use language in ways that reflect cultural practices
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored connections between language and culture and identified cultural practices associated with the target language (AC9LCHF03). They have recognised that language carries cultural meaning in everyday interactions (AC9LCH2C04). They have not yet systematically noticed how language use across a community reflects cultural practices, values and identity — or compared their own community's language use with others'.
descriptors.endpoint: Students notice that people use language in ways that reflect cultural practices — including how language use differs across communities, the role of cultural symbols and language in identity, and the relationship between language and cultural belonging.
elaborations: comparing and contrasting classroom interactions with those in target language communities
using gestures, words and phrases that reflect aspects of target language culture
identifying countries and regions where the target language is used as a language of communication
exploring symbols and language used by First Nations Australians and in target language communities in a range of contexts
discussing the role of the target language in their own lives — cultural events, food preferences, overseas travel
exploring cultural symbols and practices through stories, songs, dances, games and crafts
sharing information about their family — country of origin, languages spoken, current locations of extended family

nodes.label: Language use across communities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify ways in which language use differs across different communities and contexts where the target language is spoken.
criteria: Names at least two communities or regions where the target language is spoken
Identifies at least one way language use differs across those communities
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that language use varies across communities is the conceptual prerequisite for all subsequent work on language, culture and identity. Students who assume all target language speakers use language the same way cannot appreciate the role of cultural context in shaping communication.

width.minimum: Identify at least two communities or regions where the target language is spoken and describe at least one way language use differs across them — for example, greeting conventions, vocabulary differences, or dialect features.
width.typical: Compare and contrast classroom language use with target language use in other communities; identify countries and regions where the target language is used; notice that the same language is used differently across communities; explore how language varies across contexts within the target language community.
wider: Research how the target language is used in different countries or regions — identify specific words, expressions or conventions that differ across communities and discuss why
Compare how First Nations Australian languages and the target language are each associated with specific communities and places — discuss what language tells us about belonging and connection

modes.reason: Community language variation is understood through encounter with varied examples — images, media, guest speakers, maps. Single examples of target language use give an incomplete picture. Varied community contexts build the insight that language is socially and culturally situated.

nodes.label: Cultural symbols, practices and language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify cultural symbols and practices associated with the target language and describe how language is used in those contexts.
criteria: Identifies at least two cultural symbols or practices associated with the target language
Describes at least one piece of language used in connection with a cultural practice

width.minimum: Identify at least two cultural symbols or practices associated with the target language and describe the language used in connection with each.
width.typical: Explore cultural symbols and practices — festivals, art forms, games, crafts, community events — and the language associated with them; compare target language cultural practices with those of other communities in the class; discuss the role of language in cultural expression and identity.
wider: Examine a cultural practice in depth — identify all the language used in connection with it (greetings, wishes, descriptions, instructions) and explain what the language reveals about the cultural values behind the practice

Compare a cultural practice from the target language community with a similar practice in another community represented in the class — identify where the practices and their associated language are similar or different

modes.reason: Cultural symbol and practice knowledge is built through accumulation — students need encounter with varied practices (festivals, arts, games, food, crafts) before the connection between language and cultural practice becomes generalisable. Each encounter adds to the repertoire from which the broader insight emerges.

nodes.label: Language, identity and personal connection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on the role of the target language in their own identity and daily life, and share information about their family's language history and cultural connections.
criteria: Shares at least two personal connections to the target language — family, community, cultural practice or travel
Can identify the languages spoken in their family and describe at least one context where the target language is used

width.minimum: Share at least two ways the target language is part of their own life — family, community, cultural events, food, travel — and identify at least one language they or family members speak.
width.typical: Discuss the role of the target language in their own lives — family connections, participation in cultural events, food, community; share information about family languages and cultural backgrounds; reflect on what it means to belong to more than one language community.
wider: Create a personal language map or family language tree — showing which languages are spoken in their family and community, where, and in which contexts
Interview a family member or community elder about their language history and share what they learn with the class — reflecting on how language connects people to place, family and community

modes.reason: Personal identity reflection integrates community language awareness (node 1) and cultural practice knowledge (node 2) into a personally grounded connection. The teaching investment is in creating a genuinely inclusive, curious environment where students are invited to share their own language stories without pressure to conform to any single cultural narrative.

descriptors.title: Recognise and respond to classroom language
descriptors.description: recognise and respond to modelled classroom-related greetings, instructions and routines, and personal introductions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise meaning and communicate using modelled words, gestures and formulaic phrases with support (AC9LSF01). They have no formal curriculum experience with structured classroom routines, following instructions, or producing personal introductions in the target language.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise and respond to modelled greetings, classroom instructions, routines and personal introductions in the target language, and use modelled language to introduce themselves and express simple personal information.
elaborations: greeting and farewelling each other according to the time of the day and relationship to the person
participating in regular class routines such as stating the weather, the day and date, how they feel and making announcements
responding to simple classroom instructions and roll call
following classroom commands and imperatives using actions and gestures
following teacher instructions to complete activities or build/draw an imaginary character
introducing and describing themselves using modelled sentence structures and visual supports
using modelled statements to express likes and dislikes
using formulaic language to express thanks, apologies, praise and well wishes
asking and responding to questions using modelled sentences to discuss their personal worlds
requesting permission or seeking approval from peers using modelled expressions

nodes.label: Recognising and responding to greetings and farewells
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and respond appropriately to modelled greetings and farewells — selecting responses appropriate to time of day, relationship and context.
criteria: Responds correctly to at least three different greeting or farewell exchanges using appropriate target language or action
Uses at least two formulaic expressions (thanks, apology, praise) correctly in context
nodes.hinge_reason: Greeting and farewell routines are the daily entry point for all classroom target language use. Students who cannot manage these exchanges are excluded from the social fabric of the language classroom and cannot engage with instruction or personal introduction work.

width.minimum: Respond correctly to at least three different greeting and farewell exchanges using appropriate target language or action.
width.typical: Participate in greetings and farewells across varied time-of-day and relationship contexts; use formulaic expressions for thanks, apologies, praise and well wishes; recognise and use expressions for special occasions.
wider: Initiate a greeting independently using the appropriate contextual form without teacher prompting
Explain to a peer or family member the meaning of two or three greeting expressions and when they are used

modes.reason: Greeting and farewell language becomes automatic only through daily repetition in real routine contexts — the routine itself is the practice vehicle.

nodes.label: Following classroom instructions and routines
nodes.checkpoint: Students can follow and respond to modelled classroom instructions, commands and routine language — using action, gesture or target language response.
criteria: Follows at least four different classroom commands correctly using action or target language response
Responds to a classroom request or routine question using appropriate target language

width.minimum: Respond correctly to at least four different classroom commands or instructions using appropriate action or target language.
width.typical: Follow and respond to a range of classroom commands, activity instructions and routine exchanges (roll call, weather, day and date); respond to instructions for creative and physical activities; use target language for simple classroom requests.
wider: Follow a sequence of three or more instructions in the target language without repetition — demonstrating processing of connected instruction sets
Give a simple instruction to a partner in the target language and check that it was understood

modes.reason: Instruction-following accuracy requires daily repetition in real classroom contexts. The classroom routine itself is the practice vehicle.

nodes.label: Producing personal introductions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce personal introductions and respond to simple personal questions using modelled sentence structures — including personal details and expressions of preference.
criteria: Produces a personal introduction with at least three elements using modelled sentence structures
Responds correctly to at least two simple personal questions

width.minimum: Produce a personal introduction with at least three elements using modelled sentence structures.
width.typical: Use modelled sentence structures to introduce themselves with name, age, family members, and preferences; ask and respond to simple personal questions; use visual supports such as photos and props.
wider: Produce an extended self-introduction adding at least two personal details beyond the modelled minimum — using adapted rather than verbatim language
Ask a partner at least two personal questions and respond to two questions in a short unrehearsed exchange

modes.reason: Personal introduction language requires a bank of sentence frames across personal domains. Students need exposure to varied frame types before they can adapt them for genuine personal expression.

descriptors.title: Participate in guided play-based language activities
descriptors.description: participate in a range of guided, play-based language activities using formulaic expressions, visual and spoken cues
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise and communicate using modelled words and formulaic phrases with support (AC9LSF01). They have limited experience using the target language in structured collaborative activity.
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate in a range of guided, play-based target language activities — including games, songs, role-plays and collaborative tasks — using formulaic expressions, visual and spoken cues.
elaborations: participating in games or activities that involve taking turns, suggesting, making choices or swapping/matching items
using spontaneous expressions, phrases and non-verbal communication when playing games or engaging in activities
exchanging, sorting and classifying objects and attributes using simple question forms and affirmative/negative responses
taking part in short role-plays or skits using spoken and visual cues, props and realia
contributing to class activities or projects such as making a birthday calendar or weather board
reciting and performing chants, songs and rhymes using gestures such as clapping or dancing
using digital tools or applications collaboratively in pairs or groups to enhance learning

nodes.label: Participating in games and songs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in structured language games, songs and chants using formulaic expressions and following spoken and visual cues.
criteria: Participates in at least two activity types using appropriate target language expressions
Uses at least one spontaneous expression during a game or activity
nodes.hinge_reason: Games and songs are the primary interaction context at this band. Students who cannot use formulaic language within structured activities are excluded from the main vehicle for language development, and spontaneous expression in role-play and collaborative tasks is impossible without this base.

width.minimum: Participate in at least two different activity types using target language expressions appropriate to each.
width.typical: Participate in games involving turn-taking, matching, questioning and responding; perform songs and chants with gesture and movement; use spontaneous expressions during play; use digital tools collaboratively for language activities.
wider: Lead a familiar game or song in the target language — calling out instructions or leading a chant for classmates
Use a spontaneous target language expression in an unscripted moment during a game — demonstrating transfer beyond rehearsed contexts

modes.reason: Formulaic language in games and songs becomes automatic through repeated performance across varied activity types — the game or song is the practice vehicle.

nodes.label: Participating in short role-plays
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in short guided role-plays using spoken and visual cues, props and familiar vocabulary to exchange information with a partner.
criteria: Participates in a role-play with at least three target language exchanges
Uses at least one question-answer exchange using familiar question forms

width.minimum: Participate in a short role-play using at least three target language exchanges with a partner.
width.typical: Take part in role-plays using props and realia across familiar contexts; use question-answer exchange patterns; use actions, gestures and visual supports; exchange information about familiar objects and personal details using modelled language.
wider: Initiate at least one exchange in a role-play without teacher prompting — taking the lead role rather than only responding
Introduce a small improvised element into a role-play — adapting a familiar exchange to a slightly different scenario

modes.reason: Role-play participation requires a bank of exchange patterns across varied communicative scenarios before students can apply familiar language to new contexts.

nodes.label: Contributing to collaborative class tasks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can contribute to collaborative class tasks and projects using familiar vocabulary — including shared records, displays and class productions.
criteria: Contributes at least two target language elements to a collaborative class task
Uses familiar vocabulary correctly in at least one shared class resource

width.minimum: Contribute at least two target language elements to a collaborative class task.
width.typical: Contribute to class projects using familiar vocabulary; use digital tools collaboratively for language tasks; exchange, sort and classify items using question-answer patterns; add to shared class resources across the year.
wider: Contribute an original element to a collaborative class project using adapted target language — not only copying modelled text
Use digital tools collaboratively to create a shared target language product — dividing contributions and combining them into a shared output

modes.reason: Collaborative task participation develops through varied task types and partner conditions. Students who only contribute to one type of shared task develop narrow collaborative language schemas.

descriptors.title: Locate key information in familiar texts
descriptors.description: locate, with support, key information in familiar texts, and respond using gestures, images, words and formulaic phrases
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise meaning in target language input with support using gesture, visual cues and context (AC9LSF01). They have no prior experience locating specific information in structured target language texts or categorising information from texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students locate key information in familiar spoken, written and multimodal target language texts with support, and respond using gestures, images, words and formulaic phrases.
elaborations: listening for and identifying key words and phrases in a range of simple texts, using intonation patterns to assist understanding
participating in shared reading of print and digital texts using pictures, keywords and contextual clues to predict meaning
demonstrating comprehension by labelling, matching, drawing, miming or onscreen pointing, clicking or dragging

recognising that gestures and body language are integral to communicating in language for First Nations Australians, and showing examples of how they are also integral to communicating in the target language
participating in shared class stories and responding to and repeating keywords
listening to, reading or viewing adapted versions of familiar stories and incorporating recurring keywords and expressions
responding to questions about people, places and objects
responding to spoken, print or digital texts through play-acting, illustrating or movement
categorising information using graphic organisers such as drawings or simple tables

nodes.label: Locating key words and phrases in familiar texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate key words and phrases in familiar target language texts using context, pictures, intonation and known vocabulary as cues.
criteria: Identifies at least three key words or phrases in a familiar text with support from pictures or context
Demonstrates comprehension through an appropriate response — labelling, matching, drawing, miming or selecting
nodes.hinge_reason: Locating key information in texts is the prerequisite for all reading comprehension and text response work. Students who can only recognise isolated words cannot extract meaning from connected text — which is required for the categorisation and response work in node 2.

width.minimum: Identify at least three key words or phrases in a familiar text using context, pictures or intonation as support.
width.typical: Listen for and identify key words and phrases in simple spoken, print and digital texts — stories, songs, rhymes, simple dialogues; use intonation patterns to assist comprehension; participate in shared reading using pictures, keywords and contextual clues to predict meaning; demonstrate comprehension by labelling, matching, drawing or selecting.
wider: Sequence events from a familiar text using images or key words — demonstrating comprehension beyond isolated word recognition
Notice how gesture and body language in target language texts carry meaning — and compare with gesture conventions from other languages known to the class

modes.reason: Text comprehension strategies develop through exposure to varied familiar text types — stories, songs, rhymes, instructions — each presenting different contextual cue conditions.

nodes.label: Responding to texts and categorising information
nodes.checkpoint: Students can respond to familiar target language texts using varied response modes and begin to categorise information from texts using simple graphic organisers.
criteria: Responds to a familiar text using at least two different response modes
Categorises at least four items from a text using a simple graphic organiser

width.minimum: Respond to a familiar text using at least two response modes (e.g. gesture and words, image and phrase) and complete at least one simple categorisation task from text content.
width.typical: Respond to spoken, print and digital texts through play-acting, illustrating, movement and verbal response; answer simple questions about characters, places and objects; categorise information using graphic organisers — likes/dislikes, opposites, categories, similarities/differences; recognise that gesture and body language are integral to communication across languages including First Nations Australian languages.
wider: Create a bilingual graphic organiser from a text — categorising information in both the target language and English
Produce a simple spoken response to a text in the target language — not only gesture or image, but a formulaic phrase that communicates a reaction or finding

modes.reason: Response repertoire develops through varied response conditions — different text types, question types and response modes. Students who always respond in one mode do not develop the verbal response capacity needed at 3-4.

descriptors.title: Language carries cultural meaning
descriptors.description: notice that language carries cultural meaning in classroom-related greetings, introductions, instructions and routines
descriptors.knowledge: Students have noticed that language is connected to culture (AC9LSF03) and can use modelled classroom greetings and routines (AC9LS2C01). They have not yet analysed the cultural meaning embedded in specific greetings, forms of address, or non-verbal conventions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students notice that target language greetings, introductions, instructions and routines carry cultural meaning — including forms of address, non-verbal conventions and contextual variation — and can explain some of these connections.
elaborations: recognising the cultural significance of hand gestures and facial expressions that accompany words and phrases in the target language
explaining to others the meanings and use of simple expressions such as greetings used for different times of day, occasions and people
noticing body language and tone when using some target language words, expressions and exclamations
making class word walls or personal bilingual picture dictionaries with captions and simple descriptions to explain cultural terms
understanding that different forms of language are used with different people to show respect and familiarity, and that there may be regional variations

nodes.label: Noticing cultural meaning in greetings and forms of address
nodes.checkpoint: Students can notice that target language greetings and forms of address carry cultural meaning — that choices about how to greet and address someone signal relationship, respect and context.
criteria: Identifies at least two target language greetings or address forms and explains what relationship or context each signals
Can distinguish at least one formal and one informal address form and explain when each is appropriate
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that language choices carry cultural meaning is the conceptual foundation for all cultural and intercultural work. Students who treat greetings as arbitrary phrases cannot engage with the richer cultural meaning work in node 2 or at subsequent bands.

width.minimum: Identify at least two instances where a greeting or form of address in the target language signals something about relationship or context.
width.typical: Explain the cultural significance of contextually varied greetings, formal and informal address distinctions, and address conventions for different relationships; create resources explaining cultural terms; compare target language and English greeting conventions.
wider: Explain a target language greeting convention to someone outside the classroom — articulate what the convention means and why it matters
Compare formal and informal address conventions in the target language with equivalent conventions in English or another language known to the class

modes.reason: The connection between language form and cultural meaning must be made explicit — students need to ask 'why is this form used here?' not just 'what does this mean?'. Tasks requiring explanation of cultural reasons build the analytical habit.

nodes.label: Noticing non-verbal communication and cultural expressions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can notice that body language, tone, gesture and culturally specific expressions carry meaning in target language interaction — and that these sometimes differ from English conventions.
criteria: Identifies at least one non-verbal convention that carries cultural meaning in target language interaction and explains what it communicates
Compares at least one target language cultural expression with an English equivalent and describes the similarity or difference

width.minimum: Identify at least one non-verbal feature (gesture, body language, tone) that carries meaning in target language interaction and explain what it communicates.
width.typical: Notice body language and tone in target language expressions; compare non-verbal conventions in target language and English contexts; recognise that gesture and facial expression are integral to communication; explore culturally specific expressions and compare with English equivalents.
wider: Demonstrate a target language non-verbal convention and explain its meaning to a partner — including the equivalent or near-equivalent in English
Explore expressions in Australian English that carry cultural meaning and compare with target language equivalents — identify what each reveals about cultural priorities

modes.reason: Non-verbal and cultural meaning is most visible across varied examples in different communicative domains. Varied exposure builds the generalisation that cultural meaning is embedded in language use across all contexts.

descriptors.title: Create texts using familiar language
