descriptors.description: use words, familiar phrases and modelled language to create spoken, written and multimodal texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can communicate using modelled words and formulaic phrases (AC9LSF01) and respond to texts using gestures, images and words (AC9LS2C03). They have not yet created their own texts — they have only responded to or repeated modelled language.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use familiar words, phrases and modelled language to create spoken, written and multimodal texts about themselves, familiar topics and imaginative subjects.
elaborations: creating a self-portrait or short profile using simple statements and familiar vocabulary
creating, describing or acting out real or imaginary characters using formulaic language and supporting pictures
colouring in flags and adding labels or words in cloze exercises, then creating a personal flag with description
matching bilingual captions/labels to images of First Nations Country/Place locations
using digital tools to create informative multimodal texts such as e-books, animations, videos, voice overs or captions
adding bilingual captions or speech bubbles to a photographic display or newsletter article
making bilingual greeting cards for celebrations using greetings alongside equivalent English greetings
using key words and phrases to describe aspects of a video clip or photo story
substituting words to create alternative versions of well-known stories, songs or rhymes
labelling target language communities on a map and creating descriptions using modelled language

nodes.label: Creating texts about self
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create simple spoken and written texts about themselves — including profiles and descriptions — using familiar vocabulary and modelled sentence structures.
criteria: Creates a text about themselves with at least three target language elements using modelled structures
Produces at least one written or multimodal element (label, caption, speech bubble) alongside spoken text
nodes.hinge_reason: Creating texts about self is the first production task requiring students to select and arrange language rather than repeat it. Students who cannot move from modelled repetition to basic personal production cannot progress to imaginative or informative text creation.

width.minimum: Create a text about themselves using at least three target language elements using modelled structures.
width.typical: Create self-portraits, profiles and simple descriptions using modelled sentence structures — personal details, family members, preferences; use familiar vocabulary across personal domains; incorporate labels, captions and speech bubbles in multimodal formats.
wider: Extend a self-description beyond the modelled minimum — adding personal details not explicitly provided in the model
Create a bilingual text about themselves identifying where structures are parallel and where they differ

modes.reason: Text creation from modelled language requires students to transfer phrases from a model to their own personal content. Repeated creation tasks with varied personal content build the transferable production skill.

nodes.label: Creating imaginative and informative multimodal texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create imaginative and informative multimodal texts — describing characters, places and familiar topics — using familiar vocabulary and adapted modelled language.
criteria: Creates at least one multimodal text combining visual and target language elements about an imaginative or informative topic
Uses adapted (not verbatim) modelled language in at least one creation — demonstrating flexibility beyond direct copying

width.minimum: Create at least one multimodal text (spoken and visual, or written and visual) about a character, place or event using familiar target language.
width.typical: Create character descriptions, story re-enactments, simple informative texts and bilingual captions using familiar vocabulary; add captions to displays; substitute words to create alternative versions of known stories or songs.
wider: Substitute multiple elements to create a genuinely adapted version of a known story or song — changing character, setting and at least one action
Create a multimodal text across both imaginative and informative modes on the same topic — demonstrating flexible use of familiar language

modes.reason: Text creation skills develop through varied text types and purposes. Creating across informative and imaginative modes — and across modalities — builds flexible production capacity.

nodes.label: Creating for real audiences and purposes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create texts that serve real communicative purposes for genuine audiences — including cards, bilingual captions, event materials and labelled displays.
criteria: Creates at least one text for a genuine purpose or audience outside the immediate classroom activity
The text communicates its intended meaning clearly — a real recipient could understand it without teacher explanation

width.minimum: Create at least one text for a genuine purpose or audience beyond the immediate classroom activity.
width.typical: Make bilingual cards for real occasions; add bilingual captions to school displays or event materials; label maps or community resources; create materials for genuine school events and celebrations.
wider: Create a bilingual text for a specified real audience — making deliberate choices about which language element to use for each audience need and explaining the choice
Create a text for a real occasion that is subsequently used — displayed, sent or performed — demonstrating the text fulfilled its communicative purpose

modes.reason: Creating for real audiences integrates all prior text creation work — personal expression (N1) and imaginative/informative production (N2) — and applies it for genuine communicative purpose.

descriptors.title: Sounds and rhythms of the target language
descriptors.description: recognise and imitate the sounds and rhythms of the target language
descriptors.knowledge: Students have noticed target language sounds and imitated some with support (AC9LSF02). They have no prior systematic experience with target language phonology, vowel patterns or the full sound inventory.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise and imitate the sounds and rhythms of the target language — including vowel patterns, consonant features, intonation and sounds not present in English.
elaborations: becoming familiar with the sounds of the alphabet in the target language, noticing any letters not found in English
imitating target language sounds that do not exist in English
recognising that some sounds in the target language do not exist in English, so they may be challenging to pronounce
recognising and applying target language vowel sounds and vowel-consonant combinations
identifying additional consonants and digraphs in the target language and experimenting with tongue positioning
listening to familiar vocabulary and identifying silent letters
noticing that statements and questions have different intonation
developing pronunciation, phrasing and intonation skills by singing, reciting and repeating words in context
experimenting with sounds in onomatopoeic words related to animal sounds and actions

nodes.label: Target language sounds and alphabet features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and imitate distinctive sounds of the target language, including sounds not present in English, and apply correct sound patterns to familiar vocabulary.
criteria: Produces target language vowel patterns accurately in familiar words
Imitates at least two target language sounds not present in English with adequate accuracy for recognition
nodes.hinge_reason: Accurate target language sound patterns are the phonological foundation for all subsequent pronunciation and literacy work. Students who default to English sound patterns produce persistent errors that are increasingly difficult to remediate at higher bands.

width.minimum: Correctly produce target language vowel patterns in familiar words; imitate at least two target language sounds not present in English with adequate accuracy.
width.typical: Apply correct vowel patterns across known vocabulary; imitate distinctive consonant features; recognise silent letters and other sound conventions; differentiate sounds that are similar but distinct in the target language; participate in alphabet songs and games that embed sound-letter relationships.
wider: Explain the difference between at least two target language sounds and their nearest English approximations — demonstrating metalinguistic awareness
Compare target language and English sound conventions for common concepts (e.g. animal sounds, exclamations) — identify where conventions differ

modes.reason: Sound pattern production requires repeated practice until new sound conventions become automatic. Songs, chants and games embed high-frequency practice in engaging contexts.

nodes.label: Intonation, rhythm and statement/question distinction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and imitate target language intonation patterns — including the distinction between statements and questions — and produce spoken language with appropriate rhythm and pace.
criteria: Demonstrates different intonation for at least one statement-question pair
Produces a short familiar spoken text with appropriate rhythm and pace

width.minimum: Demonstrate the difference between statement and question intonation in at least one example pair; produce a short sentence with appropriate rhythm.
width.typical: Recognise and use intonation to distinguish statements from questions and exclamations; develop phrasing and rhythm through songs, chants and movement; notice and imitate sound patterns; apply appropriate pace and stress in familiar spoken texts.
wider: Perform a familiar chant or song with deliberate attention to rhythm, stress and pace — demonstrating prosodic control beyond word-level accuracy
Produce the same sentence as a statement and a question — demonstrating intonation distinction — and explain what changes

modes.reason: Prosodic awareness develops through varied experience with the rhythmic and melodic patterns of the language. Songs, rhymes and chants across different moods and speeds build the range of intonation patterns students need.

descriptors.title: Alphabet and language features construct meaning
descriptors.description: recognise that the Roman alphabet and features of language are used to construct meaning in the target language
descriptors.knowledge: Students have noticed basic grammatical patterns with support (AC9LSF02). They are developing early literacy in English using the Roman alphabet. They have no prior systematic knowledge of target language grammatical structures.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise how the alphabet and key grammatical features — including word class markers, agreement patterns, verb forms and basic sentence structure — are used to construct meaning in the target language.
elaborations: differentiating the alphabet used in the target language from other alphabets or scripts
using numbers for simple ideas such as telling the time, expressing age and dates, and playing games
noticing that the personal pronoun can be omitted in the target language
noticing that adjectives usually follow nouns (or vary from English placement) and are used to describe characteristics
noticing endings of simple verbs and using them in modelled and formulaic expressions
making connections between articles and word endings to understand that nouns may have a grammatical class or gender
observing gender/class in patterns of naming and using singular forms of nouns and adjectives
observing capitalisation differences between the target language and English
learning the structure of simple affirmative and negative statements
identifying basic punctuation marks that differ from English
recognising and using definite and indefinite articles with nouns
using singular possessive adjectives to show ownership

nodes.label: Grammatical markers and word class features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise how grammatical markers in the target language signal word class, agreement and relationships between words — and apply these in familiar word groups.
criteria: Uses correct grammatical markers with at least four familiar words
Produces at least two word groups with correct agreement patterns
nodes.hinge_reason: Grammatical agreement and word class markers are the foundational system governing noun-phrase and sentence production in the target language. Students who do not internalise these patterns produce systematic errors that cascade throughout all sentence production at every subsequent band.

width.minimum: Correctly use grammatical markers (e.g. articles, agreement markers) with at least four familiar words; produce at least two word groups showing correct agreement.
width.typical: Recognise and apply grammatical agreement patterns across familiar vocabulary; observe word order patterns; notice how endings and markers signal relationships between words; use possessive forms; produce simple descriptive word groups with correct agreement.
wider: Sort a set of unfamiliar target language words into grammatical categories using patterns and context clues — explain the rule applied
Identify every grammatical marker in a short familiar text and describe what each one signals

modes.reason: Grammatical agreement requires high-frequency practice across a wide range of vocabulary before it becomes automatic. Students need to encounter and produce marked forms in varied contexts — not only in drills but in real text creation and comprehension.

nodes.label: Verb forms and affirmative/negative statements
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise basic verb forms in the target language and produce simple affirmative and negative statements.
criteria: Produces at least two affirmative statements and one negative statement using correct basic verb forms
Uses at least one verb in a recognisable inflected form

width.minimum: Produce at least two affirmative statements and one negative statement using correct basic verb forms.
width.typical: Recognise and use basic verb forms; produce simple affirmative and negative statements; notice how subject information is encoded in verb forms; use number expressions for age, time and dates; use possessive forms in familiar expressions.
wider: Produce statements using at least three different verbs — demonstrating a growing verb repertoire beyond the most frequent
Find the same verb used with different subjects in a familiar text — describe the pattern that signals each person

modes.reason: Verb form recognition and basic statement production develops through accumulating examples across varied verbs and sentence contexts before inflection patterns become recognisable.

nodes.label: Sentence-level composition and target language conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce connected sentences in the target language and identify key written conventions that differ from English.
criteria: Produces at least two connected sentences that form a coherent mini-text
Identifies at least one target language written convention that differs from English and explains the difference

width.minimum: Produce at least two connected sentences; identify at least one written convention of the target language that differs from English.
width.typical: Produce connected sentences using connectors to link ideas; identify distinctive punctuation, capitalisation or orthographic conventions of the target language; notice how target language written conventions differ from English; produce simple texts with two or more connected statements.
wider: Produce three or four connected sentences about a topic — demonstrating early sentence-level composition that creates a coherent mini-text
Compare the written conventions of a target language and English sentence — identify every difference and explain each

modes.reason: Sentence-level composition develops through encountering and producing varied sentence types in real text contexts. Varied production contexts build the compositional habit beyond isolated drills.

descriptors.title: Target language and English similarities and differences
descriptors.description: notice that the target language has features that may be similar to or different from English
descriptors.knowledge: Students have noticed some similarities and differences between target language and English sounds and features with support (AC9LSF02). They are developing early English literacy. They have not yet systematically compared structural features across the two languages.
descriptors.endpoint: Students notice and describe features of the target language that are similar to or different from English — including structural patterns, shared vocabulary, text conventions and written features — drawing on both languages as reference points.
elaborations: observing features of familiar types of texts such as stories and greeting cards, and comparing them with English equivalents
understanding grammatical features present in the target language but absent in English (e.g. grammatical gender, different word order)
noticing plural forms similar to or different from English
noticing there are cognates in the target language and English, but pronunciation may differ
creating an identity card with parallel personal information in the target language and English, noticing similarities and differences
comparing how target language words used in Australian English are pronounced by speakers of each language
noticing the differences between punctuation marks in the target language and English
identifying words in the target language borrowed from other languages, and vice versa

nodes.label: Shared vocabulary and structural comparisons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify vocabulary shared across the target language and English, and notice structural patterns that are similar to or different from English.
criteria: Identifies at least three shared target language-English vocabulary items and explains what makes them recognisable
Identifies at least one structural difference between the target language and English with a supporting example
nodes.hinge_reason: Using English as a reference point for target language structure is a productive metalinguistic strategy that accelerates grammatical awareness. Students who make these comparisons explicitly build transferable understanding; students who treat the two languages as completely separate miss the scaffolding that comparison provides.

width.minimum: Identify at least three shared target language-English vocabulary items and explain what makes them recognisable; identify at least one structural difference between the two languages.
width.typical: Notice and collect shared vocabulary across the two languages; notice structural patterns — including word order, grammatical categories — that are similar to or different from English; compare how sentences are built differently; create bilingual comparison resources.
wider: Find shared vocabulary items independently and test whether their meaning is truly equivalent — identify any that appear similar but mean something different
Compare a familiar target language text with its English equivalent — list every structural difference noticed

modes.reason: Cross-language comparison requires holding both languages in mind simultaneously and describing the relationship. Structured comparison tasks — side-by-side sentence pairs, bilingual charts — scaffold this dual-language attention.

nodes.label: Text features and vocabulary borrowing across languages
nodes.checkpoint: Students can notice similarities and differences in text features across the target language and English — including text type conventions, written features and borrowed vocabulary.
criteria: Identifies at least one text feature that differs between target language and English and explains the difference
Identifies at least two borrowed vocabulary items and explains what they show about language contact

width.minimum: Identify at least one text feature that differs between target language and English texts and explain the difference; identify at least one example of vocabulary borrowing between the two languages.
width.typical: Compare text type conventions across the target language and English (e.g. story openings, greeting card language); compare written features (punctuation, capitalisation); identify vocabulary borrowed between the two languages; create identity texts with parallel information in both languages.
wider: Find examples of words borrowed from the target language into English and from English into the target language — explain what the borrowing pattern reveals about how languages influence each other
Compare a familiar target language text type with its English equivalent — annotate every difference noticed

modes.reason: Cross-language noticing develops most richly through varied comparison contexts — text types, word types, borrowings. Each new context reveals a different dimension of the language relationship.

descriptors.title: Language reflects cultural practices
descriptors.description: notice that people use language in ways that reflect cultural practices
descriptors.knowledge: Students have noticed connections between language and culture (AC9LSF03) and that greetings carry cultural meaning (AC9LS2C04). They have not yet explored the diversity of target language communities, regional language variation, or the relationship between language use and cultural identity more broadly.
descriptors.endpoint: Students notice that people use language in ways that reflect cultural practices — across the diversity of target language communities, in formal and informal contexts, and in relation to First Nations Australian and other cultural practices.
elaborations: identifying terms and concepts that can be used to help understand and discuss culture
locating target language communities on a world map and understanding that culture varies greatly among these places
recognising that the target language is an important world language spoken in different forms in many countries
exploring symbols and languages used by First Nations Australians and by target language communities in a range of contexts
noticing aspects of the lives of children in target language communities as represented in print and digital images, stories and video
comparing their own ways of communicating and making meaning, including using any other language(s) they may speak
identifying formal and informal language use between people in different contexts
noticing expressions and terms used in Australian English that reflect lifestyles and culture
identifying themselves as belonging to different groups such as family, community, class or peer groups
discussing how colours or animals can represent different meanings and identity across cultures

nodes.label: Diversity of target language communities and variation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can notice that the target language is spoken in many different communities and that language use varies across these communities.
criteria: Identifies at least two target language communities and locates them on a world map
Identifies at least one way language varies across target language communities
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that the target language is spoken by diverse communities — not a single monolithic culture — is the conceptual foundation for all subsequent cultural and intercultural work. Students who imagine a single homogeneous target language culture cannot engage with genuine cultural complexity.

width.minimum: Identify at least two target language communities or countries and at least one way language varies between them.
width.typical: Locate target language communities on a world map; recognise that the target language is spoken with cultural and linguistic variation across many communities; notice vocabulary or expression differences across regions; understand that some people speak more than one language.
wider: Research one specific target language community — find two or three cultural practices reflected in the language used there and share findings
Compare the symbols and expressions of two target language communities — identify what they reveal about each community's identity

modes.reason: Diversity awareness is built by encountering multiple communities and language variation examples. Single-community exposure produces a narrow and misleading picture of the target language.

nodes.label: Language, identity and First Nations connections
nodes.checkpoint: Students can notice how language use reflects cultural practices and identity — including formal and informal contexts, First Nations Australian language connections, and their own multilingual or multicultural backgrounds.
criteria: Identifies at least one way that language use in the target language reflects a cultural practice and explains the connection
Identifies that First Nations Australians have languages connected to Country and can give at least one local example

width.minimum: Identify at least one way that language use in the target language reflects a cultural practice; connect First Nations Australian language to place and identity.
width.typical: Explore cultural practices reflected in target language use — celebrations, family practices, address conventions; engage with First Nations language connections to Country; compare students' own ways of expressing identity; discuss belonging to multiple communities.
wider: Find one local First Nations place name and research its meaning — connect this to the idea that language carries the history and identity of a community

Compare ways of expressing cultural identity across the student's own background, a target language community and a First Nations Australian community — find at least one meaningful similarity and one difference

modes.reason: Language-identity connections are most visible across multiple cultural contexts — the student's own, target language communities and First Nations communities. Each comparison point illuminates the pattern from a different angle.

descriptors.title: Initiate exchanges and respond to questions
descriptors.description: initiate exchanges and respond to questions about home and classroom environments, using familiar expressions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interact in classroom routines, personal introductions and collaborative activities using modelled expressions (AC9LCH2C01, AC9LCH2C02). They can make polite requests, express thanks and preferences. They have not yet independently initiated exchanges, maintained multi-turn conversations, asked for clarification, or used digital communication formats in the target language.
descriptors.endpoint: Students initiate exchanges and respond to questions about home and classroom environments using familiar expressions — including initiating and sustaining multi-turn conversations, seeking clarification, and using digital formats for interaction.
elaborations: initiating conversations by asking questions in different contexts using modelled responses
playing games where students take turns to role-play the teacher and give instructions
sharing information about themselves
participating in simple spoken exchanges with peers about familiar topics such as daily routines, local places or personal interests
initiating and maintaining communication by taking turns, for example, making suggestions
asking for clarification, using appropriate formulaic expressions and gestures
seeking advice and help from others
creating short texts such as emails, letters and text messages to interact with others
using emoticons in digital communication to enhance meaning

nodes.label: Initiating and sustaining conversations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can initiate a conversation by asking a question in a familiar context and sustain it through at least three turns, using appropriate turn-taking strategies.
criteria: Initiates at least one exchange with an opening question appropriate to the context
Sustains the exchange for at least three turns without teacher prompting
nodes.hinge_reason: Initiating exchanges is the entry condition for all subsequent interaction development. Students who can only respond to teacher-led prompts cannot participate in the peer-to-peer and student-led exchanges that the Y3-4 and Y5-6 descriptors require.

width.minimum: Initiate at least one exchange by asking an opening question and sustain it for at least three turns, using at least one turn-taking strategy (suggestion, follow-up question, or response to a peer's question).
width.typical: Initiate conversations in different contexts by asking questions about familiar topics — home, school, interests, daily routines; maintain exchanges by taking turns, making suggestions and responding to peers; use emoticons or digital conventions in appropriate digital communication contexts.
wider: Initiate and sustain a conversation on a topic introduced by the partner — demonstrate flexibility in responding to an unexpected topic direction
Compare conversation initiation conventions in the target language with English — identify different ways of opening a conversation and what makes each appropriate

modes.reason: Conversation initiation requires a growing bank of opening questions and turn-taking strategies across different topics and contexts. Repeated practice across varied familiar topics — not only one scripted exchange — builds the flexible initiation capacity that the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Asking for clarification and seeking help
nodes.checkpoint: Students can ask for clarification during an exchange and seek advice or help using appropriate formulaic expressions and gesture.
criteria: Uses at least one clarification request appropriately during an exchange
Uses at least one help-seeking expression in an appropriate context

width.minimum: Use at least one clarification request and one help-seeking expression correctly in context.
width.typical: Ask for clarification using appropriate formulaic expressions and gestures; seek advice or help in appropriate contexts; recognise when to ask for clarification and select the appropriate form; use clarification requests to sustain rather than abandon an exchange.
wider: Compare how clarification is requested in the target language with English — identify where the conventions are similar and where they differ
Role-play a scenario where a communication breakdown occurs and model the use of clarification strategies to repair the exchange

modes.reason: Clarification and help-seeking are strategies needed across all interaction contexts — peer exchange, guest speaker interaction, transactional scenarios. Practising these strategies across varied contexts builds confident, flexible deployment.

nodes.label: Digital and written interaction formats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create short texts in digital or written formats to interact with others — inviting, congratulating, thanking or sharing information — using appropriate format conventions.
criteria: Creates a short interactive text using at least three target language phrases and appropriate format conventions
The text has a clear communicative purpose — invitation, thanks, or information sharing

width.minimum: Create at least one short interactive text (email, letter, message, or invitation) using appropriate format conventions and at least three target language phrases.
width.typical: Create short texts in digital and written formats — emails, letters, text messages, invitations — to interact with others; use appropriate conventions for different formats; share information about school, community or personal experiences through written interaction.
wider: Compare the conventions of a formal and an informal written or digital interaction in the target language — identify what changes (greeting, closing, vocabulary, register) and explain why
Create a digital interaction text for a specific purpose and audience — for example, a message to a peer in a target language community — selecting format and language appropriately

modes.reason: Digital and written interaction integrates initiation skills (node 1) and clarification/help-seeking strategies (node 2) into a different mode — written production for a genuine communicative purpose. The teaching investment is in making the format conventions explicit and in creating real or realistic interaction partners.

descriptors.title: Plan and transact with others
descriptors.description: participate in activities that involve planning and transacting with others, using a range of phrases, structures and modelled sentences in familiar contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can initiate and sustain exchanges, collaborate in play-based activities, and use digital formats for interaction (AC9LCH4C01, AC9LCH2C02). They can take turns, give instructions and participate in role-play. They have not yet participated in transactional exchanges (buying, ordering, negotiating), planned and presented cultural items, or interacted with guest speakers in structured contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate in activities that involve planning and transacting with others — including role-plays involving transactions, planning and presenting cultural performances, and interacting with guests — using a range of phrases, structures and modelled sentences.
elaborations: planning and presenting a cultural item such as a festive occasion by reciting a poem, singing a song or performing a dance
performing plays with allocated roles within groups, using puppets and props
participating in group activities and role-plays involving scenarios such as buying food or ordering a meal
negotiating details in a transaction, such as stating preferred size, quantity or price
participating in traditional or contemporary games involving taking turns, active listening and information exchange
following procedures or giving modelled instructions
reading their own work to others
working in teams to create word or sentence games using digital applications
interacting with guest speakers or classroom visitors during special occasions
planning and discussing cultural items to present for a school event

nodes.label: Transactional role-play language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in transactional role-plays — buying, ordering, negotiating — using appropriate request forms, quantity and price language, and transaction-closing expressions.
criteria: Participates in a transactional role-play using at least three appropriate target language phrases
Successfully completes a transaction — stating a preference, negotiating or requesting, and closing the exchange
nodes.hinge_reason: Transactional language is the functional prerequisite for all planning and negotiation activity. Students who cannot manage a basic transaction cannot participate in the more complex planning and collaborative presentation tasks this descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Participate in at least one transactional role-play (e.g. buying food, ordering a meal) using at least three appropriate target language phrases for the transaction.
width.typical: Participate in transactional scenarios — shops, restaurants, markets — making requests, stating preferences, negotiating quantity and price, and concluding transactions; use appropriate modelled language for different stages of a transaction; use real or simulated currency or props.
wider: Compare how transactions are conducted in the target language community with Australian conventions — identify differences in etiquette, bargaining norms, or interaction patterns
Extend a transactional role-play beyond a scripted exchange — add complications (wrong item, price disagreement, special request) and negotiate a resolution

modes.reason: Transactional language transfers across different transaction types — food ordering, shopping, seeking services. Practising across varied scenarios (not only one scripted shop) builds the flexible transactional capacity that the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Planning and presenting cultural items
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan and present a cultural item — a performance, cultural display, or community event contribution — collaborating with peers and using appropriate target language.
criteria: Contributes to planning and presenting a cultural item using at least four target language phrases
Collaborates with peers in at least one planning decision — role allocation, content choice, or task assignment

width.minimum: Contribute to planning and presenting at least one cultural item (performance, display, or presentation) using at least four target language phrases appropriate to the task.
width.typical: Plan and present cultural items — reciting poems, singing songs, performing dances, creating cultural displays — for school or community audiences; collaborate in group planning and decision-making; follow procedures and give instructions in the target language.
wider: Lead or coordinate a cultural presentation — making decisions about content, assigning roles, and directing the group using target language
Compare how the cultural item is presented to different audiences (classmates, families, community members) and adapt language and format accordingly

modes.reason: Planning and presenting integrates transactional and collaborative language skills into a sustained, purposeful activity with a real audience. The teaching investment is in supporting genuine collaboration — not only rehearsed performance — where students negotiate roles, content and decisions in the target language.

nodes.label: Interacting with guests and in community contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interact with guest speakers or classroom visitors using appropriate target language, and adapt their language to the context of the interaction.
criteria: Interacts with a guest or visitor using at least two appropriate target language phrases
Adapts language or manner to the guest context — for example, using more formal address or prepared questions

width.minimum: Interact with at least one guest speaker or visitor using at least two appropriate target language phrases — for example, a greeting, a question, or an expression of thanks.
width.typical: Interact with guest speakers, community visitors, or participants in special occasions using appropriate language; adapt language to context and relationship; work in teams to create collaborative digital resources or activities for sharing with others.
wider: Prepare questions in advance for a guest speaker, conduct the interaction, and report back to peers on what was learned
Compare how interaction with a guest speaker differs from peer interaction — what changes in language, register, and manner, and why

modes.reason: Interaction with guests requires explicit preparation — students need to understand what makes this interaction context different from peer exchange, and to prepare appropriately. Structured preparation tasks (generating questions, practising register-appropriate greetings) support confident participation.

descriptors.title: Locate, organise and respond to information in texts
descriptors.description: locate, organise and respond to key information related to familiar content in spoken, written and multimodal texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate key information in familiar texts and respond with opinions and retelling using modelled language (AC9LCH2C03). They can identify main points and make personal connections. They have not yet gathered, organised and re-presented information from multiple sources, nor conducted interviews or produced structured summaries or responses for an audience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students locate, organise and respond to key information in familiar spoken, written and multimodal texts — including gathering from multiple sources, organising findings, retelling and summarising, and presenting information in different forms for purpose and audience.
elaborations: watching educational television programs, listening to songs or playing digital games, and sharing personal opinions
identifying and locating familiar characters or words in texts and discussing main purpose and meaning
creating a timeline of the main events of a story using words, pictures or simple sentences
learning that First Nations Australian languages change according to connections and relationships between people, and giving examples of how this occurs in Chinese
gathering information from a range of sources and presenting findings in a different way
responding to words of songs through movement and dance
interviewing family, friends or peers about languages spoken, country of origin or cultural events
listening to, reading and viewing a range of informative and imaginative texts and retelling or summarising
reading aloud or reciting texts paying attention to pronunciation, intonation and emotion
creating performances in response to legends and folk tales using modelled language

nodes.label: Locating and identifying information in texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate familiar words and key information in a range of text types and identify the purpose, main content and key features of the text.
criteria: Locates at least three key pieces of information from a familiar text
Identifies the main purpose of the text and at least one key feature of its format
nodes.hinge_reason: Locating and identifying information is the prerequisite for all text response and re-presentation. Students who cannot extract key information from texts cannot organise, summarise or present it in a different form — the core demand of this descriptor.

width.minimum: Locate at least three key pieces of information in a familiar text and identify the text's main purpose.
width.typical: Locate familiar characters, words or information in spoken, written and multimodal texts; identify main purpose and meaning; discuss key features of different text types (stories, informative texts, songs, packaging, educational programs); notice how First Nations Australian languages change according to relationships.
wider: Compare how the same information is presented in two different text types or formats — identify what is the same and what is different about how meaning is conveyed
Investigate a real-world text (packaging, sign, advertisement) in the target language — identify all the information it contains and explain how the visual and written elements work together

modes.reason: Information location strategies transfer across text types — stories, songs, packaging, educational media, informative texts. Practising with varied text types builds flexible comprehension strategies that work beyond a single familiar format.

nodes.label: Gathering and organising information from multiple sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can gather information from more than one source and organise it to present findings in a different form.
criteria: Gathers information from at least two sources
Organises and presents the information in a different form — timeline, graph, table, or summary

width.minimum: Gather information from at least two sources and organise findings into a different format — for example, a timeline, graph, table, or summary list.
width.typical: Gather information from a range of sources — interviews, texts, surveys, media — and organise findings in a new format; create timelines, picture graphs, annotated displays or summaries; interview family or peers to collect information about cultural practices, languages or experiences.
wider: Compare findings gathered from different sources — identify where sources agree, differ, or complement each other, and discuss why
Design and conduct a class survey, analyse the results, and present findings in an annotated target language graph or display

modes.reason: Gathering from multiple sources and re-presenting requires students to hold information across sources and decide how to organise it. Scaffolded organisational tools — templates, graphic organisers, guided interview questions — support this cognitive work before students can manage it independently.

nodes.label: Retelling, summarising and performing in response to texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can retell or summarise the main information or ideas in a familiar text, and create a performance or presentation in response.
criteria: Retells or summarises main points of a familiar text using at least four target language sentences
Creates a performance or presentation in response to a text, demonstrating understanding of content

width.minimum: Retell or summarise the main points of a familiar text using at least four target language sentences, and create at least one text or performance in response.
width.typical: Retell and summarise spoken and written texts — stories, folk tales, reports — with attention to main information, sequence and key ideas; read aloud or recite texts with attention to pronunciation and intonation; create performances or presentations in response to texts.
wider: Create an alternative version of a familiar text — changing the ending, updating the setting, or retelling from a different character's perspective
Perform a cultural legend or folk tale for a specific audience, selecting language and presentation approach appropriate to that audience

modes.reason: Retelling, summarising and performing integrates information location (node 1) and multi-source organisation (node 2) into a full communicative response. The teaching investment is in creating genuine performance or presentation conditions — real audiences, real purposes — that require students to select, organise and communicate effectively.

descriptors.title: Strategies to interpret culturally-loaded language
descriptors.description: develop strategies to interpret language that conveys cultural meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students recognise that language carries cultural meaning in social interactions and can identify culturally-specific expressions (AC9LCH2C04). They understand basic politeness and address conventions. They have not yet developed explicit translation strategies, used bilingual dictionaries, or analysed the risks of literal translation for culturally-embedded expressions and idioms.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop and apply strategies for interpreting language that conveys cultural meaning — including strategies for handling untranslatable expressions, formal and informal register, gesture and cultural symbols, and dictionary use for translation tasks.
elaborations: selecting language to translate information, recognising different meanings for the same word
demonstrating levels of politeness, respect and formality in diverse contexts
explaining when to use formal and informal language in different social contexts
recognising the role that gesture plays in interactions, including taboos within target language communication
creating bilingual resources for use in the classroom or school
identifying words and expressions in the target language and English that do not readily translate
developing strategies for using bilingual print or digital dictionaries
learning the cultural value behind symbols used in cultural events
identifying culturally-specific terms and phrases and sharing insights into why cultures value certain colloquial language

nodes.label: Formal and informal register in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain when to use formal and informal language in different social contexts, demonstrating appropriate language choices.
criteria: Identifies at least two contexts requiring different register and explains why
Produces appropriate language examples for at least two different register contexts
nodes.hinge_reason: Register awareness is the prerequisite for all culturally appropriate interpretation and production. Students who cannot distinguish formal from informal language cannot develop the culturally sensitive translation and mediation strategies the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Identify at least two contexts requiring different levels of formality in the target language and produce an appropriate language example for each.
width.typical: Distinguish between formal and informal language in diverse social contexts — home, school, interactions with adults or authority figures; demonstrate appropriate language choices in context; compare language use across contexts and explain the social factors that determine register.
wider: Compare register conventions in the target language with English — identify where formal/informal distinctions map onto similar conventions and where they differ fundamentally
Analyse a short interaction text — identify the register signals (vocabulary, grammar, address forms) and explain what they reveal about the relationship between speakers

modes.reason: Register decisions require students to read the social context of an interaction and select language accordingly. Explicit discussion of the factors that determine register — relationship, setting, purpose — builds the analytical capacity before students can make spontaneous register choices.

nodes.label: Untranslatable expressions and cultural symbols
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify words and expressions in the target language that do not translate directly into English, explain their cultural meaning, and recognise cultural symbols and their significance.
criteria: Identifies at least two untranslatable expressions and explains their cultural meaning in context
Can explain why at least one expression cannot be directly translated into English

width.minimum: Identify at least two expressions or terms that cannot be directly translated and explain what each means in its cultural context.
width.typical: Identify culturally-specific terms and expressions — colloquialisms, culturally-embedded phrases, occasion-specific language — that resist direct translation; compare these with English equivalents or absence of equivalents; recognise cultural symbols and identify the language and values associated with them.
wider: Research a culturally-specific expression or symbol and create a bilingual explanation resource — explaining what it means, when it is used, and what it reveals about cultural values
Compare untranslatable expressions across two languages — identify whether they reflect fundamentally different cultural values or can be approximately explained

modes.reason: Untranslatable expressions are understood through varied cultural encounters — different occasions, relationships and contexts. Building a repertoire of examples across contexts gives students the cultural framework to approach new untranslatable expressions with strategies rather than confusion.

nodes.label: Translation strategies and dictionary use
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop and apply strategies for translating between the target language and English, including the use of bilingual dictionaries and awareness of translation limitations.
criteria: Uses a bilingual dictionary to locate at least three words, selecting context-appropriate meanings
Produces a translation that accounts for context — not only the first dictionary entry

width.minimum: Use a bilingual dictionary to locate at least three words and produce a translation that accounts for context — not just the first entry.
width.typical: Use print and digital bilingual dictionaries to assist with translation; recognise that words can have multiple meanings depending on context; create bilingual resources — glossaries, picture dictionaries, signs — for classroom use; develop awareness of when and how to use translation tools.
wider: Translate a short text from the target language to English and explain at least two translation decisions — where a direct translation would be misleading and what approach was taken instead
Compare the output of a digital translation tool with a human translation of the same text — identify differences and discuss what the human translator understood that the digital tool missed

modes.reason: Translation strategies integrate register awareness (node 1) and cultural expression knowledge (node 2) into a practical mediation task. The teaching investment is in making explicit that translation is a cultural act — not a word-for-word substitution — through tasks that require genuine translation decisions.

descriptors.title: Create and present informative and imaginative texts
descriptors.description: create and present informative and imaginative spoken, written and multimodal texts, using a range of sentence structures and modelled textual conventions, characters appropriate to context, and/or the target language writing system
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create short spoken, written and multimodal texts using modelled phrases and sentences (AC9LCH2C05). They can produce written target language and perform created texts for a purpose and audience. They have not yet created extended texts using a range of sentence structures, produced informative texts for real audiences, or created imaginative texts such as alternative story endings or original performances.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and present a range of informative and imaginative spoken, written and multimodal texts using sentence structures and textual conventions appropriate to purpose and context.
elaborations: presenting a visual display with supporting text on a topic of personal interest
supporting presentations using pictures, charts and graphs
conveying information about school and community events in written and multimodal texts
creating simple descriptions in Chinese and matching them to appropriate First Nations Country/Place locations
presenting a show and tell about an object, activity or person special to them
using familiar words, phrases or idioms to create raps or songs
creating alternative endings to familiar stories
creating and performing simple imaginative texts to share with teachers and peers
creating a mini-book relating to a familiar topic

nodes.label: Using a range of sentence structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct sentences using a range of structures — including descriptive, compound and complex sentences — appropriate to the text type being created.
criteria: Produces at least three sentences using at least two different sentence structures
Applies correct writing system conventions in at least one written text
nodes.hinge_reason: Sentence structure range is the prerequisite for creating extended, coherent texts. Students who can only produce simple or formulaic sentences cannot create the informative or imaginative texts with textual conventions that this descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Produce at least three sentences in the target language using different structures (e.g. a simple statement, a sentence with a modifier, and a question or compound sentence).
width.typical: Use a range of sentence structures in created texts — simple, compound, descriptive, and question forms; use familiar words, phrases and idioms to add variety and expression; apply appropriate writing system conventions (stroke order, direction, punctuation) to written texts.
wider: Analyse a model text and identify the sentence structures used — then deliberately vary the structures in an original text to achieve different effects
Experiment with how the same information reads differently depending on sentence structure choice — compare two versions of the same content and discuss the effect of each

modes.reason: Sentence structure range requires repeated production practice across different text types before it becomes flexible and reliable. Scaffolded writing tasks with explicit structure modelling — then progressive reduction of scaffolding — build this productive fluency.

nodes.label: Creating informative texts for a purpose and audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create informative texts in spoken, written or multimodal form using appropriate textual conventions, with supporting visual elements where relevant.
criteria: Creates an informative text using at least five target language sentences with appropriate format conventions
Uses at least one supporting visual element (image, chart, or diagram) appropriately in the text

width.minimum: Create at least one informative text (display, presentation, poster, or report) using at least five target language sentences with appropriate textual conventions.
width.typical: Create informative texts — visual displays, presentations, annotated posters, digital storyboards — about topics of personal or community interest; use supporting images, charts and graphs; convey information about school, community and cultural topics; create descriptions for real-world contexts.
wider: Create an informative text for a real external audience — for example, a travel brochure, a community newsletter, or a First Nations Country/Place description — with language and format selected for that audience
Compare the language features of two different informative text types — identify how audience and purpose shape vocabulary and structure choices

modes.reason: Informative text creation requires students to understand that different purposes and audiences call for different conventions. Varied creation tasks — presentation, poster, storyboard, digital text — build this contextual awareness before students can make independent text-type choices.

nodes.label: Creating imaginative texts and performances
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create and perform imaginative texts — stories, songs, plays, dialogues — adapting familiar narratives or creating original work for a specific audience.
criteria: Creates an imaginative text with a clear structure using at least six target language phrases
Performs the text demonstrating awareness of audience — through expression, pace or delivery choices

width.minimum: Create and perform at least one imaginative text (story, song, dialogue, or play) using at least six target language phrases, with a clear structure (beginning, middle, end or equivalent).
width.typical: Create and perform imaginative texts — alternative story endings, action songs, scripted dialogues, mini-plays — adapting familiar structures with new content; use descriptive language and expression; share creative work with teachers, peers and where possible wider audiences.
wider: Create an original imaginative text — not based on a familiar story — with a deliberate structural choice and at least one creative language decision (wordplay, descriptive phrase, or cultural reference)
Reflect on a peer's imaginative text and provide targeted feedback on at least two elements — structure, language choices, or audience impact

modes.reason: Imaginative text creation integrates sentence structure range (node 1) and informative text conventions (node 2) into a creative register where personal expression is foregrounded. The teaching investment is in creating genuine performance occasions and providing structural freedom within supported parameters.

descriptors.title: Tonal features and syllable representation
descriptors.description: recognise and use the tonal features of the target language in different contexts and understand how syllables are represented
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise and distinguish tones, represent sounds in written phonetic form, and identify syllables in target language words (AC9LCH2U01). They can recite familiar rhymes and poems with attention to tone and rhythm. They have not yet used tones across different spoken contexts with developing accuracy, explained the romanisation or phonetic system as a learning tool, or investigated dialect diversity in the target language.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise and use tonal features of the target language in different contexts with developing accuracy, understand how syllables are represented in the phonetic or romanisation system, and are aware of dialect diversity in the spoken language.
elaborations: reading aloud and reciting, focusing on phrasing, stress and intonation
engaging in activities to consolidate tonal awareness using hand gestures
differentiating the 4 tones when speaking and knowing when and how to use the neutral tone
explaining the use of Pinyin as a learning tool to reflect spoken sounds
playing pair-matching card games matching Pinyin to syllables
investigating diversity in spoken Chinese and identifying differences in phonology across dialects

nodes.label: Tonal accuracy in speech
nodes.checkpoint: Students can differentiate and produce the tones of the target language with increasing accuracy in speech, including in multi-syllable words and familiar sentences.
criteria: Produces all tones with recognisable accuracy in at least five words
Demonstrates awareness of at least one tone change rule with a correct example
nodes.hinge_reason: Tonal accuracy is a prerequisite for intelligible spoken production in tonal languages. Students who cannot reliably produce the correct tone are producing words with different or no meaning — which undermines all subsequent spoken communication.

width.minimum: Produce all tones (including neutral tone where applicable) with recognisable accuracy in at least five words and demonstrate awareness of at least one tone change rule in context.
width.typical: Differentiate and produce the full tonal system in speech — including neutral tone and tone change patterns; use hand gestures or other physical cues to demonstrate tone; read aloud and recite familiar texts with attention to phrasing, stress and intonation.
wider: Record own speech and compare tonal accuracy with a model — identify specific tones that need attention and practise targeted improvement
Investigate how tonal errors change meaning in the target language — compile examples of minimal tonal pairs and discuss the communication consequences of tonal confusion

modes.reason: Tonal accuracy requires repeated production with feedback — not conceptual understanding alone. Regular reading aloud, recitation, self-recording and peer feedback activities build the muscle memory and perceptual accuracy that tone production requires.

nodes.label: The phonetic or romanisation system as a learning tool
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the purpose and use of the target language phonetic or romanisation system, and identify sounds that differ from their English equivalents.
criteria: Explains in simple terms what the phonetic or romanisation system represents
Identifies at least two sounds that differ from English equivalents and demonstrates the correct pronunciation

width.minimum: Explain in simple terms what the phonetic or romanisation system represents and identify at least two sounds that appear similar to English letters but are pronounced differently.
width.typical: Explain that the phonetic system represents spoken sounds of the target language; match phonetic representations to syllables; identify sounds that differ from English equivalents; play matching games with phonetic forms; use the phonetic system as a reading and writing support tool.
wider: Analyse a section of target language text with phonetic annotation — identify where the phonetic form is most useful as a reading support and explain why
Investigate how the phonetic system handles sounds that do not exist in English — explain what these sounds are and how a learner could approach producing them

modes.reason: Understanding the phonetic system as a tool requires students to grasp the relationship between spoken sound, phonetic representation, and character — three distinct systems. Explicit instruction on how these relate, including common confusions between phonetic letters and English sounds, prevents systematic misreading.

nodes.label: Dialect diversity in the spoken language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that the target language has dialect diversity and describe at least one example of phonological difference across dialects.
criteria: Names at least two dialects or regional varieties of the target language
Describes at least one phonological difference across dialects with an example

width.minimum: Identify at least two dialects or regional varieties of the target language and describe at least one way the spoken language differs across them.
width.typical: Investigate diversity in spoken varieties of the target language — dialects, regional accents, varieties spoken in different communities and countries; identify differences in phonology and compare with the standard form; appreciate the value of dialect diversity within the target language community.
wider: Research a specific dialect or regional variety spoken in the target language community — identify key phonological differences and where this variety is spoken

Compare the dialect spoken in the student's own family or community with the standard spoken form — identify specific differences and discuss their significance for the student's own language identity

modes.reason: Dialect awareness integrates tonal and phonological knowledge (nodes 1–2) with the broader social and cultural contexts in which the target language is spoken. The teaching investment is in creating space for students to recognise and value non-standard varieties — including those spoken at home — rather than treating them as errors.

descriptors.title: Writing system features, sentence structures and syntax
descriptors.description: recognise and use features of the target language writing system, familiar components and/or characters, a range of sentence structures and basic syntax, in familiar texts and contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students recognise how components or characters construct meaning and can use basic grammatical structures in modelled sentences (AC9LCH2U02). They can copy and produce written target language with attention to script conventions. They have not yet applied stroke order rules systematically, built compound characters from component knowledge, or used a range of sentence structures including compound and complex forms.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise and use features of the target language writing system — including character components, stroke conventions, and writing direction — and apply a range of sentence structures and basic syntactic features in familiar texts.
elaborations: using Chinese writing conventions including direction of text and punctuation
applying rules of stroke direction and stroke order when writing characters
making connections between basic characters and related component forms such as radicals
mixing and matching Chinese characters to make new meanings
categorising Chinese characters with common components and identifying connections
recognising that there are multiple ways to structure a sentence
using reduplication adjectives in sentences to describe people, animals and objects
using adverbs to modify actions
experimenting with the use of prepositions
recognising basic structures of closed and open-ended questions
elaborating ideas in sentences including details such as time, manner and place

nodes.label: Writing system conventions and character formation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply the rules of stroke direction and stroke order when writing characters or script elements, attending to details that discriminate similar forms.
criteria: Writes at least five characters or script elements with correct stroke order and direction
Demonstrates attention to at least one discriminating detail that distinguishes similar forms
nodes.hinge_reason: Writing system conventions are the prerequisite for legible written production. Students who have not internalised stroke order and direction rules produce characters that are difficult to read and cannot be extended to compound characters or complex text in subsequent years.

width.minimum: Write at least five characters or script elements with correct stroke order and direction, demonstrating attention to discriminating details.
width.typical: Apply stroke direction and order rules when writing; attend to details that discriminate similar forms; use target language writing conventions including text direction and punctuation; practise using varied materials and digital tools.
wider: Investigate pairs of characters or script elements that differ only in small details — explain what the distinguishing feature is and why precision matters
Compare the writing conventions of the target language with English — create a guide for someone learning the target language writing system for the first time

modes.reason: Stroke order and direction require repeated, attentive practice — not occasional copying. Regular short writing practice with attention to convention builds the motor memory that allows students to write with fluency and accuracy in text creation tasks.

nodes.label: Component analysis and word building
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify components or morphemes in target language characters or words and use component knowledge to build or analyse new words.
criteria: Identifies components of at least three compound characters or words
Explains how at least one component contributes to the meaning or sound of the character or word

width.minimum: Identify the components of at least three compound characters or words and explain how each component contributes to meaning or sound.
width.typical: Identify and categorise characters or words by shared components; make connections between component forms and related meanings; mix and match known components to build new words; infer meaning of new words from known components; use digital tools to explore character structure.
wider: Investigate the six types of character formation (or equivalent morphological patterns in the target language) and identify examples of each — explain the logic behind each formation type
Use component knowledge to make an educated guess about the meaning of an unfamiliar character or word — then verify using a dictionary and discuss accuracy of the prediction

modes.reason: Component analysis requires students to apply a systematic framework to word/character structure — not just memorise individual items. Explicit instruction on component types and their semantic or phonetic roles builds the analytical capacity that supports vocabulary extension.

nodes.label: Sentence structure range and syntactic features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and use a range of sentence structures and syntactic features — including multiple sentence types, modifiers, adverbs, prepositions and elaboration patterns — in familiar texts.
criteria: Produces at least four sentences demonstrating at least three different syntactic features
Uses at least one elaboration pattern (time, manner, or place detail) correctly in a sentence

width.minimum: Produce at least four sentences demonstrating at least three different syntactic features (e.g. a sentence with a time expression, a sentence with a location preposition, a question, and a compound sentence).
width.typical: Recognise and use multiple sentence types — statements, questions (closed and open), compound sentences; use adverbs, location prepositions, reduplication adjectives, and time/manner/place elaboration patterns; apply these structures in reading and writing familiar texts.
wider: Analyse a model text and annotate each sentence to show the syntactic features used — then write an equivalent text using the same structure repertoire

Compare specific syntactic features (e.g. how time expressions or location prepositions work) across the target language and English — identify where they behave similarly and where they require different approaches

modes.reason: Sentence structure range integrates writing system knowledge (node 1) and component/word-building understanding (node 2) into a full grammatical competence for text creation. The teaching investment is in explicit modelling of each structure type followed by varied production tasks across different text contexts.

descriptors.title: Compare features of target language and English texts
descriptors.description: recognise and compare features of familiar spoken and written text in the target language and English
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare structural features, vocabulary and text features across the target language and English using simple metalanguage (AC9LCH2U03). They have used metalanguage for basic word types. They have not yet compared texts systematically by genre or feature type, used metalanguage to describe grammar rules, or analysed how English influences everyday target language use.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise and compare features of familiar spoken and written texts in the target language and English — including genre features, grammatical conventions, layout, and cross-linguistic influence — using metalanguage.
elaborations: using metalanguage to describe grammar rules
recognising language features and symbols typically associated with particular text types
identifying and comparing key words in target language and English versions of favourite stories
identifying and documenting similarities and differences in elements such as titles, layout, images and script of target language and English texts
exploring the influence of English on informal language used in daily interactions by target language speakers
recognising features of various genres and identifying which genres are most suitable for different purposes

nodes.label: Genre features and text purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify features of different text genres in the target language and English, and discuss what makes each genre appropriate for its purpose.
criteria: Identifies at least two text genres in the target language with at least two distinguishing features each
Can explain which genre would be most appropriate for a given purpose and why
nodes.hinge_reason: Genre feature knowledge is the prerequisite for all text comparison work. Students who cannot identify genre-level features cannot compare texts systematically — they can only notice surface differences. Genre awareness also underpins all text creation in the creating strand.

width.minimum: Identify at least two different text genres in the target language (e.g. narrative, procedural, informative) and describe at least two features that distinguish each genre.
width.typical: Recognise features of narratives, procedural and explanatory texts; identify language features and symbols associated with different text types; compare the features of the same genre across target language and English texts; discuss which genres suit different purposes and audiences.
wider: Compare the same genre text in target language and English — identify all the structural and language feature differences and discuss what they reveal about how the genre convention differs across the two languages
Create a short genre comparison guide for a peer — explaining how to recognise a particular genre in both languages and what conventions must be followed

modes.reason: Genre analysis requires students to apply a framework — what are the features of this genre? — to both familiar and new texts. Explicit genre study with named features (orientation, complication, resolution; materials, steps, result) builds the analytical vocabulary before students can compare independently.

nodes.label: Metalanguage for grammar comparison
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use metalanguage to describe grammar rules in the target language and compare grammatical conventions across the target language and English.
criteria: Uses at least four metalanguage terms correctly in a grammar description or comparison
Explains at least one grammatical rule in the target language using metalanguage

width.minimum: Use at least four metalanguage terms correctly in describing a grammar rule or comparison between the target language and English.
width.typical: Use metalanguage to describe placement rules, word class functions and sentence-level patterns in the target language; compare grammatical conventions with English; identify where similar terms describe different grammatical functions across the two languages.
wider: Annotate a short target language text using metalanguage labels — then compare the annotation with an equivalent English text annotation and identify structural differences
Investigate a grammatical feature that is named differently or functions differently in the target language metalanguage versus English metalanguage — explain the difference to a peer

modes.reason: Metalanguage for grammar is built through repeated use across different comparison tasks — not through a single lesson on terminology. Students need to encounter and deploy metalanguage across multiple text analysis and comparison contexts before it becomes functional vocabulary.

nodes.label: Cross-linguistic influence and text features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify examples of cross-linguistic influence in everyday target language use and compare layout, script and textual features across target language and English texts.
criteria: Identifies at least two examples of English influence on everyday target language use
Identifies at least two textual feature differences between a target language and English text of the same type

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples of English influence on everyday target language use and at least two textual feature differences between a target language and English text.
width.typical: Explore how English influences informal everyday target language use — borrowed words, code-switching, adapted expressions; compare layout, heading, script and organisational features of target language and English texts; identify similarities and differences in how the same information is organised across text types.
wider: Research the history of a specific borrowed word or expression — trace where it came from and how it entered everyday target language use
Create a bilingual comparison display showing how the same text type is structured differently in target language and English — annotate the key differences

modes.reason: Cross-linguistic influence and textual feature comparison integrates genre awareness (node 1) and grammar metalanguage (node 2) into a full text-level analysis. The teaching investment is in making visible what students often see as normal — the way English has entered everyday target language, and the distinct textual conventions of each language.

descriptors.title: Connections between language and cultural practices
descriptors.description: identify connections between target language and cultural practices
descriptors.knowledge: Students notice that people use language in ways that reflect cultural practices, and can identify cultural symbols and connect language to personal identity (AC9LCH2U04). They have explored how language reflects values and community belonging. They have not yet systematically identified how feelings, beliefs and values are embedded in specific language choices, or examined cultural identity across community and national levels.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify connections between the target language and cultural practices — including how language encodes cultural values, beliefs and identity, the role of music, ceremony and arts in cultural expression, and how cultural identity is visible in everyday language choices.
elaborations: understanding that feelings, beliefs and values can be reflected in language
