descriptors.knowledge: Students can create and present a range of informative and imaginative texts using sentence structures and textual conventions (AC9LCH4C05). They can perform and present to real audiences. They have not yet deliberately adapted texts for different purposes and audiences, used complex sentence structures to sequence information cohesively, or produced community-facing content for external audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and present informative and imaginative texts appropriate to purpose and audience, using a range of sentence structures to sequence and develop information and ideas with textual coherence.
elaborations: working in teams to prepare a presentation supported by digital media
creating displays using graphics, photographs and illustrations to document and convey ideas
preparing and creating a video clip to share with peers overseas introducing aspects of local culture
creating a print or digital advertisement or brochure in Chinese for travel to a First Nations Country/Place location
explaining a procedure or practice to others, for example, community recycling, a recipe or eating etiquette
role-playing a modified well-known children's story
producing and performing short scripted plays, experimenting with descriptive language
composing and participating in imagined interactions with characters from familiar texts
writing a letter or creating a video for their future self
creating texts for a range of audiences and purposes for school or community newsletters

nodes.label: Sequencing and cohesion in extended texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sequence information and ideas in extended texts using cohesive devices — connectives, discourse markers, time expressions — to create coherent and fluent written or spoken texts.
criteria: Produces a text of at least eight sentences using at least three cohesive devices
The text has clear logical or temporal sequencing that can be followed by a reader
nodes.hinge_reason: Cohesion and sequencing are the prerequisites for extended text production. Students who can only produce isolated sentences cannot create the informative or imaginative texts with developed ideas that this descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Produce a text of at least eight target language sentences using at least three different cohesive devices to connect ideas.
width.typical: Use a range of cohesive devices — sequence words, conjunctions, temporal and logical connectives — to organise and sequence information across a text; build more complex messages using joining words and sequence markers; apply appropriate punctuation for text-level coherence.
wider: Analyse the cohesive devices used in a model text and then reproduce the same organisational pattern with original content — compare the effect of the pattern with and without cohesive devices
Compare how cohesion is achieved in the target language with English — identify where the devices are similar (equivalent connectives) and where the languages handle sequencing differently

modes.reason: Cohesive device use requires repeated practice across text types before it becomes reliable. Explicit modelling followed by scaffolded production — with progressive removal of structural support — builds the fluency that produces cohesive extended texts.

nodes.label: Adapting texts for purpose and audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adapt language register, content and format deliberately to suit a specific purpose and audience when creating a text.
criteria: Creates a text with at least two deliberate language or format adaptations appropriate to purpose or audience
Can explain the choices made and why they suit the specified audience

width.minimum: Create a text with at least two deliberate adaptations for a specific purpose or audience — for example, formal language for an adult audience, simplified language for younger students, or persuasive language for a campaign.
width.typical: Create informative and imaginative texts adapted for different purposes and audiences — community newsletters, travel brochures, procedures, advertisements, stories; select vocabulary, register and format appropriate to the audience; support content with visual elements where appropriate.
wider: Create the same content in two different formats for two different audiences — compare the language and format choices made and explain how each serves its intended audience

Research and adopt the conventions of a specific real-world text type (e.g. a formal report, a digital advertisement) in the target language and produce a text that authentically follows those conventions

modes.reason: Audience and purpose adaptation requires students to make deliberate, reasoned language choices — not default to familiar patterns. Explicit audience analysis before drafting — who is this for? what do they need? — builds the planning capacity that underlies purposeful text creation.

nodes.label: Creating and performing imaginative texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create and perform imaginative texts — plays, stories, scripts, poems — that demonstrate language choice, structural creativity and personal voice.
criteria: Creates an imaginative text demonstrating at least one creative language choice and at least one deliberate structural decision
Performs or presents the text demonstrating awareness of audience through delivery

width.minimum: Create and perform an imaginative text demonstrating at least one creative language choice (figurative language, wordplay, structural variation, or descriptive language) and at least one deliberate structural decision.
width.typical: Create and perform imaginative texts — scripted plays, stories, modified folk tales, imagined interactions, letters to future self — using descriptive language, experimenting with structure, and demonstrating personal voice; share creative work with appropriate audiences.
wider: Create an original imaginative text in the target language with a deliberate creative vision — explain the structural and language choices made and how they serve the creative purpose
Write for a future reader — for example, a letter to themselves at graduation — using appropriate language and structure for the purpose, then compare with a peer's version

modes.reason: Imaginative text creation integrates cohesion skills (node 1) and audience-aware adaptation (node 2) in a creative register where personal expression is the primary purpose. The teaching investment is in creating genuine creative freedom within structural parameters — students decide what to express, the framework helps them shape it.

descriptors.title: Tone, intonation and stress to express feelings and opinions
descriptors.description: use tone-syllables, intonation, stress and phrasing to express feelings and opinions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can produce tones with developing accuracy and explain the phonetic system as a learning tool (AC9LCH4U01). They can recite texts with attention to tone and rhythm. They have not yet deliberately used tonal variation, intonation and stress to convey emotional register and opinion, or used digital tools to monitor and develop spoken fluency.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use tone-syllables, intonation, stress and phrasing deliberately to express feelings, opinions and emotional register in spoken target language, with developing fluency.
elaborations: reading the lyrics of Chinese pop songs, modelled texts, tongue twisters, poems and news aloud with attention to tones and pronunciation
using digital tools to check the correct pronunciation of Chinese and using voice-recording apps to check own tone and intonation
recognising syllable changes in speech, including change of tonal value
recognising how tone marks affect pronunciation and meaning
playing speaking games to demonstrate different emotions using features of pronunciation
understanding that Chinese has different regional accents spoken by people in different provinces and communities

nodes.label: Intonation and stress for emotional register
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deliberately vary intonation, stress and phrasing to convey different emotional registers — happiness, sadness, concern, emphasis — in the target language.
criteria: Reads or speaks the same sentence with at least two different emotional registers, demonstrating distinguishable intonation or stress changes
Can identify and explain what tonal or intonation feature creates the different emotional effect
nodes.hinge_reason: Deliberate use of intonation and stress is the prerequisite for expressive spoken production. Students who produce target language at a flat, uniform pitch cannot convey emotional register or opinion in speech — which undermines the authenticity and communicative effectiveness of all spoken interaction.

width.minimum: Read or say the same sentence with at least two different emotional registers, demonstrating how intonation and stress change to convey each.
width.typical: Use intonation, stress and phrasing to express different emotions and registers; read lyrics, poems, news and familiar texts aloud with attention to tonal and intonation patterns; explore how the same words with different intonation convey different meanings; play speaking games demonstrating different emotions.
wider: Investigate how intonation patterns in statements, questions and exclamations differ in the target language from English — identify where the patterns are similar and where they diverge
Compare how the same emotional register (e.g. urgency, enthusiasm, concern) is conveyed through intonation differently across the target language and English

modes.reason: Intonation and stress control requires repeated oral production practice with feedback. Regular reading aloud, performance tasks and self-recording activities build the expressive fluency that deliberate intonation control requires.

nodes.label: Tone change patterns and phrasing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and apply tone change patterns in the target language and use phrasing — pausing, grouping, rhythm — to support fluent and expressive spoken production.
criteria: Identifies at least one tone change pattern and demonstrates correct application in at least three examples
Uses phrasing and grouping to support comprehension in at least one spoken text

width.minimum: Identify at least one tone change pattern in the target language (e.g. where a standard tone changes in a specific phonological context) and demonstrate correct application in at least three examples.
width.typical: Recognise and apply tone change patterns; use phrasing — grouping words, pausing at appropriate points — to support fluency and intelligibility; understand how tone marks affect pronunciation and meaning; use context to distinguish between homophones or tonal minimal pairs.
wider: Analyse a spoken text for phrasing patterns — identify where the speaker pauses, groups words, and varies stress, and explain how these choices support comprehension
Investigate tone sandhi or tone change rules in the target language — compile examples and explain the phonological context for each change

modes.reason: Tone change patterns require explicit instruction — they are not intuitive and background learners who know spoken language may not have analysed these patterns. Systematic explanation of phonological contexts for tone change, followed by targeted practice, prevents persistent errors.

nodes.label: Using digital tools for fluency development
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use digital tools — recording apps, pronunciation checkers, digital texts — to monitor and develop their own spoken fluency.
criteria: Uses a digital tool to record and review at least one spoken production
Identifies at least one specific fluency target from the review and demonstrates a practice attempt

width.minimum: Use a digital tool to record and review at least one spoken production, identifying at least one specific feature to improve and practising improvement.
width.typical: Use digital tools to check pronunciation and tonal accuracy; record own speech and compare with models; use voice-recording apps and online resources to develop fluency; check pronunciation of target language words using digital dictionaries or reference tools.
wider: Conduct a systematic self-review of a recorded spoken performance — identify specific tonal, intonation or fluency targets, practise, re-record, and compare the two versions
Use digital tools to investigate regional accent variation in the target language — compare recordings from different communities and identify phonological differences

modes.reason: Digital tool use for fluency development integrates intonation awareness (node 1) and tone change knowledge (node 2) into a self-directed improvement cycle. The teaching investment is in establishing a sustainable self-review practice — not a one-off recording task but a regular cycle of production, review and improvement.

descriptors.title: Writing system and grammar for familiar and unfamiliar texts
descriptors.description: identify and use components and/or characters, sentence structures, syntax and writing system features to compose and respond to familiar and some unfamiliar texts and contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply writing system conventions and use a range of sentence structures and syntactic features in familiar texts (AC9LCH4U02). They can analyse character components and build compound words. They have not yet applied character knowledge to infer meaning in unfamiliar words, used complex grammatical structures such as complex clauses, aspect markers, and comparative constructions, or composed extended texts applying these features across unfamiliar contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify and use components, characters, sentence structures and writing system features to compose and respond to familiar and some unfamiliar texts — including using morphological knowledge to infer meaning and applying complex grammatical structures.
elaborations: analysing common simple and compound characters through multiple examples and identifying placement of radicals
using digital tools to write a specific character and obtain pronunciation using online dictionaries
developing understanding of types of Chinese characters such as pictographs and phono-semantic characters
inferring meaning of unfamiliar words from known morphemes
using appropriate punctuation in writing
exploring and building more complex messages using joining words, conjunction words and sequence words
discriminating between contextual meanings of characters with multiple meanings
using the function of words and structures in language to indicate completion of action
understanding different applications of grammatical rules in spoken and written language
exploring ways to express similarities and comparatives

nodes.label: Inferring meaning from morphological knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use knowledge of character components or morphemes to infer the meaning of unfamiliar words in context.
criteria: Correctly infers the meaning of at least three unfamiliar words using component or morphological knowledge
Can explain the reasoning used for at least two of the inferences
nodes.hinge_reason: Morphological inference is the prerequisite for independent reading of unfamiliar texts. Students who can only read known words cannot approach new texts strategically — and cannot meet the 'some unfamiliar contexts' demand of this descriptor.

width.minimum: Infer the meaning of at least three unfamiliar words using component or morphological knowledge, and explain the reasoning.
width.typical: Analyse common simple and compound characters through multiple examples; use digital tools to explore pronunciation and meaning of unfamiliar characters; infer meaning of unfamiliar words from known morphemes; identify the six types of character formation or equivalent morphological patterns.
wider: Apply morphological inference strategies to a text containing multiple unfamiliar words — document each inference, verify using a dictionary, and evaluate accuracy across the set
Investigate a semantic field (e.g. all characters/words related to water, plants, or communication) and identify the morphological patterns that link them

modes.reason: Morphological inference requires systematic application of component knowledge — students need a framework for analysing unfamiliar words (What components do I recognise? What semantic or phonetic pattern applies?) before they can infer reliably. Explicit strategy instruction followed by guided practice builds this capacity.

nodes.label: Complex grammatical structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and use more complex grammatical structures — including aspect markers, comparative constructions, conjunctions and compound-complex sentences — in familiar and some unfamiliar contexts.
criteria: Produces at least three sentences using different complex grammatical structures correctly
Applies appropriate punctuation in a piece of extended writing

width.minimum: Produce at least three sentences using different complex grammatical structures (e.g. aspect marker, comparative, conjunction pair) correctly in context.
width.typical: Use aspect markers to indicate completion or ongoing action; use comparative and superlative constructions; apply conjunction pairs to build complex sentences; use appropriate punctuation throughout; discriminate between contextual meanings of polysemous words; understand grammatical rules that apply differently in spoken and written registers.
wider: Analyse the grammatical structures in a model text and identify every complex structure used — then produce an equivalent text using the same grammatical repertoire in a different context
Compare how the same grammatical function (e.g. expressing completion, comparison, or conditionality) is handled differently in the target language and English

modes.reason: Complex grammatical structures require repeated production practice for accuracy and automaticity. Students need to produce these structures across varied sentence contexts — not only in grammar exercises — before they become reliable in extended text composition.

nodes.label: Composing extended texts in unfamiliar contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compose and respond to extended texts in familiar and some unfamiliar contexts, applying full writing system and grammatical knowledge.
criteria: Composes an extended text of at least 10 sentences applying writing system conventions throughout
Uses at least three different grammatical structures correctly across the text

width.minimum: Compose an extended text (at least 10 sentences) on a familiar or moderately unfamiliar topic, applying writing system conventions and at least three different grammatical structures.
width.typical: Compose and respond to texts across familiar and some unfamiliar contexts; apply full writing system knowledge including direction, punctuation and character conventions; use the full grammatical repertoire available; approach unfamiliar topics using known vocabulary and inference strategies.
wider: Compose a text on a genuinely unfamiliar topic using inference and contextual strategies — document the strategies used and evaluate their effectiveness
Create a text that deliberately experiments with register — formally written versus colloquially written — comparing the grammatical and lexical choices in each version

modes.reason: Extended text composition integrates morphological inference (node 1) and complex grammatical structure knowledge (node 2) into full productive engagement with unfamiliar text contexts. The teaching investment is in creating text composition tasks with genuine unfamiliar territory — topics or formats students haven't composed in before.

descriptors.title: Compare target language and English structures using metalanguage
descriptors.description: compare some target language structures and features with those of English, using some familiar metalanguage
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare text features, genre conventions and grammar patterns across target language and English using metalanguage (AC9LCH4U03). They can analyse cross-linguistic influence. They have not yet compared grammatical features systematically across different text types — active/passive voice, tense encoding, text cohesion, comparatives — or used metalanguage for text-level and grammatical analysis across multiple categories.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare structures and features of the target language and English across text types and grammatical categories, using metalanguage — including text organisation, grammar rules, voice, tense encoding, and cohesive devices.
elaborations: discussing aspects of grammar using metalanguage in Chinese or English
identifying and comparing language features of different text types in Chinese and English
comparing the use of passive voice and active voice in Chinese and English
comparing structural features of familiar personal, informative and imaginative texts
comparing different types of texts such as recipes, songs, stories and recounts
creating comparative lists of vocabulary used in different contexts
understanding how to create textual cohesion using adverbs of sequence and conjunctions
recognising grammatical features and how their use differs in Chinese and English
comparing the use of tenses in Chinese and English

nodes.label: Comparing grammatical features across languages
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare specific grammatical features across the target language and English — including voice, tense encoding, comparative structures, and adjectival functions — using metalanguage.
criteria: Compares at least two grammatical features across target language and English using metalanguage
Explains for each feature where the two languages work similarly and where they differ
nodes.hinge_reason: Grammatical comparison using metalanguage is the prerequisite for all analytical text work at this level. Students who cannot describe grammatical differences using metalanguage cannot analyse texts, explain language choices, or support their own writing decisions with linguistic reasoning.

width.minimum: Compare at least two grammatical features across the target language and English using metalanguage, explaining where the features work similarly and where they differ.
width.typical: Compare passive and active voice across target language and English; compare tense encoding (conjugation versus time expressions); compare comparative and superlative structures; explore adjectival verb constructions; use metalanguage from both languages to describe grammatical rules.
wider: Investigate a grammatical feature that exists in the target language but not in English (or vice versa) — explain what communicative function it serves and how the other language handles the same communicative need
Create a bilingual grammar comparison resource — explaining a specific grammatical contrast to a student learning one of the two languages

modes.reason: Grammatical comparison requires students to hold two systems in mind simultaneously and reason about structural differences. Explicit comparison frames and systematic category-by-category analysis build the analytical capacity before students can compare independently.

nodes.label: Comparing text types and cohesive conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare structural features, language conventions and cohesive devices across text types in the target language and English.
criteria: Identifies at least three structural or cohesive differences between the same text type in target language and English
Can explain how at least one cohesive device functions differently across the two languages

width.minimum: Compare the structural features of the same text type (e.g. a narrative, a procedure, a recount) in target language and English, identifying at least three differences.
width.typical: Compare features of different text types across target language and English — descriptive language in narratives, persuasive language in advertisements, procedural structure; compare audience and purpose conventions; explore how cohesive devices function differently across the two languages.
wider: Analyse the cohesive devices used in a target language text and compare with an equivalent English text — identify where the cohesion strategy is similar and where it requires a different approach
Compare how imperatives function in instruction texts across target language and English — identify differences in directness, politeness marking, and structural conventions

modes.reason: Text type comparison across languages requires encounter with varied text types — students who have only compared narratives cannot generalise their comparative strategies to procedures, recounts or persuasive texts. Varied text type comparison builds flexible analytical capacity.

nodes.label: Creating comparative analyses using metalanguage
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce a structured language comparison — written or presented — using metalanguage to explain patterns of similarity and difference across the target language and English.
criteria: Produces a comparison of at least two language features using metalanguage with examples from both languages
The comparison is accurate and clearly organised for a reader

width.minimum: Produce a structured comparison of at least two language features using metalanguage, with examples from both languages.
width.typical: Create comparative vocabulary lists, annotated text analyses, or structured presentations comparing language features; use metalanguage from both languages; discuss how language features across the two systems reflect different ways of organising meaning.
wider: Create a structured metalinguistic analysis of a target language text — annotate every grammatical and textual feature using metalanguage, then compare with an English equivalent annotation
Present a language comparison to peers as an explanation task — requiring the student to make the analysis accessible and accurate for an audience who may not know both languages

modes.reason: Producing a comparative analysis integrates grammatical comparison (node 1) and text type awareness (node 2) into a full metalinguistic task. The teaching investment is in creating genuine comparison contexts — real texts, real linguistic questions — that make the analysis meaningful rather than mechanical.

descriptors.title: Language reflects cultural practices, values and identity
descriptors.description: recognise that language reflects cultural practices, values and identity, and that this impacts on non-verbal and spoken communication
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify connections between the target language and cultural practices, and understand how language encodes values and identity (AC9LCH4U04). They can examine music, arts and cultural expression. They have not yet analysed how language variation across regional and community contexts encodes cultural identity, examined the impact of cultural language values on miscommunication, or reflected on their own intercultural positioning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise that language reflects cultural practices, values and identity — including how this shapes non-verbal and spoken communication, creates intercultural miscommunication, and connects to students' own experience as participants in two or more language communities.
elaborations: discussing language choices expected or required in diverse contexts across languages
recognising the interconnections between cultural practices and language use
noticing that language varies between regions
exploring in Chinese and English how language and culture are expressed through First Nations Australians' song, dance or artworks
identifying ways in which Chinese language and culture influence the lives of Australians
engaging with Chinese peers in diverse contexts and exploring strategies to overcome miscommunication
noticing and reflecting on how interacting in Chinese may feel different from interacting in English

nodes.label: Language choices and cultural values in communication
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how specific language choices in spoken and non-verbal communication reflect cultural practices and values, and explain the impact on interaction.
criteria: Identifies at least two examples of language choices reflecting cultural values
Explains the impact of at least one such choice on an interaction
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that language choices reflect cultural values is the conceptual prerequisite for all intercultural communication awareness. Students who cannot see the cultural logic behind language choices cannot identify miscommunication risks or develop the intercultural competence that this descriptor targets.

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples of how language choices in the target language (verbal or non-verbal) reflect specific cultural values, and explain the impact on an interaction.
width.typical: Examine how language choices across contexts — address forms, politeness conventions, topic selection, non-verbal behaviour — reflect cultural values; discuss how the same interaction would be managed differently across cultural contexts; identify the interconnections between cultural practices and language use.
wider: Analyse a recorded or simulated intercultural interaction — identify the specific moments where cultural language values are visible and discuss how each shapes the interaction

Compare how a specific cultural value (e.g. respect for elders, directness, hospitality) is encoded in language and non-verbal behaviour differently in the target language community versus Australian English-speaking contexts

modes.reason: Cultural value encoding in language requires explicit analytical scaffolding — students need to move from observing a language choice to explaining the cultural logic behind it. Guided analysis with cultural context information builds this explanatory capacity before students can reason independently.

nodes.label: Regional and community variation in language and culture
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how language varies across regions and communities within the target language world, and discuss what this variation reveals about cultural identity.
criteria: Identifies at least two regional or community language variations in the target language
Explains what at least one variation reveals about cultural identity or context

width.minimum: Identify at least two regional or community language variations in the target language and explain what each reveals about identity or cultural context.
width.typical: Notice regional variation in language — dialects, community-specific vocabulary, language contact effects; identify culturally-specific additions that mark belonging to a region or community; explore how target language communities in Australia and overseas differ in their language practices.
wider: Research language variation in a specific target language region or diaspora community — identify specific language features that mark membership and discuss what they reveal about that community's history and identity

Compare how the target language is used in the local community with how it is used in a different regional or national community — identify specific differences and discuss what they reveal about cultural diversity within the target language world

modes.reason: Regional and community language variation is understood through exposure to varied examples. Students who have only encountered one variety of the target language will treat it as monolithic. Varied community encounters — including diaspora varieties, regional dialects, and community-specific practices — build the pluralistic understanding the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Intercultural positioning and personal reflection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on their own experience of navigating between two or more language-culture communities, and identify how this shapes their communication and identity.
criteria: Reflects on at least one experience of navigating between two cultural-language contexts
Identifies at least one cultural value or communication difference that shaped that experience

width.minimum: Reflect on at least one specific experience of navigating between two cultural-language contexts — identifying what felt different, what caused difficulty, or what new perspective emerged.
width.typical: Reflect on how interacting in the target language feels different from interacting in English; identify culturally-specific behaviours and communication styles; explore how students' multilingual experience shapes their perspective on cultural difference; discuss miscommunication experiences and what caused them.
wider: Describe a specific intercultural communication experience in depth — identifying the cultural values at play, what was assumed, what caused misunderstanding, and what was learned
Compare own intercultural navigation experience with that of a peer or community member — identify what is shared and what is specific to the student's own language history and community

modes.reason: Intercultural reflection integrates cultural value analysis (node 1) and community variation awareness (node 2) into a personally grounded synthesis. The teaching investment is in creating a reflective, non-judgmental environment where students can examine their own intercultural experiences honestly — including moments of discomfort or misalignment.

descriptors.title: Initiate and sustain exchanges in familiar contexts
descriptors.description: initiate and sustain modelled exchanges in familiar contexts related to students' personal worlds and school environment
descriptors.knowledge: Students can initiate exchanges and respond to modelled questions about self, others and classroom environment (AC9LS4C01). They use formulaic expressions and modelled structures. They have not yet sustained exchanges beyond information exchange — including expressing feelings, opinions, preferences and using conversational maintenance strategies.
descriptors.endpoint: Students initiate and sustain modelled exchanges in familiar contexts — including sharing personal information, expressing feelings and opinions, and using strategies to maintain conversational flow.
elaborations: selecting forms of address and greetings appropriate to the time of day, relationship and context
sharing personal information about routines and tasks, hopes and dreams
thanking, inviting or congratulating one another using formulaic language
expressing feelings and emotions about experiences
apologising and expressing concern or sympathy to friends and family members
expressing preferences and opinions
showing reactions, understanding and interest by using strategies such as asking follow-up questions and using conversation fillers

nodes.label: Expressing feelings, emotions and opinions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express feelings, emotions, preferences and opinions in the target language — going beyond information exchange to personal response.
criteria: Expresses at least two different feelings or emotions using correct target language structures
Expresses at least one preference or opinion with a supporting reason or elaboration
nodes.hinge_reason: Moving beyond information exchange to expressing feelings and opinions is the developmental leap between 3-4 and 5-6. Students who can only exchange factual information cannot sustain exchanges about personal worlds and cannot reach the opinion and negotiation demands of subsequent standards.

width.minimum: Express at least two feelings or emotions and at least one preference or opinion using appropriate target language structures.
width.typical: Express feelings and emotions about experiences; express preferences and opinions with supporting reasons; apologise and express concern or sympathy; use appropriate register for formal and informal contexts; share personal information about hopes and future plans.
wider: Express a nuanced emotional response — not only a simple feeling but an explanation of why, connected to a specific experience
Compare how opinions and preferences are expressed differently in the target language and English — identify where the target language requires more explicit grammatical marking

modes.reason: Expressing feelings and opinions requires a bank of structures across emotional and evaluative domains. Students need varied practice expressing feelings about different experiences before this vocabulary becomes spontaneously available.

nodes.label: Sustaining exchanges using conversational strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sustain a modelled exchange using conversational strategies — showing interest, asking follow-up questions and using fillers and reaction expressions.
criteria: Sustains an exchange for at least four turns using at least two conversational strategies
Uses at least one reaction expression or filler that shows genuine response to a partner's contribution

width.minimum: Sustain an exchange for at least four turns using at least two different conversational strategies.
width.typical: Use conversational maintenance strategies — asking follow-up questions, using fillers and acknowledgement expressions, showing reactions; sustain exchanges using modelled conversation patterns; use target language for expressing agreement, disagreement and interest.
wider: Sustain an exchange on an unexpected topic — using maintenance strategies to keep the conversation going without preparation
Analyse a recorded exchange and identify every maintenance strategy used — categorise by type and evaluate which were most effective

modes.reason: Conversational sustainability develops through varied partner and topic conditions. Maintenance strategies need to transfer across varied topics and partners before they become genuinely available conversational tools.

descriptors.title: Plan and negotiate with others
descriptors.description: participate in activities that involve planning and negotiating with others, using language that expresses information, preferences and ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students can participate in collaborative planning activities using familiar phrases and modelled structures (AC9LS4C02). They allocate tasks and follow sequences. They have not yet used language to express and negotiate preferences and ideas — only to coordinate task allocation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students participate in planning and negotiation activities that require expressing preferences and ideas, checking understanding, delegating and managing decisions in the target language.
elaborations: participating in an activity for an assembly, school or class event or performance, and creating promotional materials
working with others to create resources for the school community
checking on understanding and progress during learning tasks
delegating roles and tasks with peers to plan for and participate in an event
developing a range of interview questions to ask a real or imagined target language community guest
participating in real or imagined transactions involving negotiation, requesting information and considering options
creating digital displays, presentations or performances to showcase progress in the target language
demonstrating numeracy and decision-making skills by agreeing with a partner about how to spend a set budget
working in a team to solve a puzzle or problem using target language clues

nodes.label: Expressing preferences and ideas in planning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express preferences and ideas in collaborative planning contexts — contributing personal views and negotiating with others about options and decisions.
criteria: Expresses at least two preferences or ideas in a collaborative planning task
Responds to a partner's contribution — building on, questioning or negotiating rather than simply accepting
nodes.hinge_reason: Expressing preferences in collaborative contexts — contributing personal views not only allocating tasks — is what distinguishes planning from coordination. Students who cannot negotiate preferences cannot engage with the opinion-exchange demands that continue through subsequent bands.

width.minimum: Express at least two preferences or ideas in a planning activity and respond to at least one partner's preference or idea.
width.typical: Express and negotiate preferences across planning contexts; check understanding and progress during tasks; delegate roles and tasks; develop questions for guests or interviews; promote participation in events using target language.
wider: Lead a planning negotiation — ensure all group members contribute a preference and that the final decision reflects genuine compromise
Conduct a simulated transaction involving genuine negotiation over options and decisions

modes.reason: Preference expression in planning requires students to move from describing tasks to advocating for options. Structured planning tasks with open decision points scaffold this move.

nodes.label: Problem-solving and decision-making in collaborative tasks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in planning tasks that involve decision-making with constraints — budgets, quantities, priorities — using target language to justify choices and reach agreement.
criteria: Participates in a decision-making task expressing at least two justified choices in the target language
Contributes to a shared outcome that reflects the group's negotiated decisions

width.minimum: Participate in a decision-making task using the target language — expressing at least two justified choices and contributing to a shared outcome.
width.typical: Apply decision-making skills in collaborative planning — agree on options within constraints, justify choices, express preferences; work in teams to solve problems using target language; create promotional materials for events; plan for real audiences.
wider: Design and run a simulated transaction scenario — buying, selling, negotiating and justifying decisions with a real partner
Create a complete plan specifying who, what, when, where and how — with a justification for each decision in the target language

modes.reason: Decision-making in collaborative contexts integrates preference expression (N1) with constraint management and shared outcome production. Real-stakes tasks make the integration condition authentic.

descriptors.title: Locate, process and respond to information in texts
descriptors.description: locate and process information and ideas in a range of spoken, written and multimodal texts, and respond in different ways to suit purpose
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate and respond to key information in familiar texts and categorise it using graphic organisers (AC9LS4C03). They extract information from prepared texts. They have not yet researched independently across multiple sources, processed information for specific purposes, or compared ideas across imaginative texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students locate and process information and ideas in a range of spoken, written and multimodal target language texts, and respond in ways suited to the purpose — including research, comparison, creative response and procedural tasks.
elaborations: researching topics of interest using a range of sources and organising and sharing information in print or digital format
listening to, reading and viewing authentic texts and extracting key points relating to aspects of life in target language communities
comparing main characters, events and ideas in different types of imaginative texts
listening to or viewing First Nations Australian authors' stories in English and responding using words and modelled sentences in the target language
adapting an informative or imaginative text by resequencing events, adding a new element, or creating an alternative ending
discussing key messages and cultural elements in creative texts
responding to artworks and images from target language communities
playing interpretation games with peers involving non-verbal cues
listening to a simple procedure and extracting keywords to complete a task
reading texts about destinations or conditions and making decisions as a group

nodes.label: Researching and processing information across sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can research topics of interest across multiple target language sources, extracting and organising information for a specified purpose.
criteria: Locates and extracts information from at least two sources without direct teacher prompting
Organises information in a format appropriate to the research purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Independent multi-source research is the prerequisite for the evaluation and synthesis demands of subsequent bands. Students who can only process teacher-prepared texts cannot develop source evaluation and synthesis skills.

width.minimum: Research a topic using at least two sources and organise key information in an appropriate format.
width.typical: Research topics across varied source types — print, digital, spoken, multimodal; extract key points about life in target language communities; answer questions about researched content; extract procedural language; use graphic organisers suited to purpose; read texts about real-world situations to inform decisions.
wider: Research a topic across target language and English sources — compare what each includes and excludes, and explain what each perspective adds
Evaluate two target language sources on the same topic for reliability — identify which is more credible and explain why

modes.reason: Research skills develop through varied source types and topic conditions. Each new source type builds a new strategy — varied conditions build transferable research capacity.

nodes.label: Responding to texts with personal reactions and comparisons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can respond to target language texts in varied ways — expressing personal reactions, opinions and comparisons about characters, ideas and cultural elements.
criteria: Expresses a personal reaction to a text using evaluative language
Produces at least one comparison across two texts, characters or ideas

width.minimum: Express a personal reaction to at least one text using target language evaluative language; produce at least one comparison across two texts or characters.
width.typical: Compare main characters, events and ideas across texts; discuss key messages and cultural elements; respond to artworks and images with opinions; respond to First Nations Australian authors' stories in the target language; respond to questions about characters, values and ideas.
wider: Produce a comparative written response identifying similarities and differences between two texts — using comparison language structures in the target language
Respond to a First Nations Australian cultural story — addressing both the story's content and its cultural significance

modes.reason: Evaluative and comparative response language develops through encountering varied texts and practising different response types. Students need a bank of evaluative and comparative expressions before they can respond genuinely.

nodes.label: Adapting texts for new purposes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adapt target language texts for new purposes or audiences — resequencing, adding elements, changing cultural setting or creating alternative versions.
criteria: Produces a text adaptation with at least two changed elements suited to a different purpose
The adapted text is coherent and appropriate for the intended new audience or purpose

width.minimum: Produce at least one text adaptation with at least two changed elements, suited to a different purpose or audience.
width.typical: Adapt texts by resequencing events, adding new elements or creating alternative endings; change cultural setting to a different target language community context; create versions of texts suited to different audiences; produce adapted texts for real purposes.
wider: Create an adaptation that moves a scenario to a different target language community context — explaining what changed and why
Create an adaptation designed for a genuinely different audience (younger learners, community members) — reflect on what language adjustments were needed

modes.reason: Text adaptation skills develop through working with varied text types and adaptation conditions. Each new adaptation context requires different creative and linguistic decisions.

descriptors.title: Apply strategies to interpret and convey meaning in cultural contexts
descriptors.description: apply strategies to interpret and convey meaning in the target language in familiar non-verbal, spoken and written cultural contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop and apply strategies to comprehend unfamiliar target language and adjust language for cultural meaning (AC9LS4C04). They apply comprehension strategies and formality adjustments. They have not yet worked with expressions that resist direct translation, created bilingual resources for genuine audiences, or evaluated translation tools.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply strategies to interpret and convey meaning in the target language — including managing idiomatic and culturally embedded expressions, and creating bilingual resources for genuine audiences.
elaborations: identifying words and expressions that do not translate directly from the target language into English
collecting examples of false friends and explaining how these could create confusion
interpreting words and expressions in simple texts that do not translate easily and that reflect target language cultural aspects
translating texts to identify differences in elements such as levels of politeness or directness in public signs
creating target language versions of Australian school signs, considering why some expressions require freer translation
using bilingual dictionaries and online translation tools, comparing results and noticing problems
creating bilingual resources such as flashcards and parallel expression lists to aid translation in everyday interactions
discussing strategies to resolve communication breakdowns and misunderstandings
applying active reading or listening skills to engage with and comprehend target language texts

nodes.label: Identifying and managing non-equivalent expressions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify expressions in the target language that do not translate directly into English, and apply strategies to manage them.
criteria: Identifies at least two target language expressions that resist direct translation and explains the challenge
Can explain that direct translation fails for at least one expression — providing a meaning-equivalent alternative
nodes.hinge_reason: Non-equivalent expressions are the translation challenges that most consistently mislead students relying on word-for-word strategies. Students who do not recognise these patterns make systematic errors that persist into higher bands and undermine comprehension of authentic materials.

width.minimum: Identify at least two target language expressions that resist direct translation and explain the translation challenge each presents.
width.typical: Collect and explain expressions that resist direct translation; identify vocabulary that appears similar to English but means something different; interpret culturally embedded expressions in texts; apply active reading and listening strategies for culturally complex texts.
wider: Create a guide to non-equivalent expressions for a new target language learner — including each expression, its actual meaning, and a correct usage context
Research idiomatic expressions not covered in class — explain each and find the closest English equivalent, noting where none exists

modes.reason: Awareness of non-equivalent expressions builds through accumulating examples across varied categories. A bank of examples across different semantic fields builds the recognition needed to flag potential translation traps spontaneously.

nodes.label: Creating bilingual resources and managing translation decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create bilingual resources for genuine audiences and apply translation strategies — choosing free translation or cultural explanation where word-for-word fails.
criteria: Creates a bilingual resource for a specified audience with at least one deliberate translation decision explained
Identifies at least one expression in the resource that required cultural explanation rather than word-for-word equivalence

width.minimum: Create a bilingual resource for a specified audience with at least one deliberate translation decision explained.
width.typical: Create bilingual captions, signs and resources for school or community contexts; compare translation results from different tools; create target language versions of culturally specific Australian content; discuss communication breakdown strategies; build bilingual parallel expression resources.
wider: Translate culturally specific content and annotate every decision — explaining why some expressions required free translation or cultural explanation rather than direct equivalence
Create a bilingual cultural guide for a target language community visitor — making decisions about what requires cultural explanation, not just translation

modes.reason: Bilingual resource creation develops through varied audience and purpose conditions. Creating for different audiences requires different translation and cultural explanation decisions.

descriptors.title: Create texts using varied structures and conventions
descriptors.description: create and present a range of informative and imaginative spoken, written and multimodal texts using a variety of modelled sentence structures to sequence information and ideas, and conventions appropriate to text type
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create informative and imaginative texts using formulaic expressions, simple phrases and modelled conventions (AC9LS4C05). They create for familiar formats. They have not yet used varied structures to sequence ideas, applied procedural text conventions, or created diary entries using past tense.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and present a range of informative and imaginative texts using varied modelled sentence structures to sequence information and ideas, with conventions appropriate to text type.
elaborations: representing themselves as a digital character, making choices about design, content and language
presenting factual information relating to cultural activities and events in target language communities
conveying information relating to significant people, places or events in different formats
producing a class print or digital poster describing a First Nations Country/Place location in a local or regional context
creating bilingual texts and games to engage and entertain younger children
using key features of different types of text and applying vocabulary in different contexts
creating, performing and recording texts such as advertisements, photo stories or posters
experimenting with techniques to capture character traits and emotions through speech bubbles and onomatopoeia
creating an instructive text for a procedure using appropriate language features and text structures
writing a diary entry using first person and past tense to record events and convey thoughts

nodes.label: Sequencing ideas using varied sentence structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create texts that sequence information and ideas using varied sentence structures — including time markers, connectors and tense variation — not only isolated statements.
criteria: Creates a text with at least three sentences logically connected using time markers, connectors or tense variation
Uses at least two different sentence structures across the text
nodes.hinge_reason: Sequencing ideas across sentence boundaries is the structural move from sentence-level to text-level production. Students who produce only isolated sentences cannot create coherent texts — which is required for all text creation from this band onwards.

width.minimum: Create a text using at least three different sentence structures with ideas presented in a logical sequence.
width.typical: Use varied structures to sequence information — time markers, connectors, sequencing adverbs; use tense variation for temporal meaning; apply procedural text conventions (imperative forms, step language, quantities); create diary or journal entries; use thought bubbles and commentary in visual text formats.
wider: Create a text using at least three different tenses coherently — explaining the temporal purpose of each tense choice
Create a procedural text for a real activity applying all the features of the text type — imperative forms, sequence adverbs, quantities

modes.reason: Text-level coherence requires explicit awareness of the sequencing devices that connect sentences into a whole. Students need to see and practise each device deliberately before coherent multi-sentence production becomes automatic.

nodes.label: Applying text-type conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create texts in a range of formats — applying conventions appropriate to each text type for purpose and audience.
criteria: Creates texts in at least two different formats with appropriate conventions for each
At least one text-type convention is consistently applied throughout each text

width.minimum: Create texts in at least two different formats using at least one text-type-specific convention in each.
width.typical: Create digital profiles, event materials, diary entries, instructive texts, comic strips, cultural presentations, performance scripts; apply conventions specific to each text type — diary informality, advertisement persuasion, instruction imperatives; create bilingual materials for younger learners.
wider: Create a text for a genuine audience outside the classroom — adapt text-type conventions specifically for that audience and reflect on what was changed
Compare two texts created for different purposes on the same topic — explain every difference in convention, register and structure

modes.reason: Text-type convention competence develops through creating across varied formats and purposes. Students who only create one text type develop narrow production schemas.

nodes.label: Presenting for real audiences and purposes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can present texts to real audiences — using deliberate delivery choices for voice, visual support and performance — and create texts that serve genuine communicative purposes.
criteria: Presents a text to a genuine audience using at least one deliberate delivery choice
The text serves its intended communicative purpose for the audience

width.minimum: Present at least one text to a genuine audience using at least one deliberate delivery choice.
width.typical: Present informative and imaginative texts to varied real audiences; create and perform original texts for community events, school activities or younger learners; create First Nations Country/Place descriptions for real contexts; produce target language content for genuine publication or display.
wider: Create and perform an original text in the target language for a real purpose — demonstrating deliberate selection of text type, register and conventions for the audience
Create a text presented to an audience outside the school community — reflecting on how the audience affected language choices

modes.reason: Presenting for real audiences integrates all prior text creation work — sequencing (N1) and text-type conventions (N2) — and deploys them for genuine communicative purpose. The real audience is the integration test.

descriptors.title: Apply sound knowledge for fluency
descriptors.description: apply knowledge of combinations of sounds, syllables, pronunciation and intonation patterns to develop fluency and rhythm to known words and phrases
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use sound patterns to predict spellings and produce correct intonation across sentence types (AC9LS4U01). They apply pronunciation in rehearsed contexts. They have not yet applied phonics to unknown words independently, worked with complex vowel combinations, or recognised regional variation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply knowledge of sounds, syllables, pronunciation and intonation to develop fluency and rhythm — including complex vowel combinations, consonant conventions, stress marking and regional variation.
elaborations: understanding how pitch, stress, intonation and rhythm assist meaning when individual words are unfamiliar
distinguishing the pronunciation of individual sounds in vowel combinations
using knowledge of target language pronunciation to identify and enunciate loan words
applying knowledge of consonant sounds to reproduce pronunciation across vowel combinations
recognising variation in the target language in particular regions
applying phonic knowledge to spell unknown words
understanding the function of accents to indicate where stress falls and inserting these into own work
reciting target language tongue twisters to develop pronunciation, intonation and fluency

nodes.label: Complex sound combinations and spelling conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and produce complex vowel combinations and apply consonant conventions, including stress-marking features, in familiar and unfamiliar vocabulary.
criteria: Correctly produces at least three complex vowel combinations in familiar words
Applies phonics to predict the pronunciation of at least two unfamiliar words
nodes.hinge_reason: Complex sound combination accuracy is the phonological foundation for reading and pronouncing unfamiliar vocabulary. Students who cannot apply these patterns must memorise every new word individually — severely limiting reading fluency and vocabulary acquisition.

width.minimum: Correctly produce at least three complex vowel combinations in familiar words; apply phonics to predict the pronunciation of at least two unfamiliar words.
width.typical: Distinguish and produce complex vowel combinations; apply consonant-vowel combination rules; produce borrowed vocabulary using target language phonology; apply stress-marking conventions in own writing; use phonics knowledge to spell and pronounce unfamiliar words.
wider: Compare the pronunciation of borrowed vocabulary in the target language and English — identify every sound that differs
Apply a phonological rule to a set of unfamiliar words — check predictions against a reference and identify which rules were most reliable

modes.reason: Sound rule application requires repeated practice across varied word examples until automatic. Tongue twisters, reading aloud unfamiliar texts and spelling-from-sound tasks provide high-frequency practice.

nodes.label: Fluency, rhythm and regional variation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply pronunciation knowledge for fluency and rhythm — including in unfamiliar words — and recognise that the target language varies across regions.
criteria: Reads an unfamiliar text aloud with pronunciation adequate for intelligibility
Identifies at least one regional pronunciation variation and can explain what differs

width.minimum: Read an unfamiliar short text aloud with intelligible fluency; identify at least one regional pronunciation variation in the target language.
width.typical: Apply phonics to spell and pronounce unknown words; use stress conventions correctly in own writing; understand how pitch, stress and intonation assist meaning in unfamiliar contexts; develop fluency through tongue twisters; recognise regional variation in pronunciation.
wider: Listen to target language speakers from two different regions — identify at least one pronunciation difference and explain what sounds are affected
Perform a tongue twister with accuracy, appropriate speed and natural rhythm — demonstrating genuine fluency beyond slow careful articulation

modes.reason: Fluency and regional awareness develops through exposure to varied target language speech contexts. Students who only hear one regional variety develop a narrow model of the target language.

descriptors.title: Apply grammar and punctuation to compose texts
descriptors.description: use knowledge of modelled grammatical structures and formulaic expressions to compose and respond to texts, using appropriate punctuation and textual conventions
descriptors.knowledge: Students recognise and use agreement patterns, verb forms, prepositions, adverbs and conjunctions (AC9LS4U02). They apply familiar grammatical structures in modelled contexts. They have not yet used past tense in composition, near-future structures, frequency adverbs, comparatives or consolidated agreement across complex word groups.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply modelled grammatical structures to compose and respond to texts — including tense variation, comparatives, frequency adverbs, expanded connectors and consolidated agreement patterns.
elaborations: applying appropriate writing conventions and punctuation
experimenting with multiple forms of 'to be' (or equivalent) in own texts to show different uses
constructing sentences using modelled forms of present and past tenses in context, and describing intended actions using near future structures
using conditional mode as a formulaic, modelled expression
using a range of prepositions of location to give directions
using a range of questions to make requests or ask for specific information
linking ideas and providing more information using conjunctions
indicating frequency using adverbs, noticing flexibility of word order
using ordinal numbers
consolidating the use of gender and number agreement
using a wide range of comparatives
applying the omission of subject pronouns by looking at verb endings
recognising similar spelling stems and composite words

nodes.label: Tense variation and key verb structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use present, past and near-future tense in composition — selecting the appropriate tense for temporal meaning — and apply key verb distinctions with awareness.
criteria: Produces sentences in at least two different tenses correctly in a composition context
Uses a near-future structure correctly in at least one example
nodes.hinge_reason: Tense variation is the grammatical prerequisite for all narrative and temporal text production. Students who only use present tense cannot produce recounts, diary entries or future plans — core text types from this band onwards.

width.minimum: Compose sentences in at least two different tenses; use a near-future structure correctly; use at least one key verb distinction in the target language.
width.typical: Use present, past and near-future structures in composition; use modal expressions for hypothetical or polite statements; apply key verb distinctions in the target language; apply verb forms for self and others; apply subject pronoun conventions.
wider: Write a narrative spanning past, present and future — using each tense for its correct temporal purpose and explaining the logic of the choices
Produce paired sentences demonstrating a key verb distinction — explaining the meaning difference each produces

modes.reason: Tense accuracy requires repeated production practice across varied temporal contexts. Students who understand tense conceptually still default to present tense under production pressure.

nodes.label: Agreement consolidation and comparatives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply agreement patterns consistently across complex word groups and use comparative structures to make comparisons.
criteria: Produces three word groups with correct agreement patterns in a composition task
Uses at least one comparative structure correctly

width.minimum: Produce three word groups with correct agreement patterns; use at least one comparative structure correctly.
width.typical: Consolidate agreement patterns in complex word groups; use comparative structures for making comparisons; use ordinal expressions; use a range of connectors including contrast and reason; use location expressions for giving directions.
wider: Write a text comparing two target language communities using at least four different comparative structures
Produce a word group using the same describing word in all available agreement forms — demonstrating full agreement command

modes.reason: Agreement consolidation and comparative range develops through applying these structures across varied topics and text types. Varied production builds transferable accuracy rather than context-specific competence.

nodes.label: Frequency adverbs, expanded connectors and conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use frequency adverbs with flexible word order, an expanded range of connectors, and apply appropriate punctuation and textual conventions in composition.
criteria: Uses at least two frequency adverbs correctly with appropriate word order
Uses at least two connectors beyond the most basic in connected sentences

width.minimum: Use at least two frequency adverbs correctly; use at least two connectors beyond the most basic; apply target language punctuation and capitalisation conventions.
width.typical: Use frequency adverbs with flexible word order; use expanded connectors including reason, contrast and addition; apply punctuation and capitalisation conventions of the target language; use number expressions for ordering and quantities; link ideas across sentences using varied connectors.
wider: Write a paragraph using at least five different connectors — demonstrating range across additive, contrastive, causal and temporal types
Revise a simple text by adding frequency adverbs and expanded connectors — compare before and after, explaining how each addition changes precision

modes.reason: Connector and adverb range develops through producing varied text types. Different text purposes draw on different connector types — narrative, argument and description each require different connective resources.

descriptors.title: Compare target language and English structures using metalanguage
descriptors.description: compare some target language structures and features with those of English, using some familiar metalanguage
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise familiar target language features and compare with English using grammatical metalanguage (AC9LS4U03). They apply metalanguage to grammar comparison. They have not yet compared grammatical features in text production contexts, analysed persuasive language effects, or explored informal and youth language varieties.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare target language and English language structures and features using metalanguage — including text-type conventions, persuasive language, informal variety and vocabulary pattern connections.
elaborations: comparing features of simple spoken and written texts in the target language with similar texts in English
comparing language use in advertisements and signs, noticing how different text types in each language create specific effects
using metalanguage in both the target language and English to discuss grammatical structures and features
recognising grammatical elements associated with particular texts in each language
exploring the use and popularity of abbreviations and phrases used by young people in target language communities and Australia
noticing similar word stems in the target language and English to identify meaning and extend vocabulary
compiling a graphic organiser to illustrate differences in grammar and textual conventions
comparing the use of diminutives to express affection and familiarity, with equivalents in English

nodes.label: Comparing grammatical structures and text conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare grammatical structures and text conventions across the target language and English using metalanguage — identifying what each language does differently and explaining it.
criteria: Uses at least three metalanguage terms accurately in comparing target language and English grammatical features
Identifies at least one text convention that differs between the target language and English
nodes.hinge_reason: Metalanguage precision for grammatical comparison is the analytical tool for all subsequent language analysis. Students who use metalanguage loosely cannot engage in the text evaluation and analysis work at subsequent bands.

width.minimum: Compare at least three grammatical features across the target language and English using metalanguage; identify at least one text convention that differs.
width.typical: Use metalanguage in both languages; recognise grammatical elements associated with specific text types; compare traditional text conventions across the two languages; compare subject-predicate structure and word order; compile comparison graphic organisers.
wider: Create a bilingual grammar comparison chart covering at least five features — each with a target language example, an English example and an explanation of the difference
Analyse a target language and English text of the same type side by side — use metalanguage to annotate every grammatical difference

modes.reason: Metalanguage precision develops through repeated application across multiple texts and comparison tasks before it becomes a reliable analytical tool.

nodes.label: Persuasive language, informal varieties and vocabulary patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and compare persuasive language in target language and English texts, and explore informal language varieties and vocabulary patterns.
criteria: Identifies at least two persuasive language features in a target language text and names each using metalanguage
Identifies at least one informal language feature or vocabulary pattern and explains its social or communicative function

width.minimum: Identify at least two persuasive language features in a target language text and compare them with English equivalents; identify at least one example of informal language variety or vocabulary pattern.
width.typical: Compare advertisements and public signs for persuasive and directive language across both languages; explore informal language used by young people in target language communities; compare affective language features across the two languages; notice vocabulary patterns for extending word knowledge.
wider: Create a target language persuasive text using at least three persuasive techniques — annotate each with metalanguage
Research informal language used in target language communities — explain each term, find any English parallel and describe what each reveals about youth culture

modes.reason: Persuasive language and informal variety awareness develops through exposure to varied authentic target language texts — advertisements, signs, social media, informal speech.

descriptors.title: Language reflects cultural practices, values and identity
descriptors.description: recognise that language reflects cultural practices, values and identity, and that this impacts on non-verbal and spoken communication
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify connections between the target language and cultural practices using conceptual vocabulary (AC9LS4U04). They reflect on cross-cultural comparisons. They have not yet explored contact language influences on the target language, examined cultural stereotypes critically, or analysed modern language change.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise that language reflects cultural practices, values and identity — including through contact language influences, cultural stereotypes, modern language change, and First Nations Australian cultural expressions.
elaborations: understanding that there are indigenous languages spoken in addition to the target language in target language communities, and that these languages influence the target language
researching target language communities, inviting special guests or showcasing learning about cultural aspects
recognising how the target language is widespread, and that traditions, values and practices may reflect collective identities of individuals from different target language communities
exploring how language and culture are expressed through First Nations Australians' song, dance or artworks, considering similarities and differences
sharing reactions to cultural elements witnessed in authentic materials
becoming aware of cultural stereotypes that can lead to generalisations and misconceptions
investigating modern influences on the target language such as pop culture, digital media and migration
reflecting on culturally appropriate ways of offering praise, recognition and gratitude, or declining requests
understanding that target language communities may have shared history with other languages and cultures
identifying visible and invisible elements that contribute to identity across all cultures

nodes.label: Contact language influences and cultural stereotypes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how contact with other languages has influenced the target language vocabulary, and recognise that cultural stereotypes about target language communities are oversimplifications.
criteria: Identifies at least three target language words with contact language origins and explains each
Identifies at least one cultural stereotype and explains why it is an oversimplification
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding contact language influence and the danger of stereotypes is foundational to authentic intercultural competence. Students with a single-community, stereotype-based model of target language culture cannot engage with genuine cultural diversity.

width.minimum: Identify at least three target language words derived from contact or indigenous languages and explain their origin; identify at least one cultural stereotype and explain why it oversimplifies.
width.typical: Explore contact language contributions to the target language vocabulary; recognise that contact languages remain important for identity and heritage; become aware of cultural stereotypes that lead to generalisations; recognise shared linguistic history with related language families.
wider: Research a contact language that has influenced the target language — identify several loanwords and explain what they reveal about the relationship between the two communities
Examine a cultural stereotype about target language communities — find evidence that contradicts it and explain why the stereotype persists

modes.reason: Stereotype identification and critique requires students to move from passive noticing to active analysis — identifying what a stereotype claims, finding contradicting evidence and explaining the mechanism by which stereotypes persist.

nodes.label: Modern language change and identity expression
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how modern influences shape target language change, and reflect on visible and invisible elements of identity expressed through language.
criteria: Identifies at least two modern influences on the target language and explains how each has changed it
Identifies at least one visible and one invisible element of cultural identity and explains how each is expressed through language

width.minimum: Identify at least two modern influences on the target language and explain how each has changed the language; identify at least one visible and one invisible element of cultural identity.
