width.typical: Apply character and grammatical knowledge to compose and respond to texts across familiar and some unfamiliar contexts; use morphological knowledge to approach unfamiliar vocabulary; apply cohesive devices and complex sentence constructions; differentiate morphemes with similar forms to enhance communication.
wider: Compose a text on an unfamiliar topic using morphological inference and contextual strategies — document the strategies used and evaluate their effectiveness
Analyse own extended writing for grammatical accuracy — identify patterns of error and develop a targeted revision plan

modes.reason: Composing and responding to unfamiliar texts integrates morphological inference (node 1) and writing system conventions (node 2) into full productive literacy engagement. The teaching investment is in creating text composition tasks with genuine unfamiliar elements that require strategic deployment of both skills.

descriptors.title: Compare language structures using metalanguage
descriptors.description: compare and explain similarities and differences between Chinese and English language structures and features, using familiar metalanguage
descriptors.knowledge: Students entering at Y7-8 have intuitive grammatical knowledge of the target language from home use, and English grammar knowledge from schooling. They have not previously been asked to compare the two systems analytically, name grammatical features using metalanguage, or examine text-type conventions across languages.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare and explain similarities and differences between the target language and English language structures and features, using familiar metalanguage across text types and grammatical categories.
elaborations: discussing aspects of grammar, using metalanguage in Chinese or English
comparing different ways of sequencing ideas for different audiences and purposes
reading texts and choosing expressions or sentences that appeal and explaining choices
reading samples of formal texts and identifying how language compares with everyday speech
comparing the expression of ideas in diverse traditional and contemporary literary texts

nodes.label: Metalanguage for grammatical comparison
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use metalanguage to describe grammatical features in both the target language and English, and compare how specific features function across the two languages.
criteria: Uses at least five metalanguage terms correctly
Compares at least two grammatical features across target language and English with accurate explanation
nodes.hinge_reason: Metalanguage for grammatical comparison is the prerequisite for all analytical language work. Entry students with strong intuitive grammar but no analytical framework cannot describe, compare or explain language features — which is the core demand of this descriptor.

width.minimum: Use at least five metalanguage terms correctly in comparing at least two grammatical features across target language and English.
width.typical: Use metalanguage in target language or English for grammatical description — nouns, verbs, adjectives, subject, predicate; compare grammatical features including word order, tense expression, and adjectival verb constructions; discuss aspects of grammar across both languages.
wider: Create a bilingual metalanguage comparison resource — explaining a specific grammatical contrast to a student learning one of the two languages
Investigate a grammatical feature that works fundamentally differently in the two languages — explain what communicative function it serves and how the other language handles the same need

modes.reason: Grammatical comparison requires students to hold two systems in mind and reason about structural differences. Explicit metalanguage instruction followed by systematic category-by-category comparison builds this analytical capacity.

nodes.label: Text-type and sequencing comparison
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare how different text types sequence and develop ideas in the target language and English, identifying structural and language feature differences.
criteria: Compares the structure of at least one text type across target language and English
Identifies at least three structural or language feature differences

width.minimum: Compare the structure of at least one text type (e.g. blog, email, argument, report) across target language and English, identifying at least three differences.
width.typical: Compare different ways of sequencing ideas for different audiences and purposes; compare blog versus email conventions; compare argument structure in speech versus essay; read formal target language texts and compare with everyday speech; compare traditional and contemporary literary expressions.
wider: Analyse how argument structure differs across target language and English texts — identify where the writer's position appears, how evidence is organised, and discuss the cultural logic behind the difference
Create the same text type in both languages, then compare the structural and language choices made — identify what is transferred and what is adapted

modes.reason: Text-type comparison must be applied across varied genres before students can generalise their comparative analytical capacity. Single-genre comparison produces narrow analytical skills that don't transfer.

nodes.label: Teaching and applying comparative knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply comparative language knowledge to access unfamiliar content and explain key language differences to others.
criteria: Applies comparative knowledge to access at least one unfamiliar text
Produces an explanation or resource about a key language difference for another learner

width.minimum: Apply comparative knowledge to access at least one unfamiliar text, and produce at least one explanation or resource about a key language difference for a peer or younger learner.
width.typical: Apply understanding of text and language features to access unfamiliar content; read texts and select appealing expressions to explain their choices; apply knowledge of formal text features to understand news articles and reports; explain key language differences using support resources.
wider: Create a teaching resource about a specific language difference — test it with a real or simulated learner audience and revise based on feedback
Apply comparative linguistic knowledge to analyse a genuinely unfamiliar text type — document the strategies used and evaluate their effectiveness

modes.reason: Teaching and applying comparative knowledge integrates metalanguage (node 1) and text-type comparison (node 2) into a transfer task. The teaching investment is in creating genuine transfer conditions — real unfamiliar texts, real teaching audiences — that require functional application of comparative knowledge.

descriptors.title: Identity shaped by language and culture
descriptors.description: reflect on and explain how their own and others' identity is shaped by language(s), culture(s), attitudes, beliefs and values
descriptors.knowledge: Students entering at Y7-8 have lived experience of navigating between cultural-language communities, and have implicit awareness of how their identity is shaped by their linguistic and cultural background. They have not yet systematically examined or articulated this experience, nor analysed how cultural values and attitudes are embedded in language use.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on and explain how their own and others' identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values — including how cultural values influence language use, how identity is expressed through language choices, and how humour and intercultural experience shape understanding.
elaborations: discussing identity and cultural values reflected in language use and how they influence interactions
comparing key differences between target language speaking regions and considering cultural diversity
explaining communicative practices that might be perceived differently in different cultures
examining in Chinese or English how First Nations Australians' languages have strong connections to Country/Place
identifying ways in which Chinese identity is reflected in own values, beliefs and language
exploring how known languages influence own way of communicating
identifying elements of own community and identity including involvement in cultural practices
reading jokes or cartoons in Chinese and discussing how humour is conveyed
discussing experiences of living in a target language country and comparing lifestyles and practices

nodes.label: Cultural values reflected in language use
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain how cultural values and attitudes are reflected in language use — including job titles, terms of address, compliment deflection, and community-specific expressions.
criteria: Identifies at least two examples of cultural values reflected in target language use
Explains the cultural logic behind each example
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how cultural values are reflected in language use is the conceptual prerequisite for all identity reflection at this level. Entry students who treat communication as culturally neutral cannot engage meaningfully with the intercultural dimensions of this descriptor.

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples of cultural values reflected in target language use and explain the cultural logic behind each.
width.typical: Discuss identity and cultural values in language use and interaction; explain communicative practices interpreted differently across cultures; examine how job titles and address conventions reflect respect; identify ways Chinese identity is expressed in own values, beliefs and language; explore humour across cultures.
wider: Analyse a specific communicative practice — for example, how compliments are deflected, or how thanks is expressed — across target language and English-speaking contexts, explaining the cultural values that underlie each convention
Compare how cultural identity is expressed through language in different target language community contexts — diaspora, homeland, regional — and discuss what the differences reveal

modes.reason: Cultural value analysis requires students to move from observing a language convention to explaining the cultural logic behind it. Explicit discussion with cultural context scaffolding builds this explanatory capacity.

nodes.label: Own identity across language communities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on how their own identity is shaped by their participation in multiple language and cultural communities, identifying specific ways each community has influenced their values and communication.
criteria: Identifies at least two ways different language or cultural communities have shaped own identity
Reflects on at least one specific experience of navigating between communities

width.minimum: Identify at least two specific ways different language or cultural communities have shaped own identity or communication style, and reflect on at least one experience of navigating between them.
width.typical: Explore how known languages influence ways of communicating; reflect on involvement in cultural practices and choices of language; examine how family origins reflect language use; compare cultural traditions across Chinese-speaking regions; reflect on past or possible experiences of living in a Chinese-speaking country.
wider: Interview a family member or community elder about their language and cultural identity — identify how their experience of navigating between communities differs from or resembles the student's own
Reflect on a specific moment of cultural identity navigation — describe the experience, identify what cultural values were in tension, and explain what was learned

modes.reason: Personal identity reflection is deepened through varied cultural encounter and comparison — single-context reflection produces limited insight. Varied reflective tasks across different community contexts and relationships build the richer identity understanding the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Intercultural positioning and First Nations connections
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain communicative practices that may be misinterpreted across cultures, examine how First Nations Australian language connections compare with target language cultural connections, and reflect on how humour and communication style vary across cultural contexts.
criteria: Explains at least one communicative practice that may be misinterpreted across cultures
Makes at least one connection between First Nations Australian language-country connections and target language cultural connections

width.minimum: Explain at least one communicative practice from the target language community that may be misinterpreted in an Australian English context, and make at least one connection between First Nations Australian language-country connections and target language cultural connections.
width.typical: Explain practices perceived differently across cultures; examine First Nations Australian languages' connections to Country and compare with target language cultural connections; read target language jokes and analyse how humour is conveyed; discuss how humour is interpreted across cultures; reflect on own communication style differences across languages.
wider: Conduct a comparative analysis of humour across the target language and Australian English — identify what is shared and what is culturally specific, and explain what the comparison reveals about cultural values and assumptions
Reflect on own communication style across different cultural contexts — identify specific adjustments made and explain the cultural values that motivate each

modes.reason: Intercultural positioning integrates cultural value analysis (node 1) and personal identity reflection (node 2) into a broader, outward-looking synthesis. The teaching investment is in creating genuinely comparative conditions — real intercultural encounters, real examples of misinterpretation — that require students to examine both cultures rather than only their own.

descriptors.title: Tone-syllables, intonation and phrasing for fluency
descriptors.description: use tone-syllables and apply intonation, stress and phrasing to develop fluency, and respond to and create texts in a range of contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use tonal features, intonation and stress to express feelings and opinions, apply tone change patterns, and use digital tools for fluency development (AC9LCH6U01). They have self-monitored spoken production. They have not yet developed comprehension of unfamiliar voices at varied speeds, analysed subtle regional accent differences, or applied fluency skills across a full range of text creation and response contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use tone-syllables, intonation, stress and phrasing to develop fluency in responding to and creating texts across a range of contexts — including comprehension of diverse speakers and speeds, and awareness of regional accent variation.
elaborations: listening to short interactions between unfamiliar voices at diverse speeds or levels of clarity
developing tone discrimination and identifying subtle differences in pronunciation including regional accents
differentiating pronunciation changes in tone sandhi patterns
comparing own Chinese speech patterns with target language pronunciation and making adjustments
practising ways in which tone varies according to setting and context
noticing and describing differences in accent when listening to speakers from diverse regions

nodes.label: Auditory comprehension across diverse speakers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can understand spoken target language from unfamiliar voices at varied speeds and levels of clarity, identifying key meaning and distinguishing subtle pronunciation variations.
criteria: Demonstrates comprehension of spoken target language from at least two unfamiliar voices
Identifies key information from at least one fast or less clearly articulated spoken text
nodes.hinge_reason: Comprehension of diverse, unfamiliar speakers is the prerequisite for real-world spoken language use. Students who can only understand teacher-directed or familiar speech cannot function in authentic target language listening contexts — which is the threshold the Y7-8 curriculum marks.

width.minimum: Demonstrate comprehension of at least two spoken texts from unfamiliar voices at different speeds, identifying key information from each.
width.typical: Listen to short interactions between unfamiliar voices at diverse speeds and clarity levels; develop auditory comprehension strategies; distinguish subtle pronunciation differences including regional accents; compare own speech patterns with target language models and make adjustments.
wider: Listen to spoken target language from speakers across different regions and describe specific phonological differences heard — connect these to the regional dialect knowledge developed earlier
Compare comprehension strategies for fast native-speed speech with slower learner-directed speech — identify what makes fast speech harder to process and what strategies help

modes.reason: Auditory comprehension across diverse speakers is built through repeated, varied listening exposure — different voices, speeds, accents, topics. A single familiar speaker type produces narrow comprehension that fails to generalise. Varied listening tasks build the flexible processing capacity needed.

nodes.label: Subtle tonal and pronunciation discrimination
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discriminate subtle tonal and pronunciation differences — including tone change patterns and regional accent variation — and apply this awareness to their own spoken production.
criteria: Identifies at least two subtle pronunciation differences between own speech and a model
Demonstrates a targeted improvement attempt for at least one identified difference

width.minimum: Identify at least two subtle pronunciation differences (tonal or segmental) between own speech and a target language model, and demonstrate an improvement attempt.
width.typical: Develop tone discrimination for subtle differences; distinguish between regional accent features; identify and practise tone change patterns including sandhi; compare own speech with models and make targeted adjustments; practise saying the same sentence to change meaning through tonal variation.
wider: Conduct a systematic comparison of own recorded speech with a native speaker model — identify and categorise specific pronunciation differences and design a targeted practice plan
Investigate a specific regional accent feature of the target language — describe the phonological rule, find examples, and compare with the standard form

modes.reason: Subtle tonal and pronunciation discrimination requires sustained, focused practice — these distinctions are not acquired through general exposure alone. Targeted self-monitoring activities with specific pronunciation goals build the perceptual and productive accuracy the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Fluency in text response and creation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply tonal and prosodic knowledge fluently when responding to and creating spoken texts across a range of contexts.
criteria: Responds to a spoken text demonstrating comprehension through appropriate spoken or written reply
Creates a spoken text demonstrating fluency — appropriate phrasing, stress and intonation with minimal hesitation

width.minimum: Respond to at least one spoken text and create at least one spoken text demonstrating fluency — appropriate phrasing, stress, tone and intonation — with minimal hesitation.
width.typical: Apply fluency skills across text response and creation contexts — discussions, presentations, performances, online interactions; use phrasing, grouping and intonation to support comprehension for listeners; create spoken texts that demonstrate tonal and prosodic control.
wider: Present a spoken text designed for a specific audience — demonstrate deliberate prosodic choices (pace, stress, pausing) that serve the communicative purpose
Record and review a full spoken performance across response and creation tasks — identify specific prosodic features that contribute to fluency and explain the choices made

modes.reason: Fluency in text contexts integrates auditory comprehension (node 1) and discrimination skills (node 2) into full spoken performance. The teaching investment is in creating genuine communicative conditions — real audiences, real response tasks — where fluency serves a communicative purpose.

descriptors.title: Character form and function, sentence structures and syntax
descriptors.description: apply knowledge of character form and function, sentence structures, syntax, and writing system features to infer meaning and to compose a range of texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use morphological knowledge to infer meaning in unfamiliar words and apply complex grammatical structures in extended texts (AC9LCH6U02). They have composed texts across familiar and some unfamiliar contexts. They have not yet applied grammatical knowledge to modal, tense-expression, exclamatory and response-to-negative-question structures, used digital input methods for the writing system, or composed a full range of sentence types — affirmative, negative, interrogative, imperative — systematically.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply knowledge of character form and function, sentence structures, syntax and writing system features to infer meaning and compose a range of texts — including modal structures, tense-expression patterns, and varied sentence types.
elaborations: using knowledge of components to select a character when inputting the target language digitally
categorising words containing a common morpheme to understand the relationship between morphemes and specific word meanings
applying knowledge of morphemes to create new words and confirming combinations using dictionaries
applying knowledge of punctuation in writing
understanding elements of grammar such as word order and sentence construction
understanding and using verbs to express modality
comparing how tense is expressed in the target language — completion, experience, intention, negation
recognising the purpose and effect of exclamatory sentences as opposed to statements
constructing a range of sentences in affirmative, negative, interrogative and imperative forms
recognising differences in Chinese and English responses to negative tag questions

nodes.label: Advanced morphological application and digital input
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply morphological knowledge to create new words and use digital input methods for the target language writing system.
criteria: Creates at least three new compound words using known morphemes, verified as accurate
Demonstrates competent use of at least one digital input method for the target language
nodes.hinge_reason: Advanced morphological application and digital input are the productive writing prerequisites for Y7-8 text composition. Students who cannot generate words morphologically or use digital input methods are significantly constrained in both written output quantity and quality.

width.minimum: Create at least three new compound words using known morphemes (verified as accurate), and demonstrate use of at least one digital input method for the target language writing system.
width.typical: Use morphological knowledge to create new words and confirm combinations using dictionaries or digital tools; use digital input methods for the writing system; categorise words by shared morpheme; use dictionary resources to understand subtle differences in word use.
wider: Investigate a productive morpheme in the target language — identify all the words it appears in, document the semantic pattern, and generate new combinations with verification
Compare digital input methods for the target language writing system — evaluate which method best suits different writing contexts (speed, accuracy, character discovery)

modes.reason: Digital input and morphological word creation require repeated practice for accuracy and speed. Regular writing tasks that require students to use both skills — not occasional demonstrations — build the productive fluency the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Modal, tense-expression and exclamatory structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and use modal verbs, tense-expression patterns, and exclamatory structures in the target language, understanding how these differ from English equivalents.
criteria: Produces at least four sentences demonstrating different modal or tense-expression structures correctly
Constructs at least one exclamatory sentence and explains its purpose

width.minimum: Produce at least four sentences demonstrating different modal or tense-expression structures correctly, including at least one exclamatory or response-to-negative-question construction.
width.typical: Use modal verbs to express ability, permission and obligation; use tense-expression patterns — completion, experience, intention, negation — appropriately; construct exclamatory sentences and understand their purpose; understand response conventions for negative tag questions; compare these structures with English equivalents.
wider: Analyse how tense and aspect are expressed differently in the target language compared with English verb conjugation — create examples demonstrating each pattern and explain the difference
Investigate how response conventions for negative questions can cause miscommunication between target language and English speakers — create examples and explain the cultural and linguistic logic

modes.reason: Modal and tense-expression structures require explicit instruction because they differ systematically from English — students cannot rely on L1 transfer. Explicit comparison with English equivalents, followed by targeted production practice, prevents persistent structural errors.

nodes.label: Full sentence-type range in composed texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compose texts using the full range of sentence types — affirmative, negative, interrogative, imperative — and apply full writing system and syntactic knowledge across a range of text types.
criteria: Composes a text using at least three different sentence types with correct syntax
Applies appropriate punctuation and writing system conventions throughout the text

width.minimum: Compose a text using at least three different sentence types correctly, with appropriate punctuation and writing system conventions throughout.
width.typical: Construct and use affirmative, negative, interrogative and imperative sentences for different purposes; apply understanding of word order and sentence construction including target language-specific grammatical structures; compose texts across a range of types applying full grammatical knowledge.
wider: Analyse a model text and annotate every sentence for type, modal/tense structure, and syntactic feature — then compose an equivalent text using the same full syntactic repertoire
Create a text that deliberately uses each sentence type for a different communicative function — explain how each type serves a purpose in the overall text

modes.reason: Full sentence-type range in composed texts integrates morphological production (node 1) and modal/tense structure knowledge (node 2) into complete compositional competence. The teaching investment is in extended writing tasks that require varied sentence types — not only narrative or only information tasks, but the full communicative range.

descriptors.title: Similarities and differences between target language and English using metalanguage
descriptors.description: reflect on and explain similarities and differences between the target language and English language structures and features, using metalanguage
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare language structures and features across the target language and English using metalanguage, and produce comparative analyses (AC9LCH6U03). They have compared text types, grammar and cohesive devices. They have not yet taught younger students using comparative frameworks, explored metaphorical versus literal meaning across languages, or applied comparative understanding to unlock unfamiliar content.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on and explain similarities and differences between the target language and English across a range of text types and grammatical features — using metalanguage to extend and apply comparative understanding, including to unfamiliar content and to support others' learning.
elaborations: extending understanding of metalanguage about a range of textual features in target language and English
identifying and comparing language features in target language and English texts
teaching younger students about some key differences between the target language and English using support resources
applying understanding of key features of familiar text types to understand unfamiliar content
exploring the way content is developed in different types of texts
reading samples of formal texts and identifying how language compares with everyday speech
exploring metaphorical and literal meaning in target language and English texts

nodes.label: Extended metalanguage for text and grammar analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use extended metalanguage to describe and explain a range of text-level and grammatical features in both the target language and English.
criteria: Uses at least six metalanguage terms correctly across a text or grammar analysis
Includes at least one text-level and one grammatical metalanguage term used accurately
nodes.hinge_reason: Extended metalanguage is the prerequisite for systematic language comparison and for supporting others' language learning. Students who cannot name and describe language features cannot explain similarities and differences, cannot apply comparative knowledge to unfamiliar content, and cannot teach others.

width.minimum: Use at least six metalanguage terms correctly across a text or grammar analysis that covers both languages, including at least one text-level term (e.g. paragraph, cohesion, point of view) and one grammatical term.
width.typical: Use extended metalanguage for text features — paragraphing, conjunctions, sequencing, point of view, descriptive and emotive language; compare how these features work in target language and English texts; read formal texts such as reports and news articles and compare with own everyday speech.
wider: Annotate a target language text fully using metalanguage for every grammatical and textual feature — compare the annotation with an English equivalent and identify all structural differences
Create a metalanguage comparison resource for a specific feature that differs across the two languages — designed to be used by another learner

modes.reason: Metalanguage is built through repeated deployment across varied analysis tasks — not through a single lesson. Students need to encounter and use each metalanguage term across multiple text types and comparison contexts before it becomes functional analytical vocabulary.

nodes.label: Metaphorical and literal meaning across languages
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and compare metaphorical and literal meaning in target language and English texts, and explain how metaphor functions differently across the two languages.
criteria: Identifies at least two metaphorical expressions in the target language with explanations of literal and figurative meanings
Compares at least one with the English equivalent or explains why English handles the concept differently

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples of metaphorical language in the target language, explain the literal and metaphorical meanings, and compare with English equivalents or absence of equivalents.
width.typical: Explore metaphorical and literal meaning in target language texts; compare metaphorical expressions across target language and English; identify where the same metaphor exists in both languages and where languages use different metaphors for the same concept; apply understanding to interpret unfamiliar metaphorical content.
wider: Research a specific conceptual metaphor that operates differently in the target language and English — explain how each language encodes the concept and what this reveals about cultural thinking
Analyse a target language text rich in metaphor — identify every metaphorical expression, explain its meaning, and compare with how English would express the same idea

modes.reason: Metaphorical meaning analysis requires students to hold both literal and figurative readings simultaneously and compare these across two language systems. Explicit scaffolding — identifying the literal meaning first, then the figurative, then comparing — builds this dual-level analysis capacity.

nodes.label: Applying comparative knowledge to support learning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply comparative language knowledge to access unfamiliar content and to support younger learners' understanding of key language differences.
criteria: Applies comparative knowledge to access at least one unfamiliar text, explaining strategies used
Produces a resource or explanation for a younger learner about at least one key language difference

width.minimum: Apply comparative language knowledge to access at least one unfamiliar text, explaining the strategies used, and produce at least one resource or explanation for a younger learner about a key language difference.
width.typical: Apply understanding of text and grammar features to access unfamiliar content in target language and English; teach younger students about key differences using support resources; compare content development across text types; apply comparative understanding to analyse public texts such as news articles.
wider: Create a teaching resource for younger learners about a specific language difference — test it with a real or simulated audience and revise based on feedback
Apply comparative linguistic knowledge to analyse a genuinely unfamiliar text type in the target language — document the strategies used and evaluate their effectiveness

modes.reason: Applying comparative knowledge to support learning integrates metalanguage command (node 1) and metaphor analysis (node 2) into a teaching and transfer task. The teaching investment is in creating genuine transfer conditions — real unfamiliar content, real younger learners — that require students to apply their knowledge functionally.

descriptors.title: Identity shaped by language, culture, attitudes and values
descriptors.description: reflect on and explain how their own and others' identity is shaped by language(s), culture(s), attitudes, beliefs and values
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise how language reflects cultural practices and identity, and have reflected on their own intercultural positioning (AC9LCH6U04). They have explored language variation across communities. They have not yet examined how attitudes, beliefs and values shape communication style, reflected on how cultural events and practices change across contexts, or critically examined stereotyping in intercultural interaction.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on and explain how their own and others' identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values — including how these factors influence communication style, cultural participation, and intercultural understanding.
elaborations: considering how attitudes, beliefs and values can be reflected in language and gesture
reflecting on the influence of target language culture on own communication style
reflecting on participation in cultural events noting similarities and differences across contexts and regions
examining how First Nations Australians' languages have strong connections to Country/Place and comparing with language connections in target language culture
comparing cultural elements reflected in language use and social norms such as body language, volume and silence
recognising that some target language social behaviours may be misinterpreted as lack of courtesy
developing self-awareness of possible stereotyping during interactions
discussing how family origins reflect language use, such as mixing languages while speaking

nodes.label: Attitudes, beliefs and values shaping communication
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how attitudes, beliefs and values — in both their own and others' backgrounds — shape communication choices in the target language and English.
criteria: Identifies at least two ways attitudes, beliefs or values shape communication in the target language community
Compares these with at least one parallel example from English-speaking contexts
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how attitudes and values shape communication is the conceptual prerequisite for all intercultural reflection at this level. Students who cannot see the value system behind communication choices cannot reflect meaningfully on their own identity or explain others' behaviour.

width.minimum: Identify at least two ways that attitudes, beliefs or values shape communication style in the target language community, and compare with at least one way these factors shape communication in English-speaking contexts.
width.typical: Reflect on how attitudes, beliefs and values are reflected in language and gesture in everyday conversations and media; examine how cultural background shapes communication style; compare communication norms across cultural contexts; identify how First Nations Australian languages connect to Country and compare with target language cultural connections.
wider: Analyse a real or fictional intercultural interaction — identify every moment where attitudes, beliefs or values are visible in a language or gesture choice, and explain the cultural logic behind each
Compare how a specific belief or value (e.g. about respect, family, community) shapes language use differently in the target language community and in own family or community context

modes.reason: Values-to-communication analysis requires explicit scaffolding — students need a framework for moving from 'they communicate differently' to 'this is the belief or value that produces this communication pattern.' Guided analysis with cultural context information builds this explanatory capacity.

nodes.label: Cultural participation and identity across contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on how cultural practices and events shape identity, and discuss how participation in cultural events changes across different contexts and regions.
criteria: Reflects on at least one cultural event or practice and explains how it shapes their identity
Notes at least one way the practice varies across contexts, regions, or generations

width.minimum: Reflect on at least one cultural event or practice in which they participate and explain how it shapes or expresses their identity, noting how the practice may vary across contexts or regions.
width.typical: Reflect on participation in cultural events and how practices change across contexts and regions; examine how family origins and multilingual background shape language use and identity; discuss how mixing languages reflects cultural identity; consider how cultural practices in diaspora communities differ from homeland practices.
wider: Research how a specific cultural practice has changed in the diaspora context compared with the homeland — explain the factors that caused the change and discuss what this reveals about how identity adapts across contexts

Reflect on own family's cultural practices — identify what has been maintained, what has changed, and what this reveals about the relationship between language, culture and identity across generations

modes.reason: Identity-through-cultural-participation is understood through varied reflective encounters — different events, different community contexts, different generational perspectives. Single-event reflection produces limited insight; varied cultural reflection builds the richer identity narrative the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Stereotyping, sensitivity and intercultural self-awareness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify stereotyping risks in intercultural interactions, demonstrate sensitivity in cross-cultural questioning, and reflect on their own communication adaptations when interacting across cultural contexts.
criteria: Identifies at least one stereotyping risk in intercultural interaction and explains a strategy for avoiding it
Reflects on at least one specific communication adaptation they make when interacting across cultural contexts

width.minimum: Identify at least one stereotyping risk in intercultural interaction and explain a strategy for avoiding it, and reflect on at least one specific communication adaptation they make when interacting across cultural contexts.
width.typical: Develop awareness of stereotyping in intercultural interactions; practise sensitive and considerate questioning; reflect on own communication style adaptations when interacting in different cultural contexts; discuss how some cultural behaviours may be misinterpreted across cultural contexts.
wider: Analyse a case of cultural misinterpretation — identify the stereotyping or assumption at work, explain the cultural logic of both sides, and propose how the misunderstanding could have been prevented
Reflect on a personal experience of cultural misunderstanding or misinterpretation — analyse what assumptions were made, what was misread, and what was learned from the experience

modes.reason: Stereotyping awareness and intercultural self-reflection integrate values analysis (node 1) and cultural identity reflection (node 2) into a mature intercultural stance. The teaching investment is in creating genuinely reflective conditions — real or realistic intercultural scenarios — where students examine their own assumptions rather than only others'.

descriptors.title: Initiate and sustain exchanges about experiences and views
descriptors.description: initiate and sustain exchanges in familiar and some unfamiliar contexts related to students' experiences, feelings and views, adjusting their language in response to others
descriptors.knowledge: Students can initiate and sustain modelled exchanges in familiar contexts expressing feelings, opinions and preferences (AC9LS6C01). They have not yet initiated exchanges in unfamiliar contexts, structured arguments, or adjusted language in real time in response to others.
descriptors.endpoint: Students initiate and sustain exchanges in familiar and some unfamiliar contexts about experiences, feelings and views — including structuring arguments, inviting opinions, and adjusting language in response to others.
elaborations: using appropriate register when interacting in different situations
exchanging personal information about routines and past experiences and responding to key ideas in questions
engaging in informal conversations with friends or family
developing narrative skills by exchanging accounts of significant events or milestones
initiating and extending conversations using open-ended questions and connectives
using formulaic examples to structure arguments and explain or justify a position
inviting others to give opinions, share views or make suggestions
interacting with target language community students in real or imagined contexts to convey information about Australian places, events and wildlife

nodes.label: Exchanging experiences and structuring arguments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can exchange accounts of experiences and use structured language to justify positions and invite others' opinions.
criteria: Shares at least one account of a past experience using sequenced language
Uses at least one argument-structuring expression and invites a partner's opinion during an exchange
nodes.hinge_reason: Justifying positions and inviting opinions are the interactional moves that distinguish exchange from conversation. They are required for the collaborative and analytical tasks at this band. Students who can only share information without arguing or inviting dialogue cannot reach these demands.

width.minimum: Share at least one account of a past experience using sequenced language; use at least one argument-structuring expression; invite at least one opinion from a partner.
width.typical: Develop narrative skills by exchanging significant events and milestones; use structured argument language to justify positions; invite others' opinions; use open-ended questions and connectors to initiate and extend conversations; interact with target language community peers about shared interests.
wider: Exchange a substantive account of a significant experience — providing context, sequence of events and personal reaction beyond a simple summary
Argue a position using at least three argument-structuring moves — assertion, reason and acknowledgement of a counterposition

modes.reason: Argument-structuring expressions and opinion-invitation formulae need to become automatic across varied topics before they are available spontaneously in interaction.

nodes.label: Adjusting language across contexts and registers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adjust their language in response to others and across different contexts — using appropriate register for formal and informal interactions.
criteria: Uses appropriate register in at least two different interaction contexts
Makes at least one identifiable language adjustment during an exchange in response to a partner's contribution or contextual shift

width.minimum: Demonstrate register adjustment in at least two different interaction contexts; make at least one real-time adjustment in response to a partner's contribution.
width.typical: Use appropriate register across formal and informal contexts; adjust language in response to others' contributions; use formal and informal address appropriately for varied interlocutors; sustain exchanges in some unfamiliar contexts using available strategies.
wider: Participate in an interaction that shifts register mid-exchange — demonstrate real-time adjustment without prompting
Record and review a sustained exchange — identify every instance where register was or should have been adjusted and explain the social signal that triggered each

modes.reason: Register adjustment develops through encountering varied interaction contexts. Single-register practice does not build the adjustment capacity that authentic interaction demands.

descriptors.title: Collaborate in transaction, negotiation and problem-solving
descriptors.description: collaborate in activities that involve the language of transaction, negotiation and problem-solving to plan projects and events
descriptors.knowledge: Students can participate in planning and negotiating with others, expressing preferences and ideas (AC9LS6C02). They negotiate preferences and manage decisions. They have not yet engaged in transactional or directional language, or problem-solving that addresses genuine issues for real audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students collaborate in activities involving transaction, negotiation and problem-solving — conducting transactions, giving directions, contributing perspectives on shared issues, and producing collaborative outputs for the school community.
elaborations: working together to produce class reference materials to display key vocabulary and promote target language learning
working with peers to produce bilingual signs and posters to promote sustainability within the school community
planning and participating in learning experiences such as a class outing, stating preferences, negotiating and agreeing
planning and completing tasks involving directions to real or virtual locations
participating in transaction situations and the exchange of ideas and preferences
engaging in collaborative projects such as designing a class webpage or making a short video
combining group ideas to collaboratively solve issues relating to young people, contributing and listening to others' perspectives

nodes.label: Transactional and directional language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use transactional language for purchases and services, and directional language for navigation — in simulated and real contexts.
criteria: Conducts a transaction using at least three target language exchanges including a price or option and a decision
Gives or follows at least two directional instructions using appropriate spatial language
nodes.hinge_reason: Transactional and directional language are the foundational practical tasks of the problem-solving dimension. Students who cannot manage basic transactions and directions cannot engage with the more complex collaborative problem-solving and project work in node 2.

width.minimum: Conduct a transaction using at least three target language exchanges including a price or option and a decision; give or follow at least two directional instructions.
width.typical: Role-play transactions across purchase and service contexts; give and follow multi-step directions using maps or spatial references; complete tasks requiring requesting, confirming and following directions to real or virtual locations.
wider: Conduct a full transaction — enquiry, negotiation, decision — in an unrehearsed scenario with an open outcome
Give directions to a genuinely unfamiliar destination using only the target language — including landmarks, distances and transport options

modes.reason: Transaction and direction language needs practice across varied contexts — different transaction types, locations and interlocutor conditions — before it transfers to unrehearsed situations.

nodes.label: Collaborative problem-solving and shared outputs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collaborate in problem-solving activities and produce shared outputs — including digital products and community resources — using negotiation, task delegation and reflection.
criteria: Contributes at least one perspective and negotiates at least one decision in a collaborative task
Contributes to a shared output that could serve a real communicative purpose

width.minimum: Contribute at least one perspective, negotiate at least one decision and reflect on at least one aspect of the process in a collaborative problem-solving task.
width.typical: Work in teams to solve shared problems; contribute and listen to multiple perspectives; produce collaborative outputs (bilingual resources, community materials, digital products); divide and delegate tasks; reflect on collaborative process and outcomes.
wider: Lead a collaborative project from problem identification to shared output — managing task delegation, progress checking and presentation
Produce a genuine community resource in the target language for real school use — evaluate the product's effectiveness for its intended audience

modes.reason: Collaborative problem-solving integrates transactional language (N1) with negotiation, perspective-sharing and project management — all applied in a real production task with genuine stakes.

descriptors.title: Interpret information, ideas and opinions in texts
descriptors.description: interpret information, ideas and opinions in a range of spoken, written and multimodal texts, and respond appropriately to cultural context, purpose and audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate and process information across multiple sources and respond in varied ways (AC9LS6C03). They have not yet evaluated source reliability, interpreted humour and cultural nuance, or compared perspectives across diverse community contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret information, ideas and opinions in a range of target language texts — evaluating source reliability, responding to cultural nuance and humour, and responding appropriately to context, purpose and audience.
elaborations: listening to or reading about topics of interest to young people and sharing opinions or feelings
exchanging personal preferences and perspectives on characters, attitudes and events in imaginative texts
responding to different expressions of humour in texts from target language communities and comparing with Australian humour
listening to, reading or viewing First Nations Australian authors' stories in English and responding in target language
exchanging videos or blogs with a target language community class or student, comparing community and culture
accessing a range of information sources and evaluating their reliability and accuracy
listening to reports and creating an audio or text message to invite a friend to an event

nodes.label: Evaluating sources and interpreting opinion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the reliability and accuracy of target language information sources and express opinions about text content.
criteria: Evaluates at least one source for reliability using at least one explicit criterion
Shares at least one opinion about text content using appropriate agreement or evaluative language
nodes.hinge_reason: Source evaluation is the prerequisite for the synthesis and evaluation demands of subsequent bands. Students who accept all sources at face value cannot synthesise across multiple perspectives or recognise that texts serve particular purposes.

width.minimum: Evaluate at least one source for reliability using at least one explicit criterion; share at least one opinion about text content using appropriate language.
width.typical: Access and evaluate information sources for reliability and accuracy; compare different source types for validity and perspective; share opinions on topics of interest to young people; express agreement and disagreement with authors; exchange preferences and perspectives on characters and events in imaginative texts.
wider: Compare the same event covered in two different target language sources — identify where they agree, where they diverge, and explain what the divergence reveals about each source's perspective
Evaluate a target language social media post on a factual topic — identify specific indicators of reliability and explain the evaluation criteria used

modes.reason: Source evaluation requires explicit criteria and reasoning — students need to articulate what makes a source credible or biased before they can apply this spontaneously.

nodes.label: Responding to cultural nuance, humour and diverse perspectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can respond to cultural nuance, humour and diverse community perspectives in target language texts, including First Nations Australian stories.
criteria: Identifies cultural nuance or humour in a text and explains what cultural knowledge is required
Produces a response appropriate to the text's cultural context — not only its linguistic content

width.minimum: Identify cultural nuance or humour in at least one target language text and explain what cultural knowledge is needed to understand it; produce a culturally appropriate response.
width.typical: Respond to humour in target language texts and compare with Australian conventions; exchange material with target language community peers; listen to First Nations Australian authors' stories and respond in the target language; respond to texts from diverse target language communities; select response form appropriate to cultural context.
wider: Compare target language community and Australian expressions of humour in two texts — identify what cultural knowledge each assumes and explain what this reveals about each culture
Produce a response to a First Nations Australian author's story in the target language — addressing both content and cultural significance

modes.reason: Cultural nuance and humour awareness develops through encountering diverse text types and cultural contexts. Each new cultural text context reveals different aspects of the language-culture relationship.

descriptors.title: Interpret and adjust language for cultural contexts
descriptors.description: interpret and adjust non-verbal, spoken and written language to convey meaning in the target language in familiar and some unfamiliar cultural contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply strategies to interpret and convey meaning — including managing non-equivalent expressions and creating bilingual resources (AC9LS6C04). They have not yet compared their own translations with others, interpreted context-dependent vocabulary, or created cultural responses for community audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret and adjust language to convey meaning in familiar and some unfamiliar cultural contexts — including translation comparison, context-dependent meaning, and cultural response production.
elaborations: comparing own translation of a text with classmates, commenting on similarities and differences and possible reasons
creating informative responses to cultural representations of target language communities in Australia, explaining language or images in terms of cultural associations
interpreting short messages or communications, reflecting on challenges of transferring meaning between languages
viewing authentic material of target language speakers discussing their culture and language, then responding with personal perspectives
selecting and explaining individual words or phrases whose meaning can be affected by context
presenting information gathered from different types of texts and modes to create an overview of a topic of interest

nodes.label: Context-dependent meaning and translation comparison
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret words and expressions whose meaning varies by context, and compare their translations with others' — reflecting on the choices made.
criteria: Identifies at least one target language word with context-dependent meaning and provides two different meanings with examples
Compares a translation with another version and identifies at least one difference, explaining what caused it
nodes.hinge_reason: Context-dependent meaning is a persistent comprehension challenge that produces systematic errors when unresolved. Students who do not recognise that words can shift meaning by context misread authentic texts regularly.

width.minimum: Identify at least one word with context-dependent meaning and explain two different meanings; compare a translation with at least one other version and identify at least one difference.
width.typical: Interpret context-dependent expressions across varied text types; compare translations with classmates, noting similarities and differences; reflect on challenges of meaning transfer between languages; select and explain vocabulary that shifts meaning by context; interpret short messages and informal communications.
wider: Collect target language words with context-dependent meanings — produce a mini-guide showing each meaning with a sentence example
Translate the same short text individually then compare all translations — identify every decision point where versions differ and explain what caused variation

modes.reason: Context-dependent vocabulary awareness builds through accumulating examples across different word categories and contexts. A bank of examples builds the wariness that prevents automatic misreading.

nodes.label: Creating cultural responses and explanations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create informative responses to cultural representations — reviews, vlogs, explainers — that convey cultural meaning alongside content description.
criteria: Creates a cultural response that explains at least one language or cultural element in terms of its associations — not only describes it
Incorporates personal perspective alongside cultural information

width.minimum: Create at least one cultural response that explains at least one language or cultural element in terms of cultural associations — not only content description.
width.typical: Create informative responses to target language community cultural events, exhibitions or media; explain cultural associations of specific language or images; respond to authentic discussions about culture and language incorporating personal perspectives; present information from multiple source types on a topic of interest.
wider: Produce a critical review of a target language community cultural event — incorporating cultural analysis alongside personal evaluation
Create a bilingual cultural explainer for an Australian audience — making decisions about what requires cultural explanation for an audience with no target language background

modes.reason: Cultural response production integrates context-dependent meaning interpretation (N1) with cultural knowledge and production — students must interpret what cultural elements mean and then communicate that meaning to an audience.

descriptors.title: Create texts for specific purposes with appropriate vocabulary and conventions
descriptors.description: create and present spoken, written and multimodal, informative and imaginative texts for specific purposes, selecting vocabulary, expressions, grammatical structures, features and conventions appropriate to text type and context
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create texts using varied structures and text-type conventions (AC9LS6C05). They create for familiar formats and purposes. They have not yet selected vocabulary and structures deliberately for a specific purpose or created biographical and narrative texts integrating multiple text features.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and present informative and imaginative texts for specific purposes — selecting vocabulary, grammatical structures and conventions appropriate to text type, purpose and context.
elaborations: designing a digital poster or electronic brochure to advertise a social event related to lifestyles or cultural events
using digital tools to create a slideshow with audio about a planned trip to a target language community region
reporting on own and others' experiences of events
creating a print or digital poster to promote travel to a significant cultural location on a First Nations Country/Place
composing bilingual menus, recipes or programs for target language community-themed events
creating subtitles, captions or commentaries for texts that inform the school community
creating cartoons, role-plays or short stories about a past event or a dream for the future
using voice recording and digital presentation software to create, perform or record imaginative texts
preparing a biographical account of an influential figure
using up-to-date and emerging terms relating to pop culture, technology and media when creating texts

nodes.label: Selecting vocabulary and structures for purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select vocabulary, expressions and grammatical structures deliberately to suit the purpose of a text — moving beyond default or most familiar choices.
criteria: Creates a text with at least three deliberate vocabulary or structural choices explained in terms of purpose
The text is consistently appropriate in register and vocabulary for its specific purpose
nodes.hinge_reason: Deliberate vocabulary and structure selection for purpose is the move from producing any text to producing the right text for a given context. Students who produce default texts regardless of purpose cannot meet the audience diversity demands of subsequent bands.

width.minimum: Create a text and identify at least three vocabulary or structural choices made because of the text's specific purpose — explaining the reason for each.
width.typical: Create texts with deliberate vocabulary and structure selection across varied formats — event materials, travel texts, biographical accounts, social media content; use contemporary and emerging vocabulary appropriate to context; select tense and register for purpose; apply text-type conventions consistently.
wider: Create two versions of the same content for different purposes — explicitly contrast the vocabulary, structure and register choices made for each
Annotate a produced text — marking every deliberate vocabulary or structural choice and explaining the purpose reason for each

modes.reason: Selection awareness requires metacognitive attention to language choices. Annotation tasks and contrastive production scaffold the metalinguistic awareness needed for deliberate selection.

nodes.label: Creating and presenting across formats and audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create and present texts across a range of informative and imaginative formats — using conventions appropriate to each and presenting for real audiences.
criteria: Creates texts in at least two different formats with conventions appropriate to each
Presents at least one text to an audience using appropriate delivery for the purpose

width.minimum: Create and present texts in at least two different formats using appropriate conventions for each.
width.typical: Create digital slideshows, event materials, travel texts, biographical profiles, cartoons, short stories, role-plays, subtitled content, bilingual menus and recipes, First Nations Country/Place travel materials; use voice recording and digital tools for performance and publication.
wider: Create an original short recording or performance in the target language — demonstrating command of spoken language, visual design and presentation conventions simultaneously
Create a biographical account for a specific audience and purpose — annotating every deliberate vocabulary or structural choice

modes.reason: Text creation competence across formats develops through working with varied text types and purposes. The range in the descriptor — digital, biographical, narrative, performative — is the intended development condition.

descriptors.title: Exchange information in familiar contexts
descriptors.description: interact with others using modelled language to exchange information in familiar contexts about self and personal worlds
descriptors.knowledge: No formal prior study of the target language assumed (Y7-10 Entry sequence). Students bring general communicative competence in English and may have informal or incidental exposure to the target language. They have not yet learned to operate within the conventions and structures of the target language to exchange personal information.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interact with others in the target language using modelled language structures to exchange information about themselves, their families, routines and personal worlds in familiar contexts, making appropriate choices about formality.
elaborations: exchanging greetings with others using appropriate formal or informal language
introducing and describing themselves, others and possessions
expressing likes, dislikes and preferences using simple modelled structures
interviewing others about their families, pets, likes and dislikes, hobbies and leisure time activities
responding to questions about feelings
conversing with others about routines, events and leisure activities using language associated with time and place
discussing significant or special events in their lives with peers or target language community members

nodes.label: Greetings and basic social exchanges
nodes.checkpoint: Students can exchange greetings and basic social courtesies in the target language, choosing appropriate formal or informal register.
criteria: Can produce at least two contextually appropriate greetings in the target language (one formal, one informal)
Can identify and correct a register mismatch when given a scenario (e.g. using informal language with a teacher)
nodes.hinge_reason: Greeting and register conventions are the entry point to all subsequent interaction. Students who have not internalised the formal/informal distinction will misapply register throughout EC01 and EC02 — an error that compounds across all spoken interaction descriptors.

width.minimum: Use a small set of modelled greetings and leave-takings in at least one context (e.g. greeting a teacher or peer).
width.typical: Distinguish formal and informal greetings; use modelled phrases to greet, farewell and respond to social courtesies across classroom and simulated social contexts.
wider: Compare greeting conventions across two or more cultures where the target language is spoken — identify where register rules differ from English conventions
Explore how greeting conventions shift across digital communication contexts (messaging, email) vs spoken interaction in the target language

modes.reason: Students need repeated, low-stakes exposure to greetings across varied simulated contexts before register choices become automatic. Role-play, choral practice and modelled exchanges build the repertoire from which appropriate selection can occur.
Varying the social context (peer, teacher, stranger, digital) ensures register awareness does not lock to a single modelled example.

nodes.label: Introducing and describing self and others
nodes.checkpoint: Students can introduce themselves and others and describe personal details (name, age, family, possessions) using modelled structures in the target language.
criteria: Can introduce themselves using at least three accurate modelled structures covering name, location and family
Can respond accurately to simple personal questions from a peer or teacher in the target language
nodes.hinge_reason: First- and third-person structures used for self-description underpin the grammar nodes (EU02) and all subsequent personal exchange tasks. Students who cannot produce these with basic accuracy will be unable to participate meaningfully in EC01's interview and conversation tasks.

width.minimum: Introduce themselves using at least three personal details (e.g. name, where they live, one family member) with modelled structures.
width.typical: Introduce and describe self, family members and peers; describe possessions and basic personal characteristics; respond to and ask simple questions about personal worlds using modelled language.
wider: Produce a short multimodal self-introduction (e.g. a short recorded or illustrated profile) combining spoken and written target language
Interview a peer and introduce them to the class — shifting from first person to third person structures

modes.reason: Accuracy in person agreement and possessive structures requires practice to become reliable. Errors here (e.g. person agreement, possessives) are procedural rather than conceptual — massed practice with corrective feedback is the lever.

nodes.label: Expressing likes, dislikes and preferences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express likes, dislikes and preferences about familiar topics using modelled structures in the target language.
criteria: Can express at least one like and one dislike using a modelled structure in the target language
Can respond to a peer's expressed preference with a simple agreement or contrast

width.minimum: Express at least one like and one dislike using a modelled structure tied to a familiar topic (e.g. hobbies, food).
width.typical: Use a range of modelled structures to express and compare likes, dislikes and preferences across multiple familiar topics; respond to others' expressions of preference with simple agreement or contrast.
wider: Survey peers about their preferences and compile results — shifting from personal to aggregated expression ('most people in our class like…')
Compare how preference is expressed differently across formal and informal registers in the target language

modes.reason: Students need to encounter preference expression across enough topic areas (hobbies, food, music, sport) that they can transfer the structure flexibly rather than being locked to one rehearsed topic.

nodes.label: Exchanging information about routines and daily life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interact with others to exchange information about routines, events and daily life activities using modelled language in familiar contexts.
criteria: Can ask and respond to at least three questions about daily routines in a structured exchange in the target language
Uses modelled time or place language to contextualise at least one statement in the exchange

width.minimum: Participate in a structured exchange (question and answer format) about at least one aspect of daily routine using modelled language.
width.typical: Conduct and respond to simple interviews or conversations about routines, leisure activities, significant events and daily life; use modelled language associated with time and place to add context to exchanges.
wider: Interact (via secure digital platforms where available) with peers or simulated peers from a target language community — comparing daily routines across cultural contexts
Extend exchanges to include past or future events using emerging tense structures, connecting to EU02

modes.reason: This node integrates the greetings, self-description and preference structures from nodes 1–3 into sustained, contextualised interaction. Teaching investment is in supporting students to move fluidly across structures within a single exchange rather than producing each in isolation.

descriptors.title: Develop language for classroom exchanges
descriptors.description: develop language to interact in exchanges, routines, tasks and responsibilities related to classroom and interests
descriptors.knowledge: Students can exchange basic personal information in familiar contexts using modelled language (AC9LS8EC01). They have not yet developed the functional classroom language needed to participate in the routines, tasks and responsibilities of the target language learning environment.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interact in the target language to manage classroom routines, ask for help or permission, follow and give instructions, express opinions and participate in classroom tasks and collaborative activities.
elaborations: responding appropriately to commands or requests
following and giving instructions
asking for help, information or permission
expressing opinions and thoughts using set phrases
assisting the teacher with classroom routines and duties
developing the use of spontaneous interjections, expressions and gestures to maintain simple interactions
playing games and completing activities with peers incorporating language to share, praise, encourage and take turns
making a simplified board game to reinforce learning vocabulary and grammatical points while playing with others
playing a true and false game relating to routines, interests and personal details

nodes.label: Following and giving classroom instructions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can follow modelled instructions and commands in the target language and attempt to give simple instructions to peers.
criteria: Responds correctly to at least four common classroom commands in the target language without translation support
Can give at least one simple instruction to a peer in the target language
nodes.hinge_reason: Classroom instruction language is the operational medium of the language classroom. Students who cannot follow basic commands cannot access the task structures through which all subsequent language learning occurs. This is a functional floor, not an enrichment item.

width.minimum: Follow at least four common classroom commands in the target language reliably; attempt to give one or two simple instructions.
width.typical: Follow and give a range of classroom instructions (open/close, listen, write, read, work with a partner); respond appropriately to teacher commands during regular classroom routines.
wider: Lead a class activity segment using only target language instructions — managing transitions and turn-taking
Create a bilingual classroom reference resource (poster, card set) translating common commands between the target language and English

modes.reason: Reliable response to instructions requires automaticity — students need repeated encounters with the same commands in varied classroom routines until response becomes habitual rather than effortful.

nodes.label: Asking for help, information and permission
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use modelled phrases to ask for help, clarification or permission in the target language.
criteria: Can produce at least two contextually appropriate asking phrases in the target language without prompting
Can distinguish between formal and informal address when making a request

width.minimum: Use at least two modelled phrases for asking for help or permission in a classroom context.
width.typical: Use a set of modelled phrases to ask for help, check understanding, request repetition, ask for information or seek permission; distinguish appropriately between formal and informal forms of address when making requests.
wider: Extend asking strategies to unfamiliar contexts — e.g. a simulated phone call, an email to a teacher, or a transaction scenario
Develop a personal 'survival phrase' card listing key asking strategies and add to it across the unit

modes.reason: Students need a bank of asking strategies rather than one memorised phrase. Exposure to multiple modelled forms across varied asking scenarios builds the flexibility needed to manage breakdowns in communication.

nodes.label: Expressing opinions and reactions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express simple opinions and reactions using set phrases in the target language.
criteria: Can use at least two different opinion phrases in the target language in a classroom exchange
Can respond to a peer's opinion with agreement or a simple contrasting phrase

width.minimum: Use at least two modelled set phrases to express agreement, disagreement or a simple opinion in a classroom context.
width.typical: Use a range of set phrases to express opinions, reactions and thoughts; respond to others' opinions with agreement or simple contrast; use spontaneous interjections and expressions to maintain simple interactions.
wider: Participate in a structured classroom debate or 'four corners' opinion activity using target language opinion phrases
Collect and compare opinion expressions across different registers — identify which are appropriate in which social contexts

modes.reason: Opinion expression at Y7-8 entry is phrase-dependent — students need a bank of set expressions before they can participate authentically in opinion exchanges. Varied low-stakes opinion tasks build this bank.

nodes.label: Participating in collaborative tasks and activities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in collaborative classroom tasks and games using target language for sharing, encouraging, taking turns and completing joint activities.
criteria: Uses at least one functional target language phrase (instruction, asking, opinion) spontaneously during a collaborative task — not only in a scripted exchange
Can complete a paired or group activity with the target language as the primary medium of interaction

width.minimum: Complete one collaborative classroom task using target language for at least one functional purpose (e.g. taking turns, asking a partner for information).
width.typical: Participate in games, paired activities and group tasks using target language to share, praise, encourage and coordinate; use classroom instruction language to manage the activity.
wider: Design and facilitate a simple classroom game that requires participants to use target language throughout (not just as a trigger for an English activity)
Facilitate a class routine (roll call, task distribution, instructions to peers) using only target language
