modes.reason: Collaborative tasks are where instructions, asking strategies and opinion phrases from nodes 1–3 operate simultaneously. The teaching investment is in creating task structures where students must draw on multiple functional language sets at once.

descriptors.title: Organise activities with peers
descriptors.description: engage in modelled non-verbal, spoken and written exchanges with peers to organise activities relating to daily life and school environment
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interact using modelled language for personal exchange and classroom routines (AC9LS8EC01, AC9LS8EC02). They have not yet used the target language to organise joint activities or communicate across non-verbal, spoken and written modes simultaneously.
descriptors.endpoint: Students engage in non-verbal, spoken and written exchanges in the target language with peers to plan, organise and carry out activities related to daily life and the school environment, using modelled language appropriate to context.
elaborations: working with peers to produce bilingual signs/flyers and posters to promote sustainability and waste reduction
working together to produce class reference materials such as wall charts or visuals to display key vocabulary and structures
participating in imagined scenarios such as asking for and giving directions, information and assistance
participating in real or simulated transactions such as purchasing food or tickets
emailing, messaging or using secure online applications to chat about plans and daily life experiences using present tense and immediate future

nodes.label: Coordinating and planning with peers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use modelled spoken and written exchanges to coordinate a simple joint activity with a peer in the target language.
criteria: Can produce at least three modelled phrases to coordinate a joint activity with a peer in the target language
Can exchange a short written message (note or digital message) in the target language about a planned activity

width.minimum: Participate in one structured planning or organising exchange with a peer (e.g. assigning roles, agreeing on a plan) using at least three modelled phrases.
width.typical: Use spoken and written modelled language to plan, negotiate and carry out a collaborative activity; exchange messages or notes about plans, timings or roles using present and near-future structures.
wider: Use a secure digital messaging or email platform to plan a real or simulated activity with a peer entirely in the target language
Compare how organising language differs between spoken and written modes in the target language — identify conventions specific to each

modes.reason: Students need exposure to a range of organising exchanges (assigning, scheduling, confirming, adjusting) before they can manage the planning demands of EC03's collaborative tasks. Building this repertoire through varied simulated planning scenarios is the primary lever.

nodes.label: Non-verbal communication and multimodal exchanges
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise the role of non-verbal communication in the target language context and combine non-verbal, spoken and written elements in exchanges.
criteria: Can combine at least two communication modes (spoken, written, non-verbal) in a single organised exchange
Can identify at least one non-verbal convention in the target language community that differs from Australian English norms

width.minimum: Participate in one exchange that requires combining at least two modes (e.g. spoken + gesture, written + visual) in the target language.
width.typical: Engage in modelled scenarios (e.g. simulated transactions, directions, collaborative tasks) that require coordinating spoken, written and non-verbal elements; recognise culturally specific non-verbal conventions in the target language community.
wider: Participate in a charades or mime scenario and reflect on which meanings transfer across cultures and which require cultural knowledge to interpret
Produce a bilingual resource (poster, flyer, digital notice) that combines visual and written elements to communicate to a mixed-language audience

modes.reason: Non-verbal conventions in the target language vary significantly across cultural communities. Exposure to varied scenarios prevents students from assuming that non-verbal cues are universal — a misconception with practical intercultural consequences.

nodes.label: Simulated and real transactions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in simulated or real transactional exchanges (e.g. purchasing, requesting services, following directions) in the target language.
criteria: Can complete a basic transactional exchange (request, respond, clarify) in a modelled scenario using target language
Integrates at least one asking or clarifying strategy from prior learning into the exchange

width.minimum: Participate in one scripted or semi-scripted transactional role-play in the target language (e.g. a simulated purchase, asking for and giving directions).
width.typical: Engage in a range of simulated transactional scenarios; use modelled language for requesting, responding, clarifying and completing a transaction; integrate asking strategies from EC02.
wider: Navigate a real or simulated digital service (e.g. a map, timetable or menu from a target language community) to locate and act on information
Produce a class resource (signs, posters, reference materials) in the target language that could support real transactions in a target language environment

modes.reason: Transactional exchanges require students to simultaneously manage topic vocabulary, asking strategies (EC02), appropriate register (EC01) and non-verbal conventions (node 2). Role-play scenarios that require all of these to operate together are the key teaching structure.

descriptors.title: Locate and process information in texts
descriptors.description: locate and process information and ideas in familiar spoken, written and multimodal texts, responding in ways appropriate to cultural context, purpose and audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students enter the Y7-10 sequence without prior formal target language study. They bring general literacy strategies from English and may have incidental exposure to the target language. They have not yet applied information-locating strategies to target language texts across spoken, written and multimodal modes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students locate and process specific information and ideas from familiar spoken, written and multimodal texts in the target language, and respond in ways that demonstrate awareness of cultural context, purpose and intended audience.
elaborations: identifying details and key points of information from authentic resources or teacher-created texts
locating, classifying and summarising information collected from sources such as menus, notices, timetables, packaging or brochures
conducting simple surveys or interviews with others about familiar topics, then interpreting results
listening to, reading or viewing First Nations Australian authors' stories in English and responding to them in spoken or written target language
identifying key points of information in short spoken or recorded texts such as phone messages, announcements or television segments
identifying and describing characters and events in a movie, story or comic by responding to simple questions
navigating secure online applications such as digital maps or timetables to find out about transport and services in a target language community
locating specific information about a person, place or event, describing characters, events and locations

nodes.label: Identifying key information in familiar texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific details and key points of information in familiar spoken, written or multimodal texts in the target language.
criteria: Can locate at least three specific pieces of information from a familiar target language text using comprehension strategies
Can identify the purpose and intended audience of a familiar text type in the target language
nodes.hinge_reason: Locating specific information is the prerequisite for all processing and responding tasks in EC04. Students who rely only on global comprehension (understanding 'roughly what it is about') cannot satisfy the descriptor's demand to locate and process specific ideas. EC05's translation and interpretation tasks also depend on this capacity.

width.minimum: Identify at least three specific pieces of information from one familiar text type (e.g. a menu, timetable, short announcement or simple written notice) in the target language.
width.typical: Locate and classify key information from a range of familiar text types (menus, notices, timetables, packaging, schedules); use comprehension strategies (skimming, scanning, using contextual cues) to locate specific details.
wider: Compare information located in equivalent text types from the target language community and Australia — identify differences in how information is structured or presented
Navigate an authentic digital resource (map, timetable, website) from a target language community to locate specific information for a real purpose

modes.reason: Students need explicit instruction in comprehension strategies (scanning for key words, using layout and headings, making predictions from context) before they can apply them independently to target language texts. Modelling the strategy process — not just assigning texts — is the lever.
Exposing students to a range of familiar text types ensures comprehension strategies are not locked to one text format. Scanning a menu requires different cues than scanning a timetable.

nodes.label: Processing information across text types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can process information from spoken, written and multimodal texts in the target language, summarising or classifying key ideas.
criteria: Can identify and summarise key points from a short spoken or multimodal text in the target language
Can compare or classify information from at least two texts on the same topic

width.minimum: Process information from at least one spoken or multimodal text (not only written) — e.g. identify key points from a short recording or video.
width.typical: Locate and process information from spoken, written and multimodal texts; summarise, classify or compare information across sources; conduct and report simple information-gathering tasks such as surveys or brief interviews.
wider: Compare information across two or more sources on the same topic — identify where sources agree or differ
Locate and process information from a First Nations Australian context presented in or translated into the target language — reflect on what is gained or lost in the shift

modes.reason: Processing spoken texts requires different strategies from written text processing — prosody, pace and speaker variation all carry meaning. Ensuring students process across modalities prevents over-reliance on written text as the primary comprehension mode.

nodes.label: Responding appropriately to cultural context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can respond to texts in ways that demonstrate awareness of the cultural context, purpose and audience of the original text.
criteria: Can identify at least one cultural reference or contextual feature in a target language text and explain its significance
Produces a response that is appropriate to the purpose and audience of the original text

width.minimum: Produce one response to a target language text that demonstrates awareness of at least one contextual factor (e.g. the text's purpose, its intended audience, or a cultural reference within it).
width.typical: Respond to a range of target language texts by identifying cultural references, intended purpose and audience; produce responses (written, spoken or multimodal) that are appropriate to the context and audience of the original text.
wider: Respond to imaginative texts (story, comic, film clip) from the target language community by identifying and discussing cultural assumptions or values embedded in the text
Compare responses to the same text produced by a target language community member and an Australian English speaker — identify where cultural context shapes interpretation differently

modes.reason: Cultural context awareness requires students to move beyond 'what does it say' to 'why does it say it this way, and for whom'. Explicit discussion scaffolds — who is this for? what does the writer/speaker assume? what is left unsaid? — support this shift.

descriptors.title: Interpret and convey meaning in the target language
descriptors.description: develop and begin to apply strategies to interpret, translate and convey meaning in the target language in familiar contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate and process information in familiar target language texts (AC9LS8EC04). They have not yet developed or applied explicit strategies for interpreting, translating or conveying meaning between languages — these skills are emerging and require explicit scaffolding at this entry point.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop and begin to apply a set of interpretation and translation strategies for familiar contexts, including using dictionaries, recognising cognates and false friends, inferring from context, and understanding that translation involves more than word-for-word equivalence.
elaborations: translating short texts such as public signs or community notices from the target language to English, and vice versa, identifying parts that are difficult to translate
using print and online dictionaries to assist in the translation of simple texts
recognising cognates and the possibility of encountering false friends when translating between the target language and English
identifying cognate patterns that can be used to predict meaning or obtain gist
developing techniques to infer meaning of unfamiliar vocabulary and structures in a text
understanding the distinction between literal and non-literal translation
recognising that abbreviations are used in both the target language and English texts
observing live or recorded target language interactions in different contexts and recognising that communication extends beyond words
noticing variations in language use based on the age, gender and social relationships of speakers and the context and purpose of the communication

nodes.label: Using dictionaries and reference tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use print and online dictionaries to assist with interpreting and translating familiar target language words and short phrases.
criteria: Can use a dictionary to locate the meaning of an unfamiliar word and select the contextually appropriate definition
Can identify when a dictionary definition does not fit the context and attempt an alternative interpretation
nodes.hinge_reason: Without functional dictionary use, students cannot independently interpret unfamiliar language — they are entirely dependent on teacher-provided glossaries. This limits access to the wider text encounters that develop interpretation strategies in nodes 2–4.

width.minimum: Use a dictionary (print or digital) to look up at least five unfamiliar words and check the result in context.
width.typical: Use dictionaries and reference tools to assist with translation and interpretation tasks; recognise that dictionary entries give multiple possible meanings and that context determines the right choice; develop habits of cross-checking.
wider: Compare results from multiple translation tools (dictionary, online translator, peer) for the same text — evaluate which is most accurate for a given context and explain why
Identify one case where a direct dictionary translation produces an inaccurate or awkward result — explain what additional knowledge is needed

modes.reason: Dictionary use is a procedural skill — looking up, choosing between multiple entries, checking in context. Reliable use requires practice across varied word types and contexts until the habit is automatic.

nodes.label: Recognising cognates and false friends
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify cognate patterns between the target language and English as a meaning-prediction strategy, and recognise that 'false friends' exist.
criteria: Can identify at least three cognates between the target language and English and use them to successfully predict meaning in a new text
Can identify at least one false friend and explain why it is misleading

width.minimum: Identify at least three cognates between the target language and English and use them to predict meaning in a text; identify at least one example of a false friend.
width.typical: Use cognate recognition as a systematic strategy for predicting meaning in unfamiliar texts; build awareness of false friend patterns; recognise that cognate reliability varies across target languages.
wider: Investigate cognate patterns systematically — e.g. common suffix or prefix patterns that reliably predict meaning in the target language — and create a class reference resource
Research the historical or linguistic reasons why a known false friend diverged in meaning between the target language and English

modes.reason: Cognate recognition as a strategy requires exposure to enough examples for the pattern to become intuitive. Students need to encounter cognates across multiple text types before they will apply the strategy spontaneously rather than only when prompted.

nodes.label: Inferring meaning from context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use contextual cues (surrounding text, visual elements, known vocabulary) to infer the meaning of unfamiliar words and expressions.
criteria: Can make at least one successful inference about an unfamiliar word using contextual cues and explain the reasoning
Can identify the type of cue used (surrounding words, visual, topic knowledge) for each inference attempt

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least one successful inference from context in a target language text — explain what cues they used.
width.typical: Apply a range of inferencing strategies (known vocabulary, grammatical patterns, visual context, topic knowledge) to unfamiliar words and expressions in target language texts; distinguish between high-confidence and low-confidence inferences.
wider: Observe target language interactions (recorded or live) and identify how non-verbal and contextual cues support meaning-making where linguistic knowledge is incomplete
Compare inferencing strategies with a peer — identify where different prior knowledge leads to different inferences from the same text

modes.reason: Inferencing is a strategy that must be made explicit before students will apply it independently. Think-aloud modelling of the inferencing process — 'I don't know this word, but I can see that... and the topic is... so it probably means...' — builds the reasoning habit.

nodes.label: Understanding that translation involves more than word equivalence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that direct word-for-word translation does not always convey accurate meaning, and can explain at least one reason why.
criteria: Can identify at least one expression in the target language that cannot be translated word-for-word and explain why
Can evaluate an automated or peer translation of a short text and identify at least one improvement

width.minimum: Identify one expression or phrase in the target language that does not translate word-for-word into English; explain what additional knowledge is needed.
width.typical: Recognise the distinction between literal and non-literal translation; identify idioms, fixed expressions and abbreviated forms that require interpretation beyond word equivalence; understand that abbreviations, slang and digital communication conventions vary between languages.
wider: Analyse an automated translation of a familiar text — identify specific errors or awkward renderings and explain what the tool missed
Translate a short familiar English text into the target language and compare it with a classmate's or automated version — discuss where choices diverged and why

modes.reason: Understanding translation as interpretation rather than substitution draws on all prior nodes — dictionary use, cognate awareness, contextual inferencing — and adds the conceptual insight that meaning is shaped by culture and context, not only by language structure. This prepares students for EC05's Y9-10 demands.

descriptors.title: Create informative and imaginative texts
descriptors.description: create spoken, written and multimodal, informative and imaginative texts using appropriate vocabulary, expressions, grammatical structures, and some textual conventions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate and process information in familiar texts (AC9LS8EC04) and interact using modelled language (AC9LS8EC01–03). They have not yet created extended spoken, written or multimodal texts in the target language for specific purposes and audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create spoken, written and multimodal texts (informative and imaginative) in the target language, selecting appropriate vocabulary, expressions and grammatical structures, and applying some textual conventions appropriate to the text type, purpose and audience.
elaborations: preparing a presentation by following a format that includes a greeting, introduction and sequenced ideas
composing and performing a role-play based on a real or imagined scenario
producing informative texts that combine print, digital or visual elements for specific audiences
creating a print or digital poster to promote travel to a significant cultural location on a First Nations Country
creating resources such as posters or displays to create awareness of relevant issues
writing a story by composing captions for a sequence of pictures or images
creating characters, situations or events in a range of texts designed to entertain others
writing the first part of a short narrative and exchanging with a peer to write the next section
planning and presenting a performance for non-target-language speakers, with bilingual and explanatory commentary

nodes.label: Structuring a text for purpose and audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the structural conventions of a familiar target language text type and apply them in their own text production.
criteria: Produces a text with a recognisable structure appropriate to the chosen text type (not just a list of sentences)
Can identify the intended audience for the text and explain at least one structural choice that reflects that audience
nodes.hinge_reason: Text structure awareness is the precondition for all subsequent text creation. Students who produce language without any structural frame produce utterances, not texts — they cannot meet the descriptor's demand for textual conventions or demonstrate audience awareness, both of which require a sense of the text as a whole.

width.minimum: Produce one text in the target language that follows a recognisable structural convention (e.g. a presentation with greeting, introduction and sequenced ideas; a narrative with beginning, middle and end).
width.typical: Prepare and produce texts across at least two formats (e.g. a spoken presentation and a written informative text); apply structural conventions appropriate to each text type and identify audience for each text.
wider: Compare the structural conventions of equivalent text types (e.g. a presentation, a notice, a story) in the target language and in English — identify where conventions align and where they diverge
Produce a bilingual text for a mixed-language audience — consider how structural and linguistic choices change when the audience changes

modes.reason: Students need explicit instruction in the structural conventions of target language text types before they can apply them. Annotated model texts, structural frameworks and co-constructed exemplars help students see text organisation as a deliberate choice, not a default.

nodes.label: Selecting vocabulary and expressions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select vocabulary and expressions appropriate to the topic, purpose and audience of their text rather than defaulting to the first known word.
criteria: Can identify and explain at least two deliberate vocabulary choices in their own text
Does not default entirely to direct English-to-target-language substitution — uses at least some target language expressions or set phrases

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least two deliberate vocabulary or expression choices in a target language text — can explain why each choice suits the purpose or audience.
width.typical: Select vocabulary and expressions consciously for appropriateness to topic, purpose and register; use set phrases and idiomatic expressions where appropriate; avoid over-reliance on direct translation from English.
wider: Revise a draft text by substituting more precise or contextually appropriate vocabulary — compare the original and revised versions and discuss the effect of the changes
Build a personal vocabulary journal or resource that organises known vocabulary by topic, purpose and register rather than only by translation

modes.reason: Deliberate vocabulary selection requires a repertoire — students who know only one word for each concept cannot make choices. Building vocabulary breadth across topic areas and registers is the precondition for meaningful selection.

nodes.label: Applying grammatical structures in text creation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply familiar grammatical structures accurately enough in a target language text to convey intended meaning to an audience.
criteria: Produces a text in which grammatical structures are accurate enough for the meaning to be understood by an audience unfamiliar with the student's intent
Can identify and self-correct at least one grammatical error in their own draft during revision

width.minimum: Produce a text in which the grammatical structures required for the text type (e.g. present tense verbs, basic agreement, interrogative forms) are applied with sufficient accuracy to convey meaning.
width.typical: Apply a range of grammatical structures (tense, agreement, sentence types) in both informative and imaginative texts; self-correct common errors during drafting; connect ideas using basic connectives.
wider: Review and revise a peer's draft text — identify grammatical errors that affect meaning and suggest corrections with explanations
Experiment with grammatical variation (e.g. changing sentence type, adding detail with prepositions or adjectives) to observe how it changes the effect of a text

modes.reason: Grammatical accuracy in text production is a fluency issue at Y7-8 — students typically understand the structures but apply them inconsistently under the cognitive load of text creation. Focused drafting-and-revision cycles rather than isolated grammar exercises are the most productive practice structure.

nodes.label: Creating imaginative texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create an imaginative text (narrative, role-play, performance, visual story) in the target language that communicates ideas for an intended audience.
criteria: Produces a complete imaginative text in the target language with a recognisable intent and structure
Can explain at least one deliberate creative choice in their text and its intended effect on the audience

width.minimum: Produce one imaginative text in the target language with a recognisable communicative intent and at least one deliberate creative choice (e.g. a character detail, an event sequence, a humorous or dramatic element).
width.typical: Create imaginative texts across a range of formats (narrative, role-play, performance, illustrated story, script); make deliberate creative choices about character, situation and effect; present imaginative work to an audience.
wider: Collaborate with a peer on a jointly-authored imaginative text — negotiate plot, character and language choices across the collaboration
Experiment with creative techniques from target language literary or cultural traditions (e.g. story structure conventions, poetic forms, performance styles)

modes.reason: Imaginative text creation integrates structural awareness, vocabulary selection and grammatical application from nodes 1–3 into a purposeful creative act. The teaching investment is in supporting students to see creative constraint (text type, audience, purpose) as enabling rather than limiting.

descriptors.title: Target language sound system
descriptors.description: recognise and use features of the target language sound system, including pitch, rhythm, stress, pronunciation and intonation, and demonstrate understanding of how these are represented in familiar contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students enter the Y7-10 sequence with no formal prior study of the target language sound system. They bring awareness of English phonology and may have incidental exposure to the target language's sounds. They have not yet systematically learned the phonological features of the target language or how these are represented in its writing system.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise and use the key features of the target language sound system — vowels, consonants, intonation patterns, stress and pitch — and demonstrate understanding of how these are represented in familiar written and spoken contexts.
elaborations: recognising that many letters of the target language and English have the same sounds, with some exceptions
understanding that in some target languages there is only one sound for each vowel
recognising and practising different vowel and consonant sounds through simple rhymes
spelling own name aloud in the target language
recognising variations in intonation required to form statements, questions and exclamations
listening to statements, exclamations and questions read aloud, using intonation cues and transcribing what is heard
using own phonetic notes to help pronunciation and intonation
applying pronunciation rules to common performance texts such as tongue twisters

nodes.label: Target language vowel and consonant sounds
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and produce the key vowel and consonant sounds of the target language, including those that differ from English.
criteria: Can identify at least three target language sounds that differ from English and attempt to produce them accurately
Can recognise target language vowel sounds when heard in isolation and in words
nodes.hinge_reason: Vowel and consonant accuracy underpins all spoken production. Students who do not develop accurate sound discrimination early will produce habituated errors that are progressively harder to correct as automaticity develops. EU01's pronunciation and intonation demands cannot be met without a phonological foundation.

width.minimum: Identify and attempt to produce at least three target language sounds that differ from English equivalents; recognise these sounds when heard.
width.typical: Distinguish and produce the full vowel set of the target language; recognise and practise consonant sounds that differ from English; use rhymes, tongue twisters or choral reading to build phonological accuracy.
wider: Compare the vowel systems of the target language and English — map similarities and differences using a visual reference
Research and practise regional pronunciation variations within the target language — identify at least one sound that varies across communities

modes.reason: Phonological accuracy is a fluency issue — students often understand the difference between sounds but produce them inconsistently. Repeated, corrective oral practice (choral work, minimal pairs, recording and listening back) builds the muscular habit that underpins accurate production.

nodes.label: Intonation and sentence melody
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and use appropriate intonation patterns for statements, questions and exclamations in the target language.
criteria: Can produce audibly different intonation patterns for a statement and a question in the target language
Can identify the intonation pattern used in a short spoken text when listening

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least two distinct intonation patterns (e.g. statement vs question) in spoken target language production.
width.typical: Recognise and use intonation patterns for statements, questions and exclamations; transcribe spoken texts using intonation cues; use intonation variation in role-play and spoken tasks.
wider: Listen to and compare intonation in audio texts from different target language communities — identify where melody differs from Australian English
Record own spoken target language production and compare intonation with a model — identify specific differences and practise correction

modes.reason: Intonation awareness deepens through exposure to varied spoken texts — single sentence drills do not build the sensitivity to sentence melody that natural conversation requires. A range of spoken contexts (announcements, conversations, instructions) builds the broader phonological awareness needed.

nodes.label: Stress, rhythm and phonological representation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and apply stress and rhythm patterns in the target language and understand how phonological features are represented in the writing system.
criteria: Can identify word stress correctly in at least five familiar target language words
Can connect at least one phonological feature of the writing system (e.g. accent mark, diacritic, special character) to its sound value

width.minimum: Identify word stress in at least five familiar target language words; demonstrate awareness of how stress or accent marks are represented in writing.
width.typical: Apply word stress and sentence rhythm in spoken production; use phonological notes or accent marks to support pronunciation; connect phonological representations in writing (e.g. accent marks, diacritics, special characters) to their sound values.
wider: Use phonetic notation or personal phonological notes to support the pronunciation of unfamiliar words — develop a personal pronunciation guide for challenging sounds
Practise stress and rhythm through performance texts (poems, tongue twisters, songs) and reflect on how stress choices affect meaning or emphasis

modes.reason: Stress, rhythm and phonological representation draw together the vowel/consonant knowledge from node 1 and the intonation awareness from node 2 into a unified understanding of spoken production. Performance contexts — recitation, role-play, recorded tasks — are the natural integration point.

descriptors.title: Grammar and writing systems
descriptors.description: develop knowledge of, and use structures and features of, the target language grammatical and writing systems to understand and create spoken, written and multimodal texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students enter the Y7-10 sequence without formal prior knowledge of the target language grammatical system. They bring implicit grammatical knowledge from English and may have informal exposure to the target language. They have not yet learned the grammatical structures or writing system conventions of the target language.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop knowledge of and use key grammatical structures and writing system features of the target language — including word classes, agreement, verb conjugation, sentence construction and orthographic conventions — to understand and create spoken, written and multimodal texts.
elaborations: recognising the number of consonants and vowels in the target language
noticing and applying different rules of capitalisation in the target language and English
identifying and applying graphic symbols specific to the target language on keyboards and in writing systems
understanding and applying grammatical gender rules
developing awareness of additional gender patterns in word endings
using appropriate definite and indefinite articles that agree in gender and number
understanding that adjectives and possessives agree in number and gender with nouns
developing knowledge of number and gender agreement with demonstratives
understanding the form and function of subject pronouns
understanding and using verb conjugations for the present tense of regular and common irregular verbs
recognising multiple versions of the verb 'to be' in some target languages
using verb conjugations in affirmative, negative and interrogative forms
seeking information using interrogatives
using prepositions of place and common contractions
linking ideas using connectives
recognising the functions of elements such as prefixes and suffixes

nodes.label: Writing system and orthographic conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and apply the orthographic conventions of the target language writing system, including any characters, symbols or capitalization rules that differ from English.
criteria: Applies at least three target language-specific orthographic conventions correctly in written production
Can enter target language special characters or diacritics on a device when required
nodes.hinge_reason: Orthographic accuracy is a prerequisite for written text production and comprehension. Students who do not learn target language-specific characters, diacritics or punctuation conventions produce texts that are ambiguous or incorrect, and misread texts that rely on these conventions for meaning. All subsequent writing tasks depend on this foundation.

width.minimum: Identify and apply at least three orthographic conventions of the target language that differ from English (e.g. capitalisation rules, special characters, diacritics, punctuation marks).
width.typical: Apply target language orthographic conventions consistently in written production; recognise and use special characters, diacritics and punctuation marks specific to the target language; understand how these are entered on keyboards and devices.
wider: Compare capitalisation and punctuation conventions across the target language and English — create a reference resource documenting key differences
Investigate how the target language's orthographic conventions reflect its phonological system — identify where spelling reliably predicts pronunciation

modes.reason: Orthographic conventions are procedural — students typically understand the rules but apply them inconsistently, especially under text production load. Focused practice including keyboard entry, handwriting and self-correction routines builds reliable application.

nodes.label: Grammatical gender and agreement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and apply grammatical gender and number agreement rules of the target language where these are grammatically required.
criteria: Applies gender and number agreement correctly in at least five target language phrases in written production
Can identify and correct an agreement error when one is pointed out in their own writing
nodes.hinge_reason: Gender and agreement errors propagate throughout all written and spoken production. Students who do not develop reliable agreement intuition produce texts with pervasive errors that impede comprehension and undermine all subsequent grammar nodes. EC06's text creation tasks cannot be met without basic agreement accuracy.

width.minimum: Apply gender and number agreement correctly in at least five target language phrases involving nouns and their modifiers.
width.typical: Apply gender and number agreement with nouns, articles, adjectives and possessives across spoken and written production; recognise common patterns and exceptions; use agreement rules to self-correct drafts.
wider: Research how grammatical gender is evolving in the target language (e.g. gender-neutral forms, changing norms) — compare contemporary and traditional usage
Compare grammatical gender systems across two or more languages students know — identify structural similarities and differences

modes.reason: Agreement is procedural — errors are typically in execution rather than understanding. Focused production practice with immediate corrective feedback, including self-correction during drafting, builds reliable application.

nodes.label: Verb conjugation and subject pronouns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and use subject pronouns and conjugate familiar verbs in the target language, including common irregular forms.
criteria: Can conjugate at least three regular verbs correctly across three or more persons in the present tense
Can produce affirmative, negative and interrogative forms of a familiar verb
nodes.hinge_reason: Verb conjugation is the structural spine of sentence production in most target languages. Students who cannot conjugate verbs reliably cannot produce grammatically complete sentences — all spoken and written production is blocked or severely impaired. This cascades directly into EC06 and EU02's more complex grammar nodes.

width.minimum: Conjugate at least three regular verbs correctly across at least three persons in the present tense; use subject pronouns accurately to accompany or replace nouns.
width.typical: Conjugate regular verbs across all persons in the present tense; recognise and use common irregular verb forms; use verb conjugations in affirmative, negative and interrogative forms; apply appropriate subject pronouns.
wider: Compare the verb conjugation systems of the target language and English — identify structural differences and what English omits that the target language requires
Investigate pronoun systems in the target language — map formal, informal and plural distinctions and how they reflect social relationships

modes.reason: Conjugation accuracy requires procedural fluency — understanding the rules is not sufficient for reliable production under communicative pressure. Massed conjugation practice in meaningful production contexts (not only paradigm drills) builds the automaticity required.

Conjugation accuracy is best built through varied communicative contexts (describing routines, giving instructions, interviewing peers) rather than isolated paradigm drills. Each context activates the same rules in a different production environment.

nodes.label: Sentence construction and connectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct grammatically coherent sentences in the target language, link ideas using connectives, and apply interrogative forms to ask questions.
criteria: Produces at least five grammatically coherent sentences using correct word order, agreement and verb conjugation
Uses at least one connective and at least one interrogative form correctly

width.minimum: Produce at least five grammatically coherent sentences in the target language using at least one connective and at least one interrogative form.
width.typical: Construct a range of sentence types (statements, questions, negatives) with appropriate word order; link ideas using connectives; use interrogative forms to gather information; apply prepositions of place and time.
wider: Compare word order conventions in the target language and English — identify where the target language requires different placement for adjectives, adverbs or objects
Investigate how connective use in the target language differs from English — identify connectives that do not have direct English equivalents

modes.reason: Sentence construction draws together orthographic conventions, agreement and verb conjugation from nodes 1–3 into connected text production. The teaching investment is in supporting students to maintain accuracy across multi-clause constructions, not only in isolated sentences.

descriptors.title: Compare the target language and English
descriptors.description: compare target language structures and features with English, using familiar metalanguage
descriptors.knowledge: Students are developing knowledge of target language grammatical structures and writing systems (AC9LS8EU02) and can recognise some features of the target language sound system (AC9LS8EU01). They have not yet systematically compared the target language with English using metalanguage, though they bring implicit awareness of English grammar from prior schooling.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare key structures and features of the target language with English — including grammar, word order, punctuation and register conventions — using familiar metalanguage to describe and discuss language patterns.
elaborations: developing awareness that different verbs are used in the target language and English for certain expressions
identifying do/does as an interrogative/negative auxiliary in English and how it differs in the target language
understanding the difference in expressing decimal points and numbers in the target language and English
recognising that register shifts according to familiarity and social position
building metalanguage to understand and discuss grammatical structures and vocabulary in the target language and English
comparing key structures and features of familiar target language and English texts by identifying the intended purpose and audience
discussing target language and English word order and syntax, noticing similarities and differences
comparing the ways to express 'you' in the target language and equivalent forms in English
recognising the influence of target language culture(s) on English and other languages through loan words

nodes.label: Building and using metalanguage
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a working set of grammatical metalanguage terms to describe and discuss structures in both the target language and English.
criteria: Can use at least five metalanguage terms correctly in a discussion of a language feature
Can apply metalanguage to describe a grammatical pattern in the target language
nodes.hinge_reason: Without shared metalanguage, comparison is impressionistic — students can say 'it's different' but not explain how or why. The descriptor's demand to 'compare using metalanguage' requires this vocabulary to be established before substantive comparison is possible.

width.minimum: Use at least five metalanguage terms (e.g. noun, verb, adjective, tense, agreement) correctly in describing a language feature in the target language or English.
width.typical: Build and apply metalanguage across grammatical categories (word classes, tense, agreement, sentence types); use metalanguage to describe and discuss language comparisons; develop a personal or class glossary of metalanguage in both languages.
wider: Research and compare metalanguage in the target language — identify where grammatical terms in the target language reflect its structure differently from English grammatical terms
Use metalanguage to annotate a target language text — label grammatical features and compare the pattern to an equivalent English text

modes.reason: Metalanguage is built through repeated use in meaningful contexts — defining terms once is insufficient. Students need to encounter and use metalanguage across multiple comparison tasks before it becomes functional vocabulary.

nodes.label: Comparing grammatical structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain key grammatical differences between the target language and English using metalanguage.
criteria: Can identify and explain at least two grammatical differences between the target language and English using metalanguage
Can explain why the same meaning requires different structures in the target language and English for at least one comparison

width.minimum: Identify and explain at least two grammatical differences between the target language and English (e.g. word order, agreement systems, verb forms).
width.typical: Compare grammatical structures systematically across the target language and English — including word order, agreement systems, verb forms, pronouns and interrogative constructions; explain why the same meaning requires different structures in each language.
wider: Investigate a grammatical feature present in the target language but absent in English (e.g. grammatical gender, formal/informal address distinctions, aspect) — explain what expressive or social function it serves
Compare word order and syntax across a short text in the target language and its English equivalent — map structural differences and discuss their effect on meaning

modes.reason: Grammatical comparison requires students to hold two systems in mind simultaneously and reason about structural differences. Explicit comparison frames — 'in English X, in the target language Y, because...' — scaffold the reasoning process before students can conduct comparisons independently.

nodes.label: Comparing register and contextual language use
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how register shifts in the target language and compare register conventions with English, using examples from familiar contexts.
criteria: Can identify at least one register distinction in the target language and compare it with English conventions
Can explain the social function of a specific register choice in the target language with reference to context

width.minimum: Identify at least one example of register distinction in the target language (e.g. formal vs informal address) and compare it with English conventions.
width.typical: Compare register conventions in the target language and English across familiar contexts (address forms, greeting conventions, digital communication, formal speech); identify language features that shift with register; discuss the social functions of register in each language.
wider: Compare how digital communication conventions (abbreviations, emoticons, informal syntax) differ across the target language and English — identify what is shared and what is language-specific
Investigate the influence of the target language on English or English on the target language — identify loan words and discuss what they reveal about cultural contact

modes.reason: Register is contextually defined — students who have only encountered one register context (e.g. classroom formal address) will not generalise. Exposure across digital, social, academic and formal contexts builds the register sensitivity that the descriptor requires.

descriptors.title: Identity shaped by language and culture
descriptors.description: recognise how identity is shaped by language(s), culture(s), attitudes, beliefs and values
descriptors.knowledge: Students enter the Y7-10 sequence without formal prior study of target language cultures. They bring lived experience of identity shaped by their own language(s) and cultural contexts, but have not yet examined how language and culture interact to shape identity in the target language community or reflected on how learning the target language affects their own sense of identity.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise how identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values — in target language communities and in their own experience — and identify specific language features, cultural practices and texts that reflect and reinforce identity.
elaborations: viewing interactions between target language speakers and recognising register as well as comparing culturally determined behaviours
listening to and reading traditional texts, identifying key messages, beliefs and values
identifying that a sense of identity and belonging is important across all cultures and discussing how it may be expressed differently
examining how First Nations Australian languages have strong connections to Country/Place location
exploring language features that reflect and embody cultural values and history, including regional differences
identifying elements of ways of communicating and behaving in the target language that may be unfamiliar to people from different cultural backgrounds
considering language use depending on context and relationship
understanding that languages and cultures change continuously due to contact with other languages and cultures
collecting examples of word borrowings from other languages
observing that many target language speakers may be multilingual and can move between languages to achieve different purposes
examining what is most important to them and their way of life

nodes.label: Language and cultural identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify ways in which the target language reflects and reinforces cultural identity, attitudes and values.
criteria: Can identify at least two target language features or cultural practices that reflect cultural identity or values
Can compare at least one of these with an equivalent or contrasting English-language convention

width.minimum: Identify at least two language features or cultural practices in the target language community that reflect shared values or identity (e.g. forms of address, naming conventions, greeting customs).
width.typical: Examine a range of target language features — forms of address, naming conventions, cultural references in language, regional variations — and discuss how each reflects or reinforces aspects of cultural identity; compare with English-language conventions.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian languages encode connections to Country, place and community — compare with how the target language encodes connection to place or community
Research regional identity within the target language community — identify language differences that reflect regional, national or community identity and discuss what they signal

modes.reason: Students need encounter with a range of cultural contexts where language and identity intersect before the connection becomes generalisable. Single examples (e.g. one greeting convention) tend to be treated as curiosities rather than patterns. Varied cultural encounters build the repertoire from which the general insight emerges.

nodes.label: Register, context and social identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise how language use varies according to social context, relationship and identity, and identify examples in the target language.
criteria: Can identify at least one example of language use in the target language that reflects a social relationship or context
Can explain the social or cultural reason for the language choice with reference to the target language community

width.minimum: Identify at least one example of how language use in the target language changes based on social relationship, context or purpose.
width.typical: Examine how register, formality and language choice reflect and reinforce social relationships in the target language; identify culturally specific behaviours and expressions that signal social identity; compare with Australian English conventions.
wider: Examine culturally embedded expressions or terms of address in the target language that encode social relationships not equivalently expressed in English
Investigate how multilingualism shapes identity in target language communities — interview or research bilingual speakers' experiences of moving between languages and identities

modes.reason: Students need scaffolded discussion to move from observing a language variation ('they say it differently to the teacher') to understanding the social mechanism behind it ('this reflects a social relationship structure that the language encodes'). Explicit discussion prompts and cultural context explanations support this move.

nodes.label: Personal identity and language learning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on how their own identity is expressed through language and consider how learning the target language affects or expands their sense of identity.
criteria: Can articulate at least one connection between their own language use and their personal identity
Can identify at least one new perspective introduced by learning the target language and explain why it is new

width.minimum: Articulate at least one way in which their own identity is expressed through their language use; reflect on at least one way in which learning the target language has introduced a new perspective.
width.typical: Reflect on the connections between language and personal identity in their own experience; explore how values, beliefs and attitudes are carried in language choices; consider how acquiring the target language creates a new lens through which to view their own and others' worlds.
wider: Create a personal text (slogan, visual, short reflection) in the target language that expresses an aspect of their own identity — discuss the choices made and what was translatable or not
Interview a multilingual person about their experience of identity across languages — compare insights with own reflections on the language learning experience

modes.reason: Personal identity reflection integrates the cultural and social insights from nodes 1–2 with the student's own experience. The teaching investment is in creating genuine reflective opportunities — not just asking students to describe themselves, but to examine the role language plays in how they are seen and how they see others.

descriptors.title: Apply spoken conventions to enhance fluency
descriptors.description: apply knowledge of conventions of spoken target language to enhance fluency, and to respond to and create texts in familiar and some unfamiliar contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students apply sound and pronunciation knowledge for fluency — including complex vowel combinations, consonant conventions and regional variation (AC9LS6U01). They apply pronunciation in rehearsed contexts. They have not yet worked with sentence-level stress in extended utterances or applied written doubling conventions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply spoken target language conventions to enhance fluency — including consonant nuances, sentence-level stress, written doubling conventions and intonation for expression.
elaborations: distinguishing nuances in pronunciation of consonants according to vowel combinations
using the rhythms of the target language, including intonation, tone and stress, to increase fluency and enhance expression
recognising where to place stress in extended sentences
recognising that written target language has limited double consonant combinations
applying pronunciation rules to common tongue twisters

nodes.label: Consonant nuances, sentence stress and written conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish consonant pronunciation nuances, place stress correctly in extended sentences, and apply written doubling conventions in target language spelling.
criteria: Demonstrates at least two consonant pronunciation nuances correctly in spoken production
Places stress correctly in at least two extended sentences
nodes.hinge_reason: Sentence-level stress and consonant nuance accuracy underpin intelligibility at the extended utterance level. Students with word-level accuracy but poor sentence stress sound unnatural and are harder to understand.

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least two consonant pronunciation nuances; place stress correctly in at least two extended sentences; apply written doubling conventions correctly in at least two examples.
width.typical: Distinguish consonant nuances in varied vowel and sound contexts; compare doubled consonant sounds with single equivalents; place sentence stress correctly in extended utterances; apply written doubling conventions in own writing and spelling.
wider: Read aloud a complex extended text with correct sentence-level stress throughout — demonstrating that stress placement is automatic rather than word-by-word
Compile a guide to written doubling conventions with examples — including the meaning and usage of key words

modes.reason: Sentence-level stress becomes automatic only through repeated extended production practice. Word-by-word accuracy does not automatically transfer to natural utterance-level stress.

nodes.label: Intonation and fluency in unfamiliar contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use rhythm, intonation and tone to enhance expression and fluency — including in some unfamiliar contexts — and apply these in their own spoken text creation.
criteria: Produces a spoken text with intonation and rhythm that conveys meaning and intention — not only lexical accuracy
Responds in spoken target language in an unfamiliar context with adequate fluency for communicative intent

width.minimum: Produce a spoken text in an unfamiliar context with adequate fluency — demonstrating intonation and rhythm that conveys meaning beyond word-level accuracy.
width.typical: Use target language rhythms, intonation, tone and stress to increase fluency and expression; apply pronunciation to tongue twisters and performance activities; apply spoken conventions when creating texts; respond with adequate fluency in some unfamiliar contexts.
wider: Perform a tongue twister at full speed with correct stress, rhythm and pronunciation — demonstrating fluency beyond slow careful articulation
Create and record an original spoken text applying intonation, stress and rhythm deliberately for expressive effect

modes.reason: Fluency in unfamiliar contexts develops through varied speaking conditions. Fluency that only exists in rehearsed conditions is not genuine oral competence.

descriptors.title: Apply grammatical structures to compose and respond
descriptors.description: apply understanding of grammatical structures and expressions to compose and respond to texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply modelled grammatical structures including tense variation, comparatives, agreement and frequency adverbs (AC9LS6U02). They compose in present, past and near-future. They have not yet conjugated irregular verbs across a tense range, used compound tense forms, expanded cohesive devices, or applied expressions of quantity systematically.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply grammatical structures to compose and respond to texts — including regular and irregular verb forms across a range of tenses, expanded cohesive devices, expressions of quantity, and adverbial modification.
elaborations: conjugating common regular verbs and high-frequency irregular verbs in the present, preterite and present perfect tenses
using present, past and immediate future tense verbs followed by infinitive
expanding use of cohesive devices to create compound sentences and link ideas
using adjectives to describe people and aspects of the environment
expressing quantity using a range of quantity expressions
using adverbs to modify the meaning of verbs and adjectives
indicating possession using grammatical structures appropriate to the target language

nodes.label: Irregular verb forms across a tense range
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use regular verb forms and high-frequency irregular verb forms across present, past and compound tenses, and use modal structures with infinitive.
criteria: Uses at least three high-frequency irregular verb forms correctly in at least two different tenses
Uses at least one modal structure correctly in a composition context
nodes.hinge_reason: Irregular verb accuracy across tenses is the grammatical gate for expressing past experience authentically. Students with only present tense or regular past forms cannot produce the narrative and experience-sharing texts central to this band and the next.

width.minimum: Use at least three high-frequency irregular verb forms correctly in at least two tenses; use at least one modal structure correctly.
width.typical: Use regular and high-frequency irregular verbs across present, past and compound tenses; use modal structures with infinitive for varied purposes; apply verb forms for first, second and third person; compose in connected past, present and near-future across varied topics.
wider: Compose a narrative using all three main tense forms correctly — with a margin note explaining the tense choice for each section
Identify all irregular verb forms in a given text — categorise by verb and tense, and produce the conjugation pattern for two irregular verbs

modes.reason: Irregular verb accuracy requires high-frequency production practice — students who know the rules still make errors under production pressure. Repeated composition tasks with varied topics build the automaticity needed.

nodes.label: Expanded cohesive devices and connectors
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use an expanded range of cohesive devices to create compound and complex sentences and link ideas across a text.
criteria: Uses at least two cohesive devices beyond basic connectors to connect ideas
Ideas are linked coherently across at least two sentences using varied connective resources

width.minimum: Use at least two cohesive devices beyond the most basic connectors; demonstrate that ideas are linked across at least two sentences.
width.typical: Use expanded cohesive devices across contrastive, additive and causal categories; create compound and complex sentences; link ideas within and across paragraphs; apply cohesive devices suited to different text purposes.
wider: Write a paragraph using at least four different cohesive devices — demonstrating range across additive, contrastive, causal and temporal types
Revise a simple text by adding cohesive devices — compare before and after, explaining how each addition changes the relationship between ideas

modes.reason: Cohesive device range develops through producing varied text types — narrative, argument and description each draw on different connector types.

nodes.label: Quantity expressions and adverbial modification
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a range of expressions of quantity and adverbs to modify verbs and adjectives — adding precision and nuance to composition.
criteria: Uses at least two expressions of quantity correctly in composition
Uses at least one adverb modifying a verb and one modifying a describing word correctly

width.minimum: Use at least two expressions of quantity; use at least one adverb modifying a verb and one modifying a describing word.
width.typical: Use varied expressions of quantity across different contexts; use adverbs to modify verbs and describing words with attention to placement; indicate possession using target language grammatical structures; apply adverb-verb combinations for precise meaning.
wider: Revise a simple text by adding quantity expressions and adverbial modifiers — explain how each addition changes the precision or nuance of the meaning
Produce sentences demonstrating the same verb modified by three different adverbs — showing how each changes the meaning

modes.reason: Quantity and adverbial range develops through encountering and producing these structures across varied text types and topic conditions.

descriptors.title: Reflect on target language and English structures using metalanguage
descriptors.description: reflect on similarities and differences between target language and English language structures and features, using metalanguage
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare target language and English structures using metalanguage across grammatical features, text types and persuasive language (AC9LS6U03). They have not yet used metalanguage to analyse whole-text coherence, or explored historical vocabulary influences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on similarities and differences between target language and English language structures using metalanguage — including whole-text coherence, text-type conventions, vocabulary patterns and historical influences.
elaborations: reflecting on language appropriate to different types of texts and comparing these with English
collecting examples of online and print advertisements and identifying language features used to persuade in both target language and English
understanding and comparing textual elements that provide coherence at whole-text level
comparing target language and English sentence structure
collecting cognates across categories
identifying target language words borrowed from different languages across time and through historical and social changes
understanding the conventions of several types of texts in the target language and comparing with English

nodes.label: Whole-text coherence and text-type conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use metalanguage to compare whole-text coherence features and text-type conventions across the target language and English.
criteria: Identifies at least two whole-text coherence features in a target language text using metalanguage
Compares at least one text-type convention across the target language and English, explaining the difference
nodes.hinge_reason: Whole-text metalinguistic analysis is the analytical tool for the text evaluation and synthesis work at subsequent bands. Students who only apply metalanguage at word or sentence level cannot engage with text-level evaluation.

width.minimum: Identify at least two whole-text coherence features in a target language text using metalanguage; compare at least one text-type convention across the target language and English.
width.typical: Compare descriptive, reflective and persuasive language across text types in both languages; identify and analyse language features used to create effects in different text types; compare textual coherence elements — cohesive devices, introductions, summaries, linked paragraphs; compare text conventions across communication modes.
wider: Analyse a target language and English text of the same type — use metalanguage to annotate every coherence feature and compare how each language achieves coherence
Compare advertising texts in the target language and English — annotate every persuasive feature in each and compare how each language constructs persuasion

modes.reason: Whole-text coherence analysis requires students to hold the full text in view while applying metalanguage to structural and connective features. Structured annotation tasks scaffold this whole-text analytical attention.

nodes.label: Vocabulary patterns and historical influences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect and analyse target language-English vocabulary patterns and explain how historical and cultural contact has shaped target language vocabulary.
criteria: Identifies at least three target language-English vocabulary pairs using a systematic pattern
Identifies at least one historical vocabulary influence on the target language and explains the historical context

width.minimum: Identify at least three vocabulary pairs using a systematic cross-language pattern; identify at least one historical vocabulary influence on the target language.
width.typical: Collect vocabulary pairs across systematic pattern categories; recognise systematic cross-language vocabulary patterns; identify vocabulary borrowed through historical cultural contact; explore how political, historical and social changes have introduced vocabulary into the target language.
wider: Research a historical period of cultural contact that influenced the target language — find examples of loanwords and explain what the borrowing reveals about that historical relationship
Create a visual etymology map tracing historical influences on target language vocabulary — with examples of each influence

modes.reason: Vocabulary history and pattern awareness develops through encountering varied examples across different historical influences and language families.

descriptors.title: Reflect on how identity is shaped by language and culture
descriptors.description: reflect on and explain how identity is shaped by language(s), culture(s), attitudes, beliefs and values
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise that language reflects cultural practices, values and identity including through contact language influences and modern change (AC9LS6U04). They have not yet analysed how formality signals social relationships, explored the global distribution of the target language, or examined co-official language contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on and explain how identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values — including language variation as social signal, co-official language identity, and the global distribution of the target language.
elaborations: recognising that language and cultural practices are interconnected, for example in naming conventions and changes reflecting social values
comparing elements of communication such as body language, personal space and silence in different cultural contexts
identifying levels of formality in spoken and written texts and considering what these reveal about social relationships
examining how First Nations Australian languages have strong connections to Country/Place, and comparing with language variations across target language communities
recognising that many target language communities have co-official languages and how this is an important aspect of identity
noticing components of the target language that reflect cultural histories and influences
understanding the nature of the distribution of target language speakers across the world, including communities where the target language and cultures have important presence
examining language variation in relation to vocabulary and grammatical forms across target language communities
considering the value of the influence of target language culture on the English language and other cultures

nodes.label: Language variation as identity and social signal
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how language variation in the target language — regional vocabulary, formality levels, language change reflecting social values — signals identity and social relationships.
criteria: Explains how at least two language variation features signal identity or social relationship — not only describes that they differ
Identifies at least one language change that reflects changing social values and explains the connection
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding language variation as a social and identity signal — not merely regional difference — is the conceptual prerequisite for the evaluative identity work at subsequent bands. Students who treat variation as arbitrary cannot engage with critical analysis of how language encodes values and power.

width.minimum: Explain how at least two language variation features signal identity or social relationship — not only describe that they differ.
width.typical: Recognise how cultural and religious traditions are encoded in naming conventions and common expressions; identify language changes reflecting shifting social values; compare body language, personal space and silence across cultural contexts; identify formality levels and what they reveal about social relationships; compare communicative conventions across cultural contexts.
wider: Analyse a language reform or social language debate in the target language community — explain what each position reflects about cultural values and social change
Compare how different address forms are used across at least three target language communities — explain the social and relational meanings each carries in each context

modes.reason: Explaining language variation as identity signal requires the analytical move from observation to interpretation. Structured analysis tasks — examining the same feature across different social contexts — scaffold this interpretive move.

nodes.label: Global distribution, co-official languages and First Nations connections
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the global distribution of the target language — including communities where it coexists with other languages — and reflect on co-official language identity.
criteria: Explains at least two aspects of the target language's global distribution
Explains why co-official or regional languages are significant for identity in at least one target language community

width.minimum: Explain at least two aspects of the target language's global distribution; explain why co-official or regional languages are significant for identity in at least one target language community.
width.typical: Understand the target language in global contexts; explore how target language culture has influenced other languages and cultures; examine co-official and regional language situations and their importance for identity; compare regional vocabulary variation across target language communities; examine First Nations Australian language connections to Country and compare with language variation across target language communities.
wider: Research the co-official language situation in one target language community — explain what it means for speakers' identity and compare with the situation of First Nations languages in Australia
Examine a community where the target language exists alongside other languages — explain the identity stakes for each language community involved

modes.reason: Global target language awareness and co-official language understanding develops through encountering the genuine diversity of target language communities across varied geopolitical and cultural contexts.

descriptors.title: Initiate, sustain and extend exchanges
descriptors.description: initiate, sustain and extend exchanges in a range of contexts, responding to ideas, opinions and perspectives
descriptors.knowledge: Students can initiate and sustain exchanges in familiar and unfamiliar contexts, adjusting language in response to others and using persuasive and influencing language (AC9LCH8C01). They can summarise others' views and manage real-time language adjustment. They have not yet extended exchanges into wider community and issue-based contexts, used analytical language to evaluate rules and regulations, or communicated in formal contexts such as phone calls, official enquiries, or advocacy writing.
descriptors.endpoint: Students initiate, sustain and extend exchanges in a range of contexts — including community issues, formal communication, and advocacy — responding analytically to ideas, opinions and perspectives.
elaborations: initiating and sustaining conversations to share issues from the wider target language community such as global warming
asking and responding to open-ended questions about promoting language learning
sustaining communications in a wide range of contexts such as meetings or phone calls
using analytical language to discuss and evaluate aspects of rules and regulations
using digital resources to maintain contact, express concerns or make enquiries
confirming understanding and requesting clarification
contributing to discussions and dealing with potential conflicts
writing to different audiences in a wide range of contexts to address real-life issues

nodes.label: Extending exchanges into wider community and issue contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can initiate and sustain exchanges about issues beyond personal experience — community, social, or global topics — using language appropriate to the scope of the discussion.
criteria: Initiates and sustains an issue-based exchange for at least six turns
Uses at least two analytical or evaluative language structures during the exchange
nodes.hinge_reason: Extension into wider community and issue contexts is the defining expansion from Y7-8 exchanges. Students who can only sustain personal topic exchanges cannot meet the analytical and advocacy demands of the remaining Y9-10 descriptors.

width.minimum: Initiate and sustain an exchange about a community or issue-based topic for at least six turns, using at least two analytical or evaluative language structures.
width.typical: Initiate conversations about wider community and social issues — including global topics; use analytical language to discuss and evaluate rules, policies and social questions; sustain communications across diverse contexts including meetings and extended discussions; deal with potential conflicts productively.
