wider: Participate in a structured debate or formal discussion on a community issue — sustain a reasoned position under challenge, using evidence and analytical language
Compare how issue-based discussion is conducted in target language community contexts with Australian conventions — identify differences in how authority, evidence and disagreement are managed

modes.reason: Analytical and issue-based exchange language requires a growing repertoire of structures across different topic types and positions. Repeated engagement with varied community and social issues builds the flexible analytical vocabulary and argumentation capacity needed.

nodes.label: Formal communication contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can communicate in formal contexts — phone calls, official meetings, formal written enquiries — using appropriate register, structure and language for each context.
criteria: Participates in or produces a formal communication using appropriate register throughout
Uses at least two formal register conventions appropriate to the communication context

width.minimum: Participate in or produce at least one formal communication (phone call simulation, formal meeting contribution, or formal written enquiry) using appropriate register throughout.
width.typical: Sustain communication in formal contexts — meetings, phone calls, official enquiries; use formal register and appropriate structural conventions; confirm understanding and request clarification in formal contexts; write to different audiences addressing real-life issues such as visa applications or scholarship enquiries.
wider: Compare formal communication conventions in the target language with Australian English equivalents — identify differences in register, structure, opening and closing conventions
Draft a formal written communication on a real issue of personal relevance — apply target language formal register and structural conventions appropriately

modes.reason: Formal communication contexts require students to understand what makes formal register different from informal, and to apply this consistently. Explicit register analysis of model formal texts, followed by structured production practice, builds the contextual awareness that formal communication demands.

nodes.label: Advocacy and conflict management in exchanges
nodes.checkpoint: Students can advocate for a position, address conflicting views, and use digital platforms to express concerns and contribute to wider community discussions.
criteria: Produces an advocacy communication using at least three argumentative or persuasive structures
The communication is directed at a specific audience with appropriate register and format

width.minimum: Produce at least one advocacy communication (written or spoken) addressing a real or realistic issue, using at least three argumentative or persuasive structures.
width.typical: Contribute to discussions dealing with potential conflicts; use digital resources to express concerns, make enquiries or advocate on issues; promote positions using analytical language; contribute thoughtfully to online forums and community discussions; write to different audiences on real-life issues.
wider: Produce a campaign or advocacy piece on a community issue — targeting a specific audience and using the persuasive and formal structures appropriate to that audience
Participate in a simulation of a formal meeting or community forum where positions conflict — manage the conflict productively using target language

modes.reason: Advocacy and conflict management integrates issue-based exchange skills (node 1) and formal communication capacity (node 2) into the highest-stakes interaction context. The teaching investment is in creating genuine advocacy conditions — real issues, real or realistic audiences — that require authentic persuasive engagement.

descriptors.title: Contribute to discussions with diverse views
descriptors.description: contribute to discussions that involve diverse views to negotiate outcomes, address issues and compare cultural experiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can collaborate using transacting, negotiating and justifying language to plan events (AC9LCH8C02). They have conducted community interviews and planned community-facing events. They have not yet organised authentic cultural experiences for school or community contexts, contributed to collaborative digital platforms, or collected and analysed community data for presentations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students contribute to discussions involving diverse views — negotiating outcomes, addressing issues, and comparing cultural experiences — including through collaborative digital platforms and community-facing cultural events.
elaborations: planning and making arrangements for group activities such as itineraries for school trips
collaborating to create multimodal presentations for various audiences about the impact of social media on young people
organising an authentic cultural experience for a school or local community and collaborating with target language peers
promoting inclusive cultural activities for the local community
creating a collaborative blog about language learning experiences including tips, achievements and challenges
evaluating and providing feedback on peers' blogs using direct editing, comments or spoken feedback
creating multimodal resources such as vlogs for different scenarios to help language learners
collecting data from target language communities on various topics and presenting findings

nodes.label: Negotiating outcomes with diverse views
nodes.checkpoint: Students can contribute productively to discussions where diverse views must be negotiated — managing disagreement, incorporating different perspectives, and working toward a shared outcome.
criteria: Uses at least two negotiation strategies during a discussion with diverse perspectives
Works toward a shared outcome without abandoning the target language
nodes.hinge_reason: Negotiating diverse views is the core demand of this descriptor and the prerequisite for all community-facing collaborative activity. Students who can only interact with like-minded partners cannot manage the genuine diversity of perspectives that real community and cultural engagement requires.

width.minimum: Contribute to a discussion with diverse perspectives, using at least two negotiation strategies (acknowledging a different view, finding common ground, or proposing a compromise) to work toward an outcome.
width.typical: Participate in discussions involving diverse cultural experiences and views; manage disagreements productively; incorporate different perspectives into planning; negotiate outcomes that address competing interests; promote inclusive approaches to community activities.
wider: Lead a discussion where views conflict — facilitate productive negotiation and bring the group to a shared outcome using target language

Compare negotiation strategies across cultural contexts — identify how the target language community manages disagreement differently from Australian contexts and discuss implications for intercultural collaboration

modes.reason: Productive negotiation with diverse views requires students to understand others' positions before responding — a listening-first, reasoning-second discipline. Explicit negotiation strategy instruction followed by practice in genuinely diverse discussion contexts builds this capacity.

nodes.label: Collaborative digital platforms and peer feedback
nodes.checkpoint: Students can contribute to collaborative digital platforms — blogs, vlogs, shared presentations — evaluating peers' contributions and providing justified feedback.
criteria: Contributes a substantive entry to a collaborative digital platform
Provides justified feedback on at least one peer's contribution using specific criteria

width.minimum: Contribute at least one substantive post or entry to a collaborative digital platform and provide justified feedback on at least one peer's contribution.
width.typical: Create and contribute to collaborative blogs about language learning; evaluate peers' contributions using metalanguage; create multimodal resources for Chinese learners at various levels; collect and present community data; use digital tools for collaborative planning and publication.
wider: Create a vlog or digital resource for a specific target audience — evaluate its effectiveness with that audience and revise based on feedback
Collect, analyse and present community data on a cultural topic — comparing findings across different community groups and discussing what the comparison reveals

modes.reason: Digital collaborative platforms require students to manage different roles — contributor, editor, commentator — across varied platform types. Practice across different digital contexts builds the flexible digital collaboration skills the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Organising community cultural experiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can organise authentic cultural experiences for school or community audiences — planning, promoting, executing and evaluating the event using target language.
criteria: Contributes to organising a community cultural experience with at least three target language planning decisions
Produces at least one promotional or informational material for the event

width.minimum: Contribute to organising a cultural experience for a school or community audience, participating in at least three planning decisions in target language and producing at least one promotional or informational material.
width.typical: Organise authentic cultural experiences for school or local community — cultural events, excursions, community-facing activities; create promotional materials; collaborate with target language community peers; reflect on and evaluate the experience.
wider: Lead the organisation of a community cultural event — coordinate all planning, promotion, execution and evaluation using target language, with real community participants
Evaluate the cultural event from multiple perspectives — participant, organiser, cultural community member — and synthesise these perspectives into a reflective account

modes.reason: Community event organisation integrates diverse-view negotiation (node 1) and digital collaboration (node 2) into a full real-stakes project. The teaching investment is in genuine community connections — real cultural events, real community participants — that require all collaborative and communicative skills simultaneously.

descriptors.title: Analyse and evaluate information in texts
descriptors.description: analyse and evaluate information, ideas and perspectives in a broad range of spoken, written and multimodal texts and respond appropriately to cultural context, purpose and audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interpret and analyse texts with cultural and critical awareness, evaluate source credibility, and respond with empathy and critical stance (AC9LCH8C03). They have analysed register, humour and cultural reference. They have not yet evaluated texts using formal analytical frameworks, used public speaking and debating strategies, accessed formal text types such as official policies, or referenced sources in target language academic contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and evaluate information, ideas and perspectives in a broad range of spoken, written and multimodal texts — including formal text types, literary extracts, and public discourse — responding appropriately using public speaking, debating or analytical writing strategies.
elaborations: analysing the effectiveness of actions and evaluating against own perspectives on current issues
using various communicative strategies such as public speaking, debating or negotiating to respond to texts or topics
accessing formal text types and developing specific, formal discussions
listening to or reading First Nations Australian author's stories and presenting or writing a reflective personal response in Chinese
researching a range of resources, evaluating their validity, reliability and credibility
role-playing a modified scene from a target language movie or drama
analysing key elements of language used in successful interviews and evaluating performance
analysing the plots and personalities of key characters in a story and recreating or extending the story
reading extracts from traditional target language literature and writing reflective responses

nodes.label: Evaluating formal and policy texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can access and evaluate formal text types — policies, procedures, official documents, news — assessing their validity, reliability and credibility, and citing sources in target language.
criteria: Evaluates at least two formal texts using explicit credibility criteria
Cites at least one source appropriately in target language
nodes.hinge_reason: Formal text evaluation with citation is the prerequisite for all analytical and academic response work at Y9-10. Students who cannot evaluate formal sources or cite them appropriately cannot produce the evaluative, evidence-based responses the descriptor and creating strand require.

width.minimum: Evaluate at least two formal target language texts for validity, reliability and credibility using explicit criteria, and cite at least one source appropriately in target language.
width.typical: Access formal text types — emergency procedures, policies, news, academic resources; evaluate validity, reliability and credibility; gather and cite references in target language; use formal analytical language to discuss and evaluate; compare formal target language sources with English equivalents.
wider: Conduct a research task using formal target language sources — evaluate source quality, synthesise across sources, and present findings with citations in target language
Compare how credibility is signalled differently in target language and English formal texts — identify differences in citation conventions, author authority markers, and evidence presentation

modes.reason: Formal text evaluation and citation require explicit instruction on the criteria and conventions — these are not intuitive. Explicit instruction on formal source evaluation frameworks and target language citation conventions, followed by guided practice, builds the academic literacy capacity needed.

nodes.label: Public speaking and debating strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use public speaking, debating and interview strategies to respond to a variety of text types and topics, evaluating peers' performances and demonstrating cultural knowledge.
criteria: Participates in a structured public speaking or debating task using at least two formal oral strategies
Demonstrates cultural knowledge relevant to the topic or context

width.minimum: Participate in at least one structured public speaking or debating task in target language, using at least two formal oral communication strategies appropriate to the format.
width.typical: Use public speaking, debating and interview strategies to respond to texts and topics; analyse key elements of successful interviews and speeches; simulate formal oral communication contexts; evaluate peers' performances; role-play modified scenes from target language media demonstrating cultural knowledge.
wider: Prepare and deliver a formal speech or debate contribution on an issue of significance — evaluate own performance against identified criteria and revise for a second delivery
Analyse a published target language speech or interview — identify the specific strategies used and explain how each serves the communicative purpose

modes.reason: Public speaking and debating require repeated performance practice with feedback — these are skills built through doing, not only preparation. Regular structured oral performance tasks with peer and self-evaluation build the confidence and strategic capability the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Responding to literary and cultural texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and respond to literary and cultural texts — including traditional literature and culturally significant works — with analytical and personal depth.
criteria: Produces a reflective response to a literary or cultural text of at least eight sentences
Includes at least two analytical observations about the text's language, structure or cultural context

width.minimum: Read an extract from a target language literary or cultural text and produce a reflective response of at least eight sentences, with at least two analytical observations about the text.
width.typical: Read extracts from traditional target language literature — plays, poems, novels, prose; analyse plots, characters and cultural knowledge; write and perform reflective personal responses; create or extend literary texts; keep reading journals; write reflective responses to First Nations Australian stories in target language.
wider: Compare a traditional target language literary text with a contemporary work on a similar theme — identify how cultural values and literary conventions have or have not changed
Produce a reflective literary response that situates the text in its cultural and historical context, drawing on background research

modes.reason: Literary response integrates formal text evaluation (node 1) and oral performance skills (node 2) into the full analytical and interpretive demand of this descriptor. The teaching investment is in creating genuine engagement with literary texts — real reading, real personal response — rather than only analytical exercise.

descriptors.title: Interpret and translate texts with cultural explanation
descriptors.description: interpret and translate a range of non-verbal, spoken and written texts, and explain how meaning is conveyed to reflect cultural context, purpose and audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interpret and translate across cultural contexts, manage register conversion, and produce bilingual texts for public purposes (AC9LCH8C04). They have interpreted for visitors and created bilingual resources. They have not yet interpreted puns, sarcasm and malapropisms, created multimodal bilingual resources, or justified cultural communication decisions in diverse social scenarios.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret and translate a range of texts — including humour, sarcasm, puns and culturally-complex language — explaining how meaning is conveyed to reflect cultural context, purpose and audience.
elaborations: applying strategies to overcome challenges in the translation of culturally unique concepts
demonstrating politeness, respect and formality in a range of cultural contexts
interpreting puns, idioms, humour or sarcasm between the target language and English
applying non-verbal and spoken communication strategies and justifying own actions and reactions
creating and developing multimodal target language resources incorporating bilingual subtitles
discussing and explaining malapropisms and translating hidden meanings
using secure online tools to understand emerging new words and applying knowledge in communication
composing multimodal bilingual texts for a range of audiences
changing informal spoken language into formal register to suit particular purposes and audiences

nodes.label: Interpreting humour, sarcasm and wordplay
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret puns, idioms, humour, sarcasm and malapropisms between target language and English, applying strategies to explain meaning including hidden or layered meanings.
criteria: Interprets at least two examples of puns, sarcasm, or malapropisms
Explains the literal meaning, intended meaning, and translation strategy for each
nodes.hinge_reason: Interpreting tone-dependent and culturally-layered meaning is the defining challenge of advanced translation and mediation. Students who cannot manage humour, sarcasm and wordplay cannot produce culturally appropriate interpretation for the full range of authentic texts they will encounter.

width.minimum: Interpret at least two examples of puns, sarcasm, or malapropisms, explaining the literal meaning, the intended meaning, and the strategy used to convey the correct meaning in translation.
width.typical: Interpret puns, idioms, humour and sarcasm; explain hidden meanings in malapropisms; apply strategies to make humorous intent translatable; discuss challenges of conveying tone-dependent meaning across cultural contexts; use dictionaries and digital tools to understand emerging new words and expressions.
wider: Research a specific form of target language humour — explain how it works linguistically and culturally, why it is difficult to translate, and what strategies are most effective
Compare how sarcasm or irony is signalled differently in the target language and English — identify what a translator must understand to convey the intended tone accurately

modes.reason: Humour and sarcasm interpretation requires students to analyse the literal-versus-intended meaning gap systematically, understand what cultural knowledge is required, and select a strategy. Explicit strategy instruction with varied examples builds the analytical translation capacity.

nodes.label: Justifying cultural communication decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply non-verbal and spoken communication strategies across diverse social scenarios and justify their own communication decisions in terms of cultural context.
criteria: Participates in a culturally diverse scenario and explains at least two communication decisions
Describes the cultural logic behind each decision

width.minimum: Participate in at least one culturally diverse social scenario and explain at least two communication decisions made — describing the cultural logic behind each choice.
width.typical: Apply non-verbal and spoken communication strategies in a range of cultural contexts — dining, professional meetings, social occasions; justify own communication decisions; explain cultural protocols; demonstrate politeness, respect and formality appropriate to each context.
wider: Simulate a formal cultural scenario — business card exchange, formal dining, welcoming ceremony — and provide a post-simulation analysis explaining every cultural communication decision
Compare the cultural communication conventions for a specific scenario across two different target language community contexts — identify where conventions differ and what the differences reveal

modes.reason: Cultural communication justification requires practice across varied scenarios — professional, social, ceremonial. The same ability to explain communication decisions must transfer across different cultural contexts before students can justify their choices independently.

nodes.label: Multimodal bilingual text production
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create multimodal bilingual resources — vlogs, educational blogs, subtitled video, interactive guides — that explain cultural meaning and serve a specific audience purpose.
criteria: Creates a multimodal bilingual resource with accurate meaning transfer in both languages
The resource includes at least one element of cultural explanation — not only translation of words

width.minimum: Create a multimodal bilingual resource combining at least two modes, with accurate meaning transfer and appropriate cultural explanation for the intended audience.
width.typical: Create multimodal bilingual texts — vlogs with subtitles, educational blogs, cultural awareness resources, public signs and notices — paying attention to cultural context; compose bilingual texts for diverse audiences; create resources that explain cultural meaning, not only translate words.
wider: Create a multimodal bilingual resource for a real external audience — evaluate its cultural accuracy and accessibility with a target audience member and revise accordingly

Reflect on the multimodal production process — explain how each mode contributes to meaning, what translation decisions were made, and what the production process revealed about the relationship between the two languages

modes.reason: Multimodal bilingual production integrates humour/layered meaning interpretation (node 1) and cultural communication justification (node 2) into a full creative and translation act. The teaching investment is in creating real or realistic audience conditions that require both linguistic accuracy and cultural appropriateness.

descriptors.title: Create and present texts for diverse contexts
descriptors.description: create and present informative and imaginative texts for diverse contexts and purposes, selecting vocabulary, expressions, sentence structures and textual features and conventions to engage different audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create and present extended multimodal texts with language manipulation, drafting and editing processes (AC9LCH8C05). They have produced community-facing texts with deliberate stylistic choices. They have not yet produced evaluative and persuasive writing at extended length, created procedural texts, produced literary or reflective texts for publication, or selected and applied conventions from specific literary styles.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and present informative and imaginative texts for diverse contexts and purposes — selecting vocabulary, expressions, sentence structures and conventions deliberately to engage different audiences — including evaluative, persuasive, procedural and literary forms.
elaborations: producing evaluative writing in the target language
debating or writing a text on a range of topics using persuasive language
creating multimodal bilingual texts such as a cultural awareness training information kit
reflecting on and explaining the protocols required to authentically co-create an Acknowledgement of Country/Place with a First Nations Australian
creating a range of procedural texts in the target language
creating texts for school newspaper or magazine
identifying the morals or insight of a chosen story to produce an evaluative response
creating own imaginative stories
creating written and multimodal narrative texts using a logical structure and sequence
using models of literary styles to create texts and presenting them in multiple ways

nodes.label: Evaluative and persuasive writing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce evaluative and persuasive texts — reviews, debates, analytical responses, advocacy pieces — selecting language and structure deliberately to make a case.
criteria: Produces an evaluative or persuasive text with a clear position supported by evidence
Uses at least three persuasive structures across the text
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluative and persuasive writing is the foundational productive capability for the full range of texts this descriptor requires. Students who can only produce narrative or informative texts cannot meet the evaluative, argumentative and procedural demands that follow.

width.minimum: Produce an evaluative or persuasive text of at least ten sentences using at least three persuasive structures and demonstrating a clear position supported by evidence or reasoning.
width.typical: Produce evaluative writing — reviews, analytical responses, feedback; write and debate persuasive texts on a range of topics; use evidence, logical structure and persuasive language; create texts for school newspapers and community publications; analyse and evaluate pros and cons of issues.
wider: Produce an extended persuasive text on a topic of genuine personal significance — with a documented drafting and revision process showing deliberate language choices

Compare persuasive text conventions in target language and English — identify how argument structure, evidence presentation and rhetorical strategies differ, and apply target language conventions authentically

modes.reason: Persuasive and evaluative texts require deliberate structural planning before drafting — students need to identify their position, organise evidence, and select appropriate language before producing. Explicit argument structure instruction followed by scaffolded writing practice builds this planning capacity.

nodes.label: Procedural and community texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create procedural texts and community-facing informative materials in target language, applying appropriate conventions for each text type.
criteria: Creates a procedural text applying correct genre conventions throughout
Creates a community-facing informative text appropriate for its specified audience

width.minimum: Create at least one procedural text (e.g. evacuation procedure, application checklist, operational guide) and at least one community-facing informative text using correct target language conventions for each.
width.typical: Create procedural texts — evacuation protocols, application procedures, lab checklists; produce texts for school or community newspapers; create cultural awareness resources; produce multimodal bilingual community texts; apply text-type conventions appropriately throughout.
wider: Create a complete procedural and informational resource for a real community need — evaluate its usability with an intended audience and revise
Compare procedural text conventions in target language and English — identify where the structural and linguistic conventions differ and apply the target language conventions correctly

modes.reason: Procedural and community text creation requires understanding of varied genre conventions. Practice across different procedural text types — emergency, operational, application — builds the flexible genre knowledge needed before students can apply conventions independently.

nodes.label: Literary and stylistically distinctive texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create literary and imaginative texts in target language that apply stylistic conventions, demonstrate personal voice, and engage audiences through deliberate language and structural choices.
criteria: Creates a literary or stylistically distinctive text applying at least two conventions from a specific style or genre
Demonstrates deliberate vocabulary and structural choices that serve the text's purpose

width.minimum: Create a literary or stylistically distinctive text that applies at least two conventions from a specific literary style or genre, demonstrating deliberate vocabulary and structural choices.
width.typical: Create imaginative stories about self and identity; use literary style models; produce narrative texts with logical structure; create texts using literary devices to enhance emotional impact; create Acknowledgements of Country/Place; write texts for diverse formats and audiences.
wider: Create a text that consciously applies the conventions of a specific target language literary genre — annotate the stylistic choices made and explain how each serves the text's purpose
Produce a text using a literary style model and then evaluate its success — identify where the model conventions were applied effectively and where the student's own voice emerged

modes.reason: Literary and stylistic text production integrates persuasive writing skills (node 1) and genre knowledge (node 2) into the fullest expression of creative capability at this level. The teaching investment is in creating genuine literary engagement — students as authors with a vision, not only as genre conformers.

descriptors.title: Initiate, sustain and extend exchanges
descriptors.description: initiate, sustain and extend exchanges in a range of contexts, responding to ideas, opinions and perspectives about their own and others' personal worlds
descriptors.knowledge: Students can initiate and sustain exchanges in culturally appropriate ways across digital and social contexts (AC9LCH8EC01). They can manage invitations, personal exchanges, and online interaction. They have not yet extended exchanges into debate and argument contexts, used hypothetical and spontaneous role-play scenarios, or responded formally in professional or institutional communication contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students initiate, sustain and extend exchanges in a range of contexts — including debate, formal online communication, hypothetical scenarios, and professional interaction — responding analytically to ideas, opinions and perspectives.
elaborations: applying strategies to sustain face-to-face and secure online conversations
applying effective strategies in a debate, summarising key information and presenting a balanced and reasoned argument
sharing opinions and responding to a range of school-related topics linking ideas to support a view
acknowledging strengths in others' ideas and providing evidence to contradict the ideas
engaging with educational social media to document own experiences and achievements
expressing apology, appreciation or gratitude in diverse ways and comparing practices across contexts
interacting in spontaneous, hypothetical role-plays relating to a range of contexts
responding to a range of texts such as personal letters, emails or job advertisements

nodes.label: Debate strategies and reasoned argument
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply effective debate strategies — summarising key information, presenting balanced arguments, acknowledging and challenging others' views — in structured and semi-structured discussion.
criteria: Uses at least two debate strategies during a structured discussion
Sustains a reasoned position for at least four turns
nodes.hinge_reason: Debate and argument strategies are the prerequisite for all high-level exchange work at Y9-10. Students who can only assert opinions without reasoned argument cannot meet the analytical and advocacy demands this descriptor and the broader Y9-10 band require.

width.minimum: Participate in a structured debate or discussion using at least two debate strategies (summarising, acknowledging, counter-arguing, or evidence use) and sustaining a reasoned position for at least four turns.
width.typical: Apply debate strategies; summarise key information and present balanced arguments; acknowledge strengths in others' ideas and provide contradicting evidence; share opinions on school-related and community topics linking ideas to support a view; engage with educational social media to document experiences.
wider: Lead a structured debate — facilitating argument, managing challenge, and bringing the discussion to a substantiated conclusion
Compare debate conventions in the target language community with Australian academic debate conventions — identify differences in how evidence, authority and disagreement are managed

modes.reason: Debate strategies require students to construct and deploy reasoned arguments — not only express views. Explicit strategy instruction followed by practice in genuinely contested discussions builds the argumentative capacity needed.

nodes.label: Hypothetical and spontaneous interaction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can participate in spontaneous and hypothetical role-plays — unfamiliar or unexpected scenarios — using target language flexibly without pre-prepared scripts.
criteria: Participates in a spontaneous role-play without a pre-prepared script
Sustains the interaction for at least four turns

width.minimum: Participate in at least one spontaneous or hypothetical role-play scenario without a pre-prepared script, sustaining the interaction for at least four turns.
width.typical: Participate in spontaneous hypothetical role-plays — seeing a doctor, handling personal emergencies, dealing with unfamiliar situations; sustain face-to-face and online conversations using strategies to prompt feedback; respond to open-ended questions without preparation.
wider: Participate in a series of progressively more unfamiliar hypothetical scenarios — identify which language resources transferred and which required improvisation
Reflect on the cognitive demands of spontaneous target language interaction — compare with prepared performance and discuss the strategies that help bridge the gap

modes.reason: Spontaneous interaction requires a bank of flexible language resources — strategies for managing unfamiliar situations, filler expressions, clarification moves — built through varied unscripted practice contexts.

nodes.label: Formal and professional communication
nodes.checkpoint: Students can respond formally in professional or institutional contexts — job applications, formal correspondence, apology and gratitude conventions — using appropriate register.
criteria: Produces a formal response using appropriate register throughout
Applies at least two formal register conventions for the specified context

width.minimum: Produce at least one formal response to a real or simulated professional context (job advertisement, formal invitation, or institutional enquiry) using appropriate register throughout.
width.typical: Respond to personal letters, emails and job advertisements; express apology, appreciation and gratitude in diverse ways; compare practices across contexts; write formal correspondence for professional purposes; interact in professional or institutional contexts using appropriate conventions.
wider: Compare formal communication conventions across target language and Australian English professional contexts — identify differences in register markers, structural conventions and sign-off formulas
Draft a formal communication for a real professional purpose — apply target language formal conventions and evaluate against a model

modes.reason: Formal communication integrates argument and debate skills (node 1) and spontaneous interaction capacity (node 2) into a written professional register. The teaching investment is in creating genuine professional-context tasks — real job advertisements, real institutional scenarios — that require authentic formal register.

descriptors.title: Contribute to discussions with diverse views
descriptors.description: contribute to discussions that involve diverse views to negotiate outcomes, address issues and compare cultural experiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan, transact and negotiate with peers and produce bilingual community resources (AC9LCH8EC02). They have collaborated on cultural events and community-facing projects. They have not yet led or facilitated live or online events for community audiences, contributed to sister school negotiations, or produced bilingual community initiatives on social issues.
descriptors.endpoint: Students contribute to discussions involving diverse views — including facilitating events, negotiating with diverse community stakeholders, collaborating on community initiatives, and addressing social issues in group contexts.
elaborations: planning and facilitating live or secure online events and persuading others to get involved
collaborating to create displays, presentations or performances to showcase learning
using secure online collaborative tools to produce bilingual versions of community initiatives
participating in virtual scenarios related to travelling to target language regions
collaborating to reach agreement by equally contributing ideas for a student-led activity
negotiating possible sister schools and comparing aspects of schools in target language regions
contributing to discussions about social issues to create a group presentation with balanced views
collaboratively writing reports or articles on topics such as the pros and cons of part-time work

nodes.label: Facilitating and contributing to group discussions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can contribute productively to group discussions with diverse views — facilitating equitable participation, reaching agreement, and managing competing perspectives.
criteria: Uses at least two facilitation or negotiation strategies during a group discussion
Helps move the group toward a shared outcome
nodes.hinge_reason: Group discussion facilitation is the prerequisite for all community-facing collaborative activity. Students who can only contribute without facilitating cannot lead the community events and collaborative productions this descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Contribute to a group discussion using at least two facilitation or negotiation strategies to support equitable participation and move toward a shared outcome.
width.typical: Plan and facilitate live or online events; collaborate to reach agreement by equally contributing ideas; facilitate student-led activities; contribute to collaborative reports and articles on social issues; negotiate and justify decisions with diverse peers.
wider: Lead a discussion where views conflict — facilitate negotiation and bring the group to a productive outcome using target language

Compare group discussion facilitation conventions in the target language community with Australian school contexts — identify cultural differences in how participation, turn-taking and consensus-building are managed

modes.reason: Facilitation requires students to manage group dynamics explicitly — ensuring inclusion, managing conflict, building consensus. Explicit facilitation strategy instruction followed by practice in genuinely diverse discussion contexts builds this capacity.

nodes.label: Community initiatives and sister school connections
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collaborate on bilingual community initiatives — road safety, sustainability, local activities — and negotiate with potential sister school or Chinese-speaking community connections.
criteria: Contributes to a bilingual community initiative or sister school negotiation
Produces at least one collaborative output in target language

width.minimum: Contribute to at least one bilingual community initiative or sister school negotiation, producing at least one collaborative output in target language.
width.typical: Use collaborative tools to produce bilingual versions of community initiatives; negotiate possible sister schools; consider aspects of educational systems across Chinese-speaking regions; participate in virtual exchanges involving bookings and travel negotiations; promote inclusive community activities.
wider: Lead a bilingual community initiative — coordinating the planning, production and delivery of a community-facing bilingual resource
Research and compare possible sister school partners — evaluate candidates using agreed criteria and present a justified recommendation

modes.reason: Community initiative collaboration requires students to operate across varied contexts — online platforms, community organisations, school partnerships. Exposure to varied collaboration contexts builds the flexible community engagement capacity the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Addressing social issues in group contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can contribute to discussions about social issues — presenting balanced views, supporting positions with evidence, and collaboratively writing group reports or articles.
criteria: Contributes a position supported by evidence to a group discussion or report on a social issue
Acknowledges at least one alternative view in the contribution

width.minimum: Contribute to a group discussion or report on a social issue, presenting at least one position supported by evidence and acknowledging at least one alternative view.
width.typical: Contribute to discussions about social issues with balanced views and supporting evidence; collaboratively write reports and articles on topics such as employment, education or community life; evaluate and provide feedback on peers' contributions; create multimodal resources for various audiences.
wider: Lead a group report on a social issue — coordinating contributions, synthesising diverse views, and producing a balanced, evidence-based group outcome
Compare how social issues are discussed and reported in target language media versus Australian English media — identify differences in framing, evidence use and perspective

modes.reason: Social issue discussion integrates facilitation skills (node 1) and community initiative experience (node 2) into a full evidence-based collaborative production. The teaching investment is in creating genuine social issues — real topics of relevance — that require authentic engagement rather than simulated debate.

descriptors.title: Analyse and evaluate information in texts
descriptors.description: analyse and evaluate information, ideas and perspectives in a range of spoken, written and multimodal texts, and respond appropriately to cultural context, purpose and audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate and process information across text types, evaluate sources, and respond analytically and personally (AC9LCH8EC03). They have applied comprehension strategies and produced structured responses. They have not yet evaluated information using rhetorical and analytical frameworks, created formal responses to contemporary issues, or analysed entertainment texts for their relationship to social issues.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse and evaluate information, ideas and perspectives in a range of texts — including rhetorical analysis, source evaluation with citation, and formal responses to contemporary issues.
elaborations: evaluating key messages in contemporary texts such as magazines, newspapers, websites or podcasts
listening to or reading texts and analysing how language conveys meaning such as rhetorical questions and sarcasm
applying understanding of formal text types to create own response to contemporary issues
listening to or reading a First Nations Australian author's story and presenting a reflective personal response in Chinese
accessing a range of digital and other texts to collate and present information about current affairs
analysing and evaluating information from a range of sources including statistical data
evaluating print or digital resources for reliability and referencing appropriately
exploring how forms of entertainment express or reflect contemporary issues
creating a simplified or more detailed script in response to a film or story

nodes.label: Rhetorical and analytical text analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how language conveys meaning in texts — including rhetorical questions, irony, sarcasm, and persuasive technique — and evaluate key messages in contemporary target language media.
criteria: Identifies at least two rhetorical or persuasive techniques in a text
Explains how each technique conveys meaning or influences the reader
nodes.hinge_reason: Rhetorical analysis is the prerequisite for all critical text work at Y9-10. Students who can only retrieve information cannot evaluate how meaning is constructed and cannot produce the analytical responses the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Identify at least two rhetorical or persuasive techniques in a target language text and explain how each conveys meaning or influences the reader.
width.typical: Evaluate key messages in magazines, newspapers, websites and podcasts for Chinese-speaking students; analyse how rhetorical questions, irony and sarcasm work in texts; analyse entertainment texts for their relationship to contemporary issues; identify language that influences reader response.
wider: Compare how persuasive technique is used in target language and English media on the same contemporary issue — identify differences in rhetoric and discuss what they reveal about audience expectations
Produce a rhetorical analysis of a published target language text — identify every persuasive or rhetorical device with metalanguage and evaluate the text's overall effectiveness

modes.reason: Rhetorical analysis requires an explicit framework — students need to know what to look for (rhetorical questions, irony, evidence use, framing) before they can identify and evaluate these features. Explicit analytical framework instruction followed by guided practice builds this capacity.

nodes.label: Evaluating sources and citing references
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate print and digital sources for reliability, gather information from a range of sources, and reference them appropriately in target language.
criteria: Evaluates at least two sources using explicit reliability criteria
Cites at least one source appropriately in target language

width.minimum: Evaluate at least two sources for reliability using explicit criteria, gather information from both, and cite at least one source appropriately in target language.
width.typical: Access digital and print texts to research current affairs; evaluate sources for reliability; gather and cite references in target language; use statistical data, quotations and research evidence; analyse overviews of contemporary issues from multiple source types.
wider: Conduct a research task using multiple target language sources — evaluate source quality, synthesise across perspectives, and produce a referenced summary with citations
Compare how sources are evaluated and cited in target language academic contexts with Australian English conventions — identify differences in citation format and credibility criteria

modes.reason: Source evaluation and citation require repeated practice across research tasks before the conventions become reliable. Regular research tasks with explicit citation requirements build the academic literacy skills the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Formal responses to contemporary issues
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create formal written or spoken responses to contemporary issues, applying formal text type knowledge and using evidence to develop an informed position.
criteria: Produces a formal response of at least eight sentences using at least two pieces of evidence
Applies appropriate formal text conventions throughout

width.minimum: Produce a formal response to a contemporary issue of at least eight sentences, using at least two pieces of evidence and appropriate formal conventions.
width.typical: Apply understanding of news articles and formal text types to create responses to contemporary issues; produce formal written responses to current affairs; present analytical responses to documentary or interview texts; respond to First Nations Australian stories in target language with reflective personal response.
wider: Produce an extended analytical response to a contemporary issue — drawing on multiple sources, applying formal conventions, and evaluating the issue from multiple perspectives
Compare own formal response with a published target language commentary on the same issue — identify differences in structure, evidence use and rhetorical approach

modes.reason: Formal responses to contemporary issues integrate rhetorical analysis (node 1) and source evaluation (node 2) into a full analytical production task. The teaching investment is in creating genuine contemporary issues — real current affairs, real community concerns — that require authentic analytical engagement.

descriptors.title: Interpret and translate texts
descriptors.description: interpret and translate a range of non-verbal, spoken and written texts, and explain how meaning is conveyed to reflect cultural context, purpose and audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interpret and produce bilingual texts, manage register conversion, and handle culturally-embedded language (AC9LCH8EC04). They have interpreted for others in familiar contexts. They have not yet interpreted for high-stakes cross-cultural events, managed idiom and cultural term challenges at the extended text level, or produced subtitled multimodal translations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret and translate a range of texts — including idioms, culture-specific terms, and extended texts — explaining how meaning is conveyed to reflect cultural context, purpose and audience.
elaborations: comparing and discussing various target language translations of English words, phrases and expressions
identifying words used with specific cultural assumptions such as gender, significance and formality
considering ways to translate culture-specific terms into English
interpreting for target language and English speakers for events requiring cross-cultural knowledge
comparing idioms and colloquialisms across languages and identifying challenges in mediating embedded cultural values
comparing bilingual editions of stories or poems and discussing how authors maintain stylistic devices
interpreting meaning in bilingual contexts and identifying potential issues in mediation
experimenting with translations of extended texts using dictionaries and translation tools
applying translation strategies in target language and English

nodes.label: Comparing translations and culture-specific terms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare different translations of the same text or expression, evaluate translation choices, and explain strategies for handling culture-specific terms.
criteria: Compares at least two translations of the same expression or text and evaluates the difference
Explains the strategy used to handle at least one culture-specific term
nodes.hinge_reason: Translation comparison and culture-specific term handling are the prerequisites for high-stakes interpretation. Students who cannot compare and evaluate translation choices cannot produce culturally accurate interpretations for complex or formal contexts.

width.minimum: Compare at least two translations of the same expression or short text, evaluate the difference, and explain the strategy used to handle at least one culture-specific term.
width.typical: Compare and discuss various target language translations of English words and expressions; identify words used with specific cultural assumptions — gender, formality, significance; consider strategies for translating culture-specific terms; use resources including online tools to understand emerging new words.
wider: Research the translation history of a specific culture-specific term — document different translation approaches across contexts and evaluate which works best for which audience
Compare how the same culture-specific concept is handled across multiple published bilingual texts — identify patterns in translation strategy and evaluate effectiveness

modes.reason: Translation comparison requires systematic analysis — students need a framework for evaluating what is gained and lost in each translation choice. Explicit comparative analysis with documented reasoning builds the evaluative capacity needed.

nodes.label: Interpreting for cross-cultural events
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret for Chinese and English speakers in contexts requiring in-depth cross-cultural knowledge, applying strategies to mediate embedded cultural values.
criteria: Interprets an exchange in a context requiring cross-cultural knowledge
Applies at least one strategy for mediating cultural values or embedded meaning

width.minimum: Interpret at least one exchange in a context requiring cross-cultural knowledge, applying at least one strategy for mediating cultural values or embedded meaning.
width.typical: Interpret for Chinese and English speakers at events requiring cross-cultural knowledge; compare idioms and colloquialisms across languages; identify challenges in mediating embedded cultural values; interpret meaning in bilingual contexts; identify potential issues in cultural mediation.
wider: Interpret in a complex cross-cultural scenario where embedded cultural values create mediation challenges — document the challenges and the strategies used
Compare own real-world interpreting experience with the structured approaches introduced in this descriptor — identify what is already intuitive and what requires explicit development

modes.reason: Cross-cultural interpreting requires practice across varied event types and cultural knowledge domains. Varied interpreting scenarios — formal events, community gatherings, media contexts — build the flexible cultural mediation capacity needed.

nodes.label: Extended text translation and multimodal bilingual production
nodes.checkpoint: Students can translate extended texts and produce multimodal bilingual resources — subtitled videos, captioned presentations, bilingual cultural products — that accurately convey meaning across both languages.
criteria: Translates a short extended text or produces a multimodal bilingual resource with accurate meaning transfer
Demonstrates at least two deliberate translation decisions beyond word-for-word substitution

width.minimum: Translate a short extended text (at least 8 sentences) or produce a multimodal bilingual resource, demonstrating accurate meaning transfer and at least two deliberate translation decisions.
width.typical: Experiment with translations of extended texts using dictionaries, translation tools and own knowledge; compare bilingual editions of stories or poems; produce subtitles for Chinese or English programs; create multimodal bilingual products for cultural audiences; apply translation strategies in extended contexts.
wider: Produce a fully subtitled bilingual video — evaluate accuracy and cultural appropriateness with a target audience and revise

Compare own translation of an extended text with an existing published translation — identify every difference, evaluate the choices, and discuss what the comparison reveals about translation as cultural interpretation

modes.reason: Extended text translation integrates comparison and evaluation skills (node 1) and cross-cultural interpretation (node 2) into a full sustained translation act. The teaching investment is in creating real-audience conditions — actual subtitling, real community events — where translation accuracy has genuine communicative stakes.

descriptors.title: Create and present texts for diverse contexts
descriptors.description: create and present informative and imaginative texts for diverse contexts and purposes, selecting vocabulary, expressions, sentence structures and textual features and conventions, to engage different audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create spoken, written and multimodal informative and imaginative texts for purpose and audience (AC9LCH8EC05). They have drafted, revised and produced texts for community audiences. They have not yet created evaluative and persuasive texts at extended length, produced formal procedural or policy-based texts, or created literary texts drawing on specific target language literary traditions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and present informative and imaginative texts for diverse contexts — including evaluative, persuasive, procedural and literary forms — selecting language and conventions deliberately to engage different audiences.
elaborations: creating a presentation on an issue comparing different opinions
producing multimodal presentations using tables, maps, charts or graphs
composing texts for events with specific purposes and audiences
reflecting on the protocols required to authentically co-create an Acknowledgement of Country/Place with a First Nations Australian
writing a narrative account of a character from a book or film
writing a biography of a significant person applying terms from traditional literature
creating a target language voice-over for a scene or collaborating on a drama
composing a script for a short play or video clip
composing and presenting a cultural exhibition for members of the local target language community
experimenting with ways of expressing ideas in formal contexts

nodes.label: Evaluative and persuasive texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce evaluative and persuasive texts — issue analyses, debate speeches, community presentations — using evidence, balanced perspective and persuasive language structures.
criteria: Produces an evaluative or persuasive text with a clear position supported by at least two pieces of evidence
Uses at least two persuasive structures across the text
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluative and persuasive text production is the foundational capability for all advanced text creation at Y9-10. Students who can only produce narrative or informative texts cannot meet the analytical and advocacy production demands that follow.

width.minimum: Produce an evaluative or persuasive text of at least ten sentences with a clear position, at least two pieces of supporting evidence, and at least two persuasive structures.
width.typical: Create presentations on contemporary issues analysing pros and cons; produce persuasive texts for community audiences; write evaluations comparing alternative positions; present on population, environmental, educational or community issues; use statistical data and research evidence.
wider: Produce an extended persuasive text on a topic of genuine community relevance, with a documented drafting and revision process showing deliberate language choices
Compare persuasive text conventions in target language and English — identify how argument structure, evidence use and rhetorical strategy differ across the two languages

modes.reason: Persuasive text production requires deliberate structural planning — position, evidence, counter-argument, conclusion. Explicit argument structure instruction followed by scaffolded production builds the planning capacity that produces genuinely persuasive texts.

nodes.label: Multimodal community and cultural texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce multimodal texts — presentations, exhibitions, cultural performances, community resources — combining spoken, written and visual elements for specific community audiences.
criteria: Produces a multimodal text combining at least two modes for a community or cultural audience
Demonstrates deliberate mode selection appropriate to audience and purpose

width.minimum: Produce a multimodal text combining at least two modes for a community or cultural audience, with deliberate mode selection justified by audience and purpose.
width.typical: Produce multimodal presentations using data and statistics; compose texts for events with specific purposes; create cultural exhibitions and performances; write voice-overs and scripts for drama or comedy; create resources for Chinese-speaking community audiences; reflect on co-creating Acknowledgements of Country with First Nations Australians.
wider: Create a multimodal community text for a real audience — evaluate its effectiveness with that audience and revise based on feedback
Produce a cultural performance or exhibition that draws on a specific target language cultural tradition — explain the cultural choices made and how they serve the audience

modes.reason: Multimodal community text production requires students to understand how different modes serve different purposes for different audiences. Practice across varied production formats — exhibitions, performances, presentations, community resources — builds the flexible multimodal production capacity needed.

nodes.label: Literary and formal texts using stylistic models
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create literary and formal texts using stylistic models — applying target language literary conventions, experimenting with formal language, and producing texts that demonstrate deliberate stylistic choices.
criteria: Creates a literary or formal text applying at least two conventions from a specific style
Explains at least one deliberate stylistic choice made

width.minimum: Create a literary or formal text applying at least two conventions from a specific target language literary or formal style, with at least one deliberate stylistic choice explained.
width.typical: Write narratives about characters from books or films; write biographies of significant figures using literary language; create scripts for short plays or video clips; experiment with formal versus subjective language; use literary style models; compose texts for school publications and community contexts.
wider: Create a text in a specific target language literary style — apply the conventions authentically and annotate the stylistic choices made
Reflect on the production process — explain what cultural knowledge was required to apply the literary conventions and what was learned about the target language literary tradition

modes.reason: Literary and formal text creation integrates evaluative writing skills (node 1) and multimodal production (node 2) into the fullest expression of creative and formal capability at Y9-10. The teaching investment is in creating genuine literary engagement — students as authors with a vision, not only genre followers.

descriptors.title: Features of spoken language for fluency
descriptors.description: demonstrate how features and conventions of spoken Chinese can extend fluency when responding to and creating texts appropriate to contexts, purposes and audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can examine phonological features, monitor pronunciation against standard models, and perform target language texts (AC9LCH8EU01). They have compared own speech with standard forms. They have not yet applied spoken language features to extend fluency in debate and argument contexts, prepared formal speeches for real audiences, or analysed rap, comedy and performance forms for phonological technique.
descriptors.endpoint: Students demonstrate how features and conventions of spoken target language extend fluency — including comprehension of diverse accents, performance techniques, and formal speech delivery for real audiences.
elaborations: listening to interactions between unfamiliar voices at different speeds to develop auditory and comprehension skills
discriminating between unfamiliar homophones and enhancing fluency through rap songs or stand-up comedy
identifying regional variation in pronunciation across different target language environments
experimenting with rhythm, pace, tone and stress and developing strategies to enhance communication
using dictionaries or digital tools to help with learning characters and pronunciation
presenting an argument in a debate using emphasis and persuasion with focus on fluency and audience
reading aloud a poem in different ways using intonation to convey happiness, sarcasm or jealousy

nodes.label: Comprehension and discrimination across accents and speeds
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop strategies for understanding unfamiliar voices at varied speeds and discriminating between unfamiliar homophones and regional variation.
criteria: Demonstrates comprehension of at least two spoken texts from unfamiliar voices or speeds
Identifies at least two homophone pairs and describes a strategy for discrimination
nodes.hinge_reason: Comprehension across diverse speakers and speeds is the prerequisite for authentic spoken language use at Y9-10. Students who can only understand familiar speakers or slow, teacher-directed speech cannot function in real-world target language listening contexts.

width.minimum: Demonstrate comprehension of at least two spoken texts from unfamiliar voices or speeds, identify at least two unfamiliar homophone pairs, and describe at least one strategy used for each.
width.typical: Listen to interactions between unfamiliar voices at varied speeds; apply comprehension strategies; discriminate between unfamiliar homophones; enhance fluency through rap songs or stand-up comedy; identify regional variation in pronunciation across Chinese-speaking environments.
wider: Research a specific regional variety of the target language — describe the phonological features, find examples, and explain the comprehension strategies most useful for that variety
Compare comprehension strategies across multiple regional accents encountered — identify which strategies transfer and which are variety-specific

modes.reason: Acoustic comprehension across diverse speakers is built through varied, repeated listening exposure. Systematic encounter with different voices, speeds, accents and registers builds the flexible processing capacity needed.

nodes.label: Performance techniques for rhythm and fluency
nodes.checkpoint: Students can experiment with rhythm, pace, tone and stress in performance contexts — rap, comedy, poetry, drama — and develop strategies to enhance communication for specific audiences.
criteria: Produces a performance demonstrating deliberate use of at least two prosodic features
Can explain the intended communicative or artistic effect of each prosodic choice

width.minimum: Produce at least one performance demonstrating deliberate use of at least two prosodic features (rhythm, pace, tone variation, stress) for communicative or artistic effect.
width.typical: Experiment with rhythm, pace, tone and stress; take on the role of a news reader or performer; practise rap or stand-up comedy in the target language; read poems in multiple ways to convey different meanings; watch and perform versions of target language cultural performances.
wider: Create an original performance text — rap, spoken word, or monologue — demonstrating deliberate prosodic design choices, with annotation explaining each choice
Compare the prosodic techniques used in target language and English performance genres — identify what is shared and what is culturally specific to each

modes.reason: Performance technique requires practice across varied performance forms. Students who have only practised in one format — only poetry, or only formal speech — cannot generalise their prosodic skills. Varied performance contexts build flexible prosodic production capacity.

nodes.label: Formal speech delivery for real audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deliver formal speeches to real or realistic audiences using appropriate intonation, stress and phrasing — including debate presentations, welcome speeches, and argumentative oral texts.
criteria: Delivers a formal speech of at least two minutes with appropriate prosodic conventions
Can identify and explain at least one deliberate prosodic choice made during delivery

width.minimum: Deliver a formal speech of at least two minutes using appropriate prosodic conventions, with at least one deliberate prosodic choice explained in terms of audience effect.
width.typical: Present arguments in debate using emphasis and persuasion; deliver formal speeches with focus on fluency and audience; present oral texts appropriate to formal contexts; use dictionaries and digital tools to support pronunciation; quote literary texts with appropriate intonation.
wider: Record and systematically review a formal speech delivery — identify specific prosodic choices and evaluate their effectiveness for the audience and purpose
Compare formal speech conventions in the target language with English debate or presentation norms — identify differences in pacing, pause conventions, and rhetorical delivery

modes.reason: Formal speech delivery integrates comprehension strategy awareness (node 1) and performance technique (node 2) into a full formal spoken production task. The teaching investment is in creating genuine formal audience conditions — real debates, real presentations — where prosodic control serves communicative purpose.

descriptors.title: Character form and complex grammatical structures
descriptors.description: apply knowledge of character form and function, and complex grammatical structures and features, to predict meaning and to compose a wide range of texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse character components, apply stroke conventions, and use a range of sentence structures including complex constructions (AC9LCH8EU02). They have inferred meaning from morphological knowledge. They have not yet analysed sequences of unfamiliar characters using component patterns to predict meaning, compared simplified and traditional forms systematically, or applied complex literary language and grammatical features in extended texts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply knowledge of character form and function and complex grammatical structures to predict meaning and compose a wide range of texts — including analysis of simplified/traditional forms, polysemy, literary language, and advanced grammatical features.
elaborations: analysing sequences of unfamiliar characters to determine features of form and function and predict meanings
comparing and contrasting characters in simplified and traditional forms
analysing and comparing unfamiliar characters in print media and online texts
applying understanding of word formation when comparing translations
discriminating correct forms and sounds of characters with multiple readings
inferring the meaning of unfamiliar words containing a familiar morpheme
explaining how morphology works to convey subtle and precise meanings
inferring meaning of terminology based on character analysis
applying punctuation conventions in writing and reading aloud
using language features to extend and elaborate a point of view
exploring functions of key grammatical forms in different contexts
exploring examples of literary language and how grammatical features differ from everyday speech
experimenting with abstract nouns to create procedural or creative texts

nodes.label: Advanced character analysis and prediction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse sequences of unfamiliar characters using component patterns to predict meaning, compare simplified and traditional forms, and determine precise morpheme meanings from context.
criteria: Predicts the meaning of at least three unfamiliar characters using component analysis
Determines the precise meaning of at least two polysemous morphemes from context
nodes.hinge_reason: Advanced character analysis and prediction are the prerequisites for independent reading of complex texts. Students who cannot predict meaning from component patterns cannot approach genuinely unfamiliar texts strategically — which is the threshold the Y9-10 descriptor marks.

width.minimum: Predict the meaning of at least three unfamiliar characters using component analysis, compare at least two simplified/traditional form pairs, and determine the precise meaning of at least two polysemous morphemes from context.
width.typical: Analyse sequences of unfamiliar characters to predict meanings; compare simplified and traditional character forms; analyse and compare unfamiliar characters in print and online texts; apply word formation understanding when comparing translations; discriminate correct forms and sounds of characters with multiple readings.
wider: Research the relationship between simplified and traditional forms for a set of characters — explain what was simplified, the historical rationale, and what (if anything) is lost or gained
Investigate a productive morpheme — identify all words it appears in, document the semantic pattern, and generate new combinations with verification

modes.reason: Character prediction requires systematic application of a multi-layered framework — component identification, semantic pattern, phonetic contribution, contextual disambiguation. Explicit strategy instruction with graduated practice builds this systematic analytical capacity.

nodes.label: Complex grammatical features and literary language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply complex grammatical features — modal and auxiliary verbs, abstract nouns, literary particles — and identify how grammatical features differ between literary and everyday language.
criteria: Produces a text demonstrating at least three complex grammatical features correctly
Includes at least one feature that differs between literary and everyday registers

width.minimum: Produce a text demonstrating at least three complex grammatical features correctly, including at least one that differs between literary and everyday registers.
width.typical: Apply modal and auxiliary verbs across text types; use abstract nouns in procedural and creative texts; apply advanced punctuation; explore literary language and how grammatical features differ from everyday speech; apply tense knowledge in formal and informal text types; identify how sentence structures convey messages effectively.
wider: Analyse a target language literary text for grammatical features that distinguish it from everyday speech — explain each feature and discuss the literary effect it creates
Compare own extended writing with a literary model — identify specific grammatical features of the model not present in own writing and experiment with incorporating them

modes.reason: Complex grammatical features and literary language require repeated production across varied text types before they become reliable. Regular extended writing tasks across different registers — formal, informal, literary — build the flexible grammatical competence needed.

nodes.label: Composing a wide range of texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply full character and grammatical knowledge to compose a wide range of texts — formal, informal, procedural, literary, multimodal — across diverse contexts and purposes.
criteria: Composes at least two texts of different types applying full character and grammatical knowledge
Grammatical and vocabulary choices are appropriate to each text type and purpose

width.minimum: Compose at least two texts of different types applying full character and grammatical knowledge appropriately for each text type.
width.typical: Apply character and grammatical knowledge across a wide range of text types — reports, plans, diaries, scripts, literary works, multimodal productions; adapt grammatical choices for context, purpose and audience; respond to diverse stimuli with appropriate grammatical selection.
wider: Compose a text that deliberately uses a specific grammatical or literary feature for rhetorical effect — explain the choice and compare with an alternative approach
Review and annotate own extended writing for grammatical accuracy and register appropriateness — identify patterns and develop a targeted improvement plan

modes.reason: Wide-range text composition integrates character analysis (node 1) and complex grammatical features (node 2) into full productive literacy at the highest level of this pathway. The teaching investment is in creating genuinely varied, purposeful composition tasks across text types — not only narrative or only formal.

descriptors.title: Analyse texts using metalanguage
descriptors.description: analyse a range of Chinese texts, using metalanguage to explain linguistic, textual and cultural elements
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare language structures and features across target language and English using metalanguage (AC9LCH8EU03). They have applied comparative metalanguage to text types and genre conventions. They have not yet conducted full stylistic analysis of target language texts, examined essay organisation conventions specific to the target language, analysed language in media contexts, or described genres unique to the target language literary tradition.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse a range of target language texts using metalanguage to explain linguistic, textual and cultural elements — including stylistic devices, genre organisation, content structure, and culturally-specific literary forms.
elaborations: using metalanguage in Chinese or English to identify the grammatical differences between languages
analysing the sequence of content in different text types such as blogs or news articles
explaining the use of data such as census information and surveys to support views
incorporating statistical data, quotations and research-based evidence in own texts
analysing language used in a range of text types comparing emails for different purposes
analysing language and writing techniques used in traditional target language texts
analysing the layout of magazines and online texts to identify how images and words reinforce ideas
identifying linguistic terms and how world events are reported in target language media
comparing literature across languages and recognising different features
