exploring examples of literary language and how grammatical features differ from everyday text

nodes.label: Stylistic and linguistic analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and analyse grammatical differences between languages using metalanguage, and analyse language in a range of text types for purpose and audience.
criteria: Uses metalanguage to analyse at least three linguistic features in a target language text
Compares at least one feature with its English equivalent
nodes.hinge_reason: Linguistic and textual analysis using metalanguage is the prerequisite for all sophisticated text engagement at Y9-10. Students who cannot name and analyse language features cannot produce the analytical responses the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Use metalanguage to analyse at least three linguistic features in a target language text, and compare at least one feature with its English equivalent.
width.typical: Use metalanguage to identify grammatical differences across languages — word order, verb mood, tense, possessive pronouns; analyse sequence of content in different text types; explain use of data and evidence in texts; analyse language in emails, blogs, news articles for purpose differences; identify linguistic terms in media reporting.
wider: Produce a full linguistic and textual analysis of a target language text — annotating every feature with metalanguage and explaining its contribution to the text's purpose
Compare how the same linguistic feature operates across formal and informal registers in the target language — explain the difference and discuss the cultural logic behind it

modes.reason: Metalanguage for analysis is built through repeated deployment across varied text types. Students need to encounter and apply each metalanguage term across multiple text analysis contexts before it becomes functional analytical vocabulary.

nodes.label: Genre organisation and essay conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how content is structured in target language text types — including essay organisation conventions — and compare these with English equivalents.
criteria: Analyses content organisation in at least two target language text types
Compares with English conventions for at least one, identifying at least two differences

width.minimum: Analyse the content organisation of at least two target language text types and compare with English conventions for at least one, identifying at least two differences.
width.typical: Analyse the sequence of content in different text types; examine how ideas are ordered and substantiated across genres and languages; compare essay organisation — where the author's position appears, how evidence is marshalled; analyse magazine and online text layout; compare literature across languages and cultures.
wider: Compare essay organisation conventions in the target language with English — explain the cultural logic behind each organisation pattern and discuss implications for bilingual academic writing
Apply target language essay organisation conventions in an original piece — then compare with a parallel English essay on the same topic

modes.reason: Genre organisation analysis requires students to compare across text types and languages systematically. Explicit organisational framework analysis — identifying where position appears, how evidence is structured — builds the comparative capacity before students can analyse independently.

nodes.label: Literary and cultural text analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse stylistic devices in literary texts, describe target language-specific literary forms, and explain the cultural elements embedded in literary and cultural texts.
criteria: Analyses at least two stylistic devices in a literary text using metalanguage
Describes at least one genre or form specific to the target language literary tradition

width.minimum: Analyse at least two stylistic devices in a target language literary text using metalanguage, and describe at least one genre or form specific to the target language literary tradition.
width.typical: Analyse stylistic writing techniques in target language; examine the four-step essay composition tradition; explore literary language differences from everyday text; analyse how magic and danger are portrayed in folk legends across cultures; analyse traditional Chinese literary forms and their origins.
wider: Produce a full stylistic analysis of a target language literary text — annotating every stylistic device and evaluating the text's cultural and literary significance

Research a specific target language literary form — describe its conventions, trace its historical origins, and explain its cultural significance in relation to contemporary target language literature

modes.reason: Literary and cultural text analysis integrates linguistic analysis (node 1) and genre organisation understanding (node 2) into a full cultural-literary analytical act. The teaching investment is in creating genuine engagement with the target language literary tradition — students as culturally-informed readers and analysts.

descriptors.title: Evaluate identity shaped by language and culture
descriptors.description: reflect on and evaluate how their own and others' identify is shaped by language(s), culture(s), attitudes, beliefs and values, and how these affect ways of communicating
descriptors.knowledge: Students can reflect on and explain how their own and others' identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values (AC9LCH8EU04). They have examined cultural values in language use, reflected on identity across communities, and identified stereotyping risks. They have not yet evaluated how globalisation and cultural change affect identity, examined how language is used to empower or marginalise, or reflected on the academic and professional opportunities opened by bilingualism.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on and evaluate how their own and others' identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values — including the impact of globalisation, power and marginalisation in language, and the opportunities created by bilingual identity.
elaborations: evaluating differences in perceptions, understandings and behaviours across cultures
explaining how cultural traditions and beliefs affect communication of speakers from various regions
exploring how concepts such as modesty, personal space and respect influence communication styles
reflecting on and explaining the protocols required to authentically co-create an Acknowledgement of Country/Place
examining how language may be used to empower or marginalise groups in society
accessing a range of sources and identifying content that creates bias or stereotypes
identifying how knowledge of Chinese and English opens up opportunities to expand world views
exploring cultural assumptions in language such as how terms for 'getting married' differ by gender
analysing own language and cultural backgrounds through conversations with relatives

nodes.label: Cultural change, globalisation and identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how cultural traditions and globalisation affect identity and communication, and explain how cultural beliefs shape communication differences across Chinese-speaking communities.
criteria: Evaluates how at least two cultural traditions or globalisation changes have affected communication
Explains the impact on own identity or beliefs with reasoned argument
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluating the impact of cultural change and globalisation on identity is the conceptual prerequisite for the most sophisticated identity analysis at this level. Students who can only describe cultural-language connections cannot evaluate the dynamic, contested relationship between language, culture and identity.

width.minimum: Evaluate how at least two cultural traditions or globalisation-related changes have affected communication in the target language community, and explain the impact on own identity or beliefs.
width.typical: Evaluate differences in perceptions, behaviours and communication across cultures; explain how cultural traditions and beliefs affect communication across regions; explore modesty, personal space and respect for authority in communication; reflect on how globalisation has affected own identity and beliefs.
wider: Research how a specific wave of globalisation has affected target language cultural practices and identity — evaluate whether the changes strengthen or challenge cultural continuity
Compare own intergenerational family experience of cultural change — identify what has been maintained, what has changed, and discuss the factors that drive cultural continuity or change

modes.reason: Evaluating cultural change requires students to reason about cause and effect, continuity and change, and competing values — a multi-step analytical process. Explicit frameworks for evaluating cultural impact build the critical analytical capacity the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Language, power and marginalisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine how language may be used to empower or marginalise groups in society, and identify how access to sources and critical awareness can build mutual understanding.
criteria: Identifies at least two examples of language used to empower or marginalise
Explains the impact of each with specific reference to language choices

width.minimum: Identify at least two examples of how language is used to empower or marginalise in the target language community or across cultures, and explain the impact of each.
width.typical: Examine how language empowers or marginalises groups; identify content that creates bias or stereotypes; build mutual understanding through critical source evaluation; explore how group labels influence perception; examine how cultural assumptions are embedded in language; analyse gender language conventions.
wider: Conduct an analysis of a target language text or media source for embedded bias or marginalising language — identify specific language choices and explain how they position readers or particular groups
Compare how the same social group is labelled and discussed across target language and English media — identify differences in framing and discuss the cultural values that underlie each

modes.reason: Language and power analysis must be applied across varied contexts — media, group labels, gender conventions, community discourse — before students can generalise the critical framework. Varied examples build the analytical lens that transfers across new texts and contexts.

nodes.label: Bilingual identity and world view expansion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how their bilingual identity opens opportunities to expand world views and pursue heritage and cultural connections, reflecting on the academic and personal significance of language knowledge.
criteria: Evaluates at least two ways bilingual identity opens opportunities
Reflects on at least one heritage or cultural connection made possible by target language knowledge

width.minimum: Evaluate at least two ways in which bilingual identity opens opportunities — academic, professional, cultural, or personal — and reflect on at least one heritage or cultural connection made possible by target language knowledge.
width.typical: Identify how knowledge of target language and English opens opportunities; read texts across languages to expand perspectives; analyse own language and cultural background through family conversations; discover own heritage through target language; evaluate the personal significance of bilingual identity.
wider: Produce a sustained reflective evaluation of own bilingual identity journey — tracing how it has developed, what has shaped it, and its significance for future study, community connection and professional aspiration
Interview a family member or community member about the opportunities their bilingualism has created — compare their experience with own and discuss what has changed across generations

modes.reason: Bilingual identity evaluation integrates cultural change analysis (node 1) and power/marginalisation awareness (node 2) into a personally grounded synthesis. The teaching investment is in creating genuinely reflective conditions — space for honest, complex identity examination rather than tidy resolution — where students can articulate what their bilingual identity means to them.

descriptors.title: Features and conventions of spoken target language for fluency
descriptors.description: apply features and conventions of spoken the target language to extend fluency in responding to and creating texts appropriate to contexts, purposes and audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply tonal and prosodic knowledge fluently in text response and creation, and comprehend diverse speakers (AC9LCH8U01). They have discriminated subtle tonal and regional features. They have not yet delivered formal speeches to real audiences, analysed tone and rhythm for own composition, or quoted from traditional literature with appropriate intonation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply features and conventions of spoken target language to extend fluency in responding to and creating texts — including formal speech, analysis of tone and rhythm patterns for composition, and comprehension strategies for diverse accents.
elaborations: delivering authentic speech to a range of audiences using appropriate intonation and stress
analysing a dialogue or text, identifying tone patterns and rhythm, and developing own texts with similar features
developing strategies to understand meaning when listening to diverse regional accents
comparing own Chinese speech patterns with a range of accents and creating talk show scripts
watching a range of target language performances and performing own version to the class
using appropriate intonation and pronunciation when quoting sayings from traditional literature

nodes.label: Formal speech delivery
nodes.checkpoint: Students can deliver formal speeches to real or realistic audiences using appropriate intonation, stress, phrasing and cultural conventions.
criteria: Delivers a formal speech of at least two minutes with appropriate intonation and stress for the formal register
Can identify and explain at least one deliberate prosodic choice made during delivery
nodes.hinge_reason: Formal speech delivery is the prerequisite for all formal spoken production at Y9-10. Students who cannot manage prosodic conventions in formal contexts cannot meet the public speaking, debating and presentation demands of the other Y9-10 descriptors.

width.minimum: Deliver a formal speech of at least two minutes using appropriate intonation, stress and phrasing, with at least one deliberate prosodic choice justified by communicative purpose.
width.typical: Deliver authentic speech to diverse audiences — welcome speeches, presentations, formal addresses; use appropriate intonation, stress and phrasing for formal register; quote from traditional literature with correct intonation; watch and perform target language cultural performances.
wider: Record and review a formal speech delivery — identify specific prosodic choices and evaluate their effectiveness for the audience and purpose
Compare formal speech conventions in the target language with English equivalents — identify differences in pacing, pause conventions, and intonation patterns for formal contexts

modes.reason: Formal speech delivery requires repeated performance practice with specific feedback on prosodic choices. Regular formal speech tasks — with self-review and peer evaluation — build the confidence and precision that formal delivery requires.

nodes.label: Analysing tone and rhythm for composition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse tone patterns and rhythm in spoken or written target language texts and apply insights to develop their own texts with similar prosodic features.
criteria: Analyses at least one text for tone patterns and rhythm, identifying specific features
Produces an original text demonstrating at least two prosodic features from the analysis

width.minimum: Analyse the tone patterns and rhythm of at least one target language text and produce an original text demonstrating at least two prosodic features identified in the analysis.
width.typical: Analyse dialogues and texts for tone patterns and rhythm; develop own texts applying similar prosodic features; create talk show scripts using different accents; quote traditional literature with appropriate tone and rhythm; understand variation of tones, stress and rhythm in cultural performances.
wider: Create a script or spoken text specifically designed to use tonal and rhythmic patterns for effect — explain the prosodic design decisions and how they serve the communicative purpose
Compare the tonal and rhythmic patterns of two different target language genres — identify genre-specific prosodic conventions and apply them in original compositions

modes.reason: Prosodic analysis for composition requires students to extract the underlying pattern from a model text and apply it productively — not just appreciate it. Explicit analysis frameworks followed by compositional tasks that require deliberate prosodic choices build this analytical-productive capacity.

nodes.label: Comprehension strategies for diverse accents
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop and apply strategies for understanding spoken target language from speakers with diverse regional accents, using contextual inference and accent awareness.
criteria: Identifies at least two strategies for comprehending unfamiliar regional accents
Demonstrates application of at least one strategy when listening to an unfamiliar accent

width.minimum: Identify at least two strategies for comprehending unfamiliar regional accents in the target language and demonstrate their application when listening to an unfamiliar accent.
width.typical: Develop strategies to understand meaning from diverse regional accents — contextual inference, acoustic focus, vocabulary prediction; compare own speech patterns with diverse accents; identify specific phonological features of different regional varieties.
wider: Research a specific regional accent — describe its key phonological features, find examples, and explain the comprehension strategies most useful for that variety
Compare comprehension strategies across multiple regional varieties encountered — identify which strategies transfer across accents and which are variety-specific

modes.reason: Accent comprehension strategies integrate formal speech delivery (node 1) and prosodic analysis (node 2) into a complete spoken language competence. The teaching investment is in creating genuine exposure to diverse spoken target language — real speakers, real accents — rather than only standard variety input.

descriptors.title: Character form and function, complex grammatical structures
descriptors.description: apply knowledge of character form and function, and complex grammatical structures and features, to predict meaning and to compose a wide range of texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply morphological knowledge and use the full sentence-type range in composed texts (AC9LCH8U02). They have used modal, tense-expression and exclamatory structures. They have not yet used print dictionaries for character lookup, explored polysemy across complex contexts, applied auxiliary verbs, used advanced punctuation conventions, or compared simplified and traditional character forms.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply knowledge of character form and function and complex grammatical structures and features to predict meaning and compose a wide range of texts — including using print resources, polysemy analysis, complex modality, and advanced punctuation.
elaborations: using knowledge of components to look up new characters in print dictionaries
exploring the changes of meaning for the same characters in different contexts
predicting meanings of complex characters using knowledge of pictographs
determining the precise meanings of character morphemes by context
applying knowledge of characters and functions to compose a wide range of texts
applying knowledge of punctuation in a range of complex texts
applying knowledge of modal verbs and auxiliary verbs across text types
applying knowledge of tense in formal and informal text types
responding appropriately to sarcasm, exclamatory sentences or factual statements
identifying how sentence structures convey messages effectively
comparing known simplified characters with traditional characters and discussing differences

nodes.label: Advanced character analysis and print resource use
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use knowledge of character components to look up new characters in print dictionaries, predict meanings of complex characters using pictographic knowledge, and explore polysemy in context.
criteria: Looks up at least three characters in a print dictionary using component knowledge
Identifies at least two polysemous characters and explains the different meaning in each context
nodes.hinge_reason: Advanced character analysis and print dictionary use are the productive literacy prerequisites for independent wide reading and composition at Y9-10. Students who cannot use print resources or analyse character polysemy are dependent on digital tools and cannot develop the independent literacy the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Use a print dictionary to look up at least three unfamiliar characters using component knowledge, and identify at least two examples of polysemous characters used differently in different contexts.
width.typical: Use component knowledge to look up characters in print dictionaries; predict meanings of complex characters using pictographic knowledge; determine precise meanings of morphemes by context; explore polysemous characters across different contexts; compare simplified and traditional character forms.
wider: Research the relationship between simplified and traditional character forms for a set of characters — explain what was simplified, why, and what (if anything) is lost or gained
Investigate a polysemous character — identify all its documented meanings, explain the semantic relationship between them, and create examples showing each meaning in context

modes.reason: Print dictionary use and polysemy analysis require systematic application of component and morphological knowledge — students need a framework for navigating print dictionaries and for determining which meaning of a polysemous character is active in context. Explicit strategy instruction followed by independent practice builds this capacity.

nodes.label: Complex modality and advanced grammatical features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply knowledge of modal and auxiliary verbs, complex tense expression, and advanced punctuation conventions across a range of text types.
criteria: Produces a text demonstrating correct use of at least three different complex grammatical features
Applies advanced punctuation conventions correctly in at least one text

width.minimum: Produce a text demonstrating correct use of at least three different complex grammatical features — modal verbs, auxiliary verbs, or advanced punctuation — with appropriate accuracy for the text type.
width.typical: Apply modal verbs and auxiliary verbs in a range of text types; apply knowledge of tense in formal and informal contexts; use advanced punctuation including quotation marks for sarcasm, brackets, ellipsis; respond appropriately to sarcasm, exclamatory sentences and factual statements; identify how sentence structures convey messages effectively.
wider: Analyse how modal and auxiliary verbs create different degrees of certainty, obligation or possibility — create a set of examples showing the full range and explain the distinctions
Investigate advanced punctuation conventions in the target language that have no direct English equivalent — explain the function of each and create examples demonstrating correct use

modes.reason: Complex modality and advanced grammatical features require repeated production across varied text types before they become reliable. Targeted writing tasks across different genres — formal report, personal narrative, persuasive text — build the flexible grammatical competence the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Composing a wide range of texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply full character and grammatical knowledge to compose and respond to a wide range of texts — including formal, informal, literary and multimodal — across diverse contexts and purposes.
criteria: Composes at least two texts of different types demonstrating full writing system knowledge
Grammar and vocabulary choices are appropriate for each text type and purpose

width.minimum: Compose at least two texts of different types (e.g. a formal report and a narrative) demonstrating full writing system knowledge and appropriate grammar for each text type.
width.typical: Apply full character and grammatical knowledge across a wide range of text types — reports, plans, diaries, literary texts, multimodal productions; adapt grammar and vocabulary for context, purpose and audience; respond to diverse stimuli demonstrating appropriate grammatical choices.
wider: Compose a text that deliberately uses a specific grammatical feature for rhetorical effect — explain the choice and compare the effect with an alternative grammatical approach
Review and annotate own extended writing for grammatical accuracy and appropriateness — identify patterns of error or inconsistency and develop a targeted improvement plan

modes.reason: Wide-range text composition integrates advanced character analysis (node 1) and complex grammatical features (node 2) into the full productive literacy demand of Y9-10. The teaching investment is in creating varied, genuine composition tasks across text types — not only narrative or only formal — that require students to deploy their full grammatical and textual knowledge.

descriptors.title: Analyse target language texts using metalanguage
descriptors.description: analyse a range of target language texts, using metalanguage to explain linguistic, textual and cultural elements
descriptors.knowledge: Students can reflect on and explain similarities and differences between target language and English, support younger learners, and analyse metaphorical meaning (AC9LCH8U03). They have applied comparative metalanguage across text types. They have not yet analysed stylistic devices in target language texts, compared genre organisation across languages, described genres unique to target language literary tradition, or used metalanguage to explain linguistic, textual and cultural elements simultaneously.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse a range of target language texts using metalanguage to explain linguistic, textual and cultural elements — including stylistic devices, genre conventions, structural analysis, and culturally-specific literary forms.
elaborations: analysing linguistic features using metalanguage such as double negatives and parallel sentences
analysing a range of text types and explaining how different language features suit different purposes in cultural contexts
analysing and categorising cultural and linguistic elements in target language expressions
comparing key features used in formal and informal contexts in target language and English
analysing the way content is structured in a range of target language texts
analysing the use of stylistic devices in a range of written texts and evaluating their effectiveness
reading and comparing how ideas are ordered and substantiated across genres and languages
describing the purpose and features of genres uniquely important in target language literature

nodes.label: Stylistic devices and rhetorical analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and analyse stylistic devices used in target language texts — including rhetorical, figurative and structural devices — and evaluate their effectiveness.
criteria: Identifies at least three stylistic devices in a target language text using metalanguage
Evaluates the effectiveness of at least one device with explanation
nodes.hinge_reason: Stylistic device analysis is the prerequisite for full text analysis at Y9-10. Students who cannot identify and name stylistic devices cannot produce the linguistic, textual and cultural analysis that this descriptor requires — nor can they apply these insights to their own text creation.

width.minimum: Identify at least three stylistic devices in a target language text, explain how each works using metalanguage, and evaluate the effectiveness of at least one.
width.typical: Analyse stylistic devices in target language written texts — parallel structures, double negatives, figurative devices, rhetorical questions; use metalanguage to explain their function; evaluate the effectiveness of specific devices; compare stylistic conventions in target language and English texts.
wider: Produce a full stylistic analysis of a target language text — annotating every stylistic device with metalanguage and evaluating how each contributes to the text's overall effect
Compare how the same rhetorical effect is achieved differently in target language and English texts — identify genre-specific and culturally-specific stylistic conventions

modes.reason: Stylistic device analysis requires students to identify a device, name it using metalanguage, explain its function, and evaluate its effectiveness — a multi-step analytical process. Explicit stylistic analysis instruction with varied model texts builds this systematic capacity before students can analyse independently.

nodes.label: Genre organisation and content development
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how content is structured and ideas are developed in different target language genres, including how genre conventions compare across languages.
criteria: Analyses the structural organisation of at least two different target language text types
Compares organisational conventions with English for at least one text type

width.minimum: Analyse the structural organisation of at least two different target language text types, explaining how ideas are ordered and developed in each, and comparing with English conventions for at least one.
width.typical: Analyse how text types structure content and develop ideas; compare how information is exchanged using culturally-accepted patterns; compare essay-writing conventions — position placement, argument structure — across languages; analyse linguistic features for different text purposes; categorise cultural and linguistic elements.
wider: Compare essay organisation conventions in the target language with English — explain where the author's position appears, how evidence is marshalled, and what this reveals about cultural epistemological conventions
Apply understanding of genre organisation to produce a text that authentically follows target language conventions — then compare with what the same text would look like following English conventions

modes.reason: Genre organisation analysis must be applied across varied text types — analytical essay, news article, literary prose, formal report — before students can generalise their analytical capacity. Single-genre analysis produces genre-specific rather than transferable text analysis skills.

nodes.label: Culturally-specific literary genres and traditions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the purpose and features of genres unique to target language literary tradition, exploring their origins and demonstrating cultural knowledge in text analysis.
criteria: Identifies at least one genre unique to the target language literary tradition with key features described using metalanguage
Explains the cultural origins or significance of the genre

width.minimum: Identify at least one genre unique to the target language literary tradition, describe its key features using metalanguage, and explain its cultural origins or significance.
width.typical: Describe and analyse genres unique to target language literary tradition; explore their origins in traditional literature; explain cultural purposes and conventions; compare with equivalent or non-equivalent forms in English literary tradition; apply cultural knowledge in text analysis.
wider: Produce a text in a target language literary genre — apply genre conventions authentically and reflect on what cultural knowledge was required to do so
Research the historical development of a target language literary genre — trace how it has evolved from traditional to contemporary forms and what has changed

modes.reason: Culturally-specific genre analysis integrates stylistic device knowledge (node 1) and genre organisation understanding (node 2) into a full cultural-literary analysis. The teaching investment is in creating genuine engagement with target language literary tradition — students as culturally-informed readers, not only linguistic analysts.

descriptors.title: Identity shaped by language, culture and values — evaluate
descriptors.description: reflect on and evaluate how their own and others' identity is shaped by language(s), culture(s), attitudes, beliefs and values, and how these affect ways of communicating
descriptors.knowledge: Students can reflect on and explain how their own and others' identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes and values, and can identify stereotyping risks in intercultural interaction (AC9LCH8U04). They have examined cultural participation and communication adaptation. They have not yet evaluated the impact of globalisation on cultural identity, analysed how title and address conventions reflect cultural values, or reflected on non-verbal cultural behaviour and dress codes as communication.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on and evaluate how their own and others' identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values — including the impact of globalisation, loan words, title conventions, non-verbal behaviour, and the ongoing relationship between language change and cultural identity.
elaborations: reflecting on how own identity is shaped by attitudes, beliefs, values and languages used every day
showing how the use of titles indicates respect or formality compared with Australian culture
indicating the impact of globalisation on cultural change and own identity and beliefs
reflecting on and explaining the protocols required to authentically co-create an Acknowledgement of Country/Place with a First Nations Australian
demonstrating the impact of loan words and internet language on changes in modern languages
reflecting on how non-verbal cultural behaviour such as dress codes affect communication in different cultural settings

nodes.label: Evaluating globalisation's impact on language and identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how globalisation has shaped modern target language use — including loan words, internet language, and cultural change — and reflect on the impact on their own identity and beliefs.
criteria: Identifies at least three examples of globalisation's influence on the target language
Evaluates the impact of at least one on cultural identity with reasoned argument
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluating globalisation's impact is the conceptual prerequisite for the most sophisticated identity reflection the strand requires. Students who have only described language-culture connections cannot evaluate the dynamic, contested relationship between language change, cultural identity and globalisation.

width.minimum: Identify at least three examples of globalisation's influence on the target language (loan words, internet language, or cultural change) and evaluate the impact of at least one on cultural identity.
width.typical: Examine the impact of globalisation on cultural change and language; explore loan words and internet language in modern target language use; reflect on how globalisation has affected own identity and beliefs; evaluate the relationship between language change and cultural maintenance.
wider: Research how a specific wave of globalisation — media, technology, trade — has affected target language vocabulary and cultural practices, and evaluate whether the changes strengthen or challenge cultural identity
Compare own family's language practices across generations — identify where globalisation has changed language use and what this reveals about identity negotiation across time

modes.reason: Evaluating globalisation's impact requires students to distinguish between language change as cultural enrichment and language change as cultural erosion — a genuinely contested question. Explicit frameworks for evaluating impact, rather than only describing it, build the critical analytical capacity the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Title conventions and non-verbal cultural behaviour
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how title and address conventions in the target language reflect cultural values of respect and formality, and how non-verbal cultural behaviour — dress codes, body language, space — affects communication.
criteria: Explains at least two title or address conventions and their cultural significance
Identifies at least two non-verbal cultural behaviours that affect communication across cultural contexts

width.minimum: Explain at least two title or address conventions in the target language and their cultural significance, and identify at least two non-verbal cultural behaviours that affect communication across cultural contexts.
width.typical: Analyse how titles indicate respect and formality in target language versus Australian culture; compare address and title conventions across cultural contexts; examine how non-verbal cultural behaviour — dress codes, personal space, silence, volume — affects communication; discuss how these behaviours may be misinterpreted.
wider: Compare title and address conventions across multiple target language community contexts — identify where conventions vary within the target language world and what this reveals about regional or generational cultural change
Research a specific non-verbal behaviour that differs across target language and English-speaking contexts — explain the cultural logic on both sides and discuss the miscommunication risks

modes.reason: Title, address and non-verbal conventions must be understood across varied social contexts — professional, familial, formal, informal — before students can generalise their understanding. Varied cultural context encounters build the nuanced awareness the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Evaluating own multilingual identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how their own multilingual and multicultural identity has been shaped by the languages, cultures, attitudes and values they have encountered, and how this shapes their ways of communicating.
criteria: Produces a reflective evaluation examining how at least two languages or cultural contexts have shaped own identity
Connects identity reflection to specific communication style choices or adaptations

width.minimum: Produce a reflective evaluation of at least ten sentences examining how at least two languages or cultural contexts have shaped their identity and communication style.
width.typical: Reflect on how own identity is shaped by languages, cultures, attitudes and values encountered daily; evaluate how multilingual background shapes communication choices; reflect on the protocols required for culturally authentic communication with diverse communities including First Nations Australians.
wider: Produce an extended reflective account of own language and cultural identity journey — tracing how it has developed, what has shaped it, and how it continues to evolve

Compare own multilingual identity experience with that of a peer, parent, or community member from a different generation — identify what has changed in how identity is navigated across language communities and discuss what has driven the change

modes.reason: Multilingual identity evaluation integrates globalisation analysis (node 1) and cultural behaviour understanding (node 2) into a full, personally-grounded synthesis. The teaching investment is in creating a genuinely reflective, non-prescriptive environment where students can examine their own identity honestly — including tensions, contradictions and ongoing negotiations — rather than producing a tidy, resolved account.

descriptors.title: Initiate, sustain and extend exchanges
descriptors.description: initiate, sustain and extend exchanges in familiar and unfamiliar contexts related to students' own and others' experiences of the world, adjusting their language in response to others
descriptors.knowledge: Students can initiate and sustain exchanges in familiar and some unfamiliar contexts, adjusting register and structuring arguments (AC9LS8C01). They have not yet extended exchanges into fully unfamiliar territory, sustained discussion of others' experiences, or used a full range of discussion management strategies.
descriptors.endpoint: Students initiate, sustain and extend exchanges in familiar and unfamiliar contexts about their own and others' experiences — using structured argument, discussion management, register adjustment and spontaneous interaction strategies.
elaborations: applying appropriate register and modifying behaviour, language and etiquette in familiar and unfamiliar contexts
exchanging messages with peers in a target language context to share views about aspects of teenage life
interviewing class members to elicit opinions on personal experiences and significant events
maintaining and extending conversations by following up on others' contributions
using language to achieve different purposes in interactions, including contractions and slang for speed and economy
interacting in role-plays or spontaneous skits about travelling and service situations
playing a true and false game relating to past experiences, future aspirations or topics of interest
participating in a discussion, exchanging different viewpoints using strategies such as sentence starters, asking for repetition or inviting elaboration

nodes.label: Exchanging accounts of experiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can exchange accounts of their own and others' significant experiences — using narrative, question and response strategies across familiar and unfamiliar contexts.
criteria: Shares at least one account of a significant experience using narrative structure
Asks and responds to at least two questions about another person's experience
nodes.hinge_reason: Exchanging accounts of others' experiences — not only one's own — requires perspective-taking and responsive questioning that is a prerequisite for the discussion and debate work in node 2.

width.minimum: Share at least one account of a significant experience using narrative structure; ask and respond to questions about another person's experience.
width.typical: Exchange accounts of significant events, milestones and personal experiences; use narrative techniques to develop accounts; ask follow-up questions about others' experiences; identify common themes across shared accounts.
wider: Exchange accounts with a target language community peer — adapting language and cultural references for the audience
Compare two accounts of the same type of experience from different cultural perspectives — identify what each reveals about the values of each community

modes.reason: Narrative and experiential exchange requires a bank of discourse-level strategies — not only sentence-level structures. Students need varied practice exchanging accounts across different topic areas.

nodes.label: Structuring arguments and managing discussion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can structure arguments, invite contributions and manage discussion flow using a range of discourse strategies.
criteria: Uses at least two argument-structuring moves in a sustained exchange
Uses at least two discussion management strategies effectively

width.minimum: Use at least two argument-structuring moves and at least two discussion management strategies in a sustained exchange.
width.typical: Use structured argument language to justify positions; use discussion management strategies for turn-taking, inviting elaboration and requesting clarification; maintain and extend conversations through follow-up questions and connectors; use language for different interactional purposes.
wider: Facilitate a class discussion on a contested topic — managing contributions, summarising positions and steering toward shared understanding
Participate in a discussion where a stated position is challenged — respond to the challenge without abandoning the position unless a compelling reason is given

modes.reason: Discussion management strategies develop through varied discussion contexts — different topics, interlocutors and discussion structures each require different management moves.

nodes.label: Adjusting language across unfamiliar contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adjust their language across familiar and unfamiliar contexts — using appropriate register, slang or formal language for varied interlocutors and purposes.
criteria: Demonstrates deliberate language adjustment in at least two different contexts
Responds with adequate fluency in at least one unfamiliar or unscripted situation

width.minimum: Demonstrate deliberate language adjustment in at least two different contexts — one familiar and one unfamiliar.
width.typical: Apply appropriate register across formal, informal and digital communication contexts; use contemporary language varieties including abbreviations and colloquial shortening; adjust language in response to interlocutor and context; interact in spontaneous and unscripted situations.
wider: Interact in a fully spontaneous scenario — an unrehearsed situation in an unfamiliar context — applying available language flexibly
Compare language adjustment strategies across two different unfamiliar contexts and explain what signals triggered each adjustment

modes.reason: Language adjustment across unfamiliar contexts requires encountering genuinely varied and unpredictable interaction conditions. Rehearsed scenarios do not build the spontaneous adjustment capacity needed.

nodes.label: Sustaining exchanges about complex and topical subjects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can initiate and sustain exchanges about complex and topical subjects — including social issues, global topics and shared experiences — drawing on a full range of interaction strategies.
criteria: Initiates and sustains an exchange on a complex or topical subject for at least six turns
Uses a mix of at least three different interaction strategies across the exchange

width.minimum: Initiate and sustain an exchange on a complex or topical subject for at least six turns using a mix of argument, narrative and discussion management strategies.
width.typical: Engage in discussion of topical issues, social questions and shared experiences across familiar and unfamiliar subjects; use the full range of interaction strategies developed across prior nodes; sustain extended exchanges with varied interlocutors.
wider: Participate in a sustained exchange on a topic of genuine personal significance — demonstrating that the target language can carry the full weight of the student's thinking
Initiate and maintain a target language exchange with a community member on a topic of mutual interest — adapting spontaneously to the interlocutor's responses

modes.reason: Extended exchanges on complex subjects integrate all prior interaction capabilities — narrative, argument, management and adjustment — in a sustained communicative performance.

descriptors.title: Contribute to discussions involving diverse views
descriptors.description: contribute to discussions that involve diverse views to negotiate outcomes, address issues and compare experiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can initiate and sustain exchanges using argument structures and discussion management (AC9LS10C01). They have not yet contributed systematically to multi-perspective discussions, used persuasive language for topical issues, or participated in collaborative media or broadcast contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students contribute to discussions involving diverse views — using agreement, disagreement, negotiation and persuasive language to address issues and compare experiences.
elaborations: interacting in class discussion and debates by taking turns, expressing agreement/disagreement and providing encouragement
negotiating arrangements, weighing up alternatives and reaching shared decisions in relation to planned activities
participating in real or simulated transactions such as exchanging, ordering and bargaining for consumer items
participating in collaborative projects such as a segment for a community radio or television program
using argument and expressive or persuasive language to discuss topical issues

nodes.label: Expressing agreement, disagreement and encouraging participation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express agreement and disagreement, encourage others' contributions, and use turn-taking strategies in group discussion.
criteria: Expresses at least one agreement and one disagreement using appropriate target language conventions
Uses at least one strategy to invite another person's contribution
nodes.hinge_reason: Expressing agreement and disagreement through target language conventions — not only through the logic of what is said — is the social foundation for genuine multi-perspective discussion. Students who only express opinion without these conventions cannot participate in the collaborative and persuasive tasks that follow.

width.minimum: Express at least one agreement and one disagreement using target language conventions; use at least one strategy to invite another person's contribution.
width.typical: Use varied expressions for agreement and disagreement; provide encouragement and acknowledgement in discussion; take turns and manage overlapping contributions; negotiate shared decisions in collaborative contexts.
wider: Facilitate a group discussion — ensuring balanced contribution and summarising diverse views at the end
Respond to a position that conflicts with their own — using target language conventions for polite but direct disagreement

modes.reason: Agreement and disagreement conventions require a bank of expressions for varied levels of alignment and contexts. Students need varied practice across different discussion types.

nodes.label: Negotiating outcomes and reaching shared decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can negotiate arrangements, weigh up alternatives and reach shared decisions through target language interaction.
criteria: Contributes at least one alternative and responds to another participant's contribution in a negotiation
The negotiation reaches a shared decision or outcome through target language interaction

width.minimum: Participate in a negotiation that reaches a shared decision — contributing at least one alternative and responding to at least one from another participant.
width.typical: Negotiate arrangements and alternatives across varied planning and decision contexts; weigh up options using evaluative language; reach shared decisions through compromise and persuasion; participate in simulated and real transactions involving negotiation.
wider: Negotiate a genuinely contested decision with competing constraints — demonstrating that the outcome reflects real compromise
Participate in a transaction with an unexpected complication — applying negotiation strategies spontaneously to resolve it

modes.reason: Negotiation skills develop through varied decision contexts — different stakes, different types of alternatives, different interlocutor positions each require different negotiation strategies.

nodes.label: Using persuasive language for topical issues
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use argument and persuasive language to contribute to discussion of topical issues — including social, environmental and cultural topics.
criteria: Uses at least two persuasive language moves in a discussion of a topical issue
Acknowledges at least one opposing view in the course of the discussion

width.minimum: Use at least two persuasive language moves in a discussion of a topical issue; acknowledge at least one opposing view.
width.typical: Use argument and persuasive language to discuss topical issues; structure contributions to introduce, support and conclude a position; acknowledge and respond to opposing views; participate in collaborative community media or broadcast projects.
wider: Contribute to a multi-perspective discussion on a topical issue where participants hold genuinely different positions — sustaining the argument through at least three exchange turns
Produce a persuasive contribution to a community media project — presenting a position on a real issue to a real audience

modes.reason: Using persuasive language for topical issues integrates all prior discussion capabilities — agreement/disagreement (N1), negotiation (N2) — and applies them in an argument context with genuine intellectual stakes.

descriptors.title: Evaluate and synthesise information, ideas and perspectives
descriptors.description: evaluate and synthesise information, ideas and perspectives in a broad range of spoken, written and multimodal texts and respond appropriately to cultural context, purpose and audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interpret information and evaluate source reliability in target language texts, responding to cultural nuance and diverse perspectives (AC9LS8C03). They have not yet evaluated and synthesised across a broad range of sources, distinguished fact from opinion systematically, or created responses that integrate multiple perspectives.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate and synthesise information, ideas and perspectives across a broad range of target language texts — distinguishing fact from opinion, comparing perspectives, and responding appropriately to cultural context, purpose and audience.
elaborations: comparing different perspectives about an issue from different stakeholder viewpoints and incorporating information into a multimodal text
exploring persuasive and informative texts to recognise fact versus opinion and presenting findings
reading an advertisement and responding appropriately, addressing key criteria
listening to or reading First Nations Australians' stories in English and creating a profile in the target language
summarising information from sources regarding an issue of interest, determining most important information and presenting with personal perspective
locating and researching information from reliable sources to inform decisions
synthesising information from a range of sources to group and present ideas in a logical manner
adapting and changing texts to suit different contexts, purposes and audiences
analysing published accounts of events and reporting results and highlights
composing a review of a film, story or documentary and expressing opinions about different perspectives
listening to extracts from expressive contemporary texts and identifying cultural elements
expressing responses to personal or peer experiences using evaluative and expressive language

nodes.label: Distinguishing fact from opinion and evaluating perspectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish fact from opinion in target language texts and evaluate the perspectives presented.
criteria: Identifies at least two instances of fact and two of opinion in a text
Identifies the perspective of at least one text and explains the assumptions it makes
nodes.hinge_reason: Distinguishing fact from opinion and evaluating perspective is the analytical foundation for all synthesis work. Students who cannot identify the position of a text cannot synthesise across multiple perspectives.

width.minimum: Identify at least two instances of fact and two of opinion in a text; evaluate the perspective of at least one text, identifying its position.
width.typical: Analyse persuasive and informative texts to recognise fact versus opinion; identify the perspective and assumptions of text producers; compare different stakeholder perspectives on an issue; evaluate texts for reliability, accuracy and bias.
wider: Compare two texts on the same topic from different stakeholder perspectives — explain what each perspective includes, excludes and assumes
Evaluate a target language community media text for perspective and bias — present findings with specific evidence

modes.reason: Fact-opinion distinction and perspective evaluation requires explicit analytical frameworks. Students need to be able to articulate criteria for each before applying them spontaneously.

nodes.label: Synthesising information across sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can synthesise information from multiple target language sources — grouping and presenting ideas, themes and issues in a logical and coherent manner.
criteria: Synthesises information from at least two sources into a response that organises ideas thematically
Presents a personal perspective alongside the synthesised information

width.minimum: Synthesise information from at least two sources into a coherent response that organises ideas thematically.
width.typical: Locate and research information from varied reliable sources; weigh options and organise information logically; determine what is most important or interesting from a range of sources; summarise and present synthesised information with personal perspective; create profiles of significant people or topics from multiple sources.
wider: Synthesise information from target language and English sources on the same topic — compare what each language-community source emphasises and explain what this reveals
Create a synthesis that integrates at least three different perspectives on an issue — not only summarising each but showing how they relate to each other

modes.reason: Synthesis requires students to move from juxtaposing sources to integrating them — identifying relationships, not only collecting information. Structured synthesis tasks scaffold this integrative thinking.

nodes.label: Responding to cultural context and diverse text types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can respond to target language texts appropriately for cultural context, purpose and audience — including expressive, creative and culturally embedded texts.
criteria: Produces a response to a culturally embedded text appropriate to its cultural context
Identifies at least one cultural element in the text and explains its significance

width.minimum: Produce a response to at least one culturally embedded text that is appropriate to its cultural context — not only its linguistic content.
width.typical: Respond to expressive contemporary texts — songs, poems, performances, artworks; identify cultural elements that reflect target language community experience; listen to First Nations Australian stories and create profiles in the target language; express evaluative responses using expressive language; adapt texts for different contexts and audiences.
wider: Create a profile of a First Nations Australian author or storyteller in the target language — drawing on their story as source and reflecting on the cultural significance of the work
Respond to a target language community expressive text — identifying cultural elements, explaining their significance and connecting to a parallel element in Australian culture

modes.reason: Culturally appropriate response develops through encountering diverse text types, genres and cultural contexts. Each new cultural text type reveals different dimensions of the language-culture relationship.

nodes.label: Adapting texts for context, purpose and audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can adapt target language texts for different contexts, purposes and audiences — making deliberate choices about language, register and content.
criteria: Adapts a text for a different context or audience with at least two deliberate language changes identified
The adapted text is appropriate and coherent for the new context or audience

width.minimum: Adapt a text for a different context or audience — identifying at least two deliberate language changes made for the new context.
width.typical: Adapt formal texts for informal contexts and vice versa; change text purpose (informative to persuasive; narrative to analytical); adapt for different audience knowledge levels; create texts that respond to and incorporate information from other texts.
wider: Adapt the same content for two radically different audiences — contrast every language, register and content choice made for each
Adapt a text for a genuine external audience — reflect on whether the adaptation successfully served that audience's needs

modes.reason: Text adaptation integrates evaluation and synthesis (N1-N3) with production — students draw on their analysis of source texts to create purposeful adapted versions. The real audience condition is the fullest integration test.

descriptors.title: Interpret and translate for intercultural understanding
descriptors.description: interpret and translate non-verbal, spoken and written interactions and texts to convey meaning and intercultural understanding in familiar and unfamiliar contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interpret and adjust language for cultural contexts — including context-dependent meaning, translation comparison and cultural response creation (AC9LS8C04). They have not yet worked systematically with creative text translation, evaluated translation tools critically, or reflected on intercultural miscommunication.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret and translate target language interactions and texts to convey meaning and intercultural understanding — including creative text translation, tool evaluation, and reflection on intercultural miscommunication.
elaborations: translating short familiar texts such as advertisements, songs or film clips, comparing own translation with others and analysing differences
reflecting on the difficulty of achieving equivalence in translations of creative texts
using, comparing and evaluating online translators for accuracy, efficiency and reliability
experimenting with translations of popular expressions or idioms, noticing when this creates potential for confusion
creating bilingual texts that present aspects of Australian culture for target language community audiences
considering how to maintain the integrity of original texts when translating culture-specific concepts and slang
reflecting on how meaning can be misinterpreted in intercultural interactions

nodes.label: Translating and comparing translations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can translate short target language texts and compare their translation with others' — analysing similarities, differences and possible explanations.
criteria: Translates a short text and compares with at least one other translation
Identifies at least two translation decisions and explains the reasoning for each
nodes.hinge_reason: Translation comparison — reflecting on why versions differ — is the analytical foundation for all deeper translation work. Students who translate without comparing cannot develop the metacognitive awareness of translation as decision-making.

width.minimum: Translate a short familiar text and compare with at least one other translation — identify at least two translation decisions and explain each.
width.typical: Translate short target language texts across varied text types; compare translations with classmates; analyse similarities and differences between versions; consider possible reasons for translation variation; reflect on challenges of achieving equivalence.
wider: Translate a creative text (song, poem, advertisement) and annotate every decision point — explain where literal translation was abandoned and why
Compare three different translations of the same text — identify what each prioritises (literal accuracy, cultural resonance, readability) and evaluate the trade-offs

modes.reason: Translation decision analysis requires students to articulate the reasons behind choices — not only make them. Comparative annotation tasks scaffold this explicit reasoning.

nodes.label: Evaluating translation tools and creative translation challenges
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the accuracy, efficiency and reliability of translation tools, and reflect on the specific challenges of translating creative and culturally specific content.
criteria: Evaluates at least one translation tool and identifies at least two specific limitations
Identifies at least one expression where equivalence is not achievable and explains why

width.minimum: Evaluate at least one translation tool for a specific text — identify at least two limitations; identify at least one creative or culturally specific expression where equivalence is not achievable.
width.typical: Use, compare and evaluate online translation tools for accuracy and reliability; discuss risks of over-reliance on automated translation; experiment with translating idiomatic and culturally specific expressions; reflect on the difficulty of achieving equivalence in creative texts.
wider: Evaluate an automated translation of a target language text — identify every error, ambiguity or cultural loss and explain what each reveals about the limits of machine translation
Translate a culturally specific text and produce a translator's note — explaining the most challenging decisions and the strategies used

modes.reason: Critical evaluation of translation tools requires explicit evaluation criteria — students need to be able to articulate what makes a translation accurate, appropriate and culturally sensitive.

nodes.label: Creating bilingual texts and reflecting on intercultural miscommunication
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create bilingual texts for target language community audiences and reflect on how meaning can be misinterpreted in intercultural interactions.
criteria: Creates a bilingual text with at least two deliberate decisions about cultural explanation vs translation explained
Reflects on at least one instance of potential intercultural miscommunication and proposes a strategy for managing it

width.minimum: Create a bilingual text for a target language community audience — making at least two deliberate decisions about cultural explanation vs translation; reflect on at least one instance of potential intercultural miscommunication.
width.typical: Create bilingual texts presenting aspects of Australian culture for target language community audiences; consider how to maintain integrity of original texts when translating culture-specific content; reflect on experiences of miscommunication and strategies for managing it; discuss how meaning can shift in intercultural interactions.
wider: Create a bilingual text for a real target language community audience — include a reflective note on the most challenging decisions about cultural explanation vs translation
Research and present instances where target language-English intercultural communication has produced misunderstanding — explain the mechanisms that caused each

modes.reason: Creating bilingual texts for genuine audiences integrates translation skill (N1), tool awareness (N2), and intercultural reflection — all applied in a purposeful mediating act for a real recipient.

descriptors.title: Create texts for diverse contexts and audiences
descriptors.description: create and present informative and imaginative texts for diverse contexts and purposes, selecting vocabulary, expressions, grammatical structures and a range of features and conventions to engage different audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create texts for specific purposes, selecting vocabulary and structures deliberately (AC9LS8C05). They create for defined purposes. They have not yet created for genuinely diverse contexts and audiences simultaneously, used narrative perspective deliberately, or created texts for external community audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and present informative and imaginative texts for diverse contexts and purposes — selecting vocabulary, structures and conventions to engage different audiences.
elaborations: creating a multimodal presentation comparing different perspectives on a topical issue
creating visual displays of data or information gathered from research to share with peers
composing different types of social media texts to present views on particular issues
writing a journal entry or contributing to a school newsletter reflecting on a visit to a significant First Nations Country/Place
writing the script for and presenting role-plays with characters and themes likely to appeal to specific audiences
composing and performing speeches or dialogues that reference significant celebrations or historical events
telling a story from several different perspectives and points of view
selecting images and writing descriptions from the perspective of different characters
composing a secure online cultural ID profile to exchange with target language community peers

nodes.label: Selecting features for diverse audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select vocabulary, expressions and conventions deliberately to engage specific and varied audiences — not only to meet a defined purpose.
criteria: Creates a text for a specified audience with at least three deliberate feature selections identified
The text is consistently designed for audience engagement — not only purpose compliance
nodes.hinge_reason: Designing language choices for audience engagement — not only for purpose — is the maturation of the text creation capability across the sequence. Students who only consider purpose without audience produce texts that are technically correct but communicatively flat.

width.minimum: Create a text for a specified audience and identify at least three deliberate feature selections made to engage that audience.
width.typical: Create texts across informative and imaginative purposes with audience engagement as the primary design criterion; use varied vocabulary, structures and conventions suited to each audience; create digital and print texts that present views on issues for specific audiences.
wider: Create the same content for two contrasting audiences — explicitly contrast every vocabulary, structure and convention choice made for each
Create a text for an audience with no target language background — make deliberate decisions about what requires explanation and what can be assumed

modes.reason: Audience-oriented design requires metacognitive attention to the reader's perspective. Annotation tasks and contrastive production scaffold the audience-awareness that makes language choices genuinely communicative.

nodes.label: Creating across imaginative modes and narrative perspectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create imaginative texts across varied modes — using different narrative perspectives, characters, settings and plot structures — to engage specific audiences.
criteria: Creates at least one imaginative text using a deliberate narrative perspective
Explains why the chosen perspective serves the intended audience

width.minimum: Create at least one imaginative text using a deliberate narrative perspective — identifying why that perspective was chosen for the audience.
width.typical: Create stories, plays, scripts and dialogues across varied imaginative formats; use first, second and third person narration deliberately; create texts from multiple character perspectives; use description, dialogue and action to engage audiences; create cultural and community performance texts.
wider: Tell the same story from three different points of view — explaining what each perspective reveals and conceals for the audience
Create an imaginative text for a genuinely different cultural audience — reflecting on what needed to change to make it accessible and engaging for that audience

modes.reason: Narrative perspective and imaginative mode competence develops through creating across varied perspective conditions and text formats.

nodes.label: Creating for real and community audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create and present texts for real community audiences — including target language community peers, First Nations Australian cultural contexts, and public occasions.
criteria: Creates and presents at least one text for a genuine audience outside the classroom
Reflects on whether the text achieved its communicative purpose for that audience

width.minimum: Create and present at least one text for a genuine audience outside the classroom — reflecting on whether it achieved its communicative purpose.
width.typical: Create texts for real community purposes — social media, school publications, community events, cultural exchanges with target language community peers; reflect on the impact of a visit to a significant cultural location and present in the target language; compose and perform speeches for real occasions; create cultural ID profiles for exchange with target language community peers.
wider: Create a text for a target language community peer exchange — receive and incorporate feedback about whether the text achieved its communicative purpose for that audience
Contribute to a First Nations cultural location text with appropriate permission — reflecting on the protocols followed and what they taught about cultural respect

modes.reason: Creating for real community audiences integrates all prior text creation capabilities — audience design (N1) and imaginative mode (N2) — and tests them in a genuine communicative context.

descriptors.title: Sustain interactions in varied contexts
descriptors.description: initiate and sustain interactions in familiar and some unfamiliar contexts to exchange ideas, opinions and experiences about their own and others' personal worlds
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interact using modelled language to exchange personal information in familiar contexts and manage classroom language (AC9LS8EC01, AC9LS8EC02). They have not yet initiated and sustained interactions independently or exchanged opinions and personal experiences in unfamiliar contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students initiate and sustain interactions in the target language in familiar and some unfamiliar contexts, exchanging ideas, opinions and personal experiences about their own and others' worlds, using strategies to maintain flow and authenticity.
elaborations: initiating conversations with peers, family and others using appropriate expressions
expressing, comparing and explaining likes, dislikes and preferences
interviewing other teenagers to build relationships and share views on aspects of young people's lives
developing non-verbal and spoken techniques and strategies to maintain the flow and authenticity of conversations
sharing impressions of past experiences and significant events
discussing personal views on topics such as bullying, beauty ideals and music
using appropriate discussion strategies such as active listening, showing interest, acknowledging others' opinions, responding to and inviting contributions

nodes.label: Initiating conversations and topics
nodes.checkpoint: Students can initiate conversations in the target language using appropriate opening strategies and introduce a topic for discussion.
criteria: Can initiate a conversation in the target language unprompted, using at least one natural opening strategy
Can introduce a topic for discussion without relying on a scripted or heavily modelled prompt

width.minimum: Initiate at least one conversation in the target language using an appropriate opening and introduce a topic unprompted.
width.typical: Use a range of conversation-opening strategies across social and learning contexts; introduce topics with natural, contextually appropriate openers; use small talk strategies to open and maintain early interaction.
wider: Initiate a conversation in an unfamiliar or semi-formal context (e.g. with an older speaker, in a simulated professional context) using appropriate register
Compare conversation-opening conventions in the target language community with Australian English — identify where culturally specific openers are expected

modes.reason: Conversation initiation requires a bank of opening strategies across contexts. Students who have only one rehearsed opener will stall in novel situations. Varied practice across social and topic contexts builds the flexibility needed.

nodes.label: Sustaining interaction and managing flow
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sustain an interaction in the target language using strategies to maintain flow, show interest and respond to others — including in some unfamiliar contexts.
criteria: Sustains a conversation for at least three meaningful exchanges without reverting to English or falling silent
Uses at least one active maintenance strategy (follow-up question, acknowledgement, spontaneous response) during the interaction
nodes.hinge_reason: Sustaining interaction is the structural demand of EC01 — it is what distinguishes a scripted exchange from genuine conversation. Students who can initiate but not sustain will be unable to engage with the opinion exchange and experience-sharing demands in nodes 3–4. All collaborative speaking tasks in EC02 and EC03 depend on sustained interaction capacity.

width.minimum: Sustain a conversation for at least three meaningful exchanges using at least one strategy to maintain flow (e.g. asking a follow-up question, acknowledging a partner's point).
width.typical: Use active listening, acknowledgement, follow-up questions and spontaneous interjections to maintain authentic conversational flow; manage breakdowns using repair strategies; sustain interactions across familiar and some unfamiliar topics.
wider: Participate in a discussion on a topic introduced spontaneously by a partner — adapt strategies to an unfamiliar topic in real time
Reflect on own conversation strategies after a recorded interaction — identify where flow was lost and what repair strategy could have been used

modes.reason: Conversation maintenance strategies must be practised across varied partner and topic combinations before they become automatic. Scripted role-play is insufficient — students need semi-structured and unscripted interaction opportunities to develop genuine fluency.
Strategies that work in one familiar conversational context may not transfer to an unfamiliar topic or partner. Varied conversational contexts build transferable interaction skills.

nodes.label: Exchanging opinions and personal experiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express and exchange opinions, compare views and share personal experiences in the target language, including on topics of personal and social relevance.
criteria: Expresses at least one opinion with a simple justification in the target language
Responds to a partner's contrasting view with a reasoned reply rather than only agreement or silence

width.minimum: Express and briefly justify at least one opinion on a familiar topic in the target language; respond to a partner's opinion with agreement or reasoned contrast.
width.typical: Express, compare and explain opinions and preferences; share and respond to personal experiences; discuss topics of personal and social relevance using structures for agreement, contrast and justification.
wider: Discuss a contentious or socially relevant topic — use persuasion and acknowledgement strategies to manage divergent views respectfully
