Share and compare experiences across cultural contexts — identify where experiences or values differ between own background and target language communities

modes.reason: Expressing justified opinions requires students to move beyond 'I like/I don't like' to reasoning structures ('because', 'in my opinion', 'on the other hand'). Explicit modelling of opinion structures and supported opinion exchanges scaffold this move.

descriptors.title: Question, compare and discuss ideas
descriptors.description: use the target language in exchanges to question, offer opinions and compare and discuss ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students can initiate and sustain interactions to exchange personal opinions and experiences (AC9LS10EC01) and can express basic opinions using set phrases (AC9LS8EC02). They have not yet participated in structured discussion or debate where they question others' views, compare arguments and develop position-based exchanges.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use the target language to participate in exchanges involving questioning, expressing and justifying opinions, and comparing and discussing ideas — including on topics of current or social relevance.
elaborations: participating in class discussions or activities to express opinions and reflect on those of others
expressing thoughts about the pros, cons and limitations of ideas and issues raised regarding a given topic
participating in debates about current issues of interest, using language of persuasion and suggesting possible solutions
using slogans and rhetorical devices to support arguments

nodes.label: Questioning and probing ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the target language to ask questions that probe, clarify or challenge an idea or opinion expressed by another.
criteria: Asks at least two questions that probe or extend a partner's opinion (not just factual information questions)
Can distinguish between a clarifying question and a challenging question in the target language

width.minimum: Ask at least two follow-up or probing questions in the target language in response to a partner's expressed opinion.
width.typical: Use a range of questioning strategies to probe, clarify and explore ideas; ask for evidence, examples or elaboration; use questions to steer or deepen a discussion.
wider: Use Socratic questioning techniques in the target language — practise probing without asserting, letting questions guide the reasoning
Analyse how questioning strategies differ in formal debate vs informal discussion in the target language — identify conventions specific to each

modes.reason: Probing questions require a bank of question forms beyond simple information requests. Students need exposure to a range of probing question types (why, what evidence, what if, can you give an example) in varied discussion contexts before applying them spontaneously.

nodes.label: Offering and justifying opinions in discussion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express and justify opinions on topics of current or social interest in the target language, using appropriate discussion language.
criteria: Expresses an opinion with at least one justification in the target language
Can identify and respond to a counter-argument rather than simply restating their original position
nodes.hinge_reason: Justified opinion expression is the communicative core of EC02. Students who can only assert ('I think it's good') without justification ('because...', 'however...', 'this shows that...') cannot participate meaningfully in discussion or debate. This also underpins EC06's persuasive text creation.

width.minimum: Express and briefly justify at least one opinion on a current or social topic in the target language, using at least one justification structure.
width.typical: Use a range of structures to express, justify and nuance opinions; identify pros, cons and limitations of ideas; use persuasion language and slogans or rhetorical devices where appropriate.
wider: Participate in a structured class debate on a current issue in the target language — argue an assigned position and respond to counter-arguments
Compose a short opinion text (letter, post, spoken statement) for a real or simulated audience on a topic of personal or social relevance

modes.reason: Justified opinions require explicit reasoning scaffolds — students need modelled examples of how justification structures work in the target language before they can deploy them independently. Structured debate and opinion frames provide the scaffold.
Opinion expression should be practised across a range of topics so that the structures transfer beyond one familiar topic area.

nodes.label: Comparing and evaluating ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare ideas, weigh perspectives and discuss implications in the target language, moving beyond assertion to evaluation.
criteria: Can compare at least two perspectives on a topic and identify a strength and limitation of each
Uses comparison language structures in the target language accurately enough for the comparison to be clear

width.minimum: Compare at least two perspectives on a topic in the target language; identify at least one strength and one limitation of a position.
width.typical: Compare and evaluate ideas across multiple perspectives; distinguish between fact and opinion; identify shared and divergent values underlying different positions; use comparison and evaluation language structures.
wider: Analyse a persuasive text in the target language — identify the rhetorical strategies used and evaluate their effectiveness
Compare media representations of the same topic across target language and Australian English sources — identify where framing differs and discuss why

modes.reason: Comparing and evaluating ideas integrates questioning (node 1) and justified opinion expression (node 2) into the full discussion capacity the descriptor demands. Tasks that require students to represent and evaluate multiple perspectives simultaneously are the key integration structure.

descriptors.title: Discuss and reflect with peers
descriptors.description: use non-verbal, spoken and written exchanges to discuss, plan and reflect on activities, events and experiences with peers
descriptors.knowledge: Students can engage in modelled non-verbal, spoken and written exchanges to organise activities in familiar contexts (AC9LS8EC03). They have not yet discussed, planned and reflected on activities and experiences in ways that require extended planning, negotiation and post-activity reflection in the target language.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use non-verbal, spoken and written exchanges in the target language to discuss, plan and reflect on activities, events and experiences with peers — including managing multi-stage processes and negotiating outcomes.
elaborations: planning and producing resources such as websites, posters or online features about issues related to the target language speaking world
emailing, messaging or using secure online applications to chat about and reflect on previously planned experiences
planning and playing a game of charades and reflecting on the importance of non-verbal communication and gestures to make meaning
discussing and negotiating a resolution to a common problem
organising, planning and completing all the stages of preparation for an event

nodes.label: Planning and negotiating collaboratively
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the target language to plan and negotiate with peers through a multi-stage process — assigning roles, making decisions and managing adjustments.
criteria: Participates in at least two planning stages of a collaborative task using target language for proposal, negotiation or decision
Manages at least one adjustment or disagreement during the task using target language rather than reverting to English

width.minimum: Participate in a collaborative planning task in the target language that involves at least two stages (e.g. proposal, decision, assignment of roles).
width.typical: Plan, negotiate and execute a collaborative project or event using spoken, written and digital exchanges in the target language; manage disagreements and adjustments through negotiation; use appropriate language for proposing, agreeing, disagreeing and revising.
wider: Plan and execute a real or simulated event (e.g. a class celebration, a fundraiser, a trip) using the target language as the primary medium throughout — from planning to evaluation
Compare how negotiation and planning language conventions differ in formal and informal contexts in the target language

modes.reason: Multi-stage collaborative planning integrates discussion strategies (EC02), functional classroom language (EC02 Y7-8) and transactional exchange skills (EC03 Y7-8) into a sustained, purposeful communicative task. The teaching investment is in creating genuine planning contexts, not simulated planning with predetermined outcomes.

nodes.label: Non-verbal communication and meaning-making
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and use non-verbal communication strategies in the target language context and reflect on their role in meaning-making across cultural contexts.
criteria: Can identify at least two non-verbal strategies used in a target language interaction and explain their communicative function
Can identify at least one non-verbal convention that differs between the target language community and Australian English

width.minimum: Identify at least two non-verbal strategies used in an observed or participated-in target language interaction and reflect on their contribution to meaning.
width.typical: Participate in exchanges that require coordinating non-verbal, spoken and written elements; reflect on how non-verbal conventions differ across cultural contexts; identify where non-verbal communication can clarify or obscure meaning across cultural boundaries.
wider: Participate in a charades or mime scenario in the target language and reflect explicitly on what non-verbal communication conveys vs what requires language
Research non-verbal communication conventions in the target language community and compare with Australian English conventions — present findings to peers

modes.reason: Non-verbal convention awareness requires exposure across varied interaction contexts. Single examples do not generalise — students need to encounter how gesture, posture, silence and proxemics operate differently across social contexts in the target language community.

nodes.label: Reflecting on activities and experiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect in the target language on completed activities and experiences — identifying what went well, what was challenging and what they would change.
criteria: Produces a reflection in the target language that identifies at least one strength and one challenge from a completed activity
Reflection goes beyond description of events — includes at least one evaluative or interpretive statement

width.minimum: Produce one reflective exchange (spoken or written) in the target language about a completed activity, identifying at least one strength and one area for improvement.
width.typical: Reflect on activities, events and experiences using spoken, written or digital exchanges; discuss what was challenging, surprising or significant; connect reflections to personal or cultural learning.
wider: Maintain a reflective journal or digital record in the target language across a unit of work — trace developing language and cultural understanding over time

Reflect on the experience of using the target language in a real or near-real context (e.g. interacting with a speaker, watching authentic media) — identify what was possible and what was beyond current capacity

modes.reason: Reflection in a second language requires students to produce extended, self-referential text — a cognitively demanding task. Reflection frames and sentence starters that scaffold the reflective move (first... then... I noticed... I would change...) reduce the cognitive load and allow genuine reflection rather than surface description.

descriptors.title: Interpret across a wide range of texts
descriptors.description: interpret information, ideas and perspectives in a wide range of spoken, written and multimodal texts and respond appropriately to cultural context, purpose and audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate and process information in familiar texts and respond with some awareness of cultural context (AC9LS8EC04). They have not yet interpreted information across a wide range of text types, distinguished fact from opinion, or produced responses that demonstrate nuanced awareness of cultural context and audience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret information, ideas and perspectives in a wide range of spoken, written and multimodal target language texts, and produce responses that are appropriate to the cultural context, purpose and audience of the original text — including texts with divergent perspectives.
elaborations: reading tourist brochures and travel websites about diverse locations in target language speaking communities
obtaining information about a festival, experience, event or tourist site and writing a series of postcards
accessing a range of texts on travel to target language speaking countries and writing a checklist
listening to or reading First Nations Australians' stories in English and creating a profile in the target language
watching a documentary on global issues and summarising the data
analysing and comparing information obtained from a range of sources on topics of social and cultural interest
identifying different perspectives in texts such as articles, reports or blogs, by distinguishing between facts and opinions
gathering information from a range of sources including personal commentaries by target language speaking peers and adults
responding to imaginative texts by modifying key elements
researching, presenting and taking a position on issues relating to contemporary topics

nodes.label: Interpreting a wide range of text types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret information and ideas from a wider range of text types than encountered at Y7-8, including some unfamiliar formats and longer or more complex texts.
criteria: Interprets key information from at least three different target language text types in spoken, written and multimodal modes
Can identify the purpose and intended audience of an unfamiliar text type in the target language

width.minimum: Successfully interpret key information from at least one text type not previously encountered (e.g. a documentary segment, a blog, a journalistic report, a personal commentary).
width.typical: Apply comprehension and interpretation strategies across a range of spoken, written and multimodal texts — including informative, persuasive and imaginative texts; travel and cultural texts; contemporary digital texts; and texts by First Nations authors or relating to First Nations contexts.
wider: Compare how the same event or topic is covered across two or more target language sources — identify differences in framing, emphasis or omission
Interpret a text from outside the target language community (e.g. a translated or shared cultural text) and consider how cultural context affects interpretation

modes.reason: Interpretation strategies developed through familiar text types do not automatically transfer to unfamiliar formats. Deliberate exposure to a wide range of text types — especially spoken and multimodal — builds the flexible comprehension repertoire the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Distinguishing perspective and identifying bias
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different perspectives in target language texts and distinguish between fact and opinion.
criteria: Can identify at least one factual claim and one opinion in a target language text and explain the distinction
Can identify at least one language feature in a text that signals a particular perspective
nodes.hinge_reason: Distinguishing fact from opinion and identifying perspective are preconditions for the analytical and evaluative responses required in EC04 and EC05 at Y9-10. Students who treat all text content as equally factual cannot produce appropriately critical responses — and cannot engage with the divergent perspective texts the descriptor specifies.

width.minimum: Identify at least one factual claim and one opinion or perspective in a target language text and explain the difference.
width.typical: Identify and compare different perspectives in informative and persuasive texts; distinguish fact from opinion; recognise where texts position the reader or viewer; analyse how language choices reflect and reinforce a perspective.
wider: Compare media coverage of the same issue across target language and Australian English sources — identify where perspective shapes the language choices
Investigate how language is used to position readers in a target language persuasive text — identify specific linguistic features (word choice, framing, omission) that signal perspective

modes.reason: Perspective analysis requires explicit instruction in how language encodes point of view — students need frameworks for identifying opinion markers, hedging language, framing choices and omission before they can apply these analytically to target language texts.

nodes.label: Responding with cultural and audience awareness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce responses to target language texts that demonstrate nuanced awareness of cultural context, purpose and intended audience.
criteria: Produces a response that addresses cultural context and audience — not only content
Response demonstrates awareness of the purpose of the original text and is appropriately shaped by that awareness

width.minimum: Produce one response to a target language text that addresses its cultural context, purpose and intended audience — going beyond content summary.
width.typical: Produce responses across text types (written, spoken, multimodal) that are appropriate to the cultural context and audience of the original; modify, adapt or extend texts for a different audience or purpose; respond to imaginative texts by engaging with cultural and creative elements.
wider: Adapt a target language text for a significantly different audience (e.g. produce a simplified version for a second language learner, or a version for a community unfamiliar with the cultural context) — discuss the choices made
Respond to a target language imaginative text by incorporating new cultural or creative elements — discuss how the additions relate to the original text's cultural context

modes.reason: Culturally aware response integrates text-type knowledge, perspective analysis and cultural understanding into a purposeful communicative act. Tasks that require students to produce responses genuinely tailored to a different audience — not just 'answer the questions' — are the key structure here.

descriptors.title: Interpret and translate for intercultural understanding
descriptors.description: apply strategies to interpret and translate non-verbal, spoken and written interactions and texts to convey meaning and intercultural understanding in familiar and unfamiliar contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students have developed and begun to apply interpretation and translation strategies in familiar contexts — including dictionary use, cognate recognition, contextual inferencing and understanding word-for-word limits (AC9LS8EC05). They have not yet applied these strategies in unfamiliar contexts or with the explicit goal of conveying intercultural understanding.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply a range of interpretation and translation strategies to non-verbal, spoken and written texts in familiar and unfamiliar contexts, conveying meaning and intercultural understanding — including recognising culturally embedded concepts, evaluating translation tools, and managing communication challenges.
elaborations: translating words or expressions that reflect culturally embedded references and concepts
analysing target language translations of familiar English language texts, identifying aspects that got 'lost in translation'
developing personal tools to resolve communication challenges such as rephrasing, asking for clarification or using non-verbal strategies
expanding awareness of false friends by recognising that cognate words may have diverged in meaning
identifying challenges associated with the translation of simple texts
evaluating the effectiveness and risks associated with online translation tools
identifying levels of formality in spoken and written texts and considering what these convey about social relationships

nodes.label: Translating culturally embedded meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and interpret expressions or concepts in the target language that are culturally embedded — where meaning cannot be conveyed through word-for-word translation.
criteria: Can identify at least one target language expression that requires cultural knowledge to translate and explain what that knowledge is
Can distinguish between a translation challenge caused by linguistic difference and one caused by cultural difference
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that some target language meaning is culturally embedded — and cannot be accessed through linguistic analysis alone — is the conceptual shift that distinguishes interpretation from translation. Students who have not made this shift will approach all translation as word substitution, producing inaccurate and culturally insensitive renderings that cannot satisfy EC05's intercultural understanding demand.

width.minimum: Identify and explain at least one target language expression or concept that requires cultural knowledge to translate accurately.
width.typical: Identify and interpret culturally embedded expressions, idioms and concepts; explain what is 'lost in translation' and why; distinguish between cases where a target language concept has an English equivalent and where it encodes a culturally specific idea.
wider: Research a concept embedded in the target language that has no direct English equivalent — explain the cultural or social context that gives it meaning
Compare how cultural concepts are translated or left untranslated in published bilingual texts — identify the translator's choices and evaluate their effectiveness

modes.reason: The culturally embedded concept insight requires explicit teaching — students do not arrive at it through exposure alone. Case studies of specific culturally embedded expressions, with discussion of the cultural context required to understand them, build the conceptual move.

Exposure to culturally embedded concepts across diverse target language communities (regional, national, diasporic) prevents students from assuming one cultural frame for the whole target language community.

nodes.label: Evaluating translation tools and strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of translation tools and strategies, including digital translation tools, for different contexts and purposes.
criteria: Can identify at least two specific errors or limitations in a digital translation of a target language text
Can explain what type of knowledge (linguistic, cultural, contextual) the tool lacked to produce an accurate translation

width.minimum: Evaluate one digital translation of a short target language text — identify at least two errors or limitations and explain what the tool missed.
width.typical: Evaluate translation strategies and tools across different text types and purposes; conduct 'back translations' to test accuracy; identify where automated tools produce awkward, inaccurate or culturally inappropriate renderings; develop personal evaluation criteria for translation quality.
wider: Compare multiple translation tools or strategies (dictionary, automated, peer, self) for the same text — analyse differences and develop a framework for choosing an appropriate tool
Translate a short text for a real purpose (e.g. a bilingual resource for the school community) and document translation decisions and challenges

modes.reason: Evaluating translation quality requires criteria — students need to develop explicit evaluative frameworks (accuracy, cultural appropriateness, register, audience fit) before assessment is meaningful. Guided evaluation tasks with discussion of the criteria build this analytical capacity.

nodes.label: Managing communication challenges
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply repair and adaptation strategies to manage communication challenges in the target language — including in unfamiliar contexts.
criteria: Demonstrates at least one successful repair or adaptation strategy in a target language interaction
Can identify formality levels in at least two target language texts and explain what language features signal each

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least one communication repair strategy in a target language interaction (e.g. rephrasing, asking for repetition, using a non-verbal cue to signal misunderstanding).
width.typical: Use a range of strategies to manage communication breakdowns — rephrasing, asking for clarification, adjusting formality, switching between modes; identify formality levels in spoken and written texts and adjust appropriately; manage unfamiliar communication contexts with limited language resources.
wider: Reflect on a real or simulated communication challenge in the target language — identify what broke down and evaluate which repair strategy was most effective
Investigate how register and formality conventions in the target language signal social relationships — practise adjusting formality across different simulated contexts

modes.reason: Communication repair draws on the full range of interpretation and translation strategies from nodes 1–2 plus the conversational maintenance skills from EC01–EC02. It represents the applied endpoint of the mediating strand — using strategies to keep meaning-making alive when language resources are incomplete.

descriptors.title: Create texts for diverse audiences
descriptors.description: create spoken, written and multimodal, informative and imaginative texts, selecting vocabulary, expressions, grammatical structures and textual conventions for familiar and some unfamiliar contexts and purposes, to engage different audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create spoken, written and multimodal texts using appropriate vocabulary, grammar and some textual conventions (AC9LS8EC06). They have not yet created texts for deliberately varied or unfamiliar audiences, or made strategic language selections to engage different audiences across different contexts and purposes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create spoken, written and multimodal texts (informative and imaginative) in the target language for familiar and some unfamiliar contexts, making deliberate selections of vocabulary, expressions, grammatical structures and textual conventions to engage different audiences.
elaborations: working collaboratively to create a brochure to identify aspects of their city/town/region likely to be of interest to target language speaking visitors
creating promotional and informative bilingual texts to promote events or to support activities
presenting a personal or shared perspective on topics such as fashion, music, cinema or social media
writing a journal entry or contributing to a school newsletter reflecting on the impact of a visit to a significant cultural site
selecting images and using them as creative prompts for target language writing
adapting familiar stories or fictional characters by creating new situations or different effects
composing performance texts such as skits, raps or poems to amuse, entertain and engage learners
composing simplified versions of classic stories for a second language learner audience
experimenting with poetic devices such as rhyme, repetition and onomatopoeia
writing collaboratively — exchanging a text in progress with a peer to write missing sections

nodes.label: Creating for a specific audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make deliberate language and textual decisions in a target language text based on a clearly identified audience.
criteria: Produces a text where at least two deliberate language choices are explicitly justified with reference to audience
Can explain how a different audience would require different language or format choices for the same content
nodes.hinge_reason: Audience-oriented text creation is the central move of EC06 at Y9-10 — it distinguishes text creation from language practice. Students who produce target language texts without reference to audience are still doing EC06 Y7-8 tasks. The entire descriptor's demand for 'engaging different audiences' collapses if audience awareness is not established as a production criterion.

width.minimum: Produce one target language text where at least two deliberate choices (vocabulary, structure, register, format) are explicitly made with reference to audience.
width.typical: Create informative and imaginative texts with a clearly identified audience; make deliberate vocabulary, register and format choices that reflect audience knowledge, expectations and needs; produce bilingual texts for mixed-language audiences where appropriate.
wider: Create the same content for two significantly different audiences (e.g. peers vs community members; second language learners vs fluent speakers) — compare the language choices required for each
Produce a promotional or community text in the target language for a real audience — evaluate its effectiveness based on actual reception

modes.reason: Audience awareness in production requires students to hold a mental model of the reader or viewer while making language choices — a metacognitive demand that requires explicit scaffolding. Audience analysis tasks and annotation of deliberate choices make the process visible.

nodes.label: Selecting vocabulary and grammar for effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select vocabulary, expressions and grammatical structures in the target language to achieve a specific communicative effect, purpose or tone.
criteria: Demonstrates at least two deliberate vocabulary or grammar choices in a text and can explain their intended effect
Produces texts in at least two different registers or text types with appropriate conventions for each

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least two deliberate vocabulary or grammar selections in a text that are explained with reference to intended effect or purpose.
width.typical: Select vocabulary and grammatical structures purposefully for register, tone and effect; use a range of text types (presentation, narrative, promotional, reflective, persuasive) with appropriate conventions; experiment with creative language features (rhyme, repetition, imagery) in imaginative texts.
wider: Revise a draft text with a focus on vocabulary and grammar for effect — compare before and after versions and evaluate the changes
Experiment with poetic or rhetorical devices from target language literary or oral traditions — identify the effect of each device and discuss its cultural resonance

modes.reason: Strategic selection requires having encountered vocabulary and grammar across enough registers and text types to have genuine choices. Students who have only practised one register cannot select — they default. Varied production contexts across registers and purposes build the repertoire from which selection is possible.

nodes.label: Creating imaginative texts with creative intent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create imaginative texts in the target language with deliberate creative intent — making choices that produce a specific emotional, humorous or aesthetic effect on an audience.
criteria: Produces an imaginative text with at least one deliberate creative choice that is explained with reference to intended audience effect
Text demonstrates awareness of target language textual conventions for the chosen format

width.minimum: Produce one imaginative text in the target language with at least one deliberate creative choice (structural, linguistic or thematic) and explain its intended effect.
width.typical: Create imaginative texts across formats (narrative, performance, poem, script) with deliberate creative choices; adapt familiar stories or characters for new purposes or audiences; use creative language features; produce texts designed to entertain, provoke or engage a specific audience.
wider: Adapt a familiar cultural story or text from the target language community for a different audience or purpose — discuss what is retained, changed and why
Create a collaborative imaginative text with a peer — negotiate creative choices and reflect on how collaboration shaped the final product

modes.reason: Imaginative text creation with deliberate creative intent integrates audience awareness (node 1), vocabulary and grammar selection (node 2), and knowledge of target language textual conventions into a purposeful creative act. Performance, presentation and peer response contexts are the natural integration structure.

descriptors.title: Apply target language sound system
descriptors.description: apply features of the target language sound system, including pitch, rhythm, stress, pronunciation and intonation, and show how these are represented in familiar and some unfamiliar contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise and use features of the target language sound system including vowels, consonants, intonation and stress in familiar contexts (AC9LS8EU01). They have not yet applied these features independently in unfamiliar contexts or reflected on regional pronunciation variation across target language communities.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply features of the target language sound system — including pitch, rhythm, stress, pronunciation and intonation — in familiar and some unfamiliar spoken contexts, and demonstrate understanding of how these are represented in the writing system, including awareness of regional variation.
elaborations: recognising the importance of appropriate intonation, stress, tone and pronunciation for making meaning
pronouncing consonants according to vowel combinations and double consonants
understanding variation in pronunciation across the target language speaking world
using the target language pronunciation of letters to spell words and phrases aloud
listening to and reciting texts such as poems, stories, tongue twisters or song lyrics to familiarise with rhythm and intonation
identifying the use of pitch, rhythm, stress and intonation in different audio tracks and how they affect the spoken message

nodes.label: Accurate and fluent pronunciation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce target language sounds, stress and intonation with sufficient accuracy and consistency to be understood in familiar and some unfamiliar contexts.
criteria: Produces a prepared spoken text with consistent and accurate vowel sounds, target consonants and sentence stress
Can apply phonological knowledge to attempt pronunciation of an unfamiliar word in the target language

width.minimum: Demonstrate accurate production of the key phonological features of the target language (vowels, target consonants, stress patterns) in a prepared spoken text.
width.typical: Apply accurate pronunciation, stress and intonation across prepared and semi-prepared spoken tasks; use phonological knowledge to support pronunciation of unfamiliar words; apply correct terminology for phonological features and marking conventions.
wider: Record and critically review own spoken production — identify specific phonological features to improve and practise targeted correction
Research and compare pronunciation across two or more regional varieties of the target language — discuss what the variation reveals about language change and cultural identity

modes.reason: Phonological accuracy at Y9-10 is primarily a fluency issue — students have learned the rules but need continued practice to maintain accuracy under communicative pressure. Performance tasks with self-assessment and recording support the ongoing consolidation this requires.

nodes.label: Intonation, rhythm and communicative meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use pitch, rhythm and intonation to convey communicative meaning — distinguishing mood, emphasis and intention in spoken target language production.
criteria: Produces at least two spoken utterances with audibly different intonation patterns conveying different communicative meanings
Can identify how intonation shifts meaning in at least one heard example from a target language audio source

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least two distinct intonation patterns that convey different communicative meanings (e.g. certainty vs doubt, statement vs question, excitement vs neutrality) in the target language.
width.typical: Use pitch, rhythm and intonation to convey mood, emphasis and communicative intent; recognise and reproduce intonation patterns from authentic audio sources; identify how intonation affects the meaning of target language utterances.
wider: Analyse the use of pitch, rhythm and intonation in target language audio or video texts intended for different purposes (advertisement, news, narrative, conversation) — identify how prosodic features serve each purpose
Practise prosodic features through performance texts (poems, songs, speeches) and reflect on how prosody shapes audience response

modes.reason: Intonation as a meaning-making resource is only apparent across varied communicative purposes. Exposure to target language texts across multiple genres and registers allows students to observe how prosodic choices serve different communicative ends.

descriptors.title: Select grammar to enhance meaning
descriptors.description: select and use structures and features of the target language grammatical and writing systems to enhance meaning and create spoken, written and multimodal texts
descriptors.knowledge: Students have developed knowledge of and can use key grammatical structures and writing system features of the target language — including agreement, verb conjugation, sentence construction and orthographic conventions (AC9LS8EU02). They have not yet selected and used more complex grammatical structures (comparatives, multiple tenses, complex sentences) to enhance meaning purposefully.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select and use a range of grammatical structures — including comparatives, multiple tense forms, pronoun systems, cohesive devices and complex sentence constructions — to enhance meaning in spoken, written and multimodal target language texts.
elaborations: knowing when to omit definite and indefinite articles, and adjusting for gender-change cases
using collective nouns and noticing the use of singular verbs
noticing changes in meaning when adjective position changes
using comparatives and superlatives, including some irregular forms
understanding and using indefinite adjectives and pronouns
using possessive and demonstrative pronouns
understanding the use of relative pronouns in familiar contexts
using modelled structures with direct and indirect objects
recognising different past tense forms and comparing uses with English past tense
understanding and using regular and irregular preterite/past forms
understanding and using the immediate future
recognising future and conditional tenses and their conjugational patterns
elaborating on ideas with prepositions
understanding the function of impersonal expressions
using cohesive devices in complex sentences
forming adverbs from adjectives

nodes.label: Articles, agreement and determiner refinement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply article and agreement rules with increased accuracy, including in cases where the target language differs from expected patterns.
criteria: Applies article and agreement rules correctly in complex noun phrases including at least one exception or nuanced case
Self-corrects agreement errors during drafting when reviewing own work

width.minimum: Apply definite and indefinite article rules correctly in at least five phrases, including at least one case that involves an exception or nuance from the basic rule.
width.typical: Use articles, possessives and demonstratives with accurate gender and number agreement; handle common exceptions and nuanced cases (e.g. omission rules, collective nouns, irregular patterns); apply agreement across complex noun phrases.
wider: Investigate how article use in the target language differs from English across specific contexts — create a reference guide for cases that are consistently challenging
Analyse a native speaker text for article usage — identify patterns that go beyond the rules taught and hypothesise about the additional conventions

modes.reason: Agreement accuracy is a fluency issue at Y9-10 — students typically understand rules but apply them inconsistently in production. Focused practice with nuanced cases and self-correction in drafting builds reliable application.

nodes.label: Comparatives, superlatives and intensifiers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use comparatives and superlatives — including irregular forms — and intensifiers to express and nuance comparisons in the target language.
criteria: Uses at least three comparative or superlative forms correctly including at least one irregular form
Applies comparison structures in a text where comparison is genuinely purposeful (not just a grammar drill)

width.minimum: Use at least three comparative or superlative forms correctly in a target language text.
width.typical: Use regular and common irregular comparative and superlative forms; use intensifiers to strengthen or weaken statements; apply comparison structures in informative and opinion texts.
wider: Compare how comparison is expressed across the target language and English — identify structural differences and cases where direct translation fails
Use comparatives and superlatives in a persuasive or review text — reflect on how comparison language shapes argument and evaluation

modes.reason: Comparative structures need to be practised across varied comparison contexts (people, places, ideas, options) to ensure transfer beyond one rehearsed topic area.

nodes.label: Tense variety and temporal expression
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise and use multiple tense forms in the target language — including past tenses and immediate or simple future — to express temporal relationships.
criteria: Uses at least two different tense forms correctly in a single text
Can explain the distinction between at least two tense forms in the target language
nodes.hinge_reason: Tense variety is required for the extended text production demanded in EC06 and the reflection tasks in EC03. Students who are restricted to present tense cannot produce the narrative, reflective or informative texts the Y9-10 descriptors require. This also underpins EU03's metalinguistic analysis of tense systems.

width.minimum: Use at least two different tense forms correctly in a single target language text (e.g. present and past, or past and future).
width.typical: Use present, past and future tenses in spoken and written texts; distinguish between different past tense forms where the target language requires this; use tense variation to sequence events and express temporal relationships.
wider: Compare how past tense forms in the target language differ from English past tense — identify what distinctions the target language makes that English does not require
Produce a narrative or personal account that uses at least three tense forms — reflect on how tense choice shapes the narrative perspective

modes.reason: Tense accuracy in production requires practice — students often understand tense concepts but apply them inconsistently when juggling other production demands. Narrative and reflective texts that require tense variation provide the practice context.
Tense forms need to be encountered and used across varied text types (narrative, reporting, planning, reflecting) to become flexible tools rather than practised paradigms.

nodes.label: Complex sentence construction and cohesive devices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct complex sentences and use cohesive devices in the target language to connect and develop ideas across a text.
criteria: Produces a text with at least three complex sentences using cohesive devices to connect ideas
Uses at least two different cohesive devices correctly in the same text

width.minimum: Produce at least three complex sentences in a target language text using cohesive devices to connect ideas.
width.typical: Use a range of cohesive devices to connect and develop ideas; construct sentences with subordinate clauses, relative pronouns and prepositional phrases; use impersonal expressions and discourse markers to add nuance and manage text flow.
wider: Analyse the cohesive structure of a native speaker text — identify all cohesive devices and discuss their effect on the text's coherence and flow
Compare complex sentence construction in the target language and English — identify where the target language requires different syntactic choices for the same meaning

modes.reason: Complex sentence construction integrates the grammar and vocabulary knowledge from nodes 1–3 into extended, coherent text production. The move from producing individual sentences to constructing cohesive texts is the key integration challenge — tasks requiring multi-paragraph texts with explicit cohesive marking support this.

descriptors.title: Evaluate texts using metalanguage
descriptors.description: reflect on and evaluate target language texts, using metalanguage to discuss language structures and features
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare target language structures with English using familiar metalanguage (AC9LS8EU03). They have not yet reflected on and evaluated target language texts analytically — moving from identifying features to explaining how language choices create effect, register and meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on and evaluate target language texts using metalanguage — analysing how grammatical, vocabulary and textual choices create effect, establish register and convey meaning across different text types and purposes.
elaborations: comparing language features of target language and English versions of different types of texts
understanding textual elements that provide coherence at a whole text level
reflecting on how grammatical and vocabulary choices shade meaning and establish register
researching target language words borrowed from different languages across time and through political, historical and social changes
using metalanguage to discuss language structures and features
explaining how language is used differently to achieve different purposes
investigating how social media, globalisation, technology and popular culture have influenced the target language over time

nodes.label: Analysing textual coherence and structure
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the structural and cohesive features of a target language text that contribute to its coherence.
criteria: Identifies at least two structural or cohesive features in a target language text using metalanguage
Explains how each identified feature contributes to the text's coherence or purpose

width.minimum: Identify at least two structural or cohesive features in a target language text and explain how they contribute to the text's coherence or purpose.
width.typical: Analyse how introductions, summaries, cohesive devices and paragraph structure contribute to text-level coherence; compare structural conventions across text types; use metalanguage to discuss textual organisation.
wider: Compare the structural conventions of equivalent text types across the target language and English — identify where organisation reflects different cultural or rhetorical expectations
Reconstruct or repair a structurally incomplete or incoherent target language text — explain the structural choices made

modes.reason: Textual analysis requires students to move from what a text says to how it is organised to achieve its purpose. Explicit analysis frameworks (purpose → audience → structure → cohesion) support this move before independent analysis is possible.

nodes.label: Analysing how language choices create register and effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how grammatical and vocabulary choices in a target language text establish register, shade meaning and create specific effects.
criteria: Identifies at least two specific language choices in a target language text and explains their contribution to register or effect
Uses metalanguage accurately to discuss language features rather than only describing them in general terms
nodes.hinge_reason: Analysing how language choices create register and effect is the core analytical move of EU03. Without it, students can label grammatical features but cannot explain why they matter — the 'reflect and evaluate' demand of the descriptor is not met. This also underpins EC06's purposeful text creation at Y9-10.

width.minimum: Identify at least two language choices (vocabulary or grammar) in a target language text and explain how each contributes to register or effect.
width.typical: Analyse how formal and informal registers are constructed through language choices; explain how tense, modality, vocabulary and syntax shade meaning and create tone; use metalanguage to discuss and compare language choices across texts.
wider: Compare how the same content is expressed in formal and informal target language registers — identify the specific language features that signal each register
Investigate how social media, technology or globalisation has influenced target language choices — identify specific examples of language change and discuss their implications

modes.reason: The move from describing a language feature to explaining its effect requires explicit analytical scaffolding — 'this word is X, which creates Y effect because Z'. Modelled analysis and discussion-based evaluation of choices build this metalinguistic reasoning.

Language choice analysis must be practised across varied text types and registers to be generalisable — register analysis developed only through formal texts will not transfer to digital or informal contexts.

nodes.label: Evaluating and comparing texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate and compare target language texts, using metalanguage to analyse how language structures and features serve different purposes and audiences.
criteria: Compares at least two target language texts using metalanguage, identifying differences in language choices
Explains how identified differences reflect the different purposes or audiences of the texts — not only describes the features

width.minimum: Compare at least two target language texts using metalanguage — identify at least two differences in language choices and explain how each reflects the different purpose or audience.
width.typical: Evaluate and compare texts across text types, registers and purposes; discuss how language change (globalisation, technology, social media) affects target language usage; use metalanguage to conduct and present comparative text analyses.
wider: Research the influence of other languages or cultural contact on target language vocabulary over time — identify specific examples and discuss the mechanisms of language change
Produce a text that deliberately imitates the register and conventions of a target language text type — explain the choices made with reference to the model

modes.reason: Evaluating and comparing texts integrates structural analysis (node 1) and register/effect analysis (node 2) into a full metalinguistic response. The teaching investment is in tasks that require genuine comparison rather than parallel descriptions of two separate texts.

descriptors.title: Evaluate identity and communication
descriptors.description: reflect on and explain how identity is shaped by language(s), culture(s), attitudes, beliefs and values, and how these affect ways of communicating
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise how identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values (AC9LS8EU04). They have not yet reflected on and explained these relationships analytically — moving from recognition of examples to explanation of mechanisms, and considering how identity affects ways of communicating.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on and explain how identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values — in target language communities and in their own experience — and analyse how identity affects ways of communicating, including in multilingual and cross-cultural contexts.
elaborations: recognising that the target language continues to evolve due to exposure to other cultures, globalisation, trends, technology and social change
recognising that many target language speaking countries have indigenous languages that are co-official languages
recognising that the target language co-exists with multiple indigenous languages and dialects in many communities
reflecting on and explaining the protocols required to authentically co-create an Acknowledgement of Country/Place with a First Nations Australian community
exploring the influence of popular culture in the target language speaking world
considering how regional and national perspectives influence the use of language and sense of identity relating to place/country
interviewing bilingual peers, family members or guests about the experience of using more than one language
discussing ways in which learning a different language can lead to new ways of thinking or interpreting experiences
analysing texts that show different representations of cultural identity and sense of belonging
discussing and reflecting on the nature and role of culture and its expression through language

nodes.label: Language as a carrier of cultural identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how specific features of the target language carry and reinforce cultural values, beliefs and identity — moving beyond recognition to explanation.
criteria: Explains at least two connections between specific target language features and cultural values or identity
Explanation identifies a mechanism — not only an example — for how language carries or reinforces identity

width.minimum: Explain at least two ways in which specific target language features (vocabulary, forms of address, cultural references) carry or reinforce cultural identity.
width.typical: Examine a range of target language features and explain how each reflects underlying cultural values, beliefs or identity; investigate how the target language co-exists with other languages in multilingual communities; discuss how language encodes connection to place, community and history.
wider: Investigate how indigenous languages in target language communities co-exist with the target language — research the history and current status of at least one co-official or community language
Research how a target language community's engagement with globalisation, migration or political change has affected language use and identity — identify specific language changes and their causes

modes.reason: Explaining (rather than recognising) the relationship between language and identity requires students to articulate a mechanism — 'this feature exists because this cultural value operates here'. Discussion scaffolds and case studies support the move from observation to explanation.

nodes.label: Identity and ways of communicating
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how identity — including cultural background, social role and language repertoire — shapes the ways people communicate in the target language.
criteria: Explains at least one way in which a specific identity factor (cultural background, social role, language history) shapes communication choices in the target language
Can analyse a specific communication choice in a text and explain it with reference to the communicator's identity

width.minimum: Identify and explain at least one way in which identity (cultural background, age, gender, social role, language history) shapes communication choices in the target language.
width.typical: Examine how cultural background, social identity and multilingual repertoire affect communication choices — including register selection, topic choice, language mixing and the strategies used to manage identity across cultural contexts; analyse texts that reflect different identity positions.
wider: Interview or research a multilingual speaker about their experience of identity across languages — document insights and discuss with reference to own language learning experience
Analyse a target language text (advertisement, social media post, political speech) for how identity is constructed or projected — identify the language choices that signal identity

modes.reason: The relationship between identity and communication is only apparent across varied social and cultural contexts. Students who have only encountered one context (e.g. classroom formal language) will not see how identity varies. Varied encounters — including digital, community and cross-cultural contexts — build the richer picture.

nodes.label: Reflecting on own identity as a language learner
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on and explain how learning the target language has affected their own sense of identity, perspectives and ways of communicating.
criteria: Produces a reflection that explains (not only describes) at least one way language learning has affected their perspectives or sense of identity
Reflection connects personal experience to broader insight about language, culture and identity — not only reports events

width.minimum: Produce one reflection in the target language that explains at least one way in which language learning has introduced a new perspective or affected their sense of identity.
width.typical: Reflect on the experience of operating across languages and cultures; explain how learning the target language has created new ways of thinking, new cultural empathy or new awareness of own cultural assumptions; consider the role of the target language in potential future life experiences.
wider: Produce a personal text (essay, spoken reflection, digital presentation) that traces the development of own identity and perspectives across the language learning journey
Compare own experience of language learning with that of a bilingual or multilingual person — discuss what is shared and what is unique to each experience

modes.reason: Personal identity reflection integrates the cultural insights from nodes 1–2 with the student's own experience as a language learner. This is the most personally meaningful dimension of EU04 — the teaching investment is in creating genuine reflective space, not scripted self-description tasks.

descriptors.title: Apply spoken conventions for fluency in familiar and unfamiliar contexts
descriptors.description: apply features and conventions of spoken target language to extend fluency in responding to and creating texts in familiar and unfamiliar contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students apply spoken target language conventions including consonant nuances, sentence-level stress, written doubling conventions and extended intonation (AC9LS8U01). They apply these in familiar contexts. They have not yet applied spoken conventions in genuinely unfamiliar contexts, nor created extended spoken texts for real audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply spoken conventions to extend fluency — including natural speech features, extended sentence stress, and authentic spoken production — in familiar and unfamiliar contexts.
elaborations: applying correct pronunciation to challenging letter combinations in the target language
understanding how tone can convey emotions, modify meaning and give clues about what is happening
applying knowledge of pronunciation, intonation, rhythm and pace to own use of spoken target language
experimenting with intonation and stress, improving coherence and increasing expressive range by reading from unfamiliar texts
reciting tongue twisters to develop pace and fluency

nodes.label: Natural speech features and extended sentence stress
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply natural speech features — contractions, elision, rhythm — and place stress correctly in extended and complex sentences.
criteria: Demonstrates at least two natural speech features in connected speech
Places stress correctly across at least two complex sentences
nodes.hinge_reason: Natural speech features — contractions, elision, natural rhythm — are what distinguish fluent from stilted spoken production. Students who speak only in citation forms sound unnatural and are difficult to understand in authentic interaction.

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least two natural speech features in connected speech; place stress correctly across at least two complex sentences.
width.typical: Apply contractions, elision and natural rhythm in connected speech; maintain stress patterns in complex sentences; develop fluency through tongue twisters, reading aloud and performance; apply spoken conventions in unrehearsed contexts.
wider: Produce a recording of connected speech demonstrating natural rhythm, elision and stress — compare with a native speaker sample and identify remaining differences
Apply spoken conventions in a genuine unrehearsed context — demonstrating that prosodic features are automatic rather than deliberate

modes.reason: Natural speech features become automatic only through high-frequency production in varied spoken contexts — including unrehearsed conditions. Rehearsed accuracy does not transfer automatically to natural speech.

nodes.label: Fluency in unfamiliar contexts and spoken text creation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can respond and create with adequate fluency in unfamiliar spoken contexts — applying all prior spoken conventions in extended unrehearsed production.
criteria: Produces an extended spoken text in an unfamiliar context with fluency adequate for communicative purpose
Applies natural speech features in at least one unrehearsed spoken context

width.minimum: Produce an extended spoken text in an unfamiliar context with fluency adequate for the communicative purpose.
width.typical: Apply spoken conventions in unfamiliar and spontaneous contexts; create extended spoken texts — presentations, debates, interviews, performances — applying prosodic features deliberately; sustain spoken interaction without excessive hesitation or code-switching.
wider: Participate in a fully spontaneous spoken exchange on an unfamiliar topic — sustaining fluency for at least five minutes
Create and perform an original spoken text with deliberate prosodic design — demonstrate that intonation, stress and rhythm serve the communicative and expressive purpose

modes.reason: Fluency in unfamiliar contexts requires encountering genuinely varied and unpredictable spoken conditions. Rehearsed performance does not build the spontaneous spoken fluency that authentic interaction demands.

nodes.label: Performing and recording spoken texts for real audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create and perform or record spoken texts for real audiences — applying all spoken conventions with deliberate expressive intent.
criteria: Creates and delivers a spoken text for a real audience using prosodic features deliberately
The spoken text achieves its communicative or expressive purpose for the audience

width.minimum: Create and deliver at least one spoken text for a real audience applying prosodic features deliberately.
width.typical: Create and perform debates, speeches, dramatisations, podcasts, interviews and recordings for real audiences; apply all spoken conventions — intonation, stress, rhythm, natural features — with deliberate expressive purpose; evaluate own spoken performance against authentic native speaker models.
wider: Create and record an extended spoken production — compare with an authentic native speaker text and reflect on every remaining difference
Perform a spoken text for a target language community audience — receive feedback and reflect on communicative effectiveness

modes.reason: Spoken performance for real audiences integrates all spoken convention capabilities — natural features (N1), spontaneous fluency (N2) — and deploys them for a genuine communicative purpose.

descriptors.title: Apply grammar to predict meaning and compose complex texts
descriptors.description: apply knowledge of grammatical structures to predict meaning and compose texts that contain some complex structures and ideas
descriptors.knowledge: Students apply grammatical structures including irregular verbs across tenses, expanded cohesive devices, quantity expressions and adverbial modification (AC9LS8U02). They compose in past, present and compound tenses. They have not yet worked with further tense forms for continuous or recent action, conditional or subjunctive structures, or passive constructions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply grammatical structures to predict meaning and compose texts with complex structures — including further tense forms, conditional and hypothetical structures, passive voice, and expanded complex sentence types.
elaborations: understanding and using indefinite adjectives and pronouns
applying constructions with double negation
understanding the difference between a reflexive verb and the corresponding non-reflexive verb
using modelled subjunctive mood to express doubt, uncertainty or emotion
expressing hypothetical events using modelled conditional voice structures
using cohesive devices to extend sentence complexity and sophistication
conjugating verbs to describe a range of events across time
extending understanding of symbols, acronyms, abbreviations and colloquial shortenings
recognising the different usage of imperative forms
using numbers for a range of purposes including historical and biographical timelines
using the passive, impersonal form

nodes.label: Further tense forms and conditional structures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use further tense forms for continuous or recent action, and conditional or hypothetical structures in composition.
criteria: Uses at least one further tense form correctly in composition
Uses at least one conditional or hypothetical structure correctly
nodes.hinge_reason: Further tense and conditional structures are the grammatical tools for expressing continuous, recently completed and hypothetical meaning — all required for sophisticated narrative, analytical and persuasive composition at this band.

width.minimum: Use at least one further tense form for continuous or recent action correctly; use at least one conditional or hypothetical structure correctly.
width.typical: Apply further tense forms for continuous action or recently completed events; use conditional structures for real and hypothetical scenarios; use hypothetical or subjunctive forms where appropriate in the target language; apply perfect aspect forms for completed action.
wider: Write a text using at least three different tense and aspect forms — each with a margin note explaining the temporal or aspectual purpose
Produce a conditional scenario — describing what would happen if something were different — using the correct conditional structure throughout

modes.reason: Complex tense and conditional accuracy requires repeated production practice in varied composition contexts. Understanding the distinction intellectually does not prevent production errors under pressure.

nodes.label: Passive voice and complex sentence types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use passive voice constructions and complex sentence types — including relative clauses and expanded subordinate structures.
criteria: Uses at least one passive construction correctly in a composition context
Uses at least one relative clause or complex subordinate structure correctly

width.minimum: Use at least one passive construction correctly; use at least one relative clause or complex subordinate structure correctly.
width.typical: Use passive constructions for impersonal and formal purposes; form relative clauses to embed information; use complex subordinate structures to express causation, condition and time relationships; combine structures to produce genuinely complex sentences.
wider: Produce a paragraph using at least three different complex sentence types — identify each type and explain the meaning relationship it creates
Revise a simple text by embedding information using relative clauses — compare before and after, explaining how each addition changes information density

modes.reason: Passive and complex sentence structures develop through encountering and producing them across varied text types and purposes. Each new text context draws on different complex structures.

nodes.label: Using grammar to predict meaning in complex texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use grammatical knowledge to predict and confirm meaning in complex target language texts — including texts with unfamiliar vocabulary.
criteria: Uses grammatical knowledge to predict the meaning of at least two unfamiliar items in a complex text
Explains the grammatical reasoning used for at least one prediction

width.minimum: Use grammatical knowledge to predict the meaning of at least two unfamiliar words or structures in a complex text — explain the reasoning used.
width.typical: Apply grammatical knowledge to interpret complex texts; use sentence structure and word class knowledge to predict unfamiliar meaning; identify how grammatical features signal relationships between ideas in complex texts; use grammar as a comprehension tool in authentic reading and listening.
wider: Work through a complex authentic target language text — for every unfamiliar word, use grammar and context to predict meaning before checking a reference
Explain the grammatical reasoning behind at least three predictions made in a complex text — demonstrating explicit metalinguistic awareness of the prediction process

modes.reason: Using grammar as a comprehension tool requires students to articulate the reasoning — not only guess intuitively. Structured prediction tasks with explicit reasoning make the metalinguistic process visible.

descriptors.title: Evaluate texts using metalanguage
descriptors.description: reflect on and evaluate target language texts, using metalanguage to analyse language structures and features
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use metalanguage to compare whole-text coherence features, text-type conventions, vocabulary patterns and historical influences (AC9LS8U03). They have not yet evaluated target language texts critically for effectiveness, analysed texts that challenge norms, or connected language register variation to social positioning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate target language texts using metalanguage — analysing language structures and features for effectiveness, norm deviation, register and social positioning.
elaborations: developing metalanguage to extend discussion of grammatical features such as word order, tenses and subjunctive mood
analysing and comparing different types of texts to demonstrate how language is used to create effects
identifying common textual conventions in different text types
identifying key features and functions that characterise different types of texts and reflecting on how these are used for effect
comparing the features and differences of spoken and written texts

nodes.label: Evaluating text effectiveness using metalanguage
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate target language texts for effectiveness — analysing how specific language features contribute to or undermine the text's purpose.
criteria: Identifies at least two specific language features in a text and evaluates how each contributes to or undermines the purpose
Uses metalanguage accurately to frame at least two evaluative claims
nodes.hinge_reason: Text effectiveness evaluation — not only feature identification — is the analytical foundation for all critical text work. Students who only identify features without evaluating their effectiveness cannot engage in genuine text criticism.

width.minimum: Evaluate at least one target language text for effectiveness — identify at least two specific language features and explain how each contributes to or undermines the purpose.
width.typical: Evaluate the effectiveness of texts in achieving their purpose; analyse how vocabulary, sentence structure, cohesion and text conventions contribute to effectiveness; compare effective and ineffective texts in the same genre; use metalanguage to frame evaluative claims.
wider: Evaluate a target language community media text — identify every language choice that serves the text's purpose and every one that does not, with metalanguage framing each claim
Rewrite a section of a target language text to be more effective for its stated purpose — annotate every change with a metalinguistic justification

modes.reason: Effectiveness evaluation requires a move from identification (this feature is present) to evaluation (this feature serves or undermines the purpose). Structured evaluation frameworks scaffold this analytical move.

nodes.label: Analysing norm deviation and contemporary language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how target language texts deviate from conventions to achieve effect, and evaluate contemporary and creative language use.
criteria: Identifies at least one instance of norm deviation in a text and explains its communicative or creative effect
Uses metalanguage to describe the deviation and the effect

width.minimum: Identify at least one instance of norm deviation in a target language text and explain its communicative or creative effect.
width.typical: Analyse texts that use unconventional language for creative or satirical effect; evaluate contemporary language including slang, digital and youth varieties; identify where texts break conventions deliberately; compare the language of formal and informal digital communication.
wider: Analyse a target language satirical or experimental text — identify every norm deviation, explain the effect intended, and evaluate whether it was achieved
Compare formal and informal digital communication in the target language — identify every register difference and explain the social function of each

modes.reason: Norm deviation and contemporary language analysis develops through encountering varied non-standard texts — satire, digital communication, creative writing each present different deviation conditions.

nodes.label: Register, social positioning and language across modalities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how register variation and language choices signal social positioning, and compare language structures across spoken and written modes.
criteria: Explains how at least two register features signal social positioning in a target language text
Identifies at least one structural difference between spoken and written language in the target language

width.minimum: Explain how at least two register features signal social positioning in a target language text; identify at least one structural difference between spoken and written language in the target language.
width.typical: Analyse how register choices signal social positioning, power relationships and attitudes; compare spoken and written target language for structural differences; evaluate how formality level positions the speaker or writer in relation to the audience; apply register awareness to production and comprehension.
wider: Analyse a target language interaction for power dynamics — identify every language feature that signals relative status and explain how
Compare a spoken and a written version of the same message in the target language — identify every structural difference and explain what each reveals about the conventions of each mode

modes.reason: Social positioning analysis requires explicit interpretive frameworks — students need to be able to articulate what a language choice signals about power, relationship and attitude before applying this analysis spontaneously.

descriptors.title: Reflect on how identity is shaped by language and culture
descriptors.description: reflect on and evaluate how identity is shaped by language(s), culture(s), attitudes, beliefs and values, and how these affect ways of communicating
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain how language variation signals identity and social relationships, and how co-official languages relate to community identity (AC9LS8U04). They have not yet evaluated critically how language shapes belonging and exclusion, engaged in intercultural projects for real audiences, or reflected on language learning as identity experience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on and evaluate how identity is shaped by language, culture, attitudes, beliefs and values — including belonging and exclusion, cultural change, and personal intercultural experience.
elaborations: sharing reflections on experiences of learning the target language and on reactions to aspects of the language and culture
recognising differences in the nature and function of some elements of communication in the target language compared with English
understanding how language variation can reflect cultural and social identity, and inclusion or exclusion
reflecting on the protocols required to authentically co-create an Acknowledgement of Country/Place with a First Nations Australian, to present in the target language
researching co-official target languages and investigating the history and issues surrounding such language relationships
reflecting on the development of hybrid language varieties in target language communities and evaluating debates around them
examining the meaning of proverbs and how they reflect historical cultural views and attitudes
exploring how word choices can indicate attitudes and values
comparing texts created for different audiences in different target language communities, noticing how language reflects priorities and values

nodes.label: Language, belonging, exclusion and cultural change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how language choices create belonging or exclusion and reflect on how cultural change affects language and identity.
criteria: Explains how at least one language feature creates belonging for some and exclusion for others
Identifies at least one example of cultural change affecting language or identity and explains the connection
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding language as a vehicle for belonging and exclusion is the critical conceptual leap that moves cultural understanding from description to analysis. Students who only describe cultural practices cannot engage in evaluative reflection on language and power.

width.minimum: Explain how at least one language feature creates belonging for some and exclusion for others; identify at least one example of cultural change affecting language or identity.
width.typical: Reflect on how language choices signal group membership and cultural belonging; explore how jargon, slang and specialist language create inclusion and exclusion; reflect on how cultural change — migration, globalisation, digital culture — affects identity and language; explore assumptions in daily expressions; analyse how language changes with speakers' age, relationship and setting.
wider: Examine a target language community discourse where language choice signals belonging or exclusion — explain the mechanism and evaluate the social implications
Research how a significant cultural change has shifted language or identity in a target language community — explain the before and after, and what the shift reveals about the community's values

modes.reason: Belonging and exclusion analysis requires explicit evaluative frameworks — not only descriptive observation. Students need to articulate the mechanism by which language creates inclusion or exclusion.

nodes.label: Intercultural engagement and community projects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can engage in intercultural projects for real community audiences — exploring cultural knowledge and connections through genuine target language interaction.
criteria: Contributes meaningfully to a community intercultural project using the target language
Reflects specifically on the cultural exchange dimension — not only the language production

width.minimum: Contribute meaningfully to a community intercultural project using the target language — reflecting on the cultural exchange dimension.
width.typical: Participate in cultural exchanges with target language community peers; engage in pen-pal and collaborative project work; explore how Australians of target language community background navigate dual cultural identities; produce materials for cultural knowledge exchange; participate in reciprocal cultural sharing projects.
wider: Conduct a genuine intercultural exchange with a target language community peer — reflect on what was learned about both cultures from the exchange
Explore the experience of Australians who identify with both Australian and target language community backgrounds — present findings with cultural analysis in the target language

modes.reason: Intercultural community projects integrate all prior cultural understanding — belonging and exclusion (N1), language and identity — in a genuine exchange with real stakes and real cultural participants.

nodes.label: Reflecting on language learning as identity experience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on their own language learning experience as an identity experience — examining how learning a new language changes who they are and how they communicate.
criteria: Reflects on at least two ways that learning the target language has changed how they communicate or see the world
Connects specific language learning experiences to broader insights about identity and cultural understanding

width.minimum: Reflect on at least two ways that learning the target language has changed how they communicate or see the world.
width.typical: Reflect on the experience of moving between languages and cultures; consider the identity implications of being a language learner and a bilingual communicator; explore how language learning has changed their perspective on their own language; reflect on what intercultural competence means personally; consider future use of the target language.
wider: Write a reflective essay on the identity dimensions of their target language learning journey — connecting specific experiences to broader insights about language and identity
Consider how their experience as a language learner gives them specific insight into what it means to navigate between languages and cultures — and what this insight could offer in future contexts

modes.reason: Genuine personal reflection on language learning as identity requires students to move from reporting what they did to interpreting what it meant. Structured reflection frameworks scaffold the evaluative move from observation to interpretation.
